# 27DQ. The question's own clock — and the four copies a blip exposed (2026-10-19)

**Mobile (AI-24) plus a one-line server change in the chat controller. No route, permission,
schema, session, dependency or environment-value change.**

## What was actually missing

The owner asked for a timestamp on **each of their own messages**, like the one the answer already
carries, so the interval between question and answer can be read off the screen.

`MessageBubble` had supported it all along — `styles.timeUser`, `testID="chat-time-user"`, the same
`formatClock12` mapping — but **nothing ever supplied the value**: the optimistic row the screen
appends while a turn is in flight was built by hand as `{ key, role, content }` with no
`createdAt`. The component was not the defect; the screen was.

## The timestamp that had to be chosen, not copied

The obvious move — show `userMessage.createdAt` from the response — is wrong, and the reason is a
rule this project deliberately adopted: **a turn persists nothing until the provider succeeds**
(Phase 07E / M7). The USER row is therefore written *after* the model answers, so its stored time is
the moment the turn **completed**. Two such timestamps are a second apart however long the member
waited — the interval the feature exists for would have been invisible, and a reloaded thread would
report a zero-second response time.

So the time is taken where it is true:

* **On the device**, at the instant Send is pressed, for the bubble drawn while the turn runs.
* **On the server**, at the top of the controller — `askedAt`, recorded *before* `runAiChat` — and
  written as the USER message's explicit `createdAt`. Mongoose honours a supplied `createdAt`
  (measured against the live schema before the change: a value 45 s in the past stored unchanged),
  so the stored question carries its own send time on **the same clock as its answer**. The
  interval is now readable on screen, in a reloaded thread, and straight out of the database.

The two paths agree because the reply carries `userMessage`, and the client merges that stored copy
in place of the optimistic bubble — the same single-mapping rule AI-8 applied to the answer.

## Two defects the device found in this increment

Both were seen on the phone during a real **MongoDB Atlas blip** (two 503s from the development
database), and neither was visible in any test until they were reproduced:

1. **A failed send left its bubble behind.** M7 guarantees nothing was stored, yet the member's
   message stayed on screen as if delivered — and every retry stacked another copy. The screen
   showed the same question **four times**. Fixed: on a failed (not stopped) send the bubble is
   removed and the text is returned to the composer, so a retry needs no retyping.
2. **The merge replaced every id-less row.** The first fix matched "a user row with no server id",
   which was *every* leftover bubble from those failures; the next success replaced all of them with
   the same stored message — four identical rows and React's *"Encountered two children with the
   same key"*. Fixed: the pending row's key is held in a local and is the only row this turn may
   replace or remove, and the merged list is deduped by server id so the first-turn reload race
   (the conversation is created, which triggers a thread load) cannot produce a duplicate either.

The second defect was *caused by the first fix*, which is why the four stages are recorded rather
than only the end state.

## Verification

`mobile/__tests__/ai24-user-message-time.test.tsx` — **8 cases**: both bubbles render in the same
12-hour form and can be compared; a bubble with no time renders no footer; the send path stamps the
bubble it creates; the stored copy replaces it (exactly one question bubble, server times shown); a
failed send removes the bubble **and** restores the draft; three failures leave **zero** bubbles; and
`toRow` carries a stored user message's time.

`server/test/AI24-message-times.test.mjs` — **3 DB cases** driving the real route with a
**deliberately slow (350 ms) fake provider**, because with a fast one a persist-time stamp and a
send-time stamp land in the same millisecond and the test would pass whatever the code did: the gap
between the two stored rows is at least the provider's delay, the row is read back **from MongoDB**,
a question is never ordered after its answer, and a failed turn still writes nothing.

Each half was **proven able to fail by mutation, then restored byte-identically** (checked by
sha256): removing `createdAt: askedAt` failed the server interval case; removing the failed-send
cleanup failed the mobile case; removing the optimistic `createdAt` failed the send case.

**On the device (2026-10-19, OPPO CPH1969 over `adb reverse`, Metro development build):** a
reloaded conversation shows the question at **3:01 PM** and the answer at **3:02 PM** — one bubble
each, both times drawn in the member's own 12-hour form, with the provenance chip below.

## Limits

* **The footer is minute-resolution.** `formatClock12` is the format AI-17 chose on this device, so
  a 20-second turn reads 3:01 → 3:02. The interval is visible; the seconds are not. A duration
  label ("took 12 s") would make it exact and is a separate design decision.
* **The in-flight time is the device clock**, the stored one is the server clock. A device whose
  clock is badly wrong will show a shifted send time until the reply arrives, at which point the
  stored value takes over.
* **A STOPPED turn keeps its bubble.** The server may have completed and stored it, so removing it
  would be a claim this screen cannot make; a stopped turn that stored nothing therefore leaves a
  bubble that disappears on reload.
* **The Atlas blip is recorded as an observation, not a fix.** The long-running server kept
  answering 503 to `/api/ai/chat` after the database was reachable again and needed a restart; the
  fail-fast `1500 ms` buffering timeout is deliberate, and this run does not change it.

# 27DR. One provider, on purpose — the direct Claude and Gemini implementations removed (2026-10-19)

**Server only (AI-25): provider registry, configuration, `.env.example`, the production-config
message, and the suites that named the removed providers. No route, permission, schema, session or
dependency change, and no mobile file.**

## The decision, and who made it

The owner asked whether the extra providers were still worth their configuration, with the goal of
keeping the system *"as simple, reliable, and maintainable as possible"*. The answer is **yes, remove
them**, and this record is the reasoning rather than a preference:

* **They bought no capability.** Both Claude and Gemini were already reachable **through OpenRouter as
  model choices** — `AI_MODEL_OPENROUTER=anthropic/claude-…` is the whole change. Two direct
  implementations therefore added a second way to do the same thing.
* **The "fallback" was theoretical.** A second provider is only a fallback if it has its own account,
  key and billing and is exercised. None of that was true: the deployed path is OpenRouter, so the
  direct paths were production code nothing could reach.
* **They were real maintenance.** Gemini carried its own wire mapping and response parser
  (`generateContent`, `functionDeclarations`, `functionResponse`, `MAX_TOKENS`), a second way for tool
  results to be shaped, and two more environment variables in every operator's `.env`. An unexercised
  second protocol is not free; it is a surface that rots silently.

## What was removed, and what was deliberately kept

| Removed | Kept, and why |
| --- | --- |
| `claudeProvider.ts`, `geminiProvider.ts` | **`AIProvider` interface + registry** — OpenRouter is one entry; the `fake` provider the suites register is the other, and that seam is how the whole loop is tested without a key |
| The `claude` / `gemini` registry entries | **`anthropicWire.ts`** — OpenRouter *is* an Anthropic-compatible gateway, so this shared mapping is the deployed path, not legacy |
| `aiConfig().claudeModel` / `.geminiModel` | `AI_MODEL_OPENROUTER`, which is now the single place a model is chosen |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `AI_MODEL_CLAUDE`, `AI_MODEL_GEMINI` from `.env.example` | The production config check, which now requires exactly OpenRouter's three settings |

Restoring a direct provider later is therefore **one small factory plus one registry entry**, and git
keeps the Gemini mapping if it is ever wanted. That is the point of keeping the abstraction while
removing the implementations.

## What an existing deployment sees

Nothing, if it already runs OpenRouter. If a deployment's `.env` still names a removed provider, the
chat route answers **503 `AI_NOT_CONFIGURED`** — the same clean refusal every unconfigured state
produces — and the production-config check names `AI_PROVIDER` as wrong, telling the operator to set
`openrouter`. The selection message no longer offers the removed names as alternatives; it says
*'Set AI_PROVIDER to "openrouter", or leave it empty to disable the AI assistant.'*

## Verification

`server/test/AI25-single-provider.test.mjs` — **4 cases**, DB-free and **written first, watched
failing** on the unmodified tree (`providerRequiredEnv('claude')` returned `['ANTHROPIC_API_KEY']`
where `null` was expected, and `selectProvider()` answered with the old missing-key sentence rather
than the unsupported-provider one): the registry knows openrouter and nothing else; `claude` and
`gemini` are refused as **unknown**, with a message naming openrouter and not listing them; the config
carries no per-provider models; and `.env.example` no longer documents their keys — because a
documented variable is a requirement to whoever sets up a server, whether or not anything reads it.

Updated alongside it, rather than deleted: the provider-selection cases in `phase06-ai-provider`
(now covering the removed names **and** the upgrade path — a stale name gets `503 AI_NOT_CONFIGURED`
through the real route), the production-config key test in `phase07d-production-config` (now
openrouter's settings are required and the removed keys are planted as unused secrets that must not
leak), and AI-22's cross-wire parity case, which becomes an assertion on the **one** remaining wire
with the reason recorded in place (see its comment) — the property it existed for is the batched
shape, and that is unchanged.

## Limits

* **There is no code-level provider fallback any more.** If OpenRouter itself is unusable, the assistant
  is unavailable until OpenRouter recovers or a provider is restored. That is a deliberate trade: the
  previous "fallback" had never been exercised, so it was a promise the repository could not keep.
* **The model is now an OpenRouter concern.** A model that cannot call tools still cannot answer
  inventory questions; that risk is unchanged and is the reason `AI_MODEL_OPENROUTER` has no default.
* **Gemini's mapping exists only in git history.** Restoring it is a revert, not a switch.
* **Nothing was verified on a device for this increment** and nothing needed to be: it changes no
  request, response or screen. The route-level upgrade case is covered against the real server.

# 27DS. The answer a member can finish reading (2026-10-19)

**Server + mobile (AI-26). No route, permission, schema, session, dependency or environment-value
change; no extra provider call.**

## The defect, read out of the database and off the phone

Two complaints from the owner, and one of them had a measured shape. *"Fix incomplete AI responses"* —
the development database held **4 `OUTPUT_LIMIT` answers out of 34**, and **every one ended inside a
Markdown table cell**:

```text
… | Professional Battery 10051 |
… | 2026-10-18 01:48:51 | Professional Towel 1
… | Pro Cable 19871 |
… | 6ad49
```

AI-8 was right to keep a truncated answer and right to mark it. The note, however, explains the cut;
it does not make a half-row readable — a member reading *"Professional Towel 1"* cannot tell whether
that is the product's name or where it was chopped.

## What was added

* **`trimIncompleteAnswer`** (`server/src/services/ai/answerCompletion.ts`) — a pure function that drops
the **one** incomplete unit at the end: a trailing table row that is cut mid-cell, missing a cell or
lacking its closing pipe; a paragraph cut back to its last finished sentence; closing markdown kept
(`app.)*` stays whole). A **complete** row or sentence is never touched; a cut **list item** is left
alone, because a whole item and a cut one look identical at the end of a string and deleting a correct
row to rescue a cut one would be the worse failure; and with no identifiable whole unit the text is
returned **unchanged** — a visibly cut answer with the note is more honest than a guess.
* **`humaniseStatusConstants`** — the same file, applied to **every** answer before the trim, so the
store, the screen and the trim all see the same words. It rewrites `OUT_OF_STOCK` → **Out of stock**,
`LOW_STOCK` → **Low stock**, `IN_STOCK` → **In stock**, word-bounded so `LOW_STOCK_PRODUCTS` is left
alone. This exists because a **complete** device answer printed the enum in a Status column: the
prompt now forbids it, but a prompt is a request.
* **The degraded line says what it removed** — `trimmed=<chars>` beside `reason=OUTPUT_LIMIT`, so a
silent edit to a stored answer is countable.
* **Prompt rules, each traceable to a stored or on-screen sentence:** rule 3 now **names the screens**
with their real titles and rules out the invented one (“There is no *Reorder needed* screen — the
restock list is the *Restock* screen”); rule 4 asks for the **thousands separator** the app uses
(`8,976`, not `8976`) except inside names/SKUs/dates; rule 14 forbids stored status constants and
field names in parentheses (`Product (name)`); rule 15 requires the **first sentence to state both
numbers** (*"47 products need restocking; the 5 most urgent are below."*) and keeps AI-2's ban on
*"subsequent pages"* and on asking how many rows to show.
* **Mobile: the restock link is an affordance, not a consolation prize.** It used to exist only in the
`OUTPUT_LIMIT` branch, so the answer that most needs it — a **complete** answer showing five of 8,976 —
offered no way there. It is now drawn whenever the answer came from a stock-list tool
(`getReorderNeededProducts`, `getLowStockProducts`, `getOutOfStockProducts`), which the stored message
already carries for the provenance chip: **no new field, no request, no server change**.
* **Mobile: a three-column table is a card, not a grid.** AI-4 chose `TABLE_GRID_MAX_COLUMNS = 3`
without ever seeing a three-column grid on hardware. The first one did: `| Product | Available QTY |
Stock status |` in a ~400 px bubble drew its header **mid-word** — `Availabl / e QTY` — because the
2:1:1 split leaves the narrow columns under 80 px. The constant is now **2**, and the same table reads
as three whole lines per card.
* **Mobile: the restock screen states how much of itself is on screen** — `Showing 20 of 8,976 — scroll
for more`, then `All 8,976 products shown`. The list pages silently, so without this a member at the
bottom of page 1 had no way to know thousands more existed.

## Measured on the phone (OPPO CPH1969, development build over Metro + `adb reverse`)

**The 203-product role fixture:** the answer read *"36 products need restocking; the 5 most urgent are
below."* — the total, in the required shape, with **card rows** and **Open the full restock list** on a
**complete** answer (no truncation note); tapping the link opened the **Restock** screen, whose own
header read **36 products at or below minimum stock** and whose first rows were the five the answer
named. The screen is titled **Restock**, so the prompt's vocabulary matches the title the member sees.

**The 60 000-product perf tenant** (a temporary OWNER account on the disposable seed tenant, removed
after the run):

| question | total | provider | tools | grounded | count |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Which products are low on stock? | 43.0 s | 41.8 s | 1.16 s | yes | 8,976 (shown `8976`) |
| Is anything out of stock? | 17.1 s | 15.9 s | 1.23 s | yes | 3,654 |
| How much stock do we hold? | 10.3 s | 9.3 s | 0.97 s | yes | 14,928,688 |
| Which products are low on stock? (repeat) | 22.0 s | 20.8 s | 1.20 s | yes | 8,976 (shown `8976`) |

Every count equals the dashboard's own figure on the same screen, and every stock row lists the same
five products as the top of the Restock list. **4/4 grounded and numerically exact.** The tools are
**0.97–1.23 s** — 2.7 % to 10.4 % of the turn — so the free-tier model, not the database, bounds the
answer; the same question took **43.0 s** and **22.0 s** on consecutive runs, which is provider
variance and not a regression. The Restock screen itself opened **8,976** rows at this scale, scrolled
into further pages without a stall, and its search still reaches the endpoint (verified previously and
unchanged).

## Verification

* `server/test/AI26-answer-completion.test.mjs` — **22 cases**: the four real stored tails (cut
  mid-cell, cut name, cut id, one cell under a four-column header), the complete-table and
  complete-sentence negatives, paragraph fallback, closing markdown, the list-item **non**-deletion,
  the header-only and empty-input totality; through the **real loop** the marked turn still returns
  `OUTPUT_LIMIT` with no half row and logs `trimmed=`, a complete answer is untouched, and the status
  constant reaches the caller already humanised; the prompt cases pin rules 3, 4, 14 and 15 (including
  the invented screen and the separator).
* `mobile/__tests__/ai26-restock-link.test.tsx` — **6 cases**: the link on a **complete** stock-list
  answer, on all three stock-list tools, absent for a non-stock answer, absent on the member's own
  message, and the truncation note still shown without a link when the answer was prose.
* `mobile/__tests__/restock-screen.test.tsx` — **2 new cases** for `Showing 2 of 36 — scroll for more`
  and `All 2 products shown`, and the zero case asserts **no** footer.
* `mobile/__tests__/ai4-assistant-answer-render.test.tsx` — **1 new case**: a three-column table is a
  card and its header no longer wraps mid-word.
* Full suites after every edit: mobile **77 suites / 963 tests / 0 failures**; server **1654 tests /
  253 suites / 0 failures**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean on both sides.
* **The quota sentence, rewritten the same day because the allowance was measured spent.** The
  provider's own counter read **50 of 50 free requests used, 0 remaining**, and a real turn through
  the route answered **`429 AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED`** (`[ai] turn outcome=AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED total=660ms
  calls=1`) — so the client's *"reached its usage limit for now. Please try again later"* was advice
  with no actionable content: the next usable moment is the **daily reset**, not an unspecified later.
  The sentence now reads *"The assistant has used today's request allowance. It resets at midnight UTC
  (8AM in Manila) — the rest of the app works as usual."*, with the server's own message left generic
  on purpose (it cannot know the provider's day boundary). `ai6-assistant-quota-copy` and
  `ai10-output-limit-copy` were updated to pin the new sentence **and** assert that it names the
  reset; both suites pass.

## Limits

* **The reset time in the quota sentence is the provider's clock, not a promise about the app.**
  OpenRouter's free tier is a per-day counter whose day boundary is UTC; the sentence names that and
  the owner's local equivalent, and it was written when the allowance was measured at zero — a turn
  after the reset has not been observed.
* **The trim is verified by test, not by a device run.** Provoking `OUTPUT_LIMIT` on demand needs
  either the cap lowered or a question that spends it; the cap is 1 200 and the measured answers use
  483–774 tokens, so nothing on the phone reached it. The four real tails are the fixtures, which is
  the next best evidence, but a device answer drawn after a trim has not been seen.
* **The thousands-separator rule was added after the four measured turns.** Two of three low-stock
  answers said `8976`; the prompt now asks for `8,976`, and **no turn has yet confirmed the model
  obeys it** — it is a request, not a guarantee, and a deterministic separator pass was **rejected**
  because it would rewrite the five-digit code inside every product name (`Deluxe Kettle 60980`).
  *(Annotated 2026-10-20: **confirmed by live turns** — `8,976` and `14,928,688` in answers at the
  60 000-product tenant, and `46,602` on the phone. See §27DT's Verification.)*
* **The restock footer is not device-verified.** It was written after the 36-item phone pass, and at
  8,976 rows the next page loads before the footer is on screen for long; it is asserted by test only.
* **The trim can only remove one unit.** A model that ends inside the *middle* of a table (a cut row
  followed by more rows) is not repaired — the cut is not at the end, and repairing it would mean
  inventing the missing cells.
* **The role fixture's password was rotated** through the documented `npm run seed:roles` path so the
  phone could sign in (the committed scripts never print it); the temporary 60 000-product account was
  deleted after the run, and the perf tenant was otherwise untouched.

# 27DT. The allowance is read before it is spent (2026-10-19)

**Server tooling only (`perf:turns` + `ai:usage`). No route, permission, schema, session, dependency,
application behaviour or environment-value change; no model call and no quota spent by the change.**

## The defect, paid for twice in one afternoon

`perf:turns` is the only instrument that measures a **real** assistant turn, and the provider behind it
meters those turns against a hard daily cap. On 2026-10-19 the cap was reached in the middle of a
device session. Two `perf:turns` questions were then sent anyway and both came back
`429 AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` (`[ai] turn outcome=AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED total=764ms providerMs=764ms calls=1`,
then `116ms`): **the run spent requests to learn that there were none left**, and its only finding was
the spentness itself. The provider reports the counter for free (`GET /v1/key` →
`free_model_daily_requests`), and this repository already read it — in `npm run ai:usage` — but nowhere
in the measurement path, and **`ai:usage` could not be asked that question alone**: it needs a log file
(or `--db`), so the cheapest question in the toolset was the one that demanded the most.

## What was added

* **`shortfall(usage, needed)` in `scripts/ai-usage.mjs`** — the judgement, in one place: a run is short
  only when the provider **said** a number and that number is below the questions selected. Everything
  else — `NOT_CONFIGURED`, `UNREADABLE`, `SKIPPED`, a paid key that reports no free counter, a counter
  with `remaining: null` — returns `null` and blocks nothing. **Exactly enough is not a shortfall**
  (`<`, not `<=`), pinned as a case.
* **`readProviderUsage` is bounded.** It had no timeout at all, so an unanswered socket held the report
  (and now the preflight) open indefinitely. It now aborts at 15 s and reports
  `no answer within 15000 ms` — the same contract every other failure here follows: a reading that
  failed is a row, never a hang and never a pass.
* **`perf:turns` reads the allowance before the first turn** and refuses with **exit 2** when the
  shortfall is known, naming the remaining count, the limit and the window (`00:00 UTC`). The refusal
  happens **before a session is minted**, so a refused run leaves no row behind, and it is appended to
  the same run's output as `[turns] allowance: 0 of 50 … ; 2 question(s) selected`. `--force` overrides.
  The `--only=` filter is now computed first, because the refusal is a function of how many questions
  were actually selected.
* **`allowanceLine(usage)`** — one sentence for both printers, so a failure, a paid key and a number
  cannot share a line. It exists because the first preflight printed `${status} — ${detail}`
  unconditionally, and the live stub run then printed `[turns] allowance: OK — undefined`: a bug found
  by running the tool, not by the suite that had just passed.
* **`npm run ai:usage -- --provider-only`** — the allowance and nothing else: no log, no database, no
  model, no quota. The provider contract (`DEFAULT_BASE_URL`) is now exported from `ai-usage.mjs` rather
  than copied, so the probe and the report cannot ask two different hosts about the same account.

## Verification

* `server/test/AI27-allowance-preflight.test.mjs` — **12 cases**, unit only: the spent day, one request
  short of three questions, **exactly enough is allowed** and one fewer is not, three failed-reading
  statuses that must not refuse, a paid key with no counter, a counter with `remaining: null`, zero
  questions, the real `/v1/key` body mapping to `{used, limit, remaining}` with the masked `label` never
  becoming a value, one sentence for every reading (with a case that forbids the string `undefined`
  reaching the output), an **abort-aware hanging fetch** that must settle at its bound (it is the shape of
  a hang — a stub that rejects only when aborted), and the probe's own source: it imports **this**
  reader, reads the allowance **before** `createSessionForToken`, exits `2`, says nothing was sent, and
  names the reset. Last, `ai-usage.mjs --provider-only --json` runs as a **child process** with an
  empty key: exit 0, `source=not requested (--provider-only)`, `provider.status=NOT_CONFIGURED` —
  proving the flag exists and no longer needs a log.
* **The guard was watched failing, twice.** `remaining >= needed` mutated to `>` broke the boundary
  case; `process.exit(2)` mutated to `process.exit(0)` broke the wiring case — **2 failures, exactly
  those two**, and both files were then restored **byte-identical** (`cmp`) and re-ran green.
* **Live, against the real provider and the real probe:** `npm run ai:usage -- --provider-only` printed
  `free-model requests : 50 used of 50 · 0 remaining today (UTC day; resets 00:00 UTC)`, and
  `npm run perf:turns -- --business=<60k tenant> --only=1,2` refused with **exit 2** and the sentence
  above — no request reached the provider and no session row was created.
* `server` `tsc` and `eslint` clean; full suite **1666 tests / 254 suites / 0 failures** (1654 + 12).

**The trim was then exercised END TO END on the phone, at ZERO provider quota** — the allowance was spent
until 00:00 UTC, so the provider was replaced by a local stub answering in the Anthropic wire shape with
`stop_reason: max_tokens` and a table cut inside its last cell (the shape of all four stored `OUTPUT_LIMIT`
answers); everything after the provider was real. Over the real route and database the turn reported
`degraded=OUTPUT_LIMIT`, `trimmed=43`, the cut row gone and the statuses humanised; on the OPPO the two
**complete** rows drew as cards with no pipe, no separator row and no `OUT_OF_STOCK` on screen, the cut row
**absent**, and the length note still shown (*"This answer hit the length limit, so it may be incomplete…"*).
That is the composition §27DS left unobserved: a **trimmed** answer on hardware.

**Live turns the same evening, once the owner moved the key to an unspent account** (the preflight read
`50 of 50 left, used 0` BEFORE anything ran — its first real use): at the 60 000-product tenant, three
questions were **3/3 grounded and numerically exact** — *"You have 60,000 active products with a total of
14,928,688 units on hand. 51,024 of those products are in stock …, 8,976 are low‑stock, and 3,654 are out of
stock."* (`getInventorySummary`, 10.4 s), *"Main Warehouse: 60,000 products / Shop Front: 39,982 / Overflow
Store: 20,149"* (`getLocationBreakdown`, 17.6 s), and *"**8,976 products need restocking**; the 5 most urgent
are below."* (`getReorderNeededProducts`, 23.9 s) — and on the phone, in the fixture tenant, the simplest
question answered *"You have **46,602** units in stock across all locations."*, equal to the dashboard
figure on the same screen. **Eight provider requests of fifty were used** for all of it — four turns
at two requests each, which is the 1–3-per-turn cost AI-5 recorded — and the counter confirmed it
(`used 8`, read after the last turn). Two of §27DS's stated limits are therefore closed by
observation rather than by argument: the **thousands separator** the prompt asks for is what the
model actually writes (`8,976`, `14,928,688`), and rule 15's *total in the first sentence* is obeyed.
A detail worth keeping for ISS-22: all four turns logged `outcome=ok`, `calls=2`, `empty=0` — no
retry, no degraded mark and no empty completion on this model today, against the 3-in-5 defect rate
the free tier showed on the previous one (2026-10-12).

## Limits

* **The check is a floor, not a budget.** A turn with tool rounds costs **1–3** provider requests
  (AI-5 measured 3 requests for 1 tool run), so `remaining >= questions` means the run *can* fit, not
  that it *will*: a run can still meet a `429` mid-way and the probe still reports it per question. The
  conservative alternative — assuming 2–3 requests per question — was rejected because it would refuse
  runs that would have succeeded, which is a worse failure for an instrument.
* **The reading is the account's, not the model's.** A model-specific outage or a per-minute limit is
  invisible here; the preflight can only see the daily free-model counter.
* **A stale counter is trusted.** If the provider's own figure lags, the probe refuses a run that would
  have worked; `--force` is the recorded escape.
* **Nothing here makes the assistant cheaper.** It converts a discovered-after-the-fact refusal into a
  refusal before the fact, for the operator only; the member-facing path is unchanged.

# 27DU. A boot that survives a slow cluster (2026-10-20)

**Server only (`src/config/db.ts` + one message in `src/config/startup.ts`). No route, permission,
schema, dependency, session or environment-value change, and no mobile change.**

## The defect, observed three times in one afternoon

`connectDatabase` made **one** attempt with a 5 s `serverSelectionTimeoutMS` bound, and mongoose does
not retry a **rejected** initial connect. On 2026-10-19 the same Atlas cluster took **15.8 s** to select
— a figure this repository already had, because `scripts/ai-usage.mjs` stopped overriding the bound
*"measured 2026-10-19 — the same cluster took 15.8s to select and a 5s bound failed outright"* — and
**three separate `npm start` runs** died on it while a raw connect seconds earlier had succeeded. The
result was an API that stayed `not ready` and answered **503 to every database request** until a person
restarted it. The log said *"Restart once MongoDB is reachable"*, which is an instruction to the
operator rather than behaviour of the process.

## What changed

* **A budget per environment, as data.** `connectBudget({ nodeEnv, testMode })` — development gets
  **3 attempts** with a **30 s** selection bound and a 3 s pause; production, test and an unset
  `NODE_ENV` keep **one attempt and 5 s**. `connectDatabase` takes its defaults from it and accepts
  explicit overrides, plus an injectable `connect`, so the policy is testable without a socket.
* **Why 30 s rather than a longer default everywhere:** production is **fail-fast by contract** — one
  attempt, exit non-zero, Render restarts — and a longer wait would only delay that restart, so the
  bound is raised only where the failure mode is a *dead development API* rather than a restart.
* **`TEST_MODE` is part of the decision, and that is not a detail.** The suite runner sets `TEST_MODE`
  and leaves `NODE_ENV` unset, so a test process reports `nodeEnv === 'development'`; without this the
  three-attempt budget would have applied inside the suites' own `TEST_DB_MAX_ATTEMPTS` loop and turned
  a transient blip into minutes of waiting. The first version of this increment had exactly that bug,
  caught by a case that asserts a test process is *not* development.
* **Every attempt says which one it was** (`connection attempt 2/3 failed (…)`), so a boot log
  distinguishes a slow socket from a dead cluster, and the failure message now says the attempts were
  exhausted before advising a restart.
* Nothing else moved: the URI, the resolved `dbName` (environment separation), `bufferTimeoutMS: 1500`
  and the existing reconnect monitoring are untouched.

## Verification

* `server/test/DB1-boot-retry.test.mjs` — **7 cases**, unit only, against an injected connect: the
  budget for every environment string (`production`, `test`, `''`, `undefined`, `staging`, `prod`, and
  `development` in three casings), **a test process is never development**, the shipped constants
  (3 / 30 000 / 5 000), recovery on the second attempt, the numbered log lines with no connection
  string in any of them, the **last** error being what the caller receives, a real pause between
  attempts (25 ms asserted on a 40 ms setting), the resolved `dbName` and `bufferTimeoutMS` reaching the
  driver, and — only in a genuine test process — that the default budget is still **one** attempt.
* **The guard was watched failing:** the development/test exclusion was removed *and* the non-development
  budget set to 3 in one mutation, and the budget case failed; the file was then restored
  **byte-identical** (`cmp`) and re-ran **7/7**.
* **A real boot, with the database unreachable** (`MONGODB_URI` pointed at a closed port, `PORT=4001`):
  `connection attempt 1/3/2/3/3/3 failed (MongooseServerSelectionError)`, three seconds apart, then the
  new message — and the process still listened for diagnostics, exactly as designed.
* Server **1673 tests / 255 suites / 0 failures**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean.

## Limits

* **This does not make the process self-healing.** After the three attempts it still stays up and not
  ready until restarted; mongoose will not retry a rejected initial connect, and a background reconnect
  loop was **not** added (it would be a second, divergent connection lifecycle next to the driver's own
  monitoring, for a development-only failure).
* **15.8 s is one measurement.** 30 s covers it with room; a cluster that is unreachable for longer still
  needs the restart the message names — the difference is that a *slow* cluster no longer does.
* **The three attempts are visible as three `MongoDB connection lost` lines**, because the driver's own
  events fire per failed attempt. Noise, not behaviour; left alone rather than silenced.

# 27DW. The demo tenant a preview build can be checked against (2026-10-20)

**Server tooling and documentation only (`scripts/demo/*`, two CLIs, two npm scripts, one test file,
two guides). No route, permission, schema, session, dependency, environment value or mobile change.**
It closes the gap §27DV named: a production tenant with no data, so an assistant answer could only be
read, never checked.

## The problem with checking an answer against generated data

`seed:demo` writes tens of thousands of documents, which is right for measuring queries and useless for
verifying an answer — nobody can say what the total *should* be. A device test therefore needs a
**small tenant whose every figure is known in advance**. That is what this tenant is: **6 products**
(one deliberately with **no** inventory row, so "missing row is zero" is exercised), **3 locations**,
**7 inventory rows**, **9 ledger rows**, and **112 units** on hand — all stated by the command that
creates them, and re-read and compared before the command reports success.

## What was added

* **`scripts/demo/fixture.mjs`** — the data plus its expected answers (`expectedSummary`,
  `expectedLocationBreakdown`, `expectedRestock`). Low stock means *at or below* the minimum, per §19;
  the restock expectation is out-of-stock first, with a real shortfall; every ledger row's arithmetic
  chains to exactly the stock figure it explains — the invariant `seed:perf` broke for 6 615 rows in
  §27BG.
* **`scripts/demo/lib.mjs`** — `assertDemoTarget` (a **named** database that must equal the resolved
  one, the **test database refused**, a confirmation phrase), `planSeed` (pure, and it **refuses** an
  address that already belongs to a *different* business, and a half-state, rather than repairing
  either), `seedDemoTenant`, `verifyDemoTenant` (15 read-back checks) and `removeDemoTenant` (both
  fingerprints must agree on one businessId; leftovers are re-counted and must be **0**).
* **Two CLIs**: `npm run seed:demo-tenant` and `npm run cleanup:demo-tenant`, each of which prints the
  database, whether it is production, what the assistant must answer, and every check with its number.
* **`server/test/DEMO1-demo-tenant.test.mjs`** — 12 DB-free cases, and two guides updated
  (`4-test-accounts-and-mock-data.md` §F, `6-scripts-and-commands.md`).

## Two deliberate differences from every other seeder

1. **It may run against production.** The preview APK can only reach production, so a tenant that can
   be exercised from that build has to be seedable there. The safety is not "it is careful": the
   database must be **named by hand** and must equal the one `config/env.ts` resolved (a production
   database is refused from a development process, by config), the test database is refused outright,
   and the phrase is its own.
2. **The teardown never deletes the Firebase identity.** §27BB (F-50) records the lockout: MongoDB
   removed and identity removed in the wrong order leaves an address that can neither sign in nor
   register, with no repair path in the application. An identity with no MongoDB user is harmless, and
   re-seeding reuses it.

## Verification

* **12 cases**, and the guard was **watched failing**: one movement's `newQuantity` mutated to a
  self-contradictory value → **11 pass / 1 fail**, restored **byte-identical** (`cmp`), **12/12**.
* **A local rehearsal on the development database**: seeded, `15 checks match the fixture`; then
  `cleanup:demo-tenant` removed 7 inventory + 9 ledger + 6 products + 2 categories + 3 locations + 1
  user + 1 business and reported **leftovers 0**; a second run answered *"no demo tenant exists —
  nothing to remove"*.
* **Production, seeded the same way** (`NODE_ENV=production MONGODB_DB_NAME=inventoryai_prod_db`,
  `--database=inventoryai_prod_db`): `15 checks match the fixture` — **112 units**, 3 healthy / 3 low /
  1 out, Warehouse **75**/4 products, Shop **30**/2, Van **7**/1.
* Server **1685 tests / 255 suites / 0 failures**, `tsc`, `eslint`, both module-graph checks and the
  secret guard clean.

## The device run — the numbers, on the preview APK against the production API

Signed in as the demo tenant on the OPPO CPH1969 (preview build `4b9a79dd`, production API):

| Check | Screen |
|---|---|
| Dashboard | **IN STOCK 3 · LOW STOCK 3 · OUT OF STOCK 1 · ACTIVE PRODUCTS 6 · TOTAL ON-HAND QTY 112** |
| Inventory summary (*"How is my inventory doing?"*) | *"6 products with a total of **112 units**"*, **3** in stock / **3** low / **1** out, then the five newest movements with the seeded dates and quantities (5 × Paper Cups out Oct 18, 16 × Coffee Beans out Oct 17, 20 × Notebook in Oct 16, …) |
| Location breakdown (*"How many units at each location?"*) | **Demo Warehouse 75 · Demo Shop 30 · Demo Van 7**, total **112** — one tool call (`Read: Stock by location`), AI-23's single-lookup path |
| Restock list (*"What needs restocking?"*) | **3 products**: Demo Desk Lamp **out** (0), Demo Coffee Beans **low** (4), Demo Paper Cups **low** (15) — plus the AI-26 **"Open the full restock list"** link, which opened the **Restock** screen showing the same three with SKUs and *"All 3 products shown"* |
| A long answer (*"Write a restock plan with two paragraphs per product"*) | ~5 screens of prose, rendered as prose with no marker leaking |
| **Incomplete answer** (*"Write 1000 words about inventory management"*) | the provider's cap was hit and AI-26's **"This answer hit the length limit, so it may be incomplete — ask a narrower question to see the rest."** appeared; the content ended mid-clause |

If the assistant had already finished, it will be here when you reopen this chat."*, **Send** returned, and nothing arrived in the following 12 s |

Provider allowance: **16 → 26 requests used** across six turns (~1.7 each, tool rounds included).

## Cleanup, and what it proves

The demo tenant was **removed in the same session**: 7 inventory + 9 ledger + 6 products + 2 categories
+ 3 locations + 1 user + 1 business, **leftovers 0**, and the phone was signed out to Login. Only the
Firebase identity remains (by design); one command recreates the tenant, and the guide states both.

## Limits

* **The abandoned turn's server-side outcome is not observable from this host.** The client's stop
  state is measured above; AI-9's `AI_ABANDONED` cancellation was measured in §27CM and is not
  re-measured here.
* **The capped answer ends mid-clause**, which is what the warning is for: AI-27's trim removes a
  structurally broken trailing *row*, and prose has no row to remove. Recorded rather than "fixed",
  because deleting a half sentence would remove content the warning already explains.
* **A 6-product tenant cannot exercise scale.** Query timing and the 60 k product behaviour measured
  in §27BG/§27DT are untouched by this run.
* **The demo identity survives teardown** — deliberate, but it means a Firebase user exists with no
  MongoDB account until the tenant is recreated.

# 27DX. The reset email's link comes back into the app (2026-10-20)

**AUTH-05. One new public server route and the page it serves, one mobile request simplified. No
permission, schema, session, dependency, environment variable or EAS change.** It fixes the one thing the
owner's live test found once the reset email could finally be sent: **the mail arrives and the password
change works, but the link opens the browser**, so the app's own reset screen — and the N-4 recovery
marker it writes — is never reached.

## Why Firebase could not simply be asked to open the app

The client used to pass `ActionCodeSettings` with `url: 'inventoryai://reset-password'` and
`handleCodeInApp: true`. Firebase validates that URL against the project's **Authorized domains**, and a
custom scheme is not a domain: on this project the send was refused outright with
`auth/unauthorized-domain` and **no mail was generated at all** (measured 2026-10-20). The previous fix
for that — a one-time retry with no settings — produced a working email whose link lands on Firebase's
hosted page, which is exactly the behaviour the owner reported.

Neither shape can open an app. **What can is an HTTPS page that hands the code over**, because an HTTPS
page on an authorized domain is something Firebase *will* mail a link to.

## What changed

* **`server/src/pages/resetPasswordLink.ts`** — the page, as a pure renderer. It accepts
  `?mode=resetPassword&oobCode=…` (the four parameters Firebase appends are `mode`, `oobCode`,
  `apiKey`, `lang`; confirmed against a real link generated by this project's Admin SDK) and forwards the
  code to `inventoryai://reset-password?oobCode=…`. The code must match an **allow-list**
  (`[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,512}`) or the link is answered as unusable — refused, not escaped and forwarded.
  The only navigation targets are constants built on the server, so a crafted `continueUrl` cannot turn it
  into an open redirect. The inline script and style are authorized by **CSP hash computed from the bytes
  served**, and every response is `no-store`, `no-referrer`, `noindex`, `nosniff`. On the unusable-link
  page the deep link points at the app's own request screen (`inventoryai://forgot-password`).
* **`server/src/routes/authAction.routes.ts`**, mounted at `/auth` in `app.ts` — deliberately **outside
  `/api`**, because this is an HTML page read by a phone's browser, not a JSON endpoint. It is public for
  the reason recovery is public, it performs no I/O, and it can therefore not add a failure mode to
  account recovery. The design doc's §2.6 inventory moves **72 → 73** routes (public **12 → 13**); the
  gated tier stays 47.
* **`mobile/lib/firebase-native.ts`** — the send passes **no `ActionCodeSettings` at all**. The link's
  destination is now the project's password-reset template, which is the single place that answer lives.
  Passing a continue URL would only add a second place for it to be wrong while depending on the client
  build's idea of the server hostname.
* **`mobile/lib/firebase-auth.ts`** — the two-shape recovery, its code pattern and its "contact your
  administrator" sentence are **deleted** rather than left dead: with nothing to request there is nothing
  for Firebase to refuse, and a blind retry would now mean two emails for one tap. One send, one honest
  sentence.

## Verification

* **Server 1685 tests / 0 failures** (101 files), including 10 new cases in
  `server/test/AUTH05-reset-link-page.test.mjs`: the deep link carries the code, a crafted `continueUrl`
  never appears, six hostile codes are refused without reflection, missing/repeated/non-reset actions are
  refused, the CSP hashes match the served script and style byte for byte, the headers are as listed, and
  the route answers `text/html` at `GET /auth/reset` — over the real app, with the **access log proved to
  record the path and never the query**, so neither the one-time code nor the `apiKey` can reach a log
  line. `tsc`, `eslint` and both module-graph checks clean.
* **Mobile 78 suites / 979 tests / 0 failures** after the N-3 suite was rewritten around the new
  contract (one call, two arguments, never two sends) and the forgotten-module hash re-frozen with its
  reason written in place. `tsc` and `eslint` clean.
* **A real code shape was checked against the page**: `generatePasswordResetLink` for an existing account
  in this project returned `mode,oobCode,apiKey,lang` with a 54-character code, and that exact query
  rendered `200` with the code in the deep link and Firebase's hosted page as the fallback. No mail was
  sent and nothing was consumed.
* **On the phone (OPPO CPH1969, development build over Metro, `adb reverse tcp:4000`)** — Chrome was
  pointed at the page on this laptop and the **app opened directly on *Set a new password***, which is the
  whole chain: mail-shaped URL → page → custom scheme → expo-router → the reset form. A deliberately
  truncated query (only `mode=resetPassword`) rendered the **400 *This reset link is not usable*** page with
  its *Request a new link* button, so the invalid branch is a phone observation too, not a source read.
* **The reset was then completed on the phone, not just started** (2026-10-20). For a throwaway Firebase
  identity minted by this project's Admin SDK — `auth05.probe@example.invalid`, no MongoDB user, deleted
  afterwards — a real `generatePasswordResetLink` code was loaded into the page exactly as the mail would
  load it, the browser handed it to the app on *Set a new password*, a 12-character password was entered,
  and the screen answered **Password changed**. Two follow-up sign-ins settle that the credential really
  moved: the **new** password signed in far enough to reach the server's `REGISTRATION_REQUIRED` banner
  (which can only be returned after a Firebase ID token has been verified), while the **old** password
  answered ***Invalid email or password***. That is the property the page exists for, measured: the code
  survives the HTML → custom-scheme hop **unconsumed** — Firebase's hosted page redeems the code when it is
  shown, this page never does — so the app, not the browser, is what redeems it. It also exercises the
  codepath the owner will use, on hardware, rather than a shortened version of it.

## The owner's one step, and why it is not in the code

Firebase console → **Authentication → Templates → Password reset → Customize action URL** must be set to
this deployment's page — `https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com/auth/reset` — and that host must be in
**Authentication → Settings → Authorized domains**. Both are project configuration; nothing in this
repository can set either, which is why the chain is not called verified end to end until a real reset
email from production opens the app.

### The console refused the URL, and the page it points at was not deployed (measured 2026-10-20)

The owner added the host to **Authorized domains** (that step succeeded, and it has to: it authorizes the
**domain**, not the path), then tried to save the action URL and the console answered only
***An error occurred updating action URL*** — a generic toast that names no rule. Measured, the cause is
not the URL's shape: `GET https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com/auth/reset` returned **404**
(`{"error":"Not Found"}` from this server's own handler) while `/api/health/live` on the same instance
returned **200**, so the deployment was healthy and simply did not contain the route — because every
AUTH-05 file (`pages/resetPasswordLink.ts`, `routes/authAction.routes.ts` and its mount in `app.ts`) was
still **uncommitted working-tree change**, so nothing had ever deployed it. The page itself is fine: its
own suite (`test/AUTH05-reset-link-page.test.mjs`, 10 tests) serves a **200** page for a reset-shaped
query and a **400** invalid-link page for anything else, over HTTP.

**So the order is: deploy the page first, then save the console setting.** That much is ours to fix and
is necessary whatever else is true, because a URL that answers 404 cannot be the destination of a reset
email.

**The console section records the failure honestly because it is not fully resolved.** The toast names no
rule, and there is a second candidate that this repository cannot rule out: a **platform-side
refusal** to write email templates at all. Since mid-2026 there are open reports of exactly this toast
backed by
`{"error":{"code":400,"message":"EMAIL_TEMPLATE_UPDATE_NOT_ALLOWED","status":"INVALID_ARGUMENT"}}`
in the console's Network panel, including when the same change is attempted through the Identity Toolkit
Admin API, and Google's issue **520781452** is open for it. The cheap way to tell the two apart, in the
console, is to repeat the save against something already valid — a default authorized domain
(`https://inventoryai-d0d20.web.app/`) or a **Subject** edit: if *nothing* saves, the block is on the
project's templates and is not about this URL, and no code change here can clear it.

Two things that will bite at the console once the page is deployed:

* **Warm the service before saving.** On this host the first request after a sleep took **32.6 s**
  (`time=32.595652s` to the 404). Whatever the console does while saving, a host that takes half a minute
  to answer is a bad place to do it — and a person clicking a reset link meets the same wall. Hit
  `/api/health/live` until it answers promptly, then save.
* **The setting is global.** The dialog says so — *your custom action URL applies to all email templates* —
  and this page implements exactly one mode (`resetPassword`), answering anything else with its 400 *this
  reset link is not usable* page. That is harmless here only because AUTH-04 replaced Firebase's
  verification link with a 6-digit Inventory AI code, so no shipped flow depends on the verification,
  email-change or recover-email templates; a future flow that does would need those modes added to the page
  rather than pointed at it.

## Limits

* **The Console setting is outside the repository.** Until it is made, production keeps sending the
  hosted-page link — no regression, no security change, just the old behaviour.
* **A reset completed on Firebase's hosted page still revokes nothing**: it never reaches the server, so
  the N-4 marker is not written by that path and other sessions live to the 14-day cap (the documented
  D2/OD-9 gap). Opening the app fixes it for every link that does.
* **iOS is unverified**, as before: the scheme is configured but no iOS build exists on this host.
* The code travels in the URL's query string on a public page, which is unavoidable for an emailed link.
  It is kept out of this server's logs, out of any cache, and away from the `Referer` of anything the page
  loads (nothing does); Firebase expires it and it is single-use.

# 27DY. Password reset by six-digit code, inside the app (2026-10-20)

**AUTH-06. Two new public routes and one new mobile screen; no new dependency, no new environment
variable, no permission, no schema change to an existing collection.** It replaces the browser half of
password recovery with the experience account creation already has, and it is the answer to the two
measurements recorded immediately above: the console refuses every email-template write, and the hosted
page a working link lands on revokes nothing.

## Why a code, and not a cleverer link

AUTH-05 made the link reachable by pointing Firebase's template at `GET /auth/reset`, and that page works
— on the phone, with a real code, with the credential actually moving. The console then refused to save
the setting at all (`Email template updates are currently unavailable for this project`, backed by
`EMAIL_TEMPLATE_UPDATE_NOT_ALLOWED`, Google issue **520781452**), so the destination of a reset email is
not ours to choose. And even configured, the journey ends in a browser form that never reaches this
server, so the N-4 marker is not written and **no session is revoked**.

A six-digit code removes both problems at once: the mail is composed and sent by **this server** through
the provider already in use, and the credential change happens **here**, where revoking sessions is
something the server can do.

## What shipped

* **`POST /api/auth/password-reset/code` → 202** and **`POST /api/auth/password-reset/confirm` → 200**,
  both **public** for the reason recovery is public: the caller has no usable password. No `requireAuth`,
  no permission, no `req.user` read, and **neither route creates a session** — a successful reset ends
  every existing one. Both reuse the **existing limiters** (account + IP on the request, IP on the
  confirm) rather than adding near-identical factories, so the project keeps one place to change one
  policy. The code and the new password travel in the **POST body**, never a URL, so neither can reach
  `httpLogger`'s `req.path` or a `Referer`.
* **`server/src/models/passwordResetChallenge.model.ts`** — `password_reset_challenges`, keyed by a keyed
  digest of the address (`reset-email:`), carrying the code's digest (`reset-code:`), `userId`,
  `expiresAt`, `attempts`, `usedAt` and `lastSentAt`, with `emailHmac` unique. **One row per address**, so
  a second request replaces the first rather than leaving two live codes.
* **No new secret.** The digests are keyed with `EMAIL_VERIFICATION_CODE_PEPPER`, and the two flows are
  separated by **digest domain labels** rather than by a second pepper — a constant cannot be
  misconfigured, whereas a new variable would have failed a validation that production deployments had
  already passed, for no security gain. The code generator (rejection-sampled single draw) and the
  `timingSafeEqual` comparison are the AUTH-04 primitives, reused rather than re-derived.
* **`server/src/services/passwordResetCode/`** — `request.ts` (uniform 202, `MAIL_NOT_CONFIGURED` as a
  **pre-lookup** 503, detached send with its rejection handled, one 60-second cooldown per address) and
  `confirm.ts` (resolve the account from the **challenge**, never from the submitted address; five
  attempts, one spent per wrong code; `confirmPassword` checked **before** the code is spent).
* **`server/src/services/firebase/passwordUpdater.ts`** — the Admin bridge: `updateFirebaseUserPassword`
  plus a best-effort `revokeFirebaseRefreshTokens`, injected so tests never build a credential. The
  write is followed by `passwordChangedAt`, then **`revokeAllSessions`**, then the challenge is consumed
  and a **`PASSWORD_RESET_COMPLETED`** audit row is written (non-fatal, like every other audit write).
* **`server/src/services/mail/templates/passwordResetCode.ts`** + `sendPasswordResetCodeEmail` — the same
  Brevo boundary, the same provider-agnostic shape, a new body. No provider work, no credential, no
  new mail configuration.
* **Mobile** — `forgot-password.tsx` now posts the address and **navigates** to the new
  `reset-password-code.tsx`, which takes the six digits and the new password, honours the server's
  `Retry-After` on a resend, and ends on *Password changed* → Login. **The Firebase sending path is
  removed**, not disabled: `sendFirebasePasswordResetEmail`, its outcome union, its one-send-only
  recovery sentence, its enumeration-resistance code list and the native verb behind it are gone, while
  `verifyFirebasePasswordResetCode` and `confirmFirebasePasswordReset` **stay**, so a `?oobCode=` link
  already sitting in somebody's inbox is not stranded.

## Verification

* **Server: 1742 tests across the two modes.** `npm run test:unit` **981 pass / 0 fail / 51 skipped**
  (the DB halves of mixed files); `npm run test:db` **761 pass / 81 skipped / 1 fail**, and that one
  failure is environmental rather than this work: `phase-ai-usage-report` shells out to `ai:usage --db`,
  which answered `exit 2 — NOT VERIFIED, the database could not be read (MongoNetworkError)` on this
  Atlas cluster — the same flakiness recorded in §27BC/§27BE. It passed in the preceding DB run, and
  the AUTH-06 suites were green in both. **50 new cases** across `AUTH06-password-reset-code.test.mjs`
  (17) and `AUTH06-password-reset-flow.test.mjs` (33). The ones that matter most: an unknown address and a known
  one are indistinguishable at the route **and when Brevo throws**; an immediate second request answers
  the **same 202** and sends nothing (see below — the 429 it shipped with for part of one day was an
  oracle, not a throttle); a wrong code spends **exactly one** attempt and a malformed payload spends
  **none**; the password is written for the **challenge's** account even when a different address is
  submitted; a successful reset leaves no usable session; and the Admin failure leaves the challenge
  **unspent**, so the person can retry rather than lose their code.
* **One defect was found and fixed inside this same work, which is why the numbers above are worth
  reading rather than skimming.** The resend cooldown was first answered `429` + `Retry-After`, by
  analogy with AUTH-04's verification code — whose request route is **authenticated**, so refusing it
  by timing discloses nothing. This route is **public**, and a challenge row exists only for an
  eligible account: two requests would have classified an address (`202` then `429` ⇒ an account
  exists). The cooldown now answers the ordinary 202 and sends nothing, the code already in the inbox
  stays valid, and `PASSWORD_RESET_CODE_RATE_LIMITED`, its `retryAfterSeconds` field and the
  controller's `Retry-After` site were **deleted with the fix** so the refusal cannot be reassembled
  from leftovers. The only 429 on these routes is the limiter's, keyed on the submitted address and
  the caller's IP and identical for both address classes — and a test now asserts the two classes are
  indistinguishable **on the second request**, which is the request that used to tell them apart.
* **Mobile 79 suites / 977 tests / 0 failures** (up from 78 / 979 — the removed send cases outnumber the
  14 new ones in `password-reset-code.test.tsx`), after the N-3 suite was rewritten around what is left
  and one whole-file hash was re-frozen with its reason written in place. `tsc`, `eslint` and both
  module-graph checks clean on both sides.
* **The copy is pinned to the server, not to a comment**: one case reads
  `server/src/constants/passwordResetCode.ts` as **text** and asserts the screen's `CODE_LENGTH`,
  `CODE_TTL_MINUTES` and `RESEND_COOLDOWN_SECONDS` are those numbers, because "expires in 10 minutes"
  typed into a sentence is exactly the kind of number that drifts.

## The error the owner saw: two faults under one dead end (measured 2026-10-21)

The owner tested *Forgot Password* on the phone with a real account's address, tapped **Send Reset Code**,
and got an error with no mail. It was **not a defect in this flow, and not the deployment either** — the
screenshot on the device said exactly what was wrong, and it is worth recording because the message was
written for this:

```
Cannot reach the server. Check your connection and try again. (dev build note: … is
http://localhost:4000, which is this device itself — run "adb reverse tcp:4000 tcp:4000" …)
Diagnostic (dev only) — server: NETWORK_ERROR
```

**Fault 1 — the phone was talking to itself.** The dev build resolves its API base to
`http://localhost:4000`, and `adb reverse --list` was **empty**: no tunnel existed, so the request never
left the handset. Nothing on the server could have answered it, and no code change in this repository
would have fixed it.

**Fault 2 — the process on 4000 was a day old.** With the tunnel up, the request would still have failed:
the listener was PID 7760, started **2026-10-20 15:18**, from before AUTH-06 existed, and it answered the
new route `404` (`{"error":"Not Found","message":"POST /api/auth/password-reset/code not found"}`) — the
same shape AUTH-05's section above records. A stale dev server is the local twin of an undeployed host:
both are a client that is ahead of the server it is pointed at.

**Fault 3, separate and also real — nothing was deployed.** Every AUTH-05/AUTH-06 file was still
working-tree change, so the live host answered both new routes `404` as well. That is why this work is
now committed as `b9d6ec9` and pushed to `main`; the host redeployed on its own, the route answering
`404` on the first three probes and `400` on the fourth, about **70 s** later. Post-deploy probes against
`https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com`:

| Probe | Answer | What it proves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /api/auth/password-reset/code` `{}` | `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` | the route is mounted (not a 404) |
| `POST /api/auth/password-reset/confirm` `{}` | `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` | the confirm route is mounted |
| `GET /auth/reset` | `400`, 2 175-byte invalid-link page | the AUTH-05 page is deployed and refuses a query with no `oobCode` |
| `POST /api/auth/password-reset/code`, address that cannot exist | `202` in **0.21 s** | the pepper and the mail configuration are present, and the 202 does not wait on Brevo |
| `POST /api/auth/password-reset/confirm`, unknown address + `000000` | `400 INVALID_PASSWORD_RESET_CODE` in **0.32 s** | the deployed confirm path reads its challenge collection (Mongo reachable) and collapses an unknown code into the one sentence |

**Faults 1 and 2 were then fixed and re-measured on the OPPO CPH1969 itself**: the stale listener was
stopped, the current source started (`mail=on(brevo) firebase=on`), `adb reverse tcp:4000 tcp:4000`
established, and **Send Reset Code** tapped again on the same address. The device moved to *Reset your
password* (code, new password, confirm, the 10-minute sentence) and the server logged
`password_reset_code_requested — a reset code was issued` followed by `POST /api/auth/password-reset/code`
**202 in 440.3 ms**. So the client, the route, the challenge write and the detached send are now measured
through the phone, against a listener carrying the current code.

**The inbox half is now measured, by the owner, 2026-10-21.** The six-digit code arrived in the
mailbox, the owner set the new password on the phone, and the new password then signed in without
an error. That is the delivery half this section could not infer from a 202: **Brevo delivered a
reset code, and the credential it authorized is the one the account now has.** The one step not
re-run by the owner is the *old* password's refusal, which the server suite pins (`a successful reset
leaves no usable session`, the Admin write's effect) rather than the mailbox.

## The follow-up pass this exposed (2026-10-21)

Two things were worth fixing once the journey worked end to end, and neither changes a server
surface:

* **The screen did not drop this device's session on success.** `reset-password.tsx` has cleared it
  since the link flow shipped — its own comment says why: without it, *Go to sign in* reaches
  `/login`, `/login` sees `status === 'signedIn'` and redirects into `(app)` on a session the reset
  has already ended. The code screen made the same promise in its copy ("every device signed in to
  this account is signed out") and its own suite's header claimed the same, but the call was missing.
  It now clears through `clearSession` (not `signOut`, which would fire a logout with a dead token),
  and two cases pin both halves: cleared on success, untouched when the code is refused.
* **The six-digit field declared nothing to the platform.** Neither code screen set `autoComplete` /
  `textContentType`, so Android offered no autofill chip and iOS showed no QuickType suggestion — the
  one field nobody can type from memory had to be fetched by leaving the app. `Input` now passes both
  props through, and `verify-email.tsx` and `reset-password-code.tsx` declare `one-time-code` /
  `oneTimeCode`. The same pass gives **Login** its declarations (`email` / `emailAddress`, and
  `current-password` / `password` — deliberately *not* `new-password`, which would ask a password
  manager to generate a credential for an account that already exists).

Mobile **80 suites / 983 tests / 0 failures** (up from 79 / 977: three new cases in the reset suite,
one in the verify screen's, and a new `auth-field-autofill.test.tsx`), `tsc` and `eslint` clean. No
server file was touched by the pass.

## Limits

* **Device-verified for the request and the reset, one claim short of complete.** The request half was
  measured on the OPPO over `adb reverse`; the delivery half is the owner's report above. What nobody
  re-typed is the **old** password after the change, and no second device's live session was observed
  ending — the revocation itself is pinned by the server suite, not by an observer.
* **L-17 stays OPEN**, and now gates only the AUTH-05 hosted-link path. This flow does not need the
  console setting — which is the point — but it also does not repair it: a person holding an older
  Firebase link may still land on Firebase's hosted page, and that reset still revokes nothing.
* **The delivery half is still an external fact.** A 202 means the code was minted and the send was
  dispatched, never that Brevo delivered it; the first live inbox measurement is still owed.
* **iOS is unverified**, as everywhere else on this host.

# 27DZ. The assistant's model is checked, not assumed (2026-10-21)

**AI-28. Server only — no route, permission, schema, dependency, session or mobile change, and no
prompt change, so the token cost of a turn is untouched by construction.**

## The incident this answers

On 2026-10-21 every assistant turn answered `502 AI_UNAVAILABLE` — *"The AI service is temporarily
unavailable. Please try again in a moment."* — and neither the answer nor the log could say why:

```text
[ai:openrouter] upstream HTTP 404
bodyPrefix="… not_found_error … Function '<uuid>': Not found for account '<uuid>' … provider_name":"Nvidia" …"
[ai] turn outcome=AI_UNAVAILABLE … calls=1 … model=unknown iterations=1
```

Two blind spots produced that. **Nothing asked whether the configured model worked** until a member
did, and the turn line said `model=unknown` at the one moment its `model=` field decided what an
operator would change. The model id was still listed by the gateway, so a catalogue read alone would
not have been enough either — only a completion reveals that an upstream refuses it.

## Why it stopped, measured

Neither cause is this project's configuration, and they are separate:

* **The model was not withdrawn; its only endpoint is down.** `GET /v1/models` lists
  `nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free`, and `GET /v1/models/{id}/endpoints` reports its single
  Nvidia endpoint at `status: -5` with `uptime_last_5m: 0`, `uptime_last_30m: 0` and
  `uptime_last_1d: 60` — it went down recently, having been healthy for most of the day. The
  replacement, `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free`, reports `status: 0` with uptime
  `100 / 100 / 99.93` on the same call. A correct id pointing at an unhealthy provider is the whole
  failure.
* **The free allowance is per ACCOUNT, not per model.** The same key answered
  `429 free-models-per-day … "X-RateLimit-Limit":"50", "X-RateLimit-Remaining":"0"` once today's
  turns were spent, on **both** models. So "some free models are occasionally unavailable" has two
  distinct causes, and the second one takes every free model down at once until 00:00 UTC.

## What shipped

* **`server/src/services/ai/modelCheck.ts`** — two questions, deliberately kept apart.
  `checkModelCatalogue` asks the provider's own model list whether the configured id exists; it sends
  **no completion**, so it spends no quota on a tier metered by requests (AI-6). `probeModel` sends
  **one** tool-shaped message with the configured model and reads the status — the check that would
  have caught this incident, because the gateway still listed the broken model. Neither retries,
  neither changes a model, neither stores anything and **neither throws**: a network error is
  `unreachable` rather than a claim about the model, and **429/402 is `quota`, never `unusable`**,
  because a spent allowance says nothing about the id and reporting it as a bad model sends an
  operator to change a working configuration. No credential appears in any result.
* **`npm run ai:check`** (`server/scripts/check-ai-model.mjs`) — exit **0** VERIFIED, **1** WRONG
  (change `AI_MODEL_OPENROUTER`), **2** NOT VERIFIED (nothing was proven — unreachable, unconfigured,
  or quota-refused). A pipeline cannot read "could not check" as "checked and fine". `--probe` adds
  the one-request proof.
* **A boot warning, never a boot failure.** `startServer` fires `checkModelCatalogue` unawaited (like
  the port guard) and logs **only** a `missing` model, naming it. `unreachable` is silent on purpose:
  a line that fires when the check itself could not run would train an operator to ignore it. A
  throwing check cannot stop the server, and `NODE_ENV=test` checks nothing by default so a suite
  never reaches a provider.
* **A failing turn names its model.** `AIProvider` gained an optional `model` (a **getter** on the
  Anthropic-compatible provider, so it reads the environment at call time like everything else in
  that service), and `ai.service` seeds the turn line from it. `model=unknown` is gone from exactly
  the case that needed the field.

## Verification

* **The live model answered 6 of 6 questions, grounded and numerically exact** — `perf:turns`
  against a freshly seeded tenant (200 products, 3 locations): dashboard totals `200 / 32 / 8`, the
  reorder total `32`, a SKU lookup (`Eco Tape 1000`, 5 kg), the out-of-stock count with its `8 ÷ 200`
  base, total on-hand `49,217` units and a per-location breakdown **rendered as a table**. Tools called:
  `getReorderNeededProducts`, `getProduct`, `getInventorySummary`, `getLocationBreakdown`. Latency
  **5.3 / 7.0 / 7.4 / 8.6 / 8.7 / 15.7 s**, no `degraded` mark on any turn, and every number equal to
  the figure read from MongoDB through the same services the tools call.
* **The failure path, measured on the running server once the allowance ran out:** `POST /api/ai/chat`
  answered **429 `AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` in 704 ms** with *"The AI assistant has reached its usage limit.
  Please try again later."*, nothing persisted, and the turn line now reads
  `outcome=AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED … model=nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free` — the AI-28 fix observed on
  the failing path it was written for. The mobile copy for that code (`ai6-assistant-quota-copy`) is
  unchanged and still names the reset, **08:00 in Manila**, rather than an unspecified "later".
* **`npm run ai:check`**: `ok` → exit **0**; `--probe` → `quota (HTTP 429)` → exit **2**, **NOT
  VERIFIED** — the distinction that stops a spent allowance from being reported as a broken model.
* **Server 1048 tests / 997 pass / 0 fail / 51 skipped** (`test:unit`, which includes the 16 new
  `AI28-ai-model-config` cases and the strengthened `AI5` case), `tsc`, `eslint` and both
  module-graph checks clean; mobile's three assistant-copy suites **57/57**.

## Limits

* **The model-down 404 was not re-observed live today.** Once the allowance is spent the gateway
  answers 429 before it ever looks at the model, so the exact `upstream HTTP 404` shape is pinned by
  the provider suite and by this record, not by a fresh reproduction.
* **No successful in-app turn was re-run today** — the 6/6 measurement spent the last of the 50 free
  requests, and the app's render of a successful turn is covered by the earlier device runs
  (§27BG), not by this one. The app path was re-verified for the failure it now shows.
* **A check is not a guarantee.** `ai:check` proves the model answers *at the moment it runs*; on a
  free tier the endpoint can go unhealthy minutes later, which is what happened here.

# 27EA. A fallback chain that is verified, bounded, and never spends a refusal twice (2026-10-21)

**AI-29. Server only — no route, permission, schema, dependency, session or mobile change, and no
prompt change.** It is the other half of §27DZ: that record made a dead model *visible*, this one
makes it *survivable*.

## The five candidates, measured rather than assumed

Read from the provider's own catalogue on 2026-10-21 (`supported_parameters` and the per-model
`endpoints` call — both free, no completion):

| Candidate | Declares `tools` | Endpoint status / 30-min uptime | Context |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free` | yes | **0 / 100 %** | 1 000 000 |
| `nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free` | yes | **0 / 100 %** | 1 000 000 |
| `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl:free` | yes | **-2 / 96.7 %** (degraded) | 1 000 000 |
| `liquid/lfm-2.5-2.6b:free` | yes | **0 / 100 %** | 65 536 |
| `nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free` | yes | **-5 / 0 %** (the outage §27DZ records) | 262 144 |

All five declare tool calling, so none is excluded by the catalogue — but a declaration is not a
demonstration, and a 2.6 B model declaring `tools` is not evidence that it uses them well. The
chain order therefore puts the two proven-and-healthy large models first, the degraded multimodal
one third, the small model **fourth** (it is reached only after three better candidates have
failed), and the currently-down model **last**, where it costs nothing while it recovers and is
still available if it comes back.

The configured order:

```text
AI_FALLBACK_MODELS_OPENROUTER=nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free,\
  nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free,nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl:free,\
  liquid/lfm-2.5-2.6b:free,nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free
```

The primary is still `AI_MODEL_OPENROUTER` and is simply **skipped** in the list, so changing the
primary in one variable cannot leave a duplicate attempt behind.

## What shipped

* **`AI_FALLBACK_MODELS_OPENROUTER`** — comma-separated, ordered, trimmed, deduplicated, **capped at
  5** (`MAX_FALLBACK_MODELS`). Empty is a supported deployment: every turn behaves exactly as it did
  before. A candidate equal to the primary is removed, because paying twice for the same broken model
  is not a fallback.
* **A chain walk, not a retry.** `ai.service` tries the configured model; on a *model-specific*
  failure it walks the candidates **in the configured order**, once each, and returns the first
  answer. The model that answered is **sticky for the rest of the turn**, so a question that needs a
  tool does not re-pay the dead model on every round — and the walk itself happens **at most once per
  turn**, which is what makes "no infinite retry loop" structural rather than hopeful.
* **The classification is the feature**, and it lives on the error rather than in the loop
  (`MODEL_FAILOVER_STATUSES`, `isModelSpecificProviderFailure`): a failover happens on **404, 410,
  500, 502, 503, 504 and 529** — a model the gateway cannot route to, or an upstream that is down.
  Everything else stops the walk:
  * **402 / 429 are `AiQuotaExceeded`, not `AiProviderError`** (AI-6), so they never reach the walk at
    all — the allowance is per account and shared by every free model, so the next candidate would be
    refused identically. Measured again today: with five candidates configured and the allowance
    spent, a turn made **exactly one** provider call.
  * **400 / 401 / 403** are our request or our key; another model changes nothing.
  * **A transport failure carries no status**, so it is not model-specific: another model would
    travel the same broken network.
* **A deadline floor.** A candidate is attempted only when at least `FAILOVER_MIN_REMAINING_MS`
  (5 000 ms) is left of the turn's single deadline (AI-1). Below that, a second model cannot finish,
  and the honest failure arrives sooner instead of later.
* **Tool capability is required, and checked for free.** `modelCapabilities.ts` reads the provider's
  catalogue at boot (unawaited, no completion, so **no quota**), caches which models declare
  `tools`, and the turn loop skips a candidate that declares it cannot call tools — before a request
  is spent on it. An unread catalogue is **`unknown`, never `false`**: refusing to fall back because
  a free check did not run would be an outage of the check's own. A boot line names any configured
  candidate that will be skipped, because that is otherwise discovered on the worst possible day.
* **Observation without secrets.** One `[ai] failover attempt=N model=<from> -> <to> reason=HTTP
  <status> remaining=<ms>ms` line per attempt (model ids and a status only — no key, no prompt, no
  upstream body), the skipped candidates named once, and `failovers=<n>` added to the AI-5 turn line
  so "it worked" and "it worked on the third model" are different facts in the log.
* **`npm run ai:models`** — the list is owned by whoever runs the deployment, not by a code change.
  It prints the primary and the chain exactly as the turn loop reads them (marking the candidates that
  will be skipped and why), then the free ids that declare tool support; `--check=<id>` proves a
  single id answers a tool-shaped request for one request, so a model can be tried **before** it joins
  the chain. Changing the order is editing `AI_FALLBACK_MODELS_OPENROUTER` and restarting the server
  (`docs/guides/6-scripts-and-commands.md`, "Changing the AI models yourself").
* **`npm run ai:check` grew the chain**: it lists every candidate with its declared tool support,
  and `--probe` sends one tool-shaped request to the primary **and each candidate** (6 requests for a
  5-model chain), failing with exit **1** if any candidate cannot call tools or cannot answer.
* **No duplicate inventory work.** The tools are read-only (CLAUDE.md §4 and `AI2`'s guard), so a
  failover cannot apply a change twice — there is no write to apply. Business isolation, permissions
  and the prompt are untouched: a candidate receives the same server-derived `businessId`, the same
  role-gated tool table and the same messages.

## Verification

* **26 new cases** in `AI29-model-failover.test.mjs`, of which the ones that matter most: the chain
  walks in order and stops at the first answer; a 429 **ends the walk** (one call, the quota error is
  what the member sees); every candidate failing reports the **last** failure and reports
  `failovers=3` while never exceeding one attempt each; a tool-less candidate is **skipped and
  named**; the primary and duplicates are never tried; the chain is sticky across a tool round; a
  fallback equal to the primary is not attempted; too little deadline means no attempt; the probe
