  sends the candidate's own id and calls a quota refusal `quota`, never `unusable`.
* **Server 1073 tests / 1021 pass / 0 fail / 52 skipped** (`test:unit`), `tsc`, `eslint` and both
  module-graph checks clean (464 modules).
* **Live, with the five candidates configured and the allowance spent:** `POST /api/ai/chat` answered
  **429 `AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` in 545 ms**, and the turn line read
  `outcome=AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED … calls=1 … failovers=0 … model=nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free` —
  no failover line, no second request. That is the requirement this feature could most easily get
  wrong, observed on the real route.
* **`npm run ai:check`** lists the chain with declared tool support for all five (exit 0).

## Limits

* **A real failover was not observed live today.** The account's 50 free requests were spent by the
  §27DZ measurement, so every candidate answers 429 before the model is ever consulted — the very
  case that correctly does **not** fail over. The walk is proven by the DB-gated wire test (a real
  route, real auth, a 404 from the primary answered by the fallback as an ordinary 201) and by the
  unit cases; the first live walk is owed once the allowance resets (**08:00 Manila**), and
  `npm run ai:check -- --probe` is the command that verifies the candidates themselves.
* **Declared tool support is not proven skill.** `liquid/lfm-2.5-2.6b:free` is a 2.6 B model: it
  declares `tools` and is placed last for that reason. If the probe shows it cannot ground an answer,
  it should be removed from the list rather than trusted on a technicality.
* **`nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl:free` is degraded** (-2 / 96.7 %) and
  **`nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free` is down** (-5 / 0 %) as this was written. Both stay in
  the chain — the second costs nothing while it is unavailable and is worth having if it returns.
* **The whole chain can still be down.** The member then sees the existing 502 `AI_UNAVAILABLE`
  sentence, which is accurate; a new client code was deliberately not added, because it would need a
  mobile copy and tests to say the same thing, and the per-model detail belongs in the log.

# 27EB. A model that just failed five times is not tried first on the next turn (2026-10-21)

**AI-30. Server only — no route, permission, schema, dependency, session or mobile change, and no
prompt change.** It closes the recurring cost §27EA left in place.

## The problem it removes

AI-29 makes a dead model survivable: a turn that hits it walks to a healthy candidate and still
answers. But the configured primary is tried **first on every new turn**, so a model the deployment
already knows is broken costs one failed request — and a share of the free tier's shared allowance —
on every turn until an operator edits `.env` and restarts. Survivable is not the same as cheap.

## The mechanism

`server/src/services/ai/modelBreaker.ts` is a process-local, in-memory breaker per model id:

| State | When | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **closed** | fewer than 5 consecutive model-specific failures | the model is selected normally |
| **open** | the 5th consecutive failure | skipped entirely for **30 s** |
| **half-open** | 30 s have passed | tried again; a failure **re-opens it at once**, a success closes it |

The failure count is **not** reset when the cooldown ends. Resetting it would let a dead model cost
five more requests every 30 seconds; keeping it means the first failed trial re-opens the breaker,
so the steady-state cost of a permanently dead primary is **one request per 30 s**, not one per turn.
A single 2xx clears the streak and the cooldown — the model returns to normal selection by itself.

The **primary is skipped like any other model**. When it is cooling, the turn starts directly on the
first eligible candidate; when the cooldown expires it is first in the chain again, because
configuration was never changed. Every skip is one line naming the model and the seconds left, and
the moment a breaker opens is its own line (`model cooling down for 30s after 5 consecutive
failure(s): <id>`). If **every** configured model is cooling, the turn fails fast with **zero
provider calls** and the existing 502 `AI_UNAVAILABLE` sentence — the honest answer without spending
a request to prove it a sixth time.

**What never counts.** Only `MODEL_FAILOVER_STATUSES` (404/410/500/502/503/504/529) is recorded.
Quota (429/402) is the account's shared allowance, auth and bad requests (400/401/403) travel with
us, and a configuration error never reaches the loop. None of them is evidence about a model, so none
may make a healthy model's next turn skip it. *(A status-less transport failure was also excluded
here; §27EC revisits that one — a CLASSIFIED transport failure now counts, while still never
triggering an in-turn failover.)*

## Verification

* **18 new cases** in `AI30-model-cooldown.test.mjs`: the fifth failure opens and the fourth does
  not; the window expires on its own; a failed half-open trial re-opens immediately while one
  success clears the streak; counts are per model; the primary is skipped after five failing turns
  with configuration untouched; a cooling candidate is skipped inside the walk; every model cooling
  answers with zero calls; and 429/402, 400/401/403 and an UNCLASSIFIED provider error leave the
  breaker untouched. *(A classified transport failure was excluded when this was written; §27EC
  changed that deliberately — it now counts, still without failing over.)*
* **`AI29-model-failover.test.mjs` still passes in full** (the pre-existing failover contract), with
  a breaker reset between cases because the state is process-wide by design.
* **Server 1093 tests / 1041 pass / 0 fail / 52 skipped** (`test:unit`), `tsc`, `eslint` and both
  module-graph checks clean (467 modules).

## Limits

* **Per process and not persisted.** A restart forgets every cooldown — which is the right default,
  because a restart is exactly the moment to re-test the whole chain. Two server instances keep
  independent breakers; neither learns from the other.
* **No live device run of the cooldown itself.** It is proven by the fake-provider cases; the live
  failover it builds on was measured on the phone in the same session (§27EA), and a live cooldown
  would need five real failing turns against the dead primary.
* **The breaker is not a health registry.** It remembers this process's recent failures, not the
  provider's uptime; `npm run ai:check` and `npm run ai:models` remain the way to prove a model
  answers before trusting it.

# 27EC. The model that answers becomes the model the deployment uses (2026-10-21)

**AI-31. Server only — no route, permission, schema, dependency, session or mobile change, and no
prompt change.** It turns §27EA's in-turn rescue and §27EB's cooldown into a self-managing rotation.

## The problem it removes

AI-29 rescues a turn with a fallback, and AI-30 stops a dead primary being tried first. But the
fallback was still only a fallback: the next request started on the configured primary again, so a
deployment whose primary had died re-paid for the same refusal once per cooldown window, forever. The
operator had to notice and edit `.env` — the thing this record removes.

## The mechanism

`server/src/services/ai/modelSelection.ts` holds one process-local value: the **promoted** model, or
`null` while the configured default is still the active one. `activeModel(configuredPrimary)` returns
the promotion first, and a turn's chain becomes `[active, ...configured order without it]`.

**Promotion is threshold-gated, not eager.** A fallback that answers one transient failure still
serves that turn, but does not seize the deployment — `maybePromote` requires the active model to be
**cooling**, which only happens after `AI_MODEL_FAILURE_THRESHOLD` (default **5**) consecutive
availability failures. The check is "cooling when the turn began, or cooling now": a tool-heavy
turn can outlast the 30-second window, and its fallback's success must not be discarded just because
the clock, rather than a success, ended the cooldown. When the fallback then answers a turn, it is
promoted:

```text
[ai] promoted model: <old active> -> <responder>
```

and every later turn starts there. A promoted model that later fails five times is replaced the same
way, by whichever configured model answers next; the walk keeps moving forward through the chain.

**Configuration is never overwritten.** `AI_MODEL_OPENROUTER` remains the operator's default, is what
`npm run ai:models` prints, and is what a restart returns to — deliberately, because a restart is the
moment to re-test it. Promotion is a runtime fact, not an environment edit, and the process could not
portably write `.env` anyway.

**Concurrency is a compare-and-set.** Node runs the mutator synchronously, and `promoteModel` accepts
a candidate only when the caller's `expectedActive` still matches. Two requests that both read the old
active before either promotes: the first wins, the second is refused, so they cannot overwrite one
another's decision. Failure counters are mutated synchronously in `modelBreaker`, so concurrent turns
neither lose an increment nor reset one another.

## Transport failures now count (and still do not fail over)

§27EB excluded a status-less failure from the breaker because it is not the model's fault. That is
still true of the *failover* — another model travels the same broken network — but five consecutive
ones mean the assistant cannot serve at all, and paying for the same outage on every turn is exactly
the recurring cost the breaker exists to stop. `AiProviderError` now carries a declared `kind`:
`network`, `timeout` or `invalid_response`, set at the one place that knows (`providers/http.ts`).

| Failure | Breaker counts it | In-turn failover |
|---|---|---|
| 404/410/5xx (`MODEL_FAILOVER_STATUSES`) | yes | yes |
| `network` / `timeout` / `invalid_response` | **yes** | **no** — same path would fail |
| 400/401/403 | no | no |
| 402/429 (`AiQuotaExceeded`) | no | no — one shared allowance |
| configuration error / unclassified provider error | no | no |

The kind is a declared enum, not a string match on error copy: rewording a sentence can never turn a
timeout into a model verdict. An `AiProviderError` with neither a status nor a kind still counts for
nothing, so a provider bug cannot cool a healthy model.

## Verification

* **19 cases** in `AI31-model-promotion.test.mjs`: a healthy active stays active; 1–4 failures do not
  promote (the fallback still serves); the fifth promotes; the next request starts on the promoted
  model; a promoted model failing five times is replaced by the next working one; a cooled model
  rejoins the rotation after its window; the environment order decides who is tried first; a
  configured threshold/cooldown is honoured; all models cooling fails fast with the existing 502;
  quota and 400/401/403 never promote or count; a configuration error is not counted; a tool is not
  executed twice when the model fails after it; concurrent turns keep correct counters, promote
  once, and a stale promotion is refused; and five network failures cool the active model, after
  which the first model that answers is promoted (`promoted model: fake-model -> fallback-model`).
* **`AI29` and `AI30` still pass in full.** AI-30's transport case was split into “classified counts,
  never fails over” and “unclassified counts for nothing”, so the old guarantee is pinned more
  precisely rather than dropped.
* **Server `test:unit` 1115 tests / 1063 pass / 0 fail / 52 skipped**; **`test:db` 852 tests / 764
  pass / 0 fail / 88 skipped**; `tsc`, `eslint` and both module-graph checks clean (469 modules).

## Verified live, on the real provider (2026-10-21)

A one-off script (not committed) pointed the configured primary at
**`nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free`** — a VALID id whose upstream is dead (`ai:models --
--check=…` measured `unusable (HTTP 404)`), which is the exact class this feature acts on — with
**`nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free`** as the only candidate, and ran six turns through
`runAiChat` against OpenRouter:

```text
turn 1-4  primary 404 -> failover -> OK   failures=1..4  promoted=null
turn 5    primary 404 -> failover -> OK   failures=5  model cooling down for 30s
                                         promoted model: …super-120b… -> …lightning…
turn 6    calls=1 failovers=0 model=…lightning…
```

So the five-failure threshold, the cooldown, the in-turn fallback and the promotion were all
observed on a real request path, not only on the fake provider; turn 6 is the promoted model
serving first with no failed attempt. A bogus id was tried first and answered **HTTP 400**; it was
not counted and did not fail over — the classification that keeps a bad configuration out of the
breaker, observed on the same real gateway. The 404 attempts did not change the day's free-model
allowance reading (`44 of 50` before and after); the six successful answers did not exhaust it.

**The configured order at measurement time** (`/v1/models/:author/:slug/endpoints`, no completion
and no quota): `super-vl` **-2**, 100 % / 91.7 % (degraded); `liquid/lfm-2.5-2.6b` **-5**, 100 % /
72.8 % (degraded); `lightning` **0**, 100 % / 100 %; `ultra-550b` **0**, 100 % / 100 %;
`super-120b` **-5**, 0 % / 3.75 % (down, and its completion probe answers 404). The owner's
requested order is what is configured, so the first two candidates are currently the weakest —
which is a reason to reorder the variable, not to edit the code. The live run above used
`lightning` because it is the one that answers.

## Configured order changed the same day, on that measurement

The requested initial order was recorded above rather than quietly rewritten, because the reason it
changed is the measurement beside it. Once the six-turn run and the endpoint report agreed, the
configured order was changed to put the model that had actually answered inventory questions first,
and the degraded models later:

```bash
AI_MODEL_OPENROUTER=nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free
AI_FALLBACK_MODELS_OPENROUTER=nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free,nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl:free,liquid/lfm-2.5-2.6b:free,nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free
```

`lightning` and `ultra-550b` were both at **status 0 / 100 % / 100 %**; `lightning` is first because it
is also the model with the 6/6 grounded-turn record, which uptime alone cannot show. `super-vl`
(**-2**, 91.7 % over 24 h) is third, `liquid` (2.6 B, 73.1 % over 24 h, and the weakest reasoning of the
five) is fourth, and `super-120b` (**-5**, 2.4 % over 24 h) is last. The free tier's per-model ids and
tool support were re-read at the same time; nothing in the application code or the promotion logic
changed, and the configured primary is still never overwritten at runtime.

## Production verification, and what Render actually applies (2026-10-21)

Commit **`7f3e6a1`** was pushed to `main`; Render auto-deployed it, `/api/health/ready` answered 200,
and the production environment was set to the measured order with the explicit policy values:
`AI_MODEL_OPENROUTER=nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free`,
`AI_FALLBACK_MODELS_OPENROUTER=ultra,super-vl,liquid,super-120b`,
`AI_MODEL_FAILURE_THRESHOLD=5`, `AI_MODEL_COOLDOWN_MS=30000`.

**A changed environment variable is applied by the next DEPLOY, not by a restart.** The first deploy
began before the environment write and served `super-vl`; a plain `render restart` kept serving
`super-vl`; a fresh `render deploys create` served `lightning`. The guide now states this, because
"the dashboard shows the new value" and "the running process uses the new value" were different
facts for about two minutes.

**Inventory accuracy, on the phone, against production.** The documented demo tenant was seeded into
`inventoryai_prod_db` (6 products, 3 locations, 112 units; all 15 read-back checks matched), and the
OPPO CPH1969 signed in through the production API (`https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com`). One
turn answered **112 units**; the restock turn named **Demo Desk Lamp (0), Demo Coffee Beans 1kg (4)
and Demo Paper Cups 100pk (15)**; the out-of-stock turn answered **one product, Demo Desk Lamp** —
exactly the fixture, with `getInventorySummary`, `getReorderNeededProducts` and
`getOutOfStockProducts` on the turn lines.

**Promotion was exercised on production, not inferred.** The primary was temporarily set to the
valid-but-dead `super-120b`, with `lightning` first in the fallback chain, and the phone sent real
turns. Every failed primary attempt was followed by a successful `lightning` answer; on the fifth
consecutive failure the log recorded `model cooling down for 30s after 5 consecutive failure(s)`
and then
`promoted model: …super-120b… -> …lightning…`; the next turn logged
`model cooling down, skipped: …super-120b… (9s left)`, `calls=1 failovers=0` and answered correctly
from `lightning`. Production was then restored to the lightning-first order and redeployed; the final
turn logged `model=nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free calls=1 failovers=0` and answered **112 units**.

The temporary demo tenant was removed with `cleanup:demo-tenant` (7 inventory + 9 ledger + 6 products
+ 2 categories + 3 locations + 1 user + 1 business, **leftovers 0**); the Firebase identity remains by
design. The exercise spent **11 requests** (the allowance read **42 of 50** before the promotion run
and **31** after the final verification), and the phone was signed out afterwards by clearing its
local session — no production credential was left on the device.

## Limits

* **Per process and not persisted**, like the breaker. A restart forgets the promotion and returns to
  the configured default; several instances each promote independently and converge on a model that
  answers. No shared store was introduced for a decision that is cheap to rediscover.
* **A promotion is only as good as its evidence.** It follows one usable 2xx from a model whose active
  peer is cooling; it is not a benchmark, and a model can be promoted and demoted within a minute if
  the provider is flapping. The cooldown is what keeps that from churning on every request.
* **The free tier can still be spent.** Promotion cannot create quota: when the account's 50 daily
  requests are gone, every model answers 429 and the member sees `AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED`, correctly. No
  amount of failover changes that.
* **Not device-verified in the app.** The rotation is proven by fake-provider cases AND by the live
  six-turn run above over the real provider; the in-app turn path it feeds was measured in §27EA,
  and this record changes neither the prompt nor the response shape, so no phone run was needed.

# 27ED. The model list carries live evidence, not a remembered measurement (2026-10-21)

**AI-32. Server tooling only — no route, permission, schema, dependency, session or mobile change,
and no prompt change.** It closes the gap between "the chain was measured once" and "the chain can be
re-measured by the command an operator already runs".

`readModelHealth` in `server/src/services/ai/modelCheck.ts` reads the provider's own endpoint record,
`GET /v1/models/{author}/{slug}/endpoints`, and returns every endpoint with its `status` and its
5-minute, 30-minute and 1-day uptime. It is a **GET, not a completion**, so it spends none of the
free tier's request allowance and can run on every `npm run ai:models`.

The result is deliberately raw evidence, not a verdict: the command prints the provider's code and
uptime rather than translating a negative code into "do not use". A 404 is `not_found`, an empty
endpoint list is `no_endpoints`, and any other refusal or transport error is `unreachable` — none of
those is `ok`, and none is a claim that the model cannot answer. That claim remains `probeModel`'s,
which is the only check that sends a request.

```text
[ai:models] health   : live endpoint status and uptime (GET only — no completion, no quota)
[ai:models]   primary nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free
[ai:models]           Nvidia | status 0 | 5m 100% | 30m 100% | 1d 100%
[ai:models]   2.      nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl:free
[ai:models]           Nvidia | status -2 | 5m 100% | 30m 83.3% | 1d 92.8%
```

**10 cases** in `AI32-model-health.test.mjs` pin the parsing and every failure shape (non-numeric
fields become `null`, never a guessed zero or `NaN`; the model override and URL are exact; the key
stays in the header; a `/v1` base is not doubled). `AI28` still passes unchanged. The operator guide
now explains that the health read is free and that `ai:models -- --check=<id>` shows the health before
spending its one request.

**Not a health promise.** The provider's `status: 0` and 100 % uptime are availability evidence, not
evidence that a model grounds inventory questions; §27EE's real turns are the other half. The command
does not change the configured order, the active model, the breaker or any file.

# 27EE. The comparison is measured, and the measuring instrument is fixed (2026-10-21)

**AI-33. Server tooling and tests only — no production AI path, prompt, route or mobile change.**

## The instrument had two false results

`perf:turns` checked an answer with `normalizedAnswer.includes(normalizedFact)`. That is wrong in both
directions, and both were measured:

* Lightning's correct *"none are out of stock"* was reported `MISSING 0`, because a count of zero is
often written as a word;
* an expected `2` matched the `2` inside `1281`, `12` or `24`, so a wrong answer could be reported
grounded.

The second is the dangerous one: a false PASS hides a defect. `server/scripts/perf/factCheck.mjs` now
compares numbers as **whole numbers** (so `2` is not found inside `1281` and `6` is not found inside
`64`), accepts `0`/`none`/`nothing`/`no ... products` for a zero count, and leaves text facts compared
after whitespace and case normalization. **9 cases** in `AI33-turn-fact-check.test.mjs` pin both
directions, including a control that `10` is not a zero.

## Ultra and Lightning, same tenant, same five questions

The questions were dashboard health, restock count, one SKU's name and quantity, total units, and the
per-location breakdown. Ground truth was read at run time through `dashboardService`, `productService`
and `inventoryService`; the dashboard itself was then called over HTTP with a minted session and
agreed exactly: **6 products, 1,281 units, 2 low-stock, 0 out-of-stock**, `SEEDSKU-0` **64 units** across
three locations, and **433 / 424 / 424** units per location.

| Model | Answers | Grounded | Times (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free` | 5/5 | **5/5** | 2,504 · 3,887 · 4,650 · 5,300 · 8,142 |
| `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free` | 5/5 | **5/5** after the fix | 2,962 · 3,898 · 4,535 · 6,706 · 14,528 |

Lightning's first pass printed `MISSING 0` on the zero-count answer; rerunning that one question after
the fact-check fix printed `all expected facts present`. Both models used the correct tools
(`getInventorySummary`, `getReorderNeededProducts`, `getProduct`, `getLocationBreakdown`), and both
reported the same exact figures. Ultra answered the product quantity and the location split correctly,
not merely the headline counts.

**The order did not change.** Lightning remains primary because it has the larger body of evidence
(6/6 earlier plus 5/5 here) and is already the production-proven model; Ultra remains the first
fallback, now with its own 5/5 record. One equally good run is not a reason to churn a production
primary. The comparison spent **21 of the 31 requests available at the start**; **10 remained** when the
measurement finished. No further live turns are required to justify the current order.

# 27EF. Large tenants and dependency alerts: measured, not assumed (2026-10-21)

**Measurement and review only — no production code, dependency, schema or configuration change.**

## Scale

The performance tenant was seeded deterministically at two sizes and every AI tool was timed through
the same `executeTool` the turn loop calls, with **zero model calls**:

| Size | Products | Inventory rows | Transactions | Heavy-tool medians |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 10k | 10,000 | 20,105 | 19,944 | 368–418 ms (max 656 ms) |
| 50k | 50,000 | 100,143 | 100,096 | 733–1,019 ms (one 4,780 ms outlier) |

At 50k the HTTP endpoints behind the dashboard were also timed five times: `/api/dashboard` median
**1,042 ms** (p95 1,258), `/api/products/reorder` **1,230 ms**, product search **669 ms**, product list
**435 ms**, inventory list **318 ms**, inventory history **320 ms**. No tool payload exceeded the
12,000-character cap at either size, so the model received every result whole.

The index audit reported **64 declared indexes across 16 collections, 0 declaration/database
disagreements**, and `test:db` passed **854 tests / 764 pass / 0 fail / 90 skipped**. The 50k tenant was
then removed with `cleanup:perf`: **250,256 documents removed, 0 remaining**. No bottleneck required a
code change at these sizes; the measurements are the baseline for the next scale step, not a claim
about millions of rows.

## Dependabot

Four open alerts, all in `mobile/package-lock.json` and all transitive:

| Alert | Package | Severity | Where it runs | Disposition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| #2 | `decode-uri-component@0.2.2` | medium | runtime, `expo-router` → `query-string@7.1.3` | **No safe upgrade.** The patched `0.5.0` is ESM-only; `query-string@7` is CommonJS, so forcing it would break the bundle. The real fix is an Expo SDK upgrade, which is the separate SDK 58 train. |
| #5 | `node-forge@1.4.0` | high | build only, `@expo/cli` code signing | No patched release; never shipped in the app. |
| #6 | `braces@3.0.3` | high | development only, Jest → micromatch | No patched release; not in the app runtime. |
| #8 | `sprintf-js@1.0.3` | medium | development only, Jest → js-yaml → argparse | No advisory fix; forcing the 1.1.x line under `argparse@1.0.10` is outside its supported range. |

No dependency was changed. The runtime item is a **medium-severity client denial of service**, not a
credential or data-exposure defect, and the only compatible fix would be a major Expo upgrade that
this task must not smuggle in. The alerts remain open and visible rather than being dismissed.

## Capacity ceiling — what an M0 cluster can actually hold (2026-10-21 addendum)

A read-only audit of the dev cluster (`inventoryai_dev_db`; `db.stats()` plus per-collection `collStats`)
turns the next scale step into an infrastructure question with numbers rather than a vague ambition:

| Measurement | Value |
|---|---:|
| Products / inventory rows / transactions | 79,854 / 159,080 / 110,883 |
| Logical data size | 83.9 MB |
| Index size | 140.2 MB |
| Total counted against the tier | **224.1 MB** |
| `products` bytes per product (data + index) | ~600 B |
| `inventory` bytes per row (data + index) | ~487 B |
| Footprint per product with two stock rows | **~1.6 KB** |
| `inventory_transactions` bytes per row | ~841 B |

Atlas M0's documented ceiling is **512 MB for data plus indexes**, so this shared cluster has ~288 MB
of headroom. A **1,000,000-product** tenant with two stock rows per product needs **~1.6 GB before any
transaction history**, and ~2.5 GB at the history-to-product ratio observed here. That is **not
reachable on M0**: an empty 512 MB cluster fits roughly **320,000** products of this shape, and the
current database fits roughly **180,000 more products** before it is full. The projection is linear at
this shape (catalogue + two stock rows, history excluded):

| Products | Footprint | Fits an empty M0? |
|---:|---:|---|
| 100,000 | ~160 MB | yes |
| 250,000 | ~400 MB | yes, with little headroom |
| 320,000 | ~512 MB | no — exactly at the ceiling |
| 1,000,000 | ~1.6 GB | no |

A million-product claim is therefore a **paid-tier provisioning and seeding task**, not something that
can be validated on this environment; no code change would be justified by pretending otherwise.

The 50k tenant measured above is **present again** in the dev database at audit time (**50,626
products**), which supersedes the "0 remaining" line for the current state; the earlier cleanup was real,
and these rows are a later seed. That is why the next large seed must **clean up first** rather than
stack another dataset into 288 MB of headroom. What the existing measurements do establish is narrower
and still useful: the query shapes, index coverage and 12,000-character payload cap hold at 50k with no
bottleneck; nothing below 50k is unmeasured. `test:db` passing 854 / 764 / 0 in the same window is the
correctness half of that baseline.

# 27EG. A dead model is found by a timer, not by a member's failed question (2026-10-21)

**AI-34. Server only — no route, permission, schema, dependency, session or mobile change, and no
prompt change.**

## The gap it closes

AI-28 can say whether the configured model is listed, AI-29/30/31 keep a turn alive when it is not,
and AI-32 can print live endpoint health when an operator asks. All of them are **pulled**: the
deployment learned that its model was dead on 2026-10-21 because a member asked a question and got
`502 AI_UNAVAILABLE`. Nothing watched while nobody was asking, which is the worst possible detector.

## The mechanism

`server/src/services/ai/healthWatch.ts` runs the same quota-free read AI-32 uses —
`GET /v1/models/{author}/{slug}/endpoints`, no completion, no request from the free allowance — for
the configured primary and every fallback. It classifies each model:

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ok` | a current endpoint reports status 0; best 5-minute uptime ≥ **90%** and best 30-minute uptime ≥ **95%**. |
| `degraded` | an endpoint is down while another is up, an uptime window is below its threshold, or **no endpoint reports status 0 but recent uptime is still measurable**. |
| `unavailable` | the provider publishes no endpoint, or none reports status 0 **and no recent uptime is measurable** (best 5-minute is 0 or missing). |
| `unknown` | the record could not be read. Never called an outage; two consecutive unreadable checks alert that the check itself cannot run. |

The first draft classified every `status !== 0` as unavailable. The live run on 2026-10-21 corrected
that: the provider published `status -2` with **100% five-minute uptime** for a model that was still
serving, so calling it unavailable would have sent an operator to replace a working model. The rule
is now evidence-based: **no healthy status + no current uptime = unavailable; no healthy status but
still serving = degraded.**

Alerts are **transition-only**: one message for a new problem, one for a worsening or improvement, one
for the recovery, silence while the level is unchanged. The state is per process, like the AI-30
breaker: a restart forgets it and re-sends one alert for a still-broken model, which is the correct
trade for the single-instance deployment and requires no new collection or shared store. An unreadable
check never overwrites a known outage.

**Where it goes.** `sendOperationalAlertEmail` renders the report through the existing provider-agnostic
mail boundary and sends it to `AI_HEALTH_ALERT_EMAIL`. If the address or the mail configuration is
missing, the same report is written to the server log at error level — an undeliverable alert is still
an alert. The message names model ids, endpoint statuses and uptime only: no API key, no base URL, no
tenant, no user.

**When it runs.** `startServer` starts the watchdog in production (and only when an OpenRouter model is
configured). Defaults: first check after **60 s**, then every **30 min**; both configurable, and the
timers are unref'd so a watchdog can never hold the process open. Shutdown stops it before the drain.
`npm run ai:health` runs the same check once and exits **0** healthy, **1** unavailable/degraded, **2**
could not check; `-- --alert` sends the alert too. That is the command for an external scheduler when
free hosting sleeps the process.

## Verified live, without spending quota

`npm run ai:health` against the configured chain on 2026-10-21, five GETs and zero completions:

```text
primary  nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free       ok           best 5m 100%, 30m 100%
fallback nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free   ok           best 5m 100%, 30m 100%
fallback nvidia/nemotron-3.5-super-vl:free        ok           best 5m 100%, 30m 100%
fallback liquid/lfm-2.5-2.6b:free                 degraded     status -2, 5m 100%, 30m 76.7%
fallback nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free   unavailable  status -5, 5m 0%, 30m 0%
```

Exit **1** (attention), correctly: one model is genuinely unavailable, one is degraded but serving, and
the then-dead primary replacement is last in the chain. The first run of the same command, before the
`-2` correction, reported **3 unavailable**; that is the measurement the correction is based on.

## Verification and limits

**29 cases** in `AI34-ai-health-watchdog.test.mjs`: classification (including the `-2` case), the
configured chain, transition-only alerts with recovery, unknown ≠ down, a prior outage surviving an
unreadable check, GET-only reads, no key in an alert, a failed send not throwing, the scheduler's
interval/stop, production/development/test enablement, the boot start/stop wiring, the template's
HTML escaping and empty-input refusal, and the real fake mail provider. `npm run test:unit` passed
**1168 tests / 1116 pass / 0 fail / 52 skipped** on the final re-run; an earlier 1166 / 1114 reading
was taken before the two template cases were added (the file itself reported 29 / 29 at that point).
`npm run test:db` passed **854 / 764 pass / 0 fail / 90 skipped**,
`npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint` and both module-graph checks are clean (476 modules).

Limits stated rather than discovered later: the state is **process-local**, so a restart re-alerts once
and two instances keep independent histories; a free host that **sleeps** does not check while asleep
(`npm run ai:health` is the external-scheduler answer); and the real email path was proven with the
in-process fake provider, **not** by delivering to a mailbox — the recipient has to be set on the host
and the first real alert observed.

# 27EH. Expo SDK 58 runs on the phone (2026-10-21)

The SDK 58 upgrade was committed as `93f9130` with one sentence left open — *"Not verified yet: the
Android build and the on-device pass"* — and this is that pass. The build under test is EAS
`b1fecde3-fa6f-4235-829d-5bc35a72ea58` (`development`, Android, `FINISHED` 12:39Z) **built from that
commit, not from a later one**, installed over the previous preview build on the owner's
**OPPO CPH1969, Android 11 (API 30), arm64-v8a**. The backend was the local server over
`adb reverse`, so the request log below is this repository's own code.

The point of a device pass is the class of failure a green pipeline cannot see: a native module that
compiles and never binds, a screen that renders in jsdom and not on a phone, a Kotlin/schema change
that only bites at runtime. None of that happened. Every screen in the app was opened on the phone,
and every write path was executed against the database.

## What ran, and what the server recorded

- **Sign-in** (Firebase email/password → exchange → JWT): dashboard with live counts `42,910` in
  stock / `7,716` low / `3,077` out / `50,626` active; the sessions screen listed this device with a
  correct `last active` a few minutes later, so AUTH-03's renewal wrote through.
- **Stock In** `201 / 627 ms` — `0 → 5`, alert shown, a `+5` history row, and an audit row in the
  same minute.
- **Transfer** `201 / 1,084 ms` — both legs: Main Warehouse `416 → 413`, Transit Hub `0 → 3`.
- **Stock Out** `200 / 576 ms` — `5 → 3`. **Adjust** `200 / 856 ms` — `3 → 4`.
- **AI assistant** `201 / 14.1 s` — *"You hold 12,540,196 units on hand across 50,626 active
  products"*, `getInventorySummary`, and the same population the dashboard showed minutes earlier.
  This turn also exercised **AI-29/31 on the real provider from the app**: the configured primary
  `nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free` answered **HTTP 404**, the turn walked to
  `nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free`, and the answer was correct — `failovers=1 calls=3
  iterations=2`. Reliability work that had only ever been proven by fake providers was observed on
  the device it exists to protect.
- **Label print** — the print preview rendered, *Save as PDF* wrote a 9,451-byte file, and the
  file's content stream was decoded: **30 bars, 95 modules × 4.0 pt, decoding to
  `2000053337540`**, the product's own code. That is the F-1 question (ISS-13) answered from the
  artifact instead of from paper: the printed document's bars are complete.
- **Share PDF** — share sheet with a real `*.pdf` payload. **Scanner** — permission gate → preview →
  a barcode in the room decoded as EAN-13 and answered *Product not found* with *Scan again*.
- **Registered barcode scan** — the same product's `2000053337540` label shown on the laptop was
  scanned by the phone: `GET /api/products/barcode` **200** in **326.6 ms**, and 471 ms later
  `GET /api/inventory` → 304, i.e. the product's stock record loading. This closes the earlier
  gap where only an *unregistered* code had been read (that code answered 404 at 13:06:14 the same
  session, so both outcomes of the lookup are now measured on hardware).
- **Purchase order, end to end** — created from the phone (`POST /api/purchase-orders` **201 /
  950.9 ms**, *Draft PO-0001 created*), **issued** (`POST /:id/issue` **200 / 625.9 ms**, Draft →
  Open), then **received in full** (`POST /:id/receive` **200 / 1,290.4 ms**, *Received 24 unit(s)
  across 1 line. This order is now fully received*). Read back from the API afterwards: the
  product's Shop Front stock **0 → 24**, an inventory-history row `STOCK_IN 24 — reference PO-0001`
  at the receive timestamp, and the order `RECEIVED` with `Ordered 24 · Received 24 · Remaining 0`.
- **Assistant quota copy** — a turn answered `429 AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` and the phone showed
  *"The assistant has used today's request allowance. It resets at midnight UTC (8AM in Manila) —
  the rest of the app works as usual."* It was produced by a **local pass-through proxy in front of
  the real server** that answers only `POST /api/ai/chat` with the server's own refusal: every other
  request reached the real API unchanged, and no free-model allowance was spent to manufacture it.
  That is a controlled measurement of the client's error path, not a real exhaustion.
- Read-only screens all rendered: products, categories, locations, suppliers, purchase orders,
  restock (7,716 rows), audit log, users, profile, sessions.

## The two checks that did not pass first

**`expo-sdk-pins` failed, and that is the guard working.** The upgrade made `expo-build-properties`
a direct dependency (it is how `app.json` declares `minSdk 24` and Kotlin 2.4.0 for RNFirebase 27).
The package is in the SDK's pin table, so the guard compared it and found it missing from
`.github/dependabot.yml`'s ignore list — a real gap CI would never have surfaced, because the move
it prevents is native-only. Fixed by adding the entry with its reason beside it.

**One full-suite Jest run timed out `po-form-create-navigation`** at the 5 s default while the
machine was also running the screen mirror and a build. Alone: **3.0 s, passes**. Clean full run
afterwards: **80 suites / 978 tests / 0 failures in 16.5 s**, `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean. Recorded as
a load-sensitive flake rather than a defect, but it is the second UI test to fail only under
contention, so it belongs on a list rather than in a footnote.

## The label decode is now a permanent check, not a one-off

The manual decode below was the only thing that could answer the F-1 question, and a one-off script
on a developer's machine answers it once. It is now `scripts/verify-label-barcode.mjs`, wired into the
mobile CI job in two modes: `--html` decodes the label the app generates **at that commit** (so a
regression in `mobile/lib/ean13.ts` — module width, quiet zone, run collapse — fails CI), and
`--pdf=scripts/fixtures/label-2000053337540.pdf` decodes the **real** PDF this pass printed (the one
thing CI cannot regenerate, because the rasteriser is the device's). A second PDF fixture,
`label-2000053337540-both-quiet-zones.pdf`, is the label the phone produced **after** the fix below;
both artifacts are decoded on every run. Both print the code, module
count, bar count and module width, and exit `0` only on a match; `2` means it could not look and is
never a pass. The decoder's own must-fail controls run before every report — clipped, thickened,
stray bar, damaged digit, page furniture — so a decoder that stopped catching problems fails first,
and each of those controls was watched failing against a deliberately broken decoder (disabling the
check digit, dropping the height grouping). Two real defects were found by building it: the first
version took the **tallest** rectangle as the bar height and discarded every bar on a real page (the
label PDF carries one 3300-unit rule), and a first "damaged digit" control flipped a bit inside a
pattern, which the digit tables reject anyway and which therefore proved nothing about the checksum.

**A decode cannot see geometry, so the check now reads the page too.** A label with a complete
95-module pattern decodes perfectly whether or not it has quiet zones and whether or not it fits the
page it is printed on — and two real defects lived exactly there. The printed label's SVG carried
**11 modules of white space on the left and none on the right** (`width` stopped at the last bar,
contradicting `QUIET_MODULES`' own "either side"; the on-screen preview had always padded both), and
`barcodeLabelHtml` honoured a caller's `moduleWidth` while keeping the page at 595 pt, so asking for
a 6 pt module produced **702 pt of label on a 595 pt page** — the F-1 clipping failure, reachable by
changing one argument. Both are fixed in `mobile/lib/ean13.ts` (the SVG width now adds the trailing
quiet zone; the page grows to the label rather than the label being scaled down, because a module
below a scanner's resolution is unreadable too), and `--html` now checks the geometry against the
page at module 4 and module 8, failing with the measured numbers. Reverting either fix makes it
fail: `right quiet zone is 0pt, expected 44pt`, `a 936pt label on a 595pt page would be clipped`.

The fixed label was then printed from the phone and pulled back: its clip box is **1462.5/3.125 =
468 pt = 117 modules** (the pre-fix artifact: 424 pt = 106 modules), the digit line re-centred by
22 pt, and its bars still decode to `2000053337540` at 95 modules × 4.0 pt. That is the fix observed
on the device, not only in the unit-level generator check.

## Verification and limits

Measured facts this entry adds: `minSdk 24` / `targetSdk 36` read out of the installed APK and
`compileSdk 37` from RN 0.88's own `libs.versions.toml` (ISS-06); **zero** occurrences of the
signed-in email address or Mongo user id in `adb logcat` across the whole buffer after a full
sign-in, which is the device half of **ISS-02** and what the JavaScript guard explicitly cannot read
— the fix there is upstream in RNFirebase 27, not a local patch; and no `FATAL EXCEPTION` or
`ANR in com.inventoryai.app` on the day.

Stated as limits, not as passes: **iOS** is unverified (no macOS on this host); **paper print → scan**
was not done — the PDF decode rules out clipped geometry but it is not a scan of paper; the **429
quota copy** was measured through a controlled refusal, not by exhausting the shared daily allowance,
so the *copy* is proven and a genuine end-of-allowance day is not; and the label's **right quiet zone
was added after** the first artifact was printed, so the fixed document is recorded as the second
fixture rather than by re-printing on paper.

Artifacts, including every screenshot, the printed PDF and the decoder used on it, are in
`docs/evidence/expo-sdk-58-2026-10-21/`.

## Where the branch stands — not merged, not released

`chore/expo-sdk-58` carries the SDK 58 upgrade, this acceptance pass, the label fix and the device
harness. **It is not merged and nothing has been released**, and no release decision has been made:
a successful `development` EAS build is not a production build, no store submission exists, and
**iOS has not been run at all** (no macOS on this host).

**CI is green on the branch (2026-10-21).** Workflow `ci` run `39642789958` was dispatched on
`chore/expo-sdk-58` at head `f33675f` — the device-harness commit — and **all four jobs succeeded**:
`mobile` (tests, typecheck, lint, the label decode), `server` (full suite against a real Mongo
container, boot smoke, lint, both module-graph checks), `secret-guard` and `attribution-guard`. That
is the first of the release gate's conditions now met, and met on the pushed tree rather than on a
laptop. Note that this branch's pushes do **not** trigger CI on their own — the workflow runs on
`pull_request`, on `push` to `main` and on `workflow_dispatch`, so the run above was dispatched
deliberately; a future claim of "CI green" on this branch needs the same dispatch, and the head it
was run at named with it.

What a release decision would still need: a **`preview`/`production`-profile** EAS build rather than
the `development` one the device ran, and **the iOS half** on a macOS or EAS build environment.
Until then the device evidence above is Android-only and says so.

# The device pass became a script — and found four bugs in itself (2026-10-21)

**Not an application phase.** No route, permission, role, schema, index, dependency, environment,
EAS or mobile change, and no server code was touched. It adds `scripts/device/` (a harness),
`server/test/device-harness.test.mjs` (27 cases then; **44** since the two write journeys below) and `docs/evidence/device-runs/`.

## The problem it answers

Every device acceptance pass in this project has been a hand-written sequence of
`adb shell input tap <x> <y>` coordinates, measured on one screen. They proved a great deal and left
nothing a second person could re-run: the evidence was a chat transcript, and a regression in the
same screen would be found only by repeating the whole session by hand. §27EH's SDK 58 pass was the
largest example — every write path exercised, none of it repeatable.

`scripts/device/run.mjs` drives the app **by route** (`inventoryai://dashboard`) and **by the label a
person reads**, reads the screen from `uiautomator dump`, writes `report.md`, `report.json` and
screenshots per run, and exits **0 / 1 / 2** in this repository's convention — passed, failed, or
*could not check*. A signed-out session, a missing debuggable build, a missing product id and a
missing PDF are all **2**, never a pass: the first real run reported a perfectly healthy app as a
failure because the phone had lost its session overnight, and that is exactly the inversion the exit
codes exist to prevent.

Three journeys to begin with — **`smoke`** (every main screen opens and names itself — read-only),
**`label`** (reads the 13-digit code off the screen, taps *Share PDF*, decodes the PDF the phone wrote
and fails if they disagree) and **`draft`** (creates one draft purchase order; opt-in behind
`--allow-writes`) — and **five since the same day**: `stock` and `transfer` are added just below.

## Measured on the phone, 2026-10-21

OPPO CPH1969 · Android 11 (API 30), SDK 58 development build over the USB tunnels against the local
server, signed in as `role-owner@example.invalid` on the disposable four-role fixture (§27CT):

| journey | result |
|---|---|
| `smoke` | **17/17 pass** |
| `label` | **7/7 pass** — screen `2000053300018`, PDF decoded `2000053300018`, 95 modules, 30 bars, 4 pt module |
| `draft` | **14/14 pass** — `Draft PO-0002` created through the form, its own confirmation dismissed |

## Four defects the harness had, each caught by running it

Every one of these produced a **wrong verdict about the app**, which is worse than no harness:

1. **`adb shell cat` corrupted binaries.** The first `label` run said *"contains no decodable
   EAN-13"* on a correct label. The shell's pseudo-terminal rewrote every LF as CRLF: **11,472 bytes
   for an 11,225-byte PDF**, and the 247 extra bytes fell inside a Flate stream. Fixed by reading with
   `exec-out`; a source guard fails if it regresses, with a control that must trip it.
2. **Inverted dump boxes were treated as geometry.** A dump taken mid-scroll reported
   `Create draft order` at `[48,1863][1032,1443]` — `y2` above `y1`. The centre computed to **y=1653,
   inside the quantity field**, so a tap meant for the button typed a digit instead. `parseDump` now
   marks such a node `brokenBounds`, `findTapTarget` refuses it, and `readScreen` retries an unstable
   dump the same way it already retried a blank one. Text assertions may still use the label.
3. **Typing went to whatever had focus.** `type` now takes `{ value, into: '<label>' }`, finds the
   edit box below that label (exact-then-substring, because the form says `Quantity ordered *`),
   **reads the field back** and fails if the value is not there. A form field that is empty can reach
   the dump with no label at all, so there is a geometric fallback under the label — the read-back is
   what makes that safe.
4. **The keyboard, and the previous journey's dialog.** The keyboard covers a form's buttons, so a
   swipe meant to scroll lands on keys; `type` now closes it **only when `dumpsys input_method` says
   it is open** (a blind `BACK` left the form entirely and, on one run, the app). And the `draft`
   journey now dismisses its own "order created" dialog: a leftover one covered the *next* journey's
   first screen and failed a journey that had nothing to do with it.

`tap` also scrolls to find a control below the fold, and `--until=<n>` stops after step `n` and writes
the screen to `state.json` — added after two runs were spent guessing what a mid-form failure looked
like.

## A real barcode, scanned for real (owner report, 2026-10-21)

The owner entered the barcode of a **Clearance Multi-Purpose Wipes** pack they had at home, scanned
the **physical pack** with the app, and the app opened the record they had created. That is the camera
half of the barcode feature proven against real packaging, with a real EAN-13 — a class of evidence no
harness can produce here, and the reason the device items are not closed from JavaScript alone.

- **Physical printing on paper**: no printer on this host. The PDF decode rules out clipped or
  distorted bars (and now runs on every CI run for the generator and for two real device PDFs) but it
  is **not** a scan of paper. ISS-13's print → *scan* round trip stays open.
- **iOS**: no macOS on this host. Nothing in this entry is iOS evidence, and Phase 30B stays open.
- **The camera, in general**: one product, one pack, by hand. Not automated, and not claimed to be.

## Release gate unchanged

`chore/expo-sdk-58` still carries the SDK 58 upgrade, the label fix and now the harness. **Nothing is
merged or released.** Its CI **is green** — run `39642789958` at this commit, all four jobs — but a
release decision still needs a `preview`/`production`-profile EAS build (the device ran a
`development` one) and the iOS half on a macOS or EAS build environment. **Android has now been
device-tested by a repeatable script; iOS has not been run at all** — and the two are never described
with one word.

Artifacts: `docs/evidence/device-runs/` (three passing runs, plus the first failing `label` run kept
deliberately, because it is the record of the harness blaming the app for its own bug).

# Five journeys, not three — the device pass learned to write stock and transfer (2026-10-21/22)

**Not an application phase.** It adds two journeys to `scripts/device/journeys.mjs`, fixes four
harness defects that running them exposed, and turns two **lost preconditions** into a blocked run
instead of a failed screen. `server/test/device-harness.test.mjs` grows from 27 to **44 cases**. No
route, permission, role, schema, index, dependency, environment, EAS or mobile change, and no server
production code was touched.

## The two new write journeys, and why they are net-zero

`stock` moves **5 units in and 5 out** at one location; `transfer` moves **1 unit across and 1 back**.
Both are deliberately equal and opposite, for one reason: a journey a person may run on every build
must leave the tenant where it found it. A pass count that also silently raises a product's quantity
every run stops meaning anything on the second run — and the next journey's numbers would be measured
against a moving baseline.

What they assert is stronger than "a button worked": the app's own confirmation states the arithmetic
(`Done. <product> at <location>: 33 → 38`), and the harness reads that line back and checks the
**delta**, not the absolute number. So no starting quantity is hard-coded and the tenth run is as
meaningful as the first. `stock` needs `--product=<id>` and `--source=<location name>`; `transfer`
needs `--destination=<other location name>` as well, and both are gated behind `--allow-writes` like
`draft`.

## Measured on the phone

OPPO CPH1969 · Android 11 (API 30), SDK 58 development build over the USB tunnels against the local
server, signed in as `role-owner@example.invalid` on the disposable four-role fixture:

| journey | result | what the app said |
|---|---|---|
| `stock` | **17/17 pass** | `33 → 38 (5)` after Stock In, `38 → 33 (-5)` after Stock Out |
| `transfer` | **21/21 pass** | `33 → 32, 32 → 33 (-1, 1)` for each direction |

Both had already been exercised by hand in §27EH; what is new is that the same pass is now a table of
steps another person can run, with the arithmetic asserted rather than eyeballed.

**Run again the next day** on the same fixture (2026-10-22): `stock` **17/17** and `transfer` **21/21**,
with **identical numbers** — `33 → 38 → 33` and `33 → 32, 32 → 33`. The net-zero property is measured
across two runs a day apart, not asserted from the steps' symmetry.

## Four defects the new journeys found — all in the harness

1. **`adb shell` ate the query string.** `openRoute` passed the URL unquoted, so adb joined the
   arguments into one command string and the phone's shell split
   `inventoryai://stock-in?productId=…&lock=1` at the `&`: the form arrived **unlocked and blank**.
   Fixed with `quoteForDeviceShell`, which quotes the whole URL for the device shell (and escapes the
   one character that needs it).
2. **The tap landed on the label, not the control.** A selector field renders its placeholder as a
   `Text` node inside a `Pressable` whose own label carries a chevron (`Choose a location…, ▾`). Tapping
   the text node reported success and opened nothing. `findTapTarget` now prefers a **clickable node
   containing the words** when no exact match is clickable — which is also what keeps a heading from
   being tapped in place of the button beside it.
3. **A picker tapped before its options load is silently swallowed.** The trigger is disabled while
   the list is fetched, so the tap does nothing and the next step fails on a screen that never
   changed. The tap is now repeated, bounded, **only for a picker placeholder** — a retry rule that is
   safe precisely because re-tapping an already-open picker cannot submit anything twice.
4. **The picker predicate never matched the word it was looking for.** The regex was `cho(os|se)`,
   which spells neither "choose" nor "select". Caught by the must-pass control in the unit test, not
   by reading it.

## Two preconditions that used to read as app defects

**A session the server rejects.** Mid-session on 2026-10-21 the phone kept its stored token while the
server stopped accepting it: every picker came up empty and four steps failed on a form that was fine.
The harness preflight now looks for the app's own `Session expired` banner on a screen that actually
asks the server, and exits **2** — *could not check* — with the instruction to sign in again. Nothing
is judged about the app. (The server's own record for that account shows the phone's session created
**16:30:31, never revoked, expiring 2026-11-04**, so the session did not end at the server — the
client's **access token** had expired and its renewal did not complete. Why is **not** diagnosed
here; it is recorded as an open AUTH-03 observation rather than explained away.)

**The Expo dev launcher in front.** After Metro was restarted on 2026-10-22, the dev client came back
on its launcher screen (`Development Build` / `DEVELOPMENT SERVERS`), and a route deep link cannot
reach an app that is not running. The run reported `expect "Overview"` as a **failure** — a defect
that did not exist. The harness now recognises the launcher, starts the bundle through
`expo-dev-client`'s own link (`inventoryai://expo-development-client/?url=…`, the same action as
tapping the server entry), waits a bounded while for the bundle to load, and re-opens the dashboard.
If the launcher is **still** there it exits 2 and names the fix. Verified end to end: force-stop, then
`am start -n com.inventoryai.app/.MainActivity` (which lands on `DevLauncherActivity`), then the
harness — `the Expo dev launcher is in front; starting the bundle…`, **smoke 17/17, exit 0**.

- **iOS**: no macOS on this host. Nothing in this entry is iOS evidence, and Phase 30B stays open.
- **Paper and the camera**: the PDF decode rules out clipped bars but is not a scan of paper, and a
  barcode in the room stays a manual item.
- **The mid-session sign-out above**: observed once and, later the same day, **diagnosed and fixed** —
  `POST /api/auth/renew` refused the expired token it exists to replace, so recovery could never run.
  See *"AUTH-03's recovery path never ran"* below for the reproduction, the fix and the device evidence.

Artifacts: `docs/evidence/device-runs/` — the passing `stock` and `transfer` runs, the 2026-10-22
smoke that followed the launcher recovery, and **three kept failures** (the tapped label, the expired
session, the dev launcher), because the record of the harness blaming the app is the reason each rule
exists.

**CI is green at the commit that added them.** Workflow `ci` run **`39728306119`**, dispatched on
