# AUTH-03's recovery path never ran — renewal refused the token it was meant to replace (2026-10-22)

**A defect fix inside AUTH-03, not an application phase.** One server middleware variant, one route
binding, one route count re-classified, one client-side sentence, and the tests that pin all four. No
new route, permission, role, schema, index, dependency, environment variable or API shape; the client
already called the route the way it now works.

## What was wrong, and how it was found

The device pass on 2026-10-21 ended with a phone that held a **live 14-day session** and was told
*"Session expired — please sign in again"*. The server's own record for that account showed the
session created **16:30:31, never revoked, expiring 2026-11-04** — so the session had not ended. What
had ended was the ~1-hour access token.

AUTH-03 says a live session survives that: `lib/client.ts` calls renewal **after** a `SESSION_EXPIRED`
refusal, with **the token that was just refused**, and retries once. But `/api/auth/renew` sat behind
plain `requireAuth`, whose first act is to refuse an expired token — with `SESSION_EXPIRED`, the same
code that triggered the recovery. **The recovery call could never succeed.** Proactive renewal hid it
in normal use (it runs at the 10-minute horizon, while the token is still valid), so the hole only
showed whenever the app was idle, asleep or offline long enough for the token to expire — exactly
the situation a shift worker hits.

Measured, not inferred. With `JWT_EXPIRES_IN=90s` and a fresh sign-in on the OPPO CPH1969, the phone's
token expired during a pause, and the next run produced **8 `POST /api/auth/renew` 401s** and a **401
on every data route** (`/api/dashboard`, `/api/products`, `/api/inventory`, …) while the screens still
rendered — the run reported **17/17** because the smoke journey asserts each screen's chrome, not its
data. (That is a limitation of the smoke journey, recorded below, not of the fix.) The same short-TTL
setup also proved the *other* half works: while the token was valid, **116 renewals answered 200**,
so the renewal plumbing itself was never the problem.

## The fix

`requireAuthForRenewal` — the same authentication body as `requireAuth`, with **one** relaxation:
`exp`. Signature, algorithm, issuer and audience are still verified, the `jti` is still required, the
account must exist and be `ACTIVE`, the business must be active, the password-change rule still
applies, and the named session must still be live. `/api/auth/renew` is the **only** route mounted
with it, and a source guard fails if `requireAuthForRenewal` appears on any other route — or if plain
`requireAuth` is put back on this one.

Why relaxing expiry here is safe: the route grants no data access. It verifies a **fresh Firebase ID
token** (`checkRevoked: true`), requires the verified uid to equal the account's `firebaseUid`, and
returns a token for the **same** `jti` — no session row, no new `jti`, no change to `expiresAt`. A
stolen expired JWT alone mints nothing; with the Firebase token the holder could already have opened
a session at the public exchange, and renewal is the **stricter** of the two because the session it
names must still be alive (so sign-out-everywhere still kills it).

## Verified

- **Unit / source guards** — `phaseAUTH03-session-renewal.test.mjs`: `/renew` is authenticated by the
  renewal variant, that variant is mounted once, no other route uses it, only `exp` is relaxed, and
  every surviving check is named. A must-trip control re-runs the same assertion with `requireAuth`
  put back. `phase23-authorization-contract.test.mjs` now accepts **two** authentication middlewares
  and still classifies any unknown first handler as PUBLIC; `/renew` stays `AUTHENTICATED` in the
  route tier, so §2.6's totals do not move.
- **DB behaviour** — case 6a: an **expired** token on a **live** session renews, same `jti`, same
  session `_id`, cap unmoved, no new row. Case 6b: expired-but-revoked → `401 SESSION_REVOKED`; expired
  with a bad signature → `401 INVALID_TOKEN`; expired but issued before a password change →
  `401 SESSION_INVALIDATED`. The amnesty is expiry only, and the suite proves it three ways.
- **On the phone, without signing in** — the phone still held the expired token and the live session
  from the experiment above. With the fixed server running, the next run produced **3 renewals 200**
  and `/api/dashboard` **304** (authenticated, unchanged), and the smoke journey passed **17/17**
  again — this time on data. No sign-in was performed between the failing run and the passing one.
- **Full server suite** — `npm test`: **1921 tests, 1921 pass, 0 fail** (full mode, real MongoDB).
- **Mobile** — `npx jest`: **80 suites / 979 tests / 0 failures**, `tsc` clean; the new copy case is in
  `phaseAUTH03-client-renewal.test.ts` (15 cases in that suite).

- **CI** — workflow `ci` run **`39734333329`**, dispatched on `chore/expo-sdk-58` at head
  **`dc8f7c8`**: `mobile`, `server`, `secret-guard` and `attribution-guard` all **succeeded**.

Artifacts: `docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-22T05-53-11-769Z-smoke` (the failure: 17/17 by the
journey's own count, 401 on every data route) and `.../2026-10-22T06-06-32-285Z-smoke` (the recovery,
same phone, no sign-in).

## Still open, and said so

- ~~**The copy after a genuinely transient renewal failure is misleading.**~~ **Fixed in the same
  change.** When recovery cannot complete now, `lib/client.ts` keeps the CODE and replaces the
  sentence with *"Could not refresh your sign-in. Check your connection and try again."* — so the
  classification (recoverable, never session loss) is untouched while the screen stops telling a
  member on a live 14-day session to sign in again. The suite asserts both halves: the message no
  longer matches `/expired/i`, and the code is still `SESSION_EXPIRED`.
- ~~**The smoke journey proves chrome, not data.**~~ **Fixed in the next entry** (*"The smoke journey
  asserted chrome; now it asserts data"*, below): `expectData` steps wait for a row only the server's
  data can produce, the preflight waits for the list to settle instead of reading once, and the run
  was made to fail on purpose with the API stopped (`exit 1`) before being made to pass again.

# The smoke journey asserted chrome; now it asserts data (2026-10-22)

**A harness fix, not an application phase** — it follows directly from the AUTH-03 repair above, which
is what exposed it. Two pure judgements, one step type, one preflight wait and the tests that pin
them. No route, permission, schema, index, dependency, environment variable, EAS or mobile change: the
app is untouched, and nothing about the harness's exit-code convention moved.

## What was wrong

The smoke journey's assertions were screen **headings** — `Overview`, `Inventory`, `Products`. A
heading is chrome: the app renders "Inventory" over 200 rows exactly as happily as it renders it over
a list whose every request was refused `401`. That is not a theoretical gap. Run
`2026-10-22T05-53-11-769Z-smoke` reported **17/17 pass** on a phone where every data route answered
`401 SESSION_EXPIRED` and nothing had loaded. The green report did not make the defect; it made the
defect *invisible*, which is the worse of the two.

The preflight (`Session expired` / login detection) did catch that state in general, and was the
reason the AUTH-03 defect was found at all — but in the reproduction it **looked too early**: it slept
2.5 s once and read the inventory screen before the banner had rendered, so it let the run proceed.

## The fix

- **`expectData`** (`scripts/device/lib.mjs`, `journeys.mjs`, `run.mjs`) — a step that waits for a
  label the client cannot invent and fails if the screen lands in a state that means it did not load:
  - `judgeDataRows(nodes, { match, what, min })` returns **`rows`** (pass), **`error`** (fail),
    **`empty`** (BLOCKED — this tenant has none, so data was never proven either way),
    **`pending`**/`absent` (fail once the deadline passes).
  - The order is the part that can go wrong, so it is explicit: a **`Session expired`** refusal
    outranks rows, because the app keeps its last page in memory and stale rows would otherwise read
    as data; rows come next; and loading is checked *before* empty so "still loading" is never
    mistaken for "nothing to show".
  - `describeListState` reads the app's own state copy (`Something went wrong` / `Try again`, the
    list shells' `Nothing here yet` / `Nothing to show`, `Loading…`). A copy change fails the run
    loudly rather than passing it.
- **The smoke journey now carries two of them** — the inventory screen's own arithmetic line
  (`1,281 available · 1,294 on hand`) and a product row's meta (`SKU … · Barcode …`).
- **`expectClean` covers the screens that may legitimately be empty.** Purchase orders, suppliers,
  restock, the assistant and the audit trail have no guaranteed rows, so "prove data" would block on
  a fresh tenant — but their heading renders over a failed request too. `judgeSettled(nodes)` waits
  for the screen to stop loading and **fails** if it stopped on the app's error state; a screen still
  loading at the deadline is **BLOCKED** (exit 2), because out of time is not a verdict. The smoke
  journey is **24 steps** now: 7 screens, 2 data assertions and 5 "loaded without an error" checks.
- **The patterns are anchored, because the first attempt was wrong.** `PRODUCT_ROW` began as
  `/(SKU |Barcode \d)/` and matched the screen's own search box — `Search by name, SKU or barcode…` —
  so it counted a "row" on a list with no rows and reported chrome as evidence (run `06-41-07`,
  kept). It is now `^(SKU \S|Barcode \d)`, and a unit case holds a placeholder-only screen to zero.
- **The preflight waits for the list to settle** (`appRejectsSession`, up to 10 s) instead of sleeping
  2.5 s and reading once. It ends as soon as the screen reports rows, an empty state or an error, so
the common case is faster than the fixed wait it replaced.
- **One definition of "the inventory list has data"** — `INVENTORY_ROW` is exported from the journey
  table and used by the preflight, so the two places cannot drift apart.

## Verified

- **Unit** — `server/test/device-harness.test.mjs`: **57 cases, 0 failures** (44 → 57; 9 for the data
  judgement, 4 for the "finished loading" judgement and the journey table). Every verdict is paired with the state it must reject: error
  fails, empty blocks, loading is not empty, chrome-only is `absent`, a session refusal **outranks
  stale rows**, a non-RegExp pattern matches nothing, and the placeholder-only product screen counts
  zero rows. `validateJourneys` refuses a malformed `expectData` five ways, and a journey table with
  its data assertions deleted fails.
- **On the phone, three runs, in this order** — OPPO CPH1969, Android 11 (API 30), SDK 58 development
  build over the USB tunnels, against the local server, no sign-in between any of them:
  1. `2026-10-22T06-46-06-372Z-smoke` — **19/19 pass, exit 0**. The detail lines are the evidence:
     `6 row(s), e.g. "… Shop Front, 33 available · 33 on hand …"` and
     `2 row(s), e.g. "SKU ROLESKU-202 · Household · Barcode 2000053300018"`.
  2. `2026-10-22T06-42-53-368Z-smoke` — the **must-trip control**, with the API deliberately stopped
     (`pid 20652`): **4/5, exit 1**, `expected stock rows, but the screen is showing its error state
     ("Something went wrong")`. The step that could not previously fail is the one that failed, and
     it named the state instead of the symptom. The server was then restarted, and the app — **still
     signed in, no sign-in, no reload** — went straight back to data, which is also a small second
     proof of the AUTH-03 fix above.
  3. `2026-10-22T06-41-07-892Z-smoke` — kept as a defect record: 19/19 pass, but its products detail
     reads `5 row(s), e.g. "Search by name, SKU or barcode…"`. The data assertion was still finding
     chrome. The anchored pattern in run 1 is the fix, and the run is kept because a harness that
     counts its own search box as a product is exactly what the unit case now refuses.
- **The five "may be empty" screens were proven to fail when they should** — not by a unit case
  alone. The API was moved to `:4001` and a pass-through proxy took `:4000`, refusing **only**
  `/api/purchase-orders` with `500`; everything else was served normally. The result
  (`2026-10-22T07-17-43-928Z-smoke`, **10/11, exit 1**) is exactly the defect the old journey could
  not see: `expect "Purchase Orders"` **passed** — the heading rendered over a refused list — the two
  data steps passed on the screens that were fine, and `expect Purchase Orders to load without an
  error` failed with `the screen is showing its error state ("Something went wrong")`. The proxy and
  the second server were then removed and the run repeated clean (**`07-29-33-692Z-smoke`, 24/24**).
- **The shared runner still drives a write path** — the preflight that was rewritten is used by
  every journey, so both write journeys were re-run afterwards against the disposable role fixture
  tenant: `07-04-45-117Z-stock` **17/17** and `07-06-35-250Z-transfer` **21/21**, net-zero as
  designed. Their reports also exposed a cosmetic defect that is now fixed: the step titles printed
  the raw table markers (`open inventoryai://stock-in?productId={{product}}&lock=1`) rather than the
  product that was moved, so `titleOf` now fills the placeholders — the report is the artifact a
  later reader has, and it should name the product.
- **One wrong pick, kept as a lesson in the guide** — the first `stock` attempt used a product id from
  a **neighbouring business**. The app answered `Product not found` in the form and the movement step
  failed (`expected 1 movement(s), saw 0`). That is tenant isolation working, not a defect; the guide
  now says the id must belong to the signed-in tenant, because the failure otherwise reads like a
  broken form.
- **Unchanged elsewhere** — `eslint` and `tsc --noEmit` clean in `server/`; the full server suite
  **1932 tests / 0 failures**.

Artifacts: `docs/evidence/device-runs/` — the three runs above; the README there names which is which.

## Still open, and said so

- **The products must-trip is by unit case, not on hardware.** An error state was proven on the phone
  (inventory, with the API stopped); producing an *empty* product list on this tenant would mean
  archiving its products, so the placeholder case is held by the suite instead.
- ~~**The other five screens assert only their heading.**~~ **Closed in the same change** by
  `expectClean`: every one of the seven smoke screens now fails if it ends up in the app's error
  state, and two of them additionally fail if their list has no rows. What remains unproven is the
  *data* half on the five — which is deliberate, since an empty purchase-order or supplier list is a
  normal state for a new business.
- **`expectClean` cannot tell a failed assistant turn from a successful one.** The assistant renders
  its refusals as a chat bubble (`Cannot reach the server…` / the quota sentence), not as the list
  shells' error state, so the step proves the screen loaded but says nothing about a turn. Turns are
  covered by their own suites and the quota/refusal copy by `AI6`'s mobile test; a device assertion
  for a *successful* turn would spend the shared free-model allowance on every run, which is why it
  is not part of smoke.
- **The two write journeys (`stock`, `transfer`) still check numbers, not lists** — they were already
  proving a server round trip through the app's own `from → to` line, so they never had this gap.

# Error stack traces were published unless NODE_ENV said exactly "production" (2026-10-22)

**An authentication-surface hardening fix, not an application phase.** Two helpers in
`config/env.ts`, one condition in `middlewares/errorHandler.ts`, one boot warning in
`config/startup.ts`, and a 12-case suite. No route, permission, role, session, schema, index,
dependency or environment variable changed, and the only response field affected is the one being
withheld.

## How it was found

The auth audit started from the live surface rather than from the code: ten probes against the local
API (unknown-email login, malformed bodies, a garbage reset code, missing and forged tokens, an
unauthenticated session revoke). Two things came out of it. Nine answered exactly as designed —
`INVALID_CREDENTIALS` with no enumeration signal, a uniform `202` for the reset-code request,
`AUTH_REQUIRED`/`INVALID_TOKEN` kept apart, `FIREBASE_TOKEN_INVALID` as a `401`. The tenth answered
with this:

```json
{"error":"Invalid email or password","code":"INVALID_CREDENTIALS",
 "stack":"ApiError: Invalid email or password\n    at loginWithPassword
          (file:///C:/Users/jeffe/inventory-ai/server/src/services/auth.service.ts:322:11)"}
```

Every error response carried the server's own stack. The gate was
`process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`, and that predicate is **true** for an unset, empty or
misspelled value — so `NODE_ENV=Production`, `prod`, `staging`, or a host that sets only its
platform's own variable would publish absolute local paths, module names and line numbers to any
caller who can provoke a 4xx.

## The fix

- **`isDebugNodeEnv(raw)`** in `config/env.ts` — `development` or `test` only, **fail-closed**: an
  environment nobody thought about withholds the detail instead of publishing it.
- **`nodeEnvWarning(raw)`** — the three consequences in one sentence (production config checks
  skipped, development database selected, stack traces withheld), logged once by `startServer` and
  **silent under `TEST_MODE`**, because the suite leaves `NODE_ENV` unset by design and a line that
  fires on every test boot is noise.
- **`KNOWN_NODE_ENVS`** — one list, so the predicate and the warning cannot drift.

## Verified

- **`phase-sec-debug-detail.test.mjs` — 12 cases, 0 failures.** The truth table (including
  `Production`, `PRODUCTION`, `prod`, `staging`, empty and absent), the warning's exact content, five
  integration cases over the real app, and three wiring guards (the handler no longer compares the
  variable itself; the boot calls the helper; the handler holds no private copy of the rule).
- **The control trips.** Restoring the old condition fails **3** of the 12.
- **Live at boot** — `NODE_ENV= PORT=4002 node src/index.ts` printed
  `[config] warning: NODE_ENV is not set, so this process is treated as DEVELOPMENT: … error stack
  traces are withheld from responses.` and answered `POST /api/auth/login {}` with
  `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` and **no `stack`**. The `NODE_ENV=development` server still answers with a
  stack, so local debugging is unchanged.
- **Nothing else about the error moved** — status, `error`, `code`, `fields` and `applied` are
  identical in both postures, pinned by a case that compares the two bodies.
- Server **1946 tests / 0 failures**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean.

## What the audit also established, and what it did not change

Ten probes and four modules read covered the rest of the surface: JWT verification pins `HS256`, the
issuer and the audience; `PATCH /api/auth/me` allowlists its fields, so an email cannot be changed
through it (email change has no approved phase); session listing and revocation are scoped by
`userId` in the **query filter**, not by a check after the fact; `deviceLabel` is clamped; login is
timing-equalized through the shared placeholder; and the reset/verification paths reserve attempts
atomically before comparing a digest.

Recorded rather than changed, because each is a documented decision:

- **Authenticated routes are unlimited**, including `change-password`, which spends bcrypt (~140 ms
  measured on a login comparison). Each attempt needs a live session, and the policy is explicit; it
  is an accepted availability consideration, not a finding.
- **`change-password`'s strict `iat < passwordChangedAt` window** — a token minted in the same second
  as the change survives — is pinned by the Phase 15 suite as the contract, not an oversight.
- **The wider fail-open posture is untouched**: `env.nodeEnv` still defaults to `development`, so an
  unset variable also skips the production configuration checks and selects the development
  database. That is a deployment decision, and the new boot warning now names it.

# A server must name the environment it serves (2026-10-22)

**A deployment-safety follow-up to the error-detail fix above, not an application phase.** One
classifier and two predicates in `config/env.ts`, one boot decision in `config/startup.ts`, one
published posture field on the legacy health endpoint, and the suites that pin them. No route,
permission, role, session, schema, index, dependency, mobile or new environment variable.

## What was still wrong

The previous entry made an unknown `NODE_ENV` **harmless to read**: stacks are now released only to
an explicitly development or test process. It did not stop the process from **booting**. On a
hosted deployment a missing or misspelled value still meant all three of:

- `validateProductionConfig` was **skipped** — the fail-fast that refuses a missing `JWT_SECRET`,
  an unparseable Firebase key or a half-configured mail provider never ran;
- the **development database** was selected (`resolveDatabaseName` falls back to
  `inventoryai_dev_db`), so the deployment would serve real traffic out of the wrong data set —
  real tenants writing to a developer's scratch database, or an empty one, with no error anywhere;
- error detail was withheld, which hid the only visible symptom.

A warning line in a log nobody is watching is not a control. The question this increment answers is
narrow and checkable: *should a server be allowed to start at all without saying which environment
it serves?* No. The first attempt answered a smaller version — fatal only on a host that sets
Render's markers, warning everywhere else — and that was rejected on review for the reason it is
worth recording: the same mistake was then fatal on one platform and silent on every other, which
makes the rule a property of the host rather than of the server.

## The change

- **`classifyNodeEnv(raw)`** — five answers, not a boolean: `production`, `development`, `test`,
  **`missing`** and **`unrecognised`**. The last two are kept apart deliberately, because an
  operator fixes them in different places: a variable nobody set is a deployment omission, a value
  somebody typed (`prod`, `Production`, `staging`) is a mistake with a visible cause.
- **`startServer` refuses ANY process that cannot name its environment** — one line that says
  which mistake it is (`NODE_ENV is not set` versus `does not name one of development, test,
  production`), what the variable decides, and the one-variable fix; then `exit 1` and `return
  null`, placed **first, before validation, connection or serving**. `production`, `development`
  and `test` start normally. **`TEST_MODE` is the single exception**, and only because
  `resolveDatabaseName` already pins such a process to `inventoryai_test_db` and throws when
  `NODE_ENV=production` is set — it cannot reach real data.
- **No platform marker is consulted.** The first version keyed the refusal on Render's `RENDER` /
  `RENDER_GIT_COMMIT`; `isDeployedHost` and the `deployedHost` option were removed, so the rule is
  a property of the server rather than of the host it happens to sit on.
- **`env.nodeEnv` is the classified value.** It used to be the raw string, so `NODE_ENV="
  production "` selected the production **database** while skipping the production **checks**. It
  now trims and recognises once, and every consumer reads the result.
- **The environment is not a readiness note.** `integrationReport()` no longer carries `nodeEnv`
  and `deploymentNotes()` says nothing about it: every state in that list is legal (an optional
  integration that degrades a feature), while an unnameable environment is a boot decision. The
  old `nodeEnvWarning` line and its `TEST_MODE` suppression were deleted with the move, so one
  problem is still explained once — by the refusal itself.
- **`GET /api/health` publishes the resolved posture** as `environment`, beside the commit id and
  for the same reason: "is the deployed process in the posture I configured?" was answerable only
  from the host's dashboard. It is a posture name, never a value from the environment, and
  `/ready` and `/live` are unchanged.
- **`.env.example` and the README** state that a server must name one of the three postures, and
  that `npm start` without a `.env` now refuses instead of guessing.

## Verified

- **`phase-sec-debug-detail.test.mjs` — 18 cases, 0 failures** (12 → 18): the classifier truth
  table (including `Production`, `prod`, `staging`, empty, absent and a padded value),
  `isRecognisedNodeEnv` / `isTestProcess`, and **five real `startServer` boots** — refused when
  nothing named the environment, refused on a typo, **booted** on each of `production`,
  `development` and `test`, and booted as a declared test process with no `NODE_ENV` at all. The
  posture is injected into those boots, so the suite no longer depends on what the runner exports.
- **The refusal happens before any work**: the boot case asserts no `listening` line and **no
  database connect** was reached.
- **The control trips.** Replacing the gate with `if (false)` fails **3** cases — both refusals and
  the wiring guard — and the file was restored **byte-identically** (md5 `763a4019…` before and
  after).
- **Live, four boots of the real server:** `NODE_ENV=` → `refusing to start: NODE_ENV is not set …
  Nothing was connected or served.`, exit **1**; `NODE_ENV=prod` → the same refusal naming the
  accepted values, exit **1**; `NODE_ENV=development` → the gate passes and the boot proceeds to
  the database (blocked only by the deliberately unreachable URI); `TEST_MODE=unit` with no
  `NODE_ENV` → `[server] environment=development listening on http://localhost:4324 …`.
- **The deployed service is measured, not assumed.** `https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com`
  answered `/api/health` with `commit: a0969f9…` and `POST /api/auth/login {}` with
  `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` and **no `stack`** — and at that deployed commit (`a0969f9`, before the
  error-detail fix) stacks were appended unless `NODE_ENV === 'production'` **exactly**. The live
  service therefore runs with `NODE_ENV=production`, so this gate is **inert there** and the next
  deploy cannot be refused by it. That is the one question a fatal boot gate has to answer before
  it ships, and after deployment the same endpoint states the posture outright in `environment`.
- **`DEP-1`** keeps the readiness report about integrations, gains the health-posture case (the
  field is published from the process, never a database name, and is 503-free), and passes its
  environment into every `startServer` it calls so it is runner-independent too.
- Server **`test:unit` 1246 tests / 1194 pass / 0 fail / 52 skipped**, `tsc`, `eslint` and the
  module-graph checks clean (479 files).

## Still open, and said so

- **`npm start` without a `.env` now refuses.** That is the cost of the rule and it is deliberate —
  the guess it replaces is exactly what could point a deployment at the development database. The
  message says what to set, and the documented setup (`docs/guides/1-run-on-your-laptop.md`) copies
  `.env.example` first.
- **`env.nodeEnv` still falls back to `development`** for processes that never call `startServer`
  (seed, cleanup and measurement scripts), and `resolveDatabaseName` still resolves an unset value
  to the development database. Those scripts are run deliberately by an operator against `.env`,
  and the cleanup ones carry their own confirmations; no test database was touched.
- **`TEST_MODE` is trusted as a declaration.** It is accepted at boot without `NODE_ENV`, which is
  safe for data (the resolver pins the test database and refuses production) but does mean a host
  with a stray `TEST_MODE` would serve from the test database. It would be visibly wrong on
  `/api/health` (`environment: development`, and the readiness gate would report the test
  database's state) — recorded rather than guarded, because guarding it would break the runner.
- **Nothing was verified on a deployed host for the refusal itself** — deliberately: the proof that
  production cannot hit it is the measurement above, and manufacturing a refusal there would mean
  breaking the live service.

## Deployed and measured (2026-10-22)

Merged to `main` by fast-forward and pushed, so the release line is `0c79450` — the same commit CI
ran green on (workflow `ci` run **`39756616296`**: `mobile`, `server` full suite, `secret-guard`,
`attribution-guard`, all **success**). The deployment was then verified from outside, without
touching a single environment variable on the host:

| Probe | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/health` | **200** `{"status":"ok","db":"connected","environment":"production","commit":"0c79450…"}` — the deployed build, the posture it believes it is in, and zero 5xx since boot |
| `GET /api/health/ready` / `/live` | **200** / **200** — the database gate and the dependency-free probe unchanged |
| `POST /api/auth/login {}` | **400** `VALIDATION_ERROR`, `fields` only, **no `stack`** |
| `POST /api/auth/login` unknown address | **401** `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` in **0.78 s** — the timing-equalized path, and nothing that distinguishes the address |
| `GET /api/products` without a token | **401** `AUTH_REQUIRED` |
| `POST /api/auth/renew` without a token | **401** `AUTH_REQUIRED` — the AUTH-03 route merged in this release is mounted |
| `GET /api/no-such-route` | **404** with the path echoed back, no internal detail |
| `GET /auth/reset` (no code) | **400**, the *"This reset link is not usable"* page, 2,175 bytes |

No response carried `stack`, `file:///`, `node_modules` or an absolute local path, and the
`environment` field reads `production` — which is the deployment-level proof that the new gate is
inert here and that the process is not serving from the development database.

One caveat about what this does **not** show: the probe bodies were checked for the shapes a leaked
stack takes, not every response the application can produce. The suites cover the rest, and the
refusal path itself was exercised locally rather than by breaking the live service.

# The scripts that write and delete now ask the same environment question as the server (2026-10-22)

**A follow-up to the environment work above, in the tooling rather than the server.** One shared guard
in `scripts/perf/lib.mjs`, one call added to each of the two measurement scripts, and an 11-case
suite. No route, permission, schema, dependency, mobile or environment variable change.

## What was still wrong

The server refuses to boot without naming its environment. The scripts that **write and delete data**
answered the same question with `process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'`, which says "safe" to an
unset value, to `Production`, and to `prod`. That last one is the interesting failure: `prod` is not
recognised anywhere, so `resolveDatabaseName` resolved it to **`inventoryai_dev_db`** — the guard then
passed both checks and the seeder wrote to the development database while the operator believed the
guard had considered the question. The target check ("must be exactly the development database")
prevented the catastrophic case, but the environment half of the guard was answering a question it
could not actually answer.

Two measurement tools had **no environment guard at all**. `perf:turns` writes conversation rows and
spends the shared free-model allowance, so "which database did that go to?" has to be answerable
before it starts, not from the output afterwards.

## The change

- **One classifier, the server's.** `assertSafeTarget` (the guard every seeder and its cleanup already
  called) now asks `classifyNodeEnv`, exactly as `startServer` does: `production` refuses because
  these tools never touch it, a recognised non-production value proceeds to the database check, and
  anything else — `missing`, `unrecognised`, including `prod`, `Production`, `staging` — refuses as
  **ambiguous** because it cannot prove which posture it would write under. The mistyped value is
  never echoed.
- **The existing target check is unchanged and still the stronger one**: no URI, a database that is
  not exactly `inventoryai_dev_db`, or a missing confirmation phrase all refuse *before* a connection
  exists.
- **`assertReadableTarget`** is the measurement half: a recognised non-production environment, a URI,
  and a resolved database that is the development or test one — printed before the first query. No
  confirmation phrase, because measuring is not destructive.
- **Both measurement tools call it**: `perf:measure` and `perf:turns`, before `mongoose.connect`.

## Verified

- **11 cases** in `script-environment-guards.test.mjs`, run directly with no runner variables: the
  accept path, production by name, the six ambiguous spellings, the wrong-database check (production,
  test and a stranger's name), the missing URI and phrase, and the reader guard against production
  posture, an unnamed environment and the production database **by name** under a development
  posture.
- **Source guards, because the failure mode is a script that never calls one**: all nine seeders and
  cleanups must call a target guard (the demo tenant's own `assertDemoTarget` counts — it requires
  the database to be named on the command line), both measurement tools must call
  `assertReadableTarget`, and **no script may compare `NODE_ENV` to `"production"` itself** — the old
  rule cannot grow back in a tenth file.
- **Measured on the real commands:** `cleanup:perf` with `NODE_ENV=` and with `NODE_ENV=prod` both
  refused as ambiguous and named the fix; `seed:perf` in development without its phrase still
  refused at the phrase; `perf:measure` with `NODE_ENV=production` refused before any connection;
  `perf:turns` in development printed `database : inventoryai_dev_db (environment development)` and
  then failed only because the tenant did not exist.
- Server `test:unit` **1257 tests / 1205 pass / 0 fail / 52 skipped**, `tsc`, `eslint` and the
  module-graph checks clean.

## Still open, and said so

- **The demo tenant seeder is deliberately allowed on production** — it exists to populate the
  production build's preview tenant, and its own guard requires `--database=<name>` to equal the
  resolved database and refuses the test database. That exception is a documented decision, not an
  oversight.
- **Credentials are still the operator's `.env`.** These guards decide whether a command may proceed
  and where; they do not choose the cluster or the account.
- `ai-usage` and `verify-demo-data` remain read-only with no guard; they print what they read, and
  adding one would be a different judgement (a production reading is sometimes exactly what an
  operator wants).

# AUTH-03's proactive renewal ran once per request — and asked to extend a session it could not move (2026-10-22)

**A defect fix inside AUTH-03, not an application phase.** One exported rule and two constants in
`mobile/lib/auth.tsx`, its call site, five new unit cases, two provider cases, and the one harness
pattern that reported a correct screen as a failure. No route, permission, role, schema, index,
dependency, environment variable, API shape or server change.

## What was wrong, and how it was found

The device runs in the entries above were made against a local server started with
`JWT_EXPIRES_IN=90s`, so a renewal could be watched. What they showed was not one renewal per token
expiry but **one renewal per request**: in three minutes, **121 `POST /api/auth/renew` calls and 122
`GET /api/dashboard` calls**, both in lockstep, ending only when the server's own 120/15-minute
renewal limiter answered the 121st with `429 SESSION_RENEW_RATE_LIMITED` and the client went
`degraded` with its whole budget spent.

Two independent causes, and the second is the one that is not just a test-configuration artifact:

1. **The renewal trigger used the wrong boundary.** The trigger asked whether
   `min(tokenExpiresAt, sessionExpiresAt)` was inside the 10-minute window. That minimum is the right
   thing to *display* ("your session ends at the cap") and the wrong thing to *renew on*: AUTH-03's
   own rule is that renewal never moves `expiresAt`, so when the cap is the earlier boundary the
   renewal buys nothing. For the last ten minutes of **every** session in **production**, the app
   asked for a new token on every single request.
2. **Nothing paced it.** A token minted a second earlier was immediately "due" again, because
   `Date.now()` had moved — so with a token lifetime shorter than the window (90 s here) every
   request minted a new token.

Each successful renewal calls `setToken`, and every screen's load effect depends on that token
(`dashboard.tsx` `[token, signOut, canSeePos]` → `[load]`), so each new token re-ran the load — which
issued a request, which renewed, which re-ran the load. That is the loop. It is self-sustaining
without a single tap.

## The fix

`isProactiveRenewalDue({ now, tokenExpiresAt, sessionExpiresAt, lastRenewedAt })` — a pure, exported
function, so the two subtleties are testable instead of buried in a callback:

- the **token's** `exp` must be inside the 10-minute window (`null` unknown ⇒ no proactive renewal;
  recovery on a real `SESSION_EXPIRED` still works, so the app stays correct);
- **not** when `sessionExpiresAt <= tokenExpiresAt` — the cap is the hard boundary and renewal
  cannot move it;
- **not** within `RENEWAL_MIN_INTERVAL_MS` (60 s) of the last successful renewal, unless the token is
  inside `RENEWAL_URGENT_MS` (20 s) of expiry, which is never paced away.

`lastRenewedAtRef` is stamped inside `performRenewal` — not in `renewIfDue` — so a **recovery**
(a request refused with `SESSION_EXPIRED`) counts as a renewal too, and the next proactive trigger
sees the token it minted as fresh. `clearSession` resets it, so a new sign-in is not paced by the
previous session's stamp. The 429/`Retry-After` backoff is untouched and still wins over everything.

**And a refusal for a token that has already been replaced no longer mints another one.** A screen
makes several requests in parallel, so after a renewal the rest of that load is still carrying the
old token: each refusal used to call recovery, and recovery renewed — measured on the phone as
**three renewals for ONE dashboard load** after an idle gap. `SessionRecoveryHandler` now receives
the token the refused request was sent with, and the provider answers `tokenRef.current` when that
token is no longer the current one, so the transport's existing single retry is the whole remedy.
The classification is untouched: a refusal for the CURRENT token still renews, and a terminal code
never reaches the hook.

## Verified

- **Unit (mobile)** — the `proactive renewal rule` cases: due only inside the window; **not** due
  when the cap is the earlier boundary even though the horizon is well inside it; not due again
  within the interval while the token has life left; **due** right after a renewal when the token is
  about to expire (20 s); not due when the expiry is unknown.
- **Provider (mobile)** — two cases that reproduce the device observation: a renewal answers with a
  token that is still inside the window and a second trigger **does not call the server again**; a
  renewal answers with the cap two minutes away and a token an hour away and a second trigger **does
  not call the server again**. Both failed before the change.
- **Transport (mobile)** — the recovery hook is asserted to receive the refused request's token
  (`recovery` called with `(ApiError, 'old-token')`), which is what makes the stale-token rule possible.
- **Provider (mobile)** — a sibling request refused with `the-token-it-was-sent-with` is handed the
  CURRENT token and **`api.renew` is not called again**.
- **Mobile** — `npx jest`: **80 suites / 987 tests / 0 failures**; `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.
- **On the phone, with the same 90-second server** — the app was reloaded with the new bundle and
  signed in at 10:34:25. Over the following eight minutes of use — including a full 24-step smoke
  journey — there were **6 renewals and 9 dashboard loads** in total, against **121 and 122 in three
  minutes** before; the smoke window alone was **22 requests, 1 renewal, 3 dashboard loads, zero 429s
  and zero 401s**, and the session stayed signed in throughout (`Audit Log`, i.e. still inside the
  app, at 10:43). Paced renewal is what a 90-second token should look like.

## The harness found a second defect in itself, and it was a wrong verdict about the app

With renewal fixed, the same smoke journey failed at `product rows` — `expected product rows, but
nothing matches` — on a screen the screenshot showed holding two rows. `PRODUCT_ROW` was anchored to
the **start** of the label (`^(SKU \S|Barcode \d)`), which was correct for the tenant measured when it
was written (`SKU SEEDSKU-0 · Barcode 2000053337540`) and wrong for one whose products carry a
category and no SKU: `products/index.tsx` builds the meta from the parts a product HAS, so the line
reads `Hardware · Barcode 2000053337540` and starts with the category. The anchor existed for a real
reason — the screen's own search box reads "Search by name, SKU or barcode…" — so the fix keeps the
protection and adds the separator form: `^(SKU \S|Barcode \d)|· Barcode \d`. The placeholder still
matches nothing, a `Barcode` part still has to carry digits, and five real shapes are asserted
against it (`SKU` only, `Barcode` only, `Category · Barcode`, and the full line), plus three that
must not match. `device-harness.test.mjs`: **58 cases / 0 failures**.

The smoke journey then passed **24/24, exit 0** on the same phone, which is the first time this
harness has run all 24 steps green on a tenant whose products carry categories — and again after the
stale-token rule (run `10-50-18`, `24/24`, with no new renewal or `401` in the server log for it).

## Still open, and said so

- **A renewal still re-runs the focused screen's load once.** That is expected and left alone: a new
  token is a new identity for `[token]`-keyed effects, so a screen reloads once per renewal (at most
  once a minute, and once an hour in production). Removing it would mean changing how a dozen screens
  hold their credential, which is a different change with its own risk; the loop — the reason this
  entry exists — is gone.
- **The reload was the observation, not a contrived one.** Any deployment that sets a short
  `JWT_EXPIRES_IN` now behaves correctly instead of hammering itself; nothing here changes the
  production default (1 h).
- **Not re-observed:** a renewal in the last ten minutes of a real 14-day session. The cap case is
  proven by the unit and provider cases; manufacturing a live session whose cap is minutes away
  would mean writing a session row, which no test on a real database here does deliberately.
- **iOS** remains unverified, as everywhere else on this host.

Artifacts: `docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-22T10-42-16-406Z-smoke` (24/24, paced renewal) and the
three kept failures around it — `2026-10-22T10-23-26-286Z-smoke` (the renewal storm),
`.../10-38-19-863Z-smoke` and `.../10-39-55-775Z-smoke` (the product-row matcher, twice, before it was
fixed).

## Production renewal, verified on the phone (2026-10-22, later the same day)

A `preview` build of the fixed app was made and installed, then signed in against the **production**
API. Nothing about the host was changed to make this possible.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| build | EAS `6ee0c10f-076c-4bb6-b9d2-3aa8253a6aa0`, profile **`preview`**, Android APK, artifact `bddomc_RAg…apk` (111 MB) |
| API base | `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com`, already declared by the `preview` profile in `eas.json` — no override was added |
| install | `adb install -r` over the development build on the OPPO CPH1969 (same EAS keystore, `versionName 1.0.0`) |
| sign-in | **11:46:45Z**, Firebase exchange → `403 REGISTRATION_REQUIRED` (the identity had no MongoDB user on production) → the registration screen → workspace **`joffy royal kludge`**, role OWNER, empty tenant |

The previous development build's token was signed by the **local** server's secret; the preview app
refused it at boot and showed Login — an invalid session handled securely, observed on the production
API rather than in a suite. Then, without ever re-entering credentials:

| when (UTC) | what was done | what was seen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **12:37:02** (T+50 m, token inside the 10-minute proactive window) | `am force-stop` then relaunch | session restored; dashboard, tenant name, 0/0/0 tiles — no Login screen |
| **12:48:32** (T+62 m, **past** the 1-hour access token) | `am force-stop` then relaunch | session restored again; dashboard served, `All caught up` |
| **12:49:40** | open the audit trail | **one** `Signed in` row, at 11:46:45, and nothing else — no second authentication, and the app holds no credentials to replay |

A cold start at T+62 m cannot present the token minted at sign-in under the documented `JWT_EXPIRES_IN=1h`,
so the request was authenticated with a **renewed** token; the app also has no stored password, so a
silent re-login is not available to it. That is the end-to-end production check: the deployed API
minted a replacement token for the same session, and the installed preview build used it.

**The one assumption, stated rather than hidden:** the host's `JWT_EXPIRES_IN` is not readable from
outside, and the conclusion rests on the documented 1-hour default (the same value `env.ts` falls back
to, and no record of an override exists). A host value above 62 minutes would make this observation
inconclusive rather than wrong. What is measured without any assumption: the production API accepted
the restored session 62 minutes after sign-in, from an app that could not have re-authenticated.

**Two things this leaves behind.** The verification created an empty production tenant,
**`joffy royal kludge`** (one user, one business, no products, no locations) — additive, and removable
with the existing cleanup path if the owner does not want it. And the preview APK **replaced the
development build** on the phone: the device harness needs a debuggable build, so `node
scripts/device/run.mjs` will report BLOCKED until a `development` build (or `expo run:android`) is
installed again.

**Still open:** iOS (no macOS host), and the 14-day cap on a live session — the server suite pins it

instead of recovering forever), but no live session was driven to its cap.

# 27EI. Password recovery, split into two steps (2026-10-22)

**AUTH-06UX. One new public route and one new mobile screen; the existing six-digit code, mail
boundary, limiter policy and Firebase credential write are unchanged.** The recovery journey used to
ask for the code and the new password on one form. It now proves the code on its own screen, then
takes the password on another — and the proof that the code was checked is a **server-minted,
short-lived, single-use reset authorization**, not a client flag.

## Why the split needed a server-side credential

Two screens mean the fact "this code was verified" has to survive a navigation. A boolean, a route
param or a navigation flag would all be promises the client makes to itself: the second screen could
be reached directly, and the server would still have to be willing to change a password for whoever
asked. So the verification mints something the server will honour and nothing else will:

* **`POST /api/auth/password-reset/verify`** — takes `{ email, code }`, spends one attempt, and on a
  correct code returns `{ resetToken, expiresInSeconds }`. It writes no credential, issues no session
  and changes nothing on the account. The token is 32 CSPRNG bytes as base64url; only its keyed
  digest (`reset-authorize:` domain, the same `EMAIL_VERIFICATION_CODE_PEPPER` as the other flows) is
  stored, on the challenge row, under a **sparse unique** index.
* **`POST /api/auth/password-reset/confirm`** now takes `{ resetToken, newPassword, confirmPassword }`
  and **no code and no email**. The challenge is found by the authorization's digest, so the account
  is the one recorded when the code was issued — a `userId`, `businessId` or address in the body has
  no field to travel through. A caller who navigates straight to the password screen therefore holds
  nothing the server will accept.
* **The code is single-use from verification, not from the password write.** `verifiedAt` is set on
  success and is part of the verify predicate, so replaying the six digits is refused. The password
  step gets its own **15-minute** window (`PASSWORD_RESET_AUTHORIZATION_TTL_MINUTES`), and the row's
  `expiresAt` is pushed forward so the TTL index cannot delete a live authorization. A new code
  request unsets the old verification and authorization in the same superseding write.
* **The authorization survives a failed credential write.** Unlike the code, it is consumed only
  after the Admin write succeeds, so a transient Firebase outage costs the person nothing and does
  not force a new email.
* Every refusal is the existing single generic code (`INVALID_PASSWORD_RESET_CODE` for the code,
  `INVALID_PASSWORD_RESET_AUTHORIZATION` for the token) — wrong, expired, used and exhausted stay
  indistinguishable, and the verify path answers the same 400 for an unknown address as for a wrong
  code. Both routes share the existing per-IP confirm limiter, so the two steps draw on one guess
  budget.

## Mobile

`reset-password-code.tsx` is now **code-only**: one field, *Verify code*, the resend control with its
server-stated cooldown, and a note that checking the code does not change anything yet. On success it
stores the authorization in `lib/passwordResetSession.ts` — **module memory, never a route param and
never persisted** — and `router.replace`s to the new `reset-password-new.tsx`, which takes the
password and confirmation, applies the shared policy client-side, posts only the token and the
password, then clears both the authorization and this device's session before showing *Password
changed* → Login. With no authorization in memory it renders a *Verify your code first* state instead
of a form; a definitive `INVALID_PASSWORD_RESET_AUTHORIZATION` refusal from the server drops the form
and offers *Start again*.

## Verification

Server `test:unit` **1264 tests / 1211 pass / 0 fail / 53 skipped**; `test:db` **864 / 774 pass / 0
fail / 90 skipped**; `tsc`, `eslint` and both module-graph checks clean. Mobile **81 suites / 997
tests / 0 failures**, `tsc` clean. New cases cover: a correct code mints an authorization whose
token is never stored; a wrong code spends exactly one attempt and mints nothing; the same code
cannot be verified twice; a new code request invalidates an outstanding authorization; a password
cannot be changed without a verification (blank, junk and code-as-token all refused); the
authorization is bound to its account even when the body names another; it cannot be replayed after a
successful reset; it expires on its own window; and it survives a failed credential write. Route
inventory 75 → **76** (public 15 → **16**), recorded in design §2.6, the Phase 23 public register and
the Phase 26B recovery-surface guard.

## The six-box code field (2026-10-22)

Both screens that ask for a six-digit code — **Forgot password** step one and **Create Account's**
email verification — now use one shared control, `mobile/components/CodeInput.tsx`, instead of a
single text input. Six boxes, one per digit, with the active box ringed and a drawn caret.

The boxes are decoration over **one real, invisible `TextInput`**, and that is what makes the three
behaviours work rather than needing to be emulated:

* **auto-advance** is "the caret is after the last digit", so the ringed box is the next one by
  construction — no per-field focus transfer, and so no `setTimeout` to survive Android's focus races;
* **paste** is native: the whole six-digit string arrives in one `onChangeText`, is filtered to
  digits and capped, and every box fills. The platform's own copy/paste, selection and
  `one-time-code`/`oneTimeCode` autofill all still work, because the control *is* a text field;
* **backspace** is a shorter value, so the last box empties and holding the key clears the field, with
  no "which box was focused" state to get wrong.

Filtering happens **before** the cap, not through `maxLength`: `maxLength` truncates the raw string,
so a pasted `" 481 902 "` would have lost its last three digits before they were filtered. The
component decides nothing else — it never validates, submits or counts attempts, so the screens keep
their own *Verify* control and a mistyped sixth digit is not a request nobody asked for.

A real defect was caught by `tsc` before the device run: RN 0.88's generated types no longer expose
`StyleSheet.absoluteFillObject`, so the overlay's positioning spread resolved to nothing and the
invisible field would have sat in the layout flow, shifting the boxes. It is now sized explicitly.

## Device verification (2026-10-22)

An EAS **`development`** build — the environment that carries the development Firebase files — was
installed on the owner's **OPPO CPH1969 (Android 11 / API 30)** and pointed at the local server over
`adb reverse` (`http://localhost:4000`, database `inventoryai_dev_db`). Every step below was observed

| Step | Observed |

| Wrong code (`999999`) | 400 `INVALID_PASSWORD_RESET_CODE`, the generic sentence on screen, **one** attempt spent on the challenge row, **no** authorization minted |
| Expired code (row past `expiresAt`) | the same 400 and the same sentence — expired is not distinguishable from wrong |
| Typing | digits fill left to right and the ring moves with them; two backspaces empties the last two boxes |
| Paste | the OS paste (`KEYCODE_PASTE`) filled **all six** boxes in one action |
| Correct code | 200, authorization stored in memory, *Set a new password* opened with the address in its subtitle |
| Empty / weak / mismatched password | the local rules fired before any request; no attempt was spent |
| New password | *Password changed*; challenge `usedAt` set |
| Credential | old password `REJECTED (INVALID_LOGIN_CREDENTIALS)`, new password `ACCEPTED`, and signing in on the phone reached the dashboard |
| Revocation | a session issued **before** the reset answered `GET /api/auth/me` → **401 `SESSION_INVALIDATED`**, twice (once per reset) |

**Create Account** was driven end to end on the same build: registration → the *Verify your email*
screen with the same six boxes → a challenge minted for the throwaway address → code typed → **Verify**

**What this does not cover.** The codes were minted by a throwaway script rather than read from an

# 27EJ. The audit that found three open doors, and closed them (2026-10-23)

**Security audit. Server + documentation; no route, permission, role, schema, index, dependency,
session model or mobile change.** An owner-requested review of the whole authentication surface —
registration, the AUTH-04 code, AUTH-06 recovery, login, sessions and renewal, enumeration, error
hygiene, validation, every auth limiter and the production proxy configuration — plus the wider API's
authorization, tenant isolation, query construction, headers and logging. The full record, including
the findings that needed no change, is **checklist §52**; this entry records the engineering.

## What was actually wrong

1. **`POST /api/auth/change-password` had no rate limiter (High).** It is the one authenticated route
   whose body carries a **password** — and `currentPassword` is the only re-authentication it does.
   Anyone holding a live session could therefore guess the account's password at machine speed, and a
   correct guess installs a new credential (and revokes the sessions, so the real owner is signed out
   last). Each attempt also costs a bcrypt comparison, which made it a CPU lever for any member. The
   route now has **two** buckets after `requireAuth`: **10 per account+address / 15 min**, then **30 per
   address / 15 min** as an address-rotation backstop, with every attempt counted because a refusal
   must spend budget. 429 `CHANGE_PASSWORD_RATE_LIMITED`.
2. **`POST /api/auth/firebase/link` and `POST /api/auth/credentials-changed` were unlimited (Medium).**
   Both were written when the Firebase check was assumed local; it is an **outbound** `checkRevoked`
   verification, and the second also writes a `revokeAllSessions` update. They now have per-account
   buckets (10 and 20 per 15 min). `credentials-changed` is deliberately the larger of the two because
   the recovery handoff retries it.
3. **A proxy without `TRUST_PROXY` silently breaks every per-IP limiter (Medium, operational).** On a
   host that terminates TLS in front of the process, `req.ip` is the proxy for every request, so all
   per-IP buckets collapse into one: **60 failed logins from anywhere** would answer 429 to every member
   for 15 minutes, and registration (30/h), reset (20/h), exchange (30/15 min), verification (30/15 min)
   and renewal (120/15 min) collapse the same way. Nothing in a response reveals it, so it can only be
   noticed as "the app is weirdly locked" — which is exactly how it would have been noticed. The fix is
   detection, not a default: `proxyTrustNote()` in `config/deploymentReadiness.ts` is a pure function
   over `NODE_ENV` + `TRUST_PROXY`, and `startServer` logs a `[config] warning:` naming the variable and
   the consequence. It is a warning rather than a refusal because the readiness contract already says a
   degraded deployment keeps serving; the existing fail-fast list stays unchanged.
4. **Auth responses had no cache directive (Low).** A 200 carrying an access token, a 202 about an
   address or a 200 carrying a reset authorization could be stored by an intermediary. `/api/auth` now
   sends `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Pragma: no-cache`, applied once at the mount point and pinned
   by a test that also asserts the header does **not** appear on ordinary API responses.

## What was checked and left alone

Code generation and storage (CSPRNG, keyed domain-separated HMAC, timing-safe compare), expiry and
attempt caps as atomic predicates, AUTH-06's single-use verify→authorize chain, uniform 202/400 on both
recovery surfaces, timing-equalized login, uid-only Firebase joins, `jti`-backed sessions with the
14-day cap and `passwordChangedAt` invalidation, claim-free tokens, server-derived tenant filters on
every service (AI conversations by business **and** user), escaped `$regex`, capped pagination, the
100 kb body limit, fail-closed stack traces, path-only access logging, default-deny CORS, helmet, and
the mobile client's 429 / `Retry-After` handling. Each is listed with its evidence in checklist §52.

## Limiter inventory after the audit

| Endpoint | Buckets | Window / cap | Counts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /auth/login` | IP+account, IP | 15 min / 10 failed, 15 min / 60 failed | failures only |
| `POST /auth/register` | IP | 1 h / 30 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/firebase/exchange` | IP | 15 min / 30 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/firebase/register` | IP | 1 h / 30 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/session/renew` | IP | 15 min / 120 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/email-verification/request` | IP (+ 60 s per-identity cooldown in the service) | 15 min / 30 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/email-verification/confirm` | IP (+ 5 attempts per challenge) | 15 min / 30 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/password-reset/code` | IP+address, IP | 1 h / 5, 1 h / 20 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/password-reset/verify` | IP (shared with confirm) | 15 min / 20 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/password-reset/confirm` | IP (shared with verify) | 15 min / 20 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/forgot-password` | IP+address, IP | 1 h / 5, 1 h / 20 | every attempt |
| `POST /auth/reset-password` | IP | 15 min / 20 | every attempt |
| **`POST /auth/change-password`** | **account+IP, IP** | **15 min / 10, 15 min / 30** | **every attempt** |

All eight new variables are optional and documented in `server/.env.example` and the README table
(thirty variables, fifteen pairs); every documented default is the production value.

## Verification

**12 new cases, 4 existing guards updated** — and each updated guard still asserts `requireAuth`
comes first and no permission or role gate was added. Server `test:unit` **1269 tests / 1216 pass / 0
fail / 53 skipped**, `test:db` **871 / 781 pass / 0 fail / 90 skipped**, `tsc`, `eslint` and both
module-graph checks clean (486 modules). Mobile **83 suites / 1016 tests / 0 failures** (`tsc`
clean), including the suite added for the half that was only asserted in prose before:
`mobile/__tests__/change-password-rate-limit.test.tsx` mounts the real screen and pins that a 429
shows the **server's** sentence and keeps the session, that the form survives the refusal, that a
400 `fields` refusal lands **under its input**, and that a 401 **ends** the session rather than
reporting it.

## Device verification (2026-10-23, OPPO CPH1969)

The behaviour above was then measured **on the phone**, against a local server over `adb reverse`,
using a disposable legacy account (no Firebase identity, so the app takes its documented legacy
fallback) and the documented demo tenant:

- **Sign-in and authenticated requests.** Firebase-first sign-in reached
  `POST /api/auth/firebase/exchange` **200**, then `/api/dashboard`, `/api/products/reorder` and
  `/api/purchase-orders` **200/304**, and the dashboard rendered **6 active / 3 in stock / 3 low /
  1 out of stock / 112 units** — exactly the fixture's figures. A legacy account's sign-in answered
  `POST /api/auth/login` **200** after Firebase refused it, which is the fallback reached only for
  the two codes that mean "no Firebase identity for this address".
- **Validation.** An empty change-password form answered *Password is required* under the field and
  sent **no request**; a wrong current password on the Firebase-native screen produced its own
  sentence and no server call, because that step re-authenticates locally.
- **429 keeps the session.** With the account+address bucket spent, the phone's submit answered
  `429 CHANGE_PASSWORD_RATE_LIMITED` in **177 ms**, the screen showed the server's own sentence
  (*"Too many password change attempts. Please wait a moment and try again."*), the form stayed
  usable — and the next `GET /api/dashboard` still answered **304**, so nothing signed the person
  out.
- **401 ends it.** Bumping `passwordChangedAt` server-side made the next two requests answer
  **401**; the app cleared the stored session and returned to Login **with no error banner**.
- **A real change succeeds and revokes.** The correct current password answered **200** and replaced
  the credential; the follow-up `POST /api/auth/logout` answered **401** because that session had
  already been invalidated by the change, and the app still returned to Login cleanly. The **new**
  password signed in afterwards, which is the credential itself proven live.

Residual risks the audit accepted for V1
— in-process limiter state, distributed stuffing, the shared-address lockout, per-IP rather than
per-recipient email bounds, and the absent per-user session cap — are enumerated in checklist §52
with the reason each is a V4 concern rather than a release blocker.

# 27EK. The Firebase verification email had no sender left (2026-10-23)

**Mobile only — one dead capability removed. No route, permission, schema, dependency,
session, environment or Firebase-console change, and no behaviour change.**

An owner review asked whether Firebase's password-reset and email-verification machinery is
still needed now that both journeys belong to this application. Traced from call site to SDK
verb, the answer splits cleanly.

**Everything Firebase does as the identity provider stays.** Native email/password and Google
sign-in, the forced ID token, `reload()`/`emailVerified`, and on the server the Admin SDK's
`verifyIdToken`, the `emailVerified` and password writes, and `revokeRefreshTokens` are all
live and were not touched.

**No code asks Firebase to send an email.** AUTH-06 removed `sendPasswordResetEmail`, and
AUTH-04 had already replaced the verification message with this server's six-digit code —
which left `nativeSendEmailVerification` exported with **no caller anywhere in `app/` or
`lib/`**, only its own test. It is now removed, with its two boundary cases replaced by the
equivalent pair for `nativeUpdatePassword`: that credential write shares the same
no-current-user contract (Android resolves a user-scoped call with no user while iOS rejects
it) and previously had no direct test. The verb also leaves the suite's SDK mock, so the
mocked surface cannot assert a call the boundary can no longer make. This is the same
principle AUTH-06 applied to `sendPasswordResetEmail`: a permitted capability with no caller
is one nobody reviews, and the boundary exists to keep the reachable set small.

**What was deliberately NOT removed, and why.** The AUTH-05 landing page (`GET /auth/reset`),
its `?oobCode=` redemption in `reset-password.tsx`, and the console's *Customize action URL*
all stay. They are reachable without this app: Firebase's own `accounts:sendOobCode`
endpoint answers to the project key that ships inside the binary, and the console's
per-user *Reset password* action uses it too — so a real reset link can still reach a real
inbox. When one does, our page forwards it into the app, which writes the N-4 recovery
marker and, after the automatic sign-in and `credentials-changed`, **revokes every
session**. Firebase's own hosted form changes the password and revokes nothing (D2/OD-9),
so deleting the page would remove the only session-revoking destination such a link has.
That makes the path a security asset rather than dead weight, and the earlier justification
— "a link already in somebody's inbox" — is superseded here rather than in the file, because
action codes are short-lived and any pre-AUTH-06 link has expired, while
`lib/firebase-auth.ts` is pinned byte-for-byte by the frozen-module tripwire (a comment-only
edit moves that hash, so the deliberation belongs in this record instead). The Firebase email templates themselves
need no change: nothing the app does consults them, and the verification template is simply
unused.

**Verification.** Mobile `tsc` clean; **83 suites / 1016 tests / 0 failures**, including the
Phase 1 inertness guard and the Phase 16 verification suites, which pass unchanged. No
server file was touched.

# 27EL. The deployment learns from the provider before it spends a request (2026-10-23)

**Server + documentation. No route, permission, schema, index, dependency, session or mobile
change, and no prompt change.** Five increments on top of AI-29/30/31's failover. Every one uses
data the provider publishes for free — endpoint-health `GET`s and response headers — so none of
them buys a completion to check a model.

**AI-35 — a model the provider says is down is not tried first.** AI-28 could see a
listed-but-dead model, and AI-34 alerted on it, but neither changed selection: a cold process
still tried the configured model first, every turn, until five refusals opened AI-30's cooldown.
On a 50-request day that is a tenth of the allowance, spent inside a member's turn, before any
surviving model is asked. `modelHealthGate.ts` now holds such a model out of selection. The
reading is the same free `GET /v1/models/{author}/{slug}/endpoints`: fired unawaited at boot and
re-run by the watchdog. Only `unavailable` marks — `degraded` is still serving, `unknown` is a
check that could not run. A mark lasts until the next reading (31 min, one watchdog interval plus
grace) and is cleared by an answer, so it cannot outlive reality. **The safety valve is the part
that makes it safe to ship:** if a reading would remove every configured model, the configured
primary is released, so a wrong reading costs requests but can never refuse service.

**AI-36 — the allowance is visible, and an exhausted one is not re-tested every turn.** The free
tier is metered at 50 requests a day, shared by every free model, which is why AI-29 never fails
over on a quota refusal. The number was invisible until a member's turn failed, and once spent,
every turn still paid a round-trip to be told. `quota.ts` parses `x-ratelimit-remaining` /
`x-ratelimit-limit` from every response; the turn line reports `quota=12/50` (or `quota=unknown`,
never an invented zero). A refusal that reports **zero** starts a 30-second fail-fast
(`AI_QUOTA_BLOCK_MS`) that answers the normal 429 with **zero provider calls**; a 429 without a
reading keeps AI-6's behaviour exactly, and any success lifts the block immediately. `postJson`
returns `{ data, quota }` and `AiQuotaExceeded` carries the reading.

**AI-37 — a promotion ends by itself.** AI-31's promotion was sticky until a restart or until the
promoted model failed five times: a recovery ten minutes later went unnoticed. The watchdog now
ends it after **two consecutive** healthy readings of the configured model — one reading is a
sample, two is a recovery — logs `returning to it: <id>` once, and clears the health mark in the
same pass. A healthy fallback never ends it, and there is no paid probe: the evidence is the free
health read.

**AI-38 — an optional per-attempt slice, OFF by default.** AI-29 only fails over when the first
model REFUSES; a model that hangs gets the whole remaining budget, so the turn waits out its
deadline and the fallback never starts. `AI_ATTEMPT_MAX_MS` (default **0**) bounds one attempt
while another candidate remains; the **last** attempt always keeps everything left, so a
slow-but-working answer is never cut short when there is nowhere else to go. A capped expiry is
treated as model-specific — it fails over and counts toward the breaker — while a transport
failure still does not fail over, because another model would travel the same broken path. The
default stays off deliberately: the correct value is a measurement (5.3–19.4 s measured on this
tier, so 25 000 ms is the documented starting point), and enabling it is one variable after
re-measuring.

**AI-39 — the configuration is stated.** A fallback list longer than the five-model cap used to be
truncated with no message, so a pasted candidate looked configured and was never used. The parser
now returns the ignored ids and boot warns with them; the effective chain is logged once
(`[ai] chain order: …`). The watchdog's run line also carries the live state —
`active=<promoted> (configured=<primary>) cooling=<ids|none> quota=<reading>` — so "is production
on its preferred model right now?" is answerable without grepping for a promotion that may be
hours old.

**Context handling was verified, then deliberately left alone.** `npm run ai:models` (free GETs)
measured the configured chain at **66k / 262k / 1000k** context tokens — the smallest is the
fourth candidate — against a worst realistic prompt of **~40–58k tokens** (20 history messages at
the 4 000-char cap plus 12 000-char tool results over six rounds). A per-model trim would be
machinery without a present fault, so none was added; the measurement is the reason, and it must
be re-run before adding a model with a small context.

**Files.** New: `server/src/services/ai/modelHealthGate.ts`, `server/src/services/ai/quota.ts`.
Changed: `ai.service.ts`, `aiConfig.ts`, `aiErrors.ts`, `healthWatch.ts`, `providers/http.ts`,
`providers/index.ts`, `providers/anthropicWire.ts`, `config/startup.ts`, `.env.example`,
`README.md`, `docs/guides/6-scripts-and-commands.md`, this record, `CLAUDE.md`.

**Verification.** **47 new cases** in `AI35-health-aware-selection`, `AI36-quota-header-awareness`,
`AI37-primary-recovery`, `AI38-attempt-budget` and `AI39-ai-config-diagnostics`; the existing
AI29/30/31/34 suites pass unchanged (one assertion updated for `postJson`'s new envelope, in
AI6's harness positive control). Server `test:unit` **1316 tests / 1263 pass / 0 fail / 53
skipped**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean, both module-graph checks clean (494 modules).

**Residual limits.** The health marks and the quota block are process-local, like the breaker:
several instances each learn separately, and a restart re-reads health (which is the intended
moment to). The quota block is intentionally short and success-cleared, so it is a saving rather
than a hard gate. AI-38 ships off, so the hanging-model case is unchanged until an operator
enables it. The free allowance is still shared by every model, so a total outage still spends up
to five requests before the breaker settles.
