# 27EM. The answer arrives while it is being written (2026-10-23)

**Server + mobile + documentation. No new route, permission, schema, index, dependency, session or
environment change, and no prompt change.** The assistant's measured latency on the free tier is
5–19 s per turn, and until now the screen showed a spinner for all of it: the member read the
first word of the answer at the same moment as the last. `POST /api/ai/chat` can now deliver the
answer as it is written, and the ordinary JSON response is untouched for every client that does
not ask for it.

**Negotiated on `Accept`, not on a second path.** `Accept: text/event-stream` selects the streamed
form; anything else gets the exact response it got before. That was chosen over a second route or
a body flag because the route table, the permission gate (`ai.use`) and the rate limiter are then
provably unchanged — the Phase 23 classification, the route inventory and the RBAC mirror have
nothing new to describe — and because a client that cannot stream cannot reach the new code by
accident. `prepareTurn` was extracted so validation, conversation ownership, the AI-24 asked-at
timestamp and the AI-1 abort listener happen **once, before any header is written**: a bad request
therefore still answers the ordinary JSON `400` envelope on both paths, which is what keeps
every existing error sentence and its mobile copy working.

**The wire contract is three event names.** `delta { text }` for answer text in order, `done { … }`
carrying the stored turn (identical to the JSON body), and `error { status, code, message }` mapped
by the same `mapAiFailure` the JSON path uses. **`done` is the authority, not the deltas:** the
server rewrites status constants and trims a cut-off unit before storing, so the client replaces
what it rendered with the final message. Deltas make the wait visible; `done` makes the result
correct. Persistence is unchanged and still happens only after the provider has answered — a
failed turn writes nothing, on either path — and a `: ping` comment every 15 s holds the
connection through a mobile network or a proxy. `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform`,
`X-Accel-Buffering: no` and an explicit `flush()` are there because a buffering proxy defeats the
feature while still returning 200.

**The provider layer learned to read a stream, and refuses to guess.** `providers/http.ts` reads
the upstream SSE, and `providers/anthropicWire.ts` assembles text deltas and the JSON fragments of
a tool call into the **same** response shape the non-streaming path produces, so the turn loop,
the tools, the breaker and the failover did not change shape at all. Three rules keep a stream from
becoming a new failure mode: a `2xx` that carried no event is `invalid_response`, never an empty
answer; a gateway that ignores `stream: true` gets **one** ordinary request as a fallback, but
**never** after text has been delivered; and the existing empty-completion retry is untouched
because an empty completion emits nothing. `ai.service` counts **delivered characters** and stops
the failover walk once any exist — text on screen cannot be taken back, so a second model would
show the answer twice. A transport failure still does not fail over, for the same reason it never
did.

**Mobile.** `mobile/lib/sse.ts` is an incremental parser and a byte-stream reader: it holds a
partial event until its blank-line separator arrives, strips exactly one space after `data:`, skips
comment lines, and decodes through **one stateful `TextDecoder`** so a character split across two
chunks (an em dash, an accented product name) is not corrupted. CRLF is normalised **on the buffer
rather than the chunk** — a network chunk can end between `\r` and `\n`, and normalising each chunk
separately left that pair untouched, delivering the whole answer as one payload; the split-CRLF
case in `ai40-sse-parser.test.ts` fails if that moves back. `aiApi.chatStream` cannot go through
`apiFetch` (that client parses one JSON body and owns retry, renewal and timeout together), so the
three things that must behave identically were made explicit rather than reimplemented: the token
comes from `resolveRequestToken`, newly exported from `lib/client.ts` **because the streamed
request is the one request that would otherwise let a nearly-expired token answer 401 and sign the
member out** — the exact defect AUTH-03 exists to prevent; the turn keeps `AI_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`
and distinguishes the caller's abort from its own (`REQUEST_CANCELLED` versus `NETWORK_TIMEOUT`);
and a refusal that arrives before streaming is parsed from the ordinary error envelope into the
same `ApiError`. `expo/fetch` is imported lazily — a native streaming implementation the rest of
the app has no reason to load. `AiChat` renders the arriving text in the answer bubble, keeps the
thinking row only until the first character, replaces everything with the `done` payload, and
retries through the ordinary route **only** when no text was shown and the failure is a transport
one; a quota refusal, an ended session, a stop and an answer that was already partly read are
never retried.

**Two defects were found before release, one in review and one on the phone.** (1) The upstream
transport normalised CRLF **per chunk**, so a `\r\n` split across two network writes left the pair
in the buffer, `\n\n` never matched, and a CRLF gateway delivered **no events at all** until EOF —
streaming silently became one late paint. It is normalised on the buffer now, and the `sse-crlf`
case reports **1** event instead of **7** if that regresses (verified by reverting the fix and
watching it fail). (2) The phone showed the more serious one: a stream that went **silent without
closing** left `reader.read()` parked, so even the 75 s budget could not settle the call — the
spinner stayed for minutes with no sentence and no way out but killing the app. `readSseStream` now
has a **20-second idle window** (one server heartbeat plus grace) and an abort that settles the read
even when the body ignores `cancel()`; `chatStream` races its own call against the abort as the last
line of defence, and `fetchImpl` is injectable for the same reason `readModelHealth` takes one — the
wedge cannot be produced by the real transport on demand. `ai40-chat-stream-transport.test.ts`
(6 cases) pins both failures and the healthy path beside them. The same review consolidated the
JSON path onto `prepareTurn` — it had been duplicated, with a comment claiming otherwise, which is
exactly the drift the extraction exists to prevent — and add nothing else to the request path.

**Verification.** **18 server cases** in `AI40-ai-streaming.test.mjs` (classified MIXED: SSE
framing across chunk boundaries incl. the split-CRLF case, the no-event `2xx`, an `error` event,
tool-fragment assembly, the unstreamed fallback and its prohibition after text, delta forwarding
without changing any non-streaming request, no failover after text, the empty-completion retry,
authentication, and the wire contract — deltas then one `done`, the JSON path unchanged, a failed
turn persisting nothing and validation still a plain 400). **25 mobile cases**: 10 in
`ai40-sse-parser.test.ts`, 9 in `ai40-assistant-streaming.test.tsx`, 6 in
`ai40-chat-stream-transport.test.ts` (live text then the stored message, fallback when the stream
never started, no retry after text was shown, quota/session/stop not treated as stream failures,
and the idle/abort/timeout settlement) — with `ai9-assistant-stop` and `ai24-user-message-time`
updated for the new transport and still asserting what they existed to assert. Server `test:unit`
**1330 / 1276 pass / 0 fail / 54 skipped**, `test:db` **879 / 786 pass / 0 fail / 93 skipped**,
`tsc`/`eslint`/both module-graph checks clean (499 files) and the secret guard clean (22 controls);
mobile **86 suites / 1042 tests / 0 failures**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean.

**Device-verified on the OPPO CPH1969, 2026-10-23** against the local server over `adb reverse`, on
the documented demo fixture, with a local fault-injecting proxy in front of the server so each
transport failure could be produced on demand. Six scenarios, all recorded in
`docs/evidence/ai-streaming-2026-10-23/`: a **normal turn with a tool call** (one `POST`, `200` in
16 232 ms, `calls=2 toolRuns=1 tools=getReorderNeededProducts`, the three fixture products with
their quantities); a stream **cut before any text** (two POSTs 281 ms apart — the JSON retry
answered `201` in 4 238 ms and the member saw the complete answer); a stream **cut after the first
delta** (the partial `Three` stayed on screen with the error sentence, **one** POST, the server's
`AI_ABANDONED` and nothing persisted — no retry, because retrying would show the answer twice); a
**Stop** pressed mid-turn (*You stopped waiting for this answer…*, the AI-9 state); a **429 quota
refusal** (the exact quota sentence, one POST, no provider request); and a stream that **went
silent and never closed** (the client gave up after **20.5 s** and the ordinary retry answered in
9 431 ms). That the streamed path served the normal turn is read off the log rather than assumed:
the fallback would have been a second `POST`, and there was exactly one. The frames taken during
the early wait contain no text because the turn spends its first ~12 s in the tool round — a model
writes no answer while it is asking for one — so incremental delivery rests on the
character-at-a-time and split-chunk cases, not on a static image. **AI-35 was observed live in the
same session**: the provider's own health read marked `liquid/…` and `…super-120b…` unavailable at
boot and on every turn, both were skipped before a request was spent on them, and `npm run
ai:health` reproduced exactly those two verdicts (with `super-vl` degraded and still selected).
**AI-37's return is proven at the decision level** ("does not return on a single healthy reading",
"returns after two consecutive healthy readings, and says so once", "resets the count when a reading
in between is not healthy") rather than live, because a live demonstration needs a promotion in
progress plus two 30-minute watchdog cycles — a real cadence this session could not compress
without faking the clock the suite already injects.

**Production (deployed 2026-10-23, commit `3294387`).** Render serves the commit that
`/api/health` names, with `environment: production`, the database connected, **66 responses and
zero server errors** (no 5xx) after the deploy. `POST /api/ai/chat` and `GET
/api/ai/conversations` without a session answer **401 `AUTH_REQUIRED` as JSON — including when the
request sends `Accept: text/event-stream`**, which is the property that matters: streaming cannot be
reached before `requireAuth`, no SSE header is written on a refused request, and the new code adds
no way past the gate. **An authenticated streamed turn through Render was then measured
(2026-10-23, the same day), separately from the local server.** The demo tenant was seeded into
`inventoryai_prod_db` by naming the database, its Firebase identity was created in the project the
deployment verifies, and the identity was signed in through Firebase and exchanged at
`POST /api/auth/firebase/exchange` (**200**, a 293-character token). One streamed turn answered
**200** `text/event-stream`, and the body arrived as **36 network chunks carrying 98 `delta`
events over 1 044 ms** (13 477 → 14 521 ms) before one `done` at 14 734 ms — so the Cloudflare edge
in front of Render does **not** buffer it, which is the only thing an authenticated production call
could add. The answer was the fixture's: 112 units, the three restock products, model
`nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free`, tools `getInventorySummary` +
`getReorderNeededProducts`. It was stored **once**: 1 conversation, 2 messages (`USER`,
`ASSISTANT`). On the same deployment an **unauthenticated** streamed request answered **401** JSON
with no SSE header, an **empty message** answered **400** `VALIDATION_ERROR` as the ordinary JSON
envelope (so `prepareTurn` really does precede the headers), and a turn **abandoned at 2 180 ms**
left both counts unchanged. Afterwards the counters read **77 responses, 0 5xx, 0 server errors**;
the tenant was torn down with **0 leftovers** and the database returned to its pre-test shape
(3 users / 3 businesses / 1 product / 0 conversations). Render's own log stream was **not**
available from this host, so that review used the deployment's counters, the rows and the request
telemetry rather than log lines — recorded as a narrower instrument, not as a log review. The run
first ran **API-level**, and was then **repeated on the phone** (same day, 21:08–21:17 Manila,
scrcpy over USB): Metro was started with `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com`
and the fetched bundle was checked to contain that host — a `development` client's JS comes from
Metro, so this needed no new APK — `adb reverse tcp:4000` was removed so nothing could fall back to
the local server, and the app signed in as the seeded production demo OWNER (dashboard: 3 in stock /
3 low / **1** out / 6 active / **112** on hand, and a session row in `inventoryai_prod_db` at
13:08:50 UTC). **Four turns** answered from production with the fixture's numbers — 112 units and
its health split, the movement history, and low stock with a **6** and **5** unit shortfall — and
one was screenshotted every ~0.74 s: **12.9 s** showed the intro plus two bullets cut off
mid-sentence with **Stop** still up, **15.2 s** a third bullet and a fourth trailing at `on 2026-`,
and the final frame the whole answer with *Read: Stock movements*. Stored **once**: 3 conversations,
2 / 4 / 2 messages, no duplicate row, all on the configured primary model. `5xx` stayed **0**. `X-Accel-Buffering` was not
visible to the client (Cloudflare answers first); it is a proxy hint, delivery was incremental, and
nothing was changed for it. CI green on `main` (workflow `ci`, run `39951211533`).

**A teardown defect found while cleaning up, and fixed.** Deleting the production demo tenant
after the phone run printed `leftovers: 0 — verified over every tenant collection` while **3
conversations and 8 messages stayed in `ai_conversations` / `ai_messages`**, found by counting the
collections directly. `clearTenantData` listed inventory, transactions, purchase orders, products,
categories, locations and suppliers — but the assistant's history cannot join that list, because a
MESSAGE carries no `businessId` (only its conversation does). It is now handled as two steps in
`scripts/perf/lib.mjs`: resolve the tenant's conversations, delete their messages, then the
conversations — and `countTenantLeftovers` uses the same two steps, so a collection that is removed
is necessarily also verified. The effect is wider than the demo command: re-seeding the demo tenant
(`clearTenantData`) now resets its assistant history instead of leaving it to accumulate, and any
future tenant removal cannot leave orphans. **5 DB cases** in `DEMO2-tenant-ai-teardown.test.mjs`
(target removed and counted, empty tenant a no-op, and a positive control proving the counter can
see a conversation it did not remove), added to the runner's classification.

**The same audit then found two more gaps, so the list is now exhaustive rather than repaired.**
Comparing every model against what the teardown touched turned up `audit_logs` (which does carry
`businessId` and was simply missing) and the account-scoped rows a tenant owns **indirectly** —
`sessions`, `password_reset_tokens` and `password_reset_challenges`, which carry only `userId`.
Audit rows now sit in `TENANT_DATA_COLLECTIONS`, so a data reset clears a fixture tenant's own
governance trail and a removal does too; and `removeTenant` resolves the tenant's user ids **before**
deleting the users and removes those three collections by owner, with their counts — deleting the
users first is what would have stranded them, since afterwards no query could tie them to the tenant
again. The demo cleanup's closing line also stopped overstating itself: it now says it verified
*every collection carrying the businessId (and the assistant messages, through their conversation)*,
because a `userId`-only row cannot be found by that predicate and its removal is evidenced by the
counts above it instead. `email_verification_challenges` are deliberately untouched — they are
keyed by a keyed digest of the address, carry no user or tenant id, and expire on their own TTL.
The two new cases create a whole tenant (business, user, session, reset token, reset challenge,
audit row) and prove each one is removed and counted while a second tenant keeps all of its own.
**Observed on the real command, in the dev database:** `cleanup:demo-tenant` reported removing
**20 `ai_messages`, 5 `ai_conversations`, 4 `audit_logs` and 3 `sessions`** before the users and the
business — rows the previous version would have left behind — and closed with the corrected
sentence. The fixture was then re-seeded and its 15 checks matched.

That run's own rows —
3 conversations, 8 messages and the account's session — were removed by that same two-step rule
(applied once by hand, before the command learned it), and the database returned to its pre-test
shape: 3 users, 3 businesses, 1 product, 0 conversations for the demo tenant, with the 4
conversations belonging to the real accounts untouched.

**Files.** New: `mobile/lib/sse.ts`, `server/test/AI40-ai-streaming.test.mjs`,
`mobile/__tests__/ai40-sse-parser.test.ts`, `mobile/__tests__/ai40-assistant-streaming.test.tsx`,
`mobile/__tests__/ai40-chat-stream-transport.test.ts`, `docs/evidence/ai-streaming-2026-10-23/`.
Changed: `ai.controller.ts`, `ai.service.ts`, `providers/anthropicWire.ts`, `providers/http.ts`,
`providers/index.ts`, `mobile/lib/api.ts`, `mobile/lib/client.ts`, `mobile/components/AiChat.tsx`,
`scripts/run-tests.mjs`, `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, this record.

**Residual limits.** A dropped connection is not resumed: the answer is written once, so a stream
that breaks after showing text is shown as a failure and is **not** retried (retrying would show
the answer twice), while one that breaks before any text falls back to the ordinary route. There is
no `Last-Event-ID` bookkeeping, deliberately — the server does not store a partial answer, so there
is nothing to resume from. A proxy that ignores `no-transform` can still buffer, which no app-side
code can detect beyond the heartbeat. A streamed turn that fails after its headers have gone out is
a **200 on the wire** by necessity, so the failure lives in the `error` event, the turn's outcome
line and the client's sentence rather than in the access log's status — an operator counting failed
turns must count outcomes, not statuses. iOS remains unverified (no macOS on this host).

# 27EN. The auth screens stop making people guess (2026-10-23)

**Mobile only — no route, permission, schema, dependency, session-model or environment change.**
Five behaviours on the screens a person meets before they are inside the app. Each was chosen
because it was a real moment of friction, not because a checklist named it.

**1. Autofill on Create Account.** The registration fields declared nothing about what they hold,
so a password manager could not fill the address it already had or offer to generate a password —
on the one screen where generating one matters most. The address now declares `email` /
`emailAddress`, the password `new-password` / `newPassword` (not `current-password`, which asks for
a credential that cannot exist yet), and the two name fields declare `name` and capitalise words.
Login and the new-password screen already did this; the three cannot drift apart silently now
(`auth-flow-continuity.test.tsx`).

**2. A corrected field stops looking wrong.** Login, Create Account, Forgot Password and the
reset password step left a field's red message in place while the value was being replaced, so a
form that was already right still looked wrong until the next submit. Editing a field now clears
that field's message and nothing else — the same rule the code field already used.

**3. A code's lifetime is counted, not restated.** Both six-digit screens printed "expires in 10
minutes" as fixed text, which describes when the code was issued rather than how long it has left —
so an expired code was indistinguishable from a wrong one until the server refused it. Each screen
now counts down from its own send instant (the verify screen's `verificationCodeIssuedAt`, the reset
screen's `sentAt`, both reset by a successful resend) and says *That code has expired. Send a new
one to continue.* when the window closes. The numbers are the server's constants, already pinned
to its source by the existing drift guard.

**4. The code screens name the inbox.** A code that has not arrived is the commonest way these
screens stall, and the first question is "which address did I use?". Verify says which address it
sent to when this run knows it; the reset screen always does, because the previous screen collected
it. The reset screen's "Wrong address? Start over" is directly below, so the fact makes the next
step obvious instead of adding a second one.

**5. A cold start no longer strands a verified identity.** A `REGISTRATION_REQUIRED` refusal arms
the business-name form from **in-memory** state, and a cold start restores no session — so someone
refused, who then closed the app, arrived at Login holding a verified Firebase identity the app
could see but could not act on. The only way back was retyping a password Firebase had already
accepted. The read-only boot probe now reports `hasResumableFirebaseIdentity` alongside the
verification state, Login offers **Continue with saved account**, and the tap performs the ordinary
exchange. **The rule is intact:** a launch still mints nothing and exchanges nothing; only a tap
opens a session, and the action re-checks `emailVerified` at the moment of use rather than trusting
a launch-time snapshot. A refusal arms onboarding exactly as a password sign-in does, so the journey
the person lost is the one they land back in.

**What was deliberately not done.** No persisted flag, token, uid or address; the address used in
point 4 is in-memory for the run and never a route parameter on the verify path (`firebaseAccountEmail`).
No new native or provider boundary: the resume control reuses the existing probe, `currentFirebaseIdToken`
and `firebaseExchange`. No visual redesign — the existing `AuthLayout`, tokens and contrast work are
untouched. No change to any limiter, code lifetime, attempt budget or session rule.

**Verification.** Mobile `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean, **88 suites / 1063 tests / 0 failures** (two new
suites: `auth-flow-continuity.test.tsx` — 14 cases on the five behaviours — and
`auth-resume-identity.test.tsx` — 7 cases proving the probe mints nothing, only a tap exchanges,
verification is re-checked, and `REGISTRATION_REQUIRED` still arms onboarding). Every pre-existing
auth suite passes unchanged. No server file was touched, so the server baselines are unchanged.
**Device-verified 2026-10-23** on the OPPO CPH1969 against the local server (see the evidence in
`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-23-auth-polish/`): Login offered **Continue with saved account**
and one tap opened the tenant's dashboard, and the offer was **gone** after signing out. iOS remains
unverified (no macOS on this host).

**Still open from the review this came from:** a new-device sign-in email. Two of the three items
this sentence used to list have since shipped — the **per-user session cap** in §27FL and
**invitation-based onboarding** in §27FB — so only the control that *detects* a takeover is left. The
live password rule and the shared helpers landed in §27EO.

# 27EO. The rule is stated while it is typed, and six digits verify themselves (2026-10-23)

**Mobile only — no route, permission, schema, dependency, session-model or environment change, and
no server file touched.** Three follow-ups from the auth review in §27EN, each small enough to check
by hand and each removing a moment where the screen knew more than it said.

**1. The password rule is stated live, not after a refusal.** The server has exactly one password
policy — 8 to 72 characters — and the four screens that *choose* a password said only "Min 8
characters", so a 73-character password and a 5-character one both travelled to the server and came
back in a developer's words. `passwordRuleHint` in `lib/validation.ts` now reports distance from that
one policy while the value is being typed — *3 of 8 characters — 5 more to go.*, *12 characters —
within the limit.*, *Too long by 3 characters.* — on Create Account, the reset password step, the
emailed-link reset screen and Change Password. It deliberately **invents no complexity rule**: a
checklist of "one number, one symbol" would refuse passwords the server accepts, which is a client
guardrail nobody asked for. The numbers are the shared constants, already pinned to the server's own
source by `auth-validation-rules.test.ts`.

**2. Six digits verify without a tap — after a beat.** Both code screens waited for a press even
when all six boxes were full. They now submit themselves **400 ms** after the sixth digit, which is
long enough to replace a mistyped last digit and short enough that nobody reaches for the button.
A deliberate action wins: pressing Verify or Resend **cancels** the pending request, so one code is
never submitted twice, and an in-flight guard covers the press that lands while the automatic request
runs. Nothing is scheduled for a partial code (the challenge allows five attempts and an unfinished
entry would spend one) or for a code the screen already knows has expired (the remedy is a new code,
and the helper says so; a phone whose clock disagrees can still press Verify). The same rule is on
both screens, so the verify screen and the reset screen behave alike.

**3. The copied helpers have one home.** `fieldMap` had been pasted into nine auth screens and
`formatRemaining` into three; copies drift one sentence at a time, and the person then reads two
explanations of the same refusal depending on which screen they were on. `lib/authCopy.ts` now holds
both, imported everywhere they were duplicated. A source scan in `auth-copy.test.ts` fails if any
auth screen defines its own again, with a positive control so the scan cannot pass by seeing nothing.
This is the mechanical half of "one failure vocabulary"; the sentences screens *own* — which are
genuinely different per step — stay where they are.

**Verification.** Mobile `tsc` and `eslint` clean; **89 suites / 1082 tests / 0 failures**, 19 new
cases (`auth-copy.test.ts`, four auto-verify cases on each code screen, three on the password hint
and its rendering). No server file changed, so the server baselines stand as last measured
(unit 1330 tests / 1276 pass / 0 fail / 54 skipped; db 884 / 791 / 0 / 93).

**Device-measured 2026-10-23** on the OPPO CPH1969 through `scrcpy`, against the local server:
the Create Account hint moved *Between 8 and 72 characters.* → *3 of 8 characters — 5 more to go.*
→ *12 characters — within the limit.* as characters were typed; the reset screen named the inbox and
counted *Code expires in 8m 48s*; and typing `123456` produced **exactly one**
`POST /api/auth/password-reset/verify` (400) **without pressing anything**, with the server's refusal
rendered as the banner. The success half of auto-verify (a correct code opening the password step)
was **not** driven — it needs a live code and the probe address has no inbox — and is covered by the
suites; the verify-email screen's identical path was not reached on the device either. Evidence and
the run's limits: `docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-23-auth-polish/README.md`. iOS unverified.

**Device-measured 2026-10-24 — the success half.** The run above could only
type a *wrong* code, because nothing can read a probe address's inbox. This one had the app make the
request (its own Forgot password screen, so the real route minted the code) and then read the mailed
digits back out of the stored keyed digest with the server's own `hashResetCode` and pepper, so the
value typed on the phone was **the value that was sent**. Typing those six digits **opened the
password step with no press**: *Set a new password — Your code was verified for
auth.probe.…@example.com* — a step reached this way twice in the run (frames at 12:32 and
12:43). The reset screen still named the inbox and counted *Code expires in 6m 27s* down to
*5m 6s*; the password step reported *28 characters —
within the limit.* while it was typed and put *Confirm password is required* **under the empty
confirmation** without submitting; and the credential that code authorized then signed in **on the
phone** and rendered the tenant's dashboard. Two limits stayed recorded rather than papered over:
the password step's own button was **not** carried to *Password changed* in that pass (the
confirmation was applied through the route pair afterwards), and the **verify-email** screen's
identical auto-verify was still not reached. Evidence, the cleanup re-count (0 users, 0 businesses,
0 sessions, 0 audit rows, 0 challenges) and two harness notes (typed text goes to whatever has
focus; the dev build lost Metro and needed a reload):
`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-24-auth-auto-verify/README.md`.

**Both of those were then closed on the device the same day, in one pass, from the app's own
screens.** Create Account was filled and submitted on the phone, which created the Firebase
identity and asked for the code (`POST /api/auth/email-verification/request` **200**); the six mailed
digits typed into the boxes, **with no press of Verify**, produced `confirm` **200** →
`firebase/register` **201** → `firebase/exchange` **200**, and the new tenant's dashboard — so the
registration ordering gate and the auto-verify success path are both measured end to end. The same
account was then signed out and reset from Forgot password: the app requested the code (**202**),
the digits opened the password step with no press (`verify` **200**), both fields were filled (the
rule reading *13 characters — within the limit.*), and **Set new password was pressed on the phone**
→ `password-reset/confirm` **200** → *Password changed*. The **old** password was then refused by the
app itself (*Invalid email or password*) and the **new** one signed in to the same tenant
(`exchange` **200**) — no credential write was performed by hand in this run. Still not proven: a
pre-reset session being revoked on the device (the account was signed out first; suite-backed and
device-measured 2026-10-22, §27EI), mail arriving in a real inbox (the digits came from the stored
digests), and a production build. Evidence, the request-by-request table and three harness traps
(`uiautomator dump` failing silently onto the previous screen's file while a countdown repaints; typed
text going to whatever holds focus; the two code rows sitting at different heights):
`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-24-auth-end-to-end/README.md`. iOS unverified.

**Still open:** a new-device sign-in email. The **per-user session cap** shipped in §27FL, and
invitation-based onboarding — the prerequisite for retiring legacy password login — shipped in
§27FB.

# 27EP. The installed app updates itself, and a launch without a network stays signed in (2026-10-24)

**Mobile only — no route, permission, schema, index, session-model or server change; one new direct
dependency (`expo-updates`, SDK-pinned) and one new documentation guide.** Two things that had been
asked for and never measured: an installed build that can receive new JavaScript **without being
rebuilt and reinstalled**, and a cold start with no network that does not throw the session away.
The second was found *during* the first, by doing it.

**1. The update runtime is configured, and every rule that could send the wrong bundle is pinned.**
`expo-updates` is installed at the SDK's own version (`~58.0.17`) and added to Dependabot's
SDK-pinned ignore list, because a dependency Expo owns is taken with the SDK, not on its own. Each
build profile has its own channel (`development`, `preview`, `production`) — the channel is compiled
into the APK, so a preview publish physically cannot reach a production install — and
`runtimeVersion` is `{ policy: "appVersion" }`, so the compatibility label is derived from
`expo.version` rather than typed by hand. `checkAutomatically: ON_LOAD` with
`fallbackToCacheTimeout: 0` means a launch never waits on the update host: the download completes in
the background and is used on the next launch. `mobile/__tests__/ota-update-config.test.ts` (10
cases) pins all of it, including a positive control for the channel resolver and a scan that no two
profiles share a channel.

**2. The `fingerprint` policy was tried first and FAILED, measured.** It was the more attractive
policy because it derives the label automatically. Build `71d63d16-c6f2-403e-8f62-eadcdf6f8f5e`
aborted in the `Configure expo-updates` phase, before compiling anything, with
`Runtime version calculated on local machine: e32953a7894593a4e41d1ca76592f3df00d5eeae` against
`Runtime version calculated on EAS: 6217b878d4238c37f68b848c2649d2a2c617181f`. The cause is this
project's dynamic config: `app.config.js` resolves the Firebase configuration **file paths** from EAS
*file* environment variables, and the files they name exist only on the build runner, so the laptop
cannot reproduce the project EAS hashes. The sources EAS reported were `expoConfigExternalFile` and
`bareNativeDir`. `appVersion` removes that class of mismatch at the price of one manual rule, now
written down in the guide: **a change that alters native code must bump `expo.version`.**

**3. Delivery was measured on the phone, not just configured.** Preview build
`ea941bb7-95f0-4e8e-88be-4c5af08aa73e` (channel `preview`, runtime `1.0.0`) was installed over the
previous preview APK and signed in to the **production** API with the reserved demo tenant —
dashboard **3 in stock / 3 low / 1 out / 6 active / 112 on hand**, matching `seed:demo-tenant`'s
fixture. An update was published (`9e3936aa-b502-4b41-8e8d-b71a80ffe752`, runtime `1.0.0`,
Android) containing the boot fix below. **The bundle was inspected before upload**: the export
contains `ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com` once, `localhost:4000` **zero** times, and the new
`inventoryai.auth.userSnapshot` key — so the publish carried both the right server and the new code.

**4. The first publish was not served to the device, and that is recorded rather than smoothed
over.** For at least 19 minutes the installed app answered `CheckCompleteUnavailable` / "No update
available" while the manifest endpoint returned the update to `curl` with the same platform, runtime
and channel headers. `eas update:republish --group 9e3936aa…` (group `6e14b317-2729-465b-9746-449f8b3c272a`)
was picked up on the very next launch: `DownloadCompleteWithUpdate`, `isUpdateAvailable=true`,
`isUpdatePending=true`, manifest `01a16c95-…`, runtime `1.0.0`. **The cause is not established**, so
the guide records the observation and the one-command remedy rather than a theory. Also measured:
`eas update` **without `--platform android` fails** while building the web bundle (`expo-router` →
`react-native-web`); this project ships Android and iOS, so publishes are Android-only.

**5. The update fixed a real defect the same run had exposed: a launch with no network threw the
session away.** With the phone in aeroplane mode, a cold start landed on **Login** although the
stored Inventory AI token was still valid. The boot restore asks `api.me` for the account, and a
network failure fell through to the signed-out state — exactly the rule AUTH-03 removed from
`refresh()` and left in place here. The fix stores the **server-confirmed profile** beside the token
(`inventoryai.auth.userSnapshot`, written only from a `user` the API returned, never from a
login form) and, when the boot request fails for a **non-session** reason, restores that profile with
status `signedIn` and phase `degraded`. A **session** refusal still signs out and deletes the
profile with the token, so a disowned account cannot be resurrected offline; a missing or corrupt
profile falls back to the old signed-out outcome rather than inventing an account; and a healthy
launch rewrites the profile, so a role change made elsewhere does not go stale. `auth-offline-boot.test.ts`
adds **6 cases** (keep on network failure, do not invent, corrupt profile, refused boot, refused live
session, healthy refresh), and two existing guards were updated to count **token writes by key**
rather than "how many entries a session writes".

**6. Verified on hardware after the update.** The downloaded bundle ran on the next launch; with
**aeroplane mode on** and the app force-stopped, the cold start showed the **signed-in app shell** —
*INVENTORY AI · Demo Tester · Owner* — and the dashboard's own offline state
(*Couldn't load the dashboard — Cannot reach the server…* + *Try again*). Before the update the same
sequence produced Login, so this single frame proves delivery **and** behaviour. Network restored,
*Try again* returned the same production figures (3 / 3 / 1 / 6 / 112). The demo tenant was then
removed with `cleanup:demo-tenant` (**0 leftovers**; the Firebase identity is left in place by that
script's design) and the temporary password file deleted.

**7. The seeder now sets the password it was given, every time.** Found while preparing the run: an
existing demo identity kept whatever password the FIRST seeding run chose, so a second test cycle had
a login nobody could sign in as and no message saying why. `resolveIdentity` now updates an existing
identity's password to `DEMO_ACCOUNT_PASSWORD` (and leaves it `emailVerified`, because this is a
reserved test credential), reporting *"password refreshed from DEMO_ACCOUNT_PASSWORD"*; a newly
created identity reports creation and does not claim a refresh that did not happen. Guide 4 states
the behaviour.

**Verification.** Mobile `tsc` and `eslint` clean, **91 suites / 1098 tests / 0 failures**;
`check-build-env` clean for all four profiles; `npx expo config --type public --json` resolves the
runtime policy, update URL, `ON_LOAD` and a zero fallback; the APK's own manifest confirms
`EXPO_RUNTIME_VERSION` = `1.0.0`, channel header `preview`, and the update URL for this project. No
server source file changed, so the server baselines stand. Artifacts:
`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-24-preview-ota/` (four frames plus the `expo-updates` log
excerpt); operator guide `docs/guides/7-over-the-air-updates.md`.

**Not verified, stated rather than implied:** a store-signed production build, iOS (no macOS on this
host), code signing (available and deliberately off until a public release owns the key), and the
rollback commands (`update:roll-back-to-embedded`, `update:rollback`), which exist but were not
exercised. The first-publish refusal above remains unexplained.

# 27EQ. The preview build against production: channel isolation, and every account journey on the installed app (2026-10-24)

**No production code, route, permission, schema, index, session-model or dependency change.** One
configuration variable was added to an EAS environment, and the run found and fixed a latent defect
that would have made any production-channel update unreachable. This entry records measurements the
previous one could not make: that a preview install cannot receive a production update, and that
registration, verification, reset and an offline cold start all work on the installed build that
points at the deployed server.

**1. Isolation, measured at the service and on the phone.** Only one update channel exists
(`preview`, pointing at branch `preview`, holding groups `9e3936aa…` and `6e14b317…`). A manifest
request at the build's runtime version (`1.0.0`) naming `production` or `development` answered
**404** (*There is no channel named production…*). A probe was then published to `production`
(`d165e4cb…`, manifest `01a16cb2…`) and a second, **visible marker** publish followed
(`3c777c22…`, manifest `01a16cb5…`, temporarily changing the Login tagline) — newer than the
`preview` manifest `01a16c95…` the phone was running. Requests then showed the split cleanly:
`preview` → `01a16c95…` (unchanged), `production` → `01a16cb5…`. The phone, cold-launched **twice**
while the marker was live, kept the real tagline and logged **zero** references to `01a16cb5…`.
The `production` channel and branch were deleted, and the 404 returned. The channel is compiled into
the APK, so this is a property of the binary, not a policy that could be forgotten.

**2. A defect found while setting that up: the production EAS environment had no API URL.**
`eas env:list --environment production` showed the Firebase values but **not**
`EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL`; the preview environment had it. `mobile/lib/config.ts` falls back to
`http://localhost:4000` when the variable is absent, and `eas update` reads `--environment`, not the
build profile — so the first production publish would have shipped a bundle that could reach no
server. The variable was added to that environment. Proof it took: the next production publish
produced the **same asset key** (`mX841Vs3…`) as the preview publish, whose bytes had already been
grepped to contain `ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com` once and `localhost:4000` zero times. Guide 7
now tells the operator to check this before any production publish, with the command and the fix.

**3. Every account journey, on the installed build, against production.** A probe account
(`auth.preview.1024@example.invalid`, *Preview Probe Co*) was created **from the phone**: the form
accepted five fields and reported *19 characters — within the limit.*; the verify screen named the
inbox and counted from **8m 29s**; six digits typed with **no press of Verify** completed
confirm → register → exchange and opened the **new tenant's dashboard**. Production rows afterwards:
`role=OWNER`, `status=ACTIVE`, `emailVerified=true`, `firebaseUid` present, business `ACTIVE`, one
session, challenge `attempts=1 usedAt` stamped. Then: aeroplane mode, force-stop, cold launch →
**signed in**, dashboard offline state with *Try again* (not Login); network restored, the first tap
12 s later still failed, the second loaded the dashboard. Password reset followed the two-step
journey — code screen (inbox named, **9m 50s**, resend **50 s**), six digits with no press
(`attempts=1`, `verifiedAt`, authorization minted), new-password step with an **18-character** hint,
*Password changed* (`usedAt` stamped, four `audit_logs` rows for the business), the **old password
refused** (*Invalid email or password*), the **new password signed in** to the same tenant, and the
platform offered to save the credential (the `new-password` / `newPassword` field declarations
working).
Codes were recovered from the stored keyed digests with the server's own labels and pepper — the
probe address has no inbox — and the helper scripts were deleted; no code or pepper is committed.

**4. Cleanup verified, not assumed.** The probe's Firebase identity was deleted and every
collection was scanned for its `businessId`: users 0, businesses 0, reset challenges 0, audit rows 0,
the business name 0. The phone was signed out and left on Login. (The first teardown used slightly wrong collection
names for some business-scoped rows — `auditlogs` instead of `audit_logs` — so the sweep by
`businessId` across the real collection list is what actually closed it out; four audit rows were
removed.)

**Verification.** Mobile `tsc`/`eslint` clean, **91 suites / 1098 tests / 0 failures**; server
`tsc`/`eslint` clean, `test:unit` **1330 tests / 1276 pass / 0 fail / 54 skipped**. Artifacts:
`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-24-preview-journeys/` (eleven frames plus the isolation frame and
the README with the measurements above).

**Not verified, stated rather than implied:** a store-signed production build; iOS (no macOS on this
host); a real inbox in *this* run (delivery to one was measured on 2026-10-22 and is unchanged); an
induced 5xx (error handling was exercised by an unreachable network, not a failing server); and the
cause of the one failed *Try again*, recorded as observed.

# 27ER. The production profile on the phone: build, journeys, OTA and a measured rollback (2026-10-24)

**Mobile build configuration only (temporarily), one test case added — no route, permission, schema,
server, session-model or dependency change.** The previous entry proved the *preview* profile. This
run did the same for the **production** profile, and closed the rollback item that had been recorded
as untested since the update runtime shipped.

**1. The build is the production profile, honestly described.** EAS `12829e5d-fb93-4ae4-858d-7f58e962f495`,
profile `production`, signed with the project's production keystore (`Build Credentials 84JNqqnITp`),
`versionName 1.0.0` / `versionCode 1`, `minSdk 24` / `targetSdk 36`, runtime `1.0.0`, channel
`production`, `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` = the production API. Two settings were changed **for the run and
restored in the same commit series**: `android.buildType: apk` (a Play artifact is an AAB and cannot
be installed with `adb`) and `autoIncrement: false` (to keep the version equal to the publishes).
**The AAB path was not built**, so Play packaging and Play App Signing remain unproven; the release
*code path* and the release *update channel* are what this run proves. `adb install -r` over the
preview APK succeeded, which also proves both profiles share one signing key.

**2. Every journey passed on it, against production.** Create Account → *Verify your email* (inbox
named, 8m 49s) → six digits with **no press of Verify** → new tenant dashboard; production rows
`OWNER`/`ACTIVE`/`emailVerified`, one session, one audit row. Aeroplane mode + force-stop + cold
launch stayed **signed in** with the dashboard's offline state; network restored, the **first** *Try
again* loaded the dashboard. Reset: code screen → code verified (`attempts=1`, `verifiedAt`,
authorization minted) → password step → *Password changed* (`usedAt`) → **old password refused** →
**new password signed in** to the same tenant.

**3. The old "first Try again failed" finding is explained, not waved away.** The client's budgets are
`REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 15 s` once the server has answered recently and `COLD_START_TIMEOUT_MS = 60 s`
while it has not. The 2026-10-24 preview run screenshot the failure **12 s** after the tap, so it was
not a timeout — the request had failed immediately, which is what a radio that has not yet attached
produces. This run waited **20 s** after aeroplane mode was switched off and the **first** tap worked.
The app behaved correctly in both runs (error state, session kept, retry available).

**4. OTA delivery to a release build, and the rollback that had never been exercised.** The
`production` channel did not exist (manifest 404). A marker publish (`197d0367…`, manifest
`01a16cfb…`) was applied by the phone, changing the Login tagline; then
`eas update:roll-back-to-embedded --channel production --platform android --runtime-version 1.0.0`
(`5516d353…`, manifest `01a16cfe…`) returned it to the **embedded** tagline after two cold launches,
proving the rollback path on an installed release build. The CLI **requires `--runtime-version`** in
non-interactive mode — a fact the guide now states. The channel and branch were then deleted and the
404 returned, so production currently offers no updates.

**5. The 5xx gap is closed at the client rule, not pretended closed on a device.**
`auth-offline-boot.test.tsx` gains one case: a **500** at boot keeps the session, restores the stored
profile, marks the phase `degraded` and does **not** end the Firebase session — a server fault is not
a refusal. A live injected 5xx on the handset was still not performed, and is recorded as such.

**6. Cleanup.** The probe tenant, user, sessions, reset challenge, 5 audit rows and Firebase identity
were removed (0 leftovers); the phone was left signed out on the release build's Login screen; helper
scripts were deleted.

(17 controls passed); production configuration restored (`autoIncrement: true`, no `buildType`).

# 27EV. The privacy policy, served by the server that creates the obligation (2026-10-24)

**Server and documentation only — one new PUBLIC page route, no permission, schema, dependency,
session-model or mobile change.** §27EU named the missing privacy policy as one of two Play blockers.
This ships it as a page rather than a document, so it cannot drift from the code it describes.

**1. What exists.** `GET /privacy` — mounted **outside `/api`** in `server/src/app.ts`, beside the
AUTH-05 reset page and for the same reason: it is HTML a person or a store reviewer opens in a
browser, at the address the Play listing will point to. `server/src/pages/privacyPolicy.ts` holds the
content and `server/src/routes/privacy.routes.ts` the route. Public by requirement — a policy behind
a login cannot be read by someone deciding whether to create an account — and it performs no I/O, so
it adds no failure mode.

**2. What it says, checked against the code.** The policy names each processor the application
actually uses — **Firebase Authentication** (identity), **Brevo** (verification and reset mail),
**OpenRouter** (the assistant's question, recent conversation and the inventory data it reads, with
no name/email/password unless typed), **MongoDB Atlas** (database) and **Render** (hosting); it
states what is deliberately **not** collected (location, contacts, photos, microphone, advertising
identifiers) and that there is **no advertising, analytics or crash-reporting SDK**; it describes
HTTPS, the password never reaching this application, secure token storage, per-business filtering and
path-only request logs; retention; children (not intended under 18); and change control (the date at
the top moves with the content).

**3. Deletion is described as it exists today.** The page tells the reader to email the address on
the account, which is the only path that works before the §27EU deletion design ships. That is
deliberate: a policy promising an in-app button that does not exist would be a false statement to a
reviewer. **The deletion work must edit this page in the same change** — and
`PRIVACY-page.test.mjs` asserts the mailto sentence, so the page cannot silently keep claiming a
route that no longer exists without a test failing.

**4. Why it is safe to serve.** No script at all: CSP is `default-src 'none'` plus the stylesheet's
**SHA-256 hash computed from the bytes served** (the AUTH-05 technique), so a policy can never
describe a different document. `no-store`, `no-referrer`, `nosniff`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`, no
`X-Powered-By`. No request data reaches the page, so there is nothing to reflect, and `POST /privacy`
is a 404 rather than a write endpoint.

**5. Ownership detail to confirm.** The contact address is the owner's, hardcoded in one constant;
the wording deliberately **does not claim a jurisdiction or legal entity**, because inventing either
would be worse than omitting it. Replacing the address, or adding an entity line, is a one-line edit
plus the date.

**Verification.** `PRIVACY-page.test.mjs` — 6 cases: served at `GET /privacy` with no auth; **CSP
hash matches the stylesheet in the response** and no `script-src`/`unsafe-*`; `no-store`,
`no-referrer`, `nosniff`, no `X-Powered-By`; every processor named; no placeholder text and the
mailto deletion path pinned; `POST` → 404. Route inventory **76 → 77** (public **16 → 17**), recorded
in design §2.6 and re-measured by `phase-docs-route-inventory`. Server **`test:unit` 1336 tests /
1282 pass / 0 fail / 54 skipped**, `tsc`/`eslint`/both module-graph checks clean (510 modules).

**Not verified:** the page is **not live** — it ships with the next server deploy, so the Play
listing cannot point at it yet, and no reviewer has seen it. No device pass applies (no mobile
change). The deletion half of the Play requirement remains open, and iOS is untouched (no macOS).

# 27EW. Account deletion — in the app and on the web (2026-10-24)

**Server + mobile + documentation — one AUTHENTICATED route, one PUBLIC page and one mobile screen;
no new permission, dependency, schema migration or session-model change.** §27EU recorded the second
Play blocker: Play requires an **in-app** way to delete an account *and* a **web URL** for people who
no longer have the app. The retained data is the hard part, not the deletion: every audit row,
inventory transaction and purchase order cites a `User`, so erasing the row would make another
member's inventory history point at nothing.

**1. The decision: delete the person, tombstone the row.** A deletion removes everything that
identifies the person or grants them access — name, real email address, password hash, Firebase
identity, all sessions, password-reset and email-verification records, and their assistant
conversations with their messages — and **keeps** the business's own records, with the person's
`userId` set to `null`. The `User` row survives as a placeholder (`status: 'DELETED'`, name
`Deleted user`, address `deleted+<id>@deleted.invalid`, no credential, no identity link), so the
business's trail still resolves while the person is no longer named. The address is genuinely freed:
`deleted.invalid` is RFC 2606's never-delivered TLD, so the placeholder cannot become an inbox.

**2. `DELETE /api/auth/me`** (`controllers/auth.controller.ts`, `services/accountDeletion.service.ts`).
The account is **`req.user.id`** — `validateAccountDeletion` returns only `confirmation`,
`currentPassword` and `idToken`, so there is no field through which a request could name another
account, tenant, role or uid. Two proofs are required and they answer different questions:

- the typed word `DELETE` (a `VALIDATION_ERROR` field under the input, re-checked by the service for
direct callers);
- **re-authentication**: a Firebase ID token whose `uid` must equal the account's own
  (`409 FIREBASE_IDENTITY_CONFLICT` otherwise, naming nothing), or the current password for a legacy
  account (`400 INVALID_CURRENT_PASSWORD`). A Firebase-only account cannot fall through to the
  password branch: with no stored hash it is answered `400 FIREBASE_REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED`.

Both refusals are **400/409, never 401**, so a typo cannot end a session. The last active `OWNER` is
refused `409 LAST_OWNER_TRANSFER_REQUIRED`; a second active owner unlocks it. The write is conditional
on `status: 'ACTIVE'`, so a concurrent or repeated request converges (`200 { deleted: true,
changed: false }`) instead of deleting a second identity or writing a second audit row.

**3. The order is the safety property.** The **Firebase identity is deleted first**, then the
tombstone is written, then the owned records are erased and the audit row is written. A crash after
the provider delete leaves an ACTIVE row that a retry can still tombstone (the second provider delete
answers `auth/user-not-found`, reported as `deleted: false`), while a provider outage happens
**before** anything is written, so the account stays usable and the session alive (503). A deletion
that left a working Firebase identity would be an account that is gone and still able to sign in —
the state a deletion promise must rule out.

**4. The trail.** Audit rows that named the person are KEPT with `userId: null` (the business's
governance record), and the deletion itself writes one `ACCOUNT_DELETED` row with `userId: null`,
`entityId` the tombstone's id and `metadata.role` — so the event is visible without re-identifying
the account the transaction just anonymized. `AUDIT_ACTIONS.ACCOUNT_DELETED` and the mobile label
("Account deleted") were added together, so the audit screen cannot render a raw enum.

**5. The web half.** `GET /account-deletion` (`pages/accountDeletionPage.ts`,
`routes/accountDeletion.routes.ts`) is mounted outside `/api`, public and unauthenticated — somebody
who cannot sign in is exactly one of the people who needs it — and describes the same operation: the
in-app steps, the confirmation word, the last-owner rule, what is deleted, and what is kept. No
script; CSP is `default-src 'none'` plus the stylesheet's SHA-256 hash computed from the bytes
served; `no-store`, `no-referrer`, `nosniff`, `noindex`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`; `POST` is a 404.

**6. The mobile half.** `lib/accountDeletion.ts` owns the two decisions the screen must not make:
the confirmation constant (pinned to the server's copy by a test that reads the file) and **which
credential** the account has (`authMethods.firebase` → a forced-refresh ID token; otherwise the
password). `app/(app)/delete-account.tsx` states the consequences before the button, refuses a
blank/mistyped word or a missing password client-side, shows every server refusal in place (last
owner, wrong password, 429), and only clears the session on success or a genuine 401. Profile links
to it **below** Sign out, as a quieter secondary action: closing the account is rarer and more
consequential, not more prominent. The destructive button is deliberately **not** disabled while the
word is untyped — a disabled control cannot be focused, so it cannot say why — and `submit()` refuses
instead, under the field.

**7. Limiter.** The route is budgeted per account at **5 per hour** (`AUTH_ACCOUNT_DELETION_*`,
`createAccountDeletionLimiter`), mounted `requireAuth → limiter → controller` so an anonymous caller
is refused 401 without spending a bucket. Enough for a mistyped confirmation and a retry after a
transient provider failure; far below what makes an irreversible operation worth fuzzing.

**Verification.** `ACCOUNT-DELETION.test.mjs` — **12 cases, 0 failures** over a real database:
unauthenticated 401; mistyped word and wrong password refused with the account **and session**
intact; the last-owner 409 then a co-owner unlocking it; the tombstone field by field (status, name,
address, `deletedAt`, no `passwordHash`, no `firebaseUid`); sessions, reset tokens, reset challenges
and AI conversations/messages gone; the audit row `userId: null` and the `ACCOUNT_DELETED` row; the
old token refused; the real address free to register again; the repeat call converging; another
business and its member untouched; a deleted member hidden from `GET /api/users` and `GET
/api/users/:id`; Firebase mismatch/absence/attempt ordering; the provider-failure rollback; and the
429. `PRIVACY-page.test.mjs` grew to **9 cases** (privacy + deletion page: no auth, CSP hash, headers,
processors, camera, the shipped deletion wording, no placeholder, GET only). Mobile
`account-deletion.test.tsx` — **9 cases**: the consequences, the word gate, the password path, the
Firebase path (and no password field), the no-identity refusal, the last-owner/wrong-password/429
refusals keeping the session, and the success path clearing it. Two existing guards were updated on
purpose: Phase F-1's `$unset firebaseUid` prohibition now permits **exactly one** file by name
(`services/accountDeletion.service.ts`) and separately asserts that its tombstone also removes the
credential and is terminal, and the design §2.6 route inventory moved **77 → 79** (authenticated
**13 → 14**, public **17 → 18**). The Firebase delete bridge lives in its own module
(`services/firebase/identityDeleter.ts`) rather than beside the AUTH-04-B2 updater, because that
bridge's guards exist to keep it a single non-destructive field write; all 32 of them still pass.
Server **`test:unit` 1343 / 1288 pass / 0 fail / 55 skipped**; targeted DB suites (users,
pagination, Phase 24 matrix, 26A sessions, AUTH-02, AUTH-03, deletion) **92 tests / 0 fail**; mobile
**93 suites / 1114 tests / 0 failures**; `tsc`/`eslint`/both module-graph checks clean.

**Not verified:** the URLs are **not live** until the next server deploy, so neither has been opened
by a reviewer or in a private browser window; the **in-app flow has not been run on a device** — it
destroys the account it is used on, so it needs a disposable account, and the store-installed build
is the only place Play's entry points would be exercised end to end; Play App Signing and upload
remain unexercised; iOS is untouched (no macOS). Business deletion (as opposed to person deletion)
is deliberately **not** in scope and would be its own confirmed action, because it destroys history
other members rely on. *(Corrected the same day by §27EX: a business whose **only member** deletes
their account is now closed with it — the refusal above survives only while somebody else remains.)*

# 27EX. A business whose only member leaves closes with them (2026-10-24)

**Server + mobile + documentation — no new route, permission, dependency, schema migration or
session-model change; one new module, moved rather than invented.** §27EW shipped deletion and
locked the last-OWNER refusal. Walking the Play requirement end to end exposed that the refusal was
a **dead end for the product's primary persona**: registration creates an OWNER who is alone in
their business, and there was **no invitation, no ownership-transfer and no business-deletion
route** (verified by reading every `router.delete`/`router.patch` and the business routes). A
reviewer who registers a fresh account and taps *Delete account* would have been told to promote
somebody who does not exist — and a sole proprietor could never close their account at all.

**1. The owner's decision (2026-10-24): close the business too.** Deletion now has two shapes, and
the service decides which by reading the business, never the request:

- **Somebody else remains.** The old rule stands: an OWNER with no second active OWNER is refused
  `409 LAST_OWNER_TRANSFER_REQUIRED` (now worded *"Other people still use this business…"*) and the
  business keeps its owner. A second OWNER unlocks the ordinary account-only deletion.
- **Nobody else remains.** The account **and the whole tenant** are removed. Keeping the records
  served nobody, retained personal data for no one's benefit, and left the account unclosable.

**2. One definition of "the tenant's rows", moved into the application.**
`services/tenantTeardown.service.ts` now owns `TENANT_DATA_COLLECTIONS`,
`clearTenantData`/`removeTenant`/`countTenantLeftovers`, which previously lived only in
`scripts/perf/lib.mjs` — and that script **re-exports them from `src/`**, so `seed:*`, `cleanup:*`,
the demo seeder and `DEMO-2` all keep one import site. A second copy in the service is how a
teardown eventually deletes less than a seed created; the collection list already has that scar
(`suppliers`/`purchase_orders`, then `audit_logs` at AI-40). Module graph **520 modules**, 0 stale
specifiers.

**3. The order, and why this branch has no tombstone.** Re-authenticate → decide the business's
fate → **delete the Firebase identity** → **re-check** that the caller is still the only active
member (a member created in between means the business must survive) → remove the tenant. There is
no tombstone and no `ACCOUNT_DELETED` audit row in this branch **deliberately**: the collections
that would hold them are part of what is being removed, and a row pointing at a business that no
longer exists is worse than no row. The request is still in the structured access log.

**4. The screens and pages say it.** `app/(app)/delete-account.tsx` gained an *If you are the only
member* paragraph stating that closing the account closes the business, before the button; the
retained-records paragraph is now qualified with *while other people still use your business*.
Both public pages were corrected in the same change — `GET /account-deletion` and `GET /privacy`
both described the old absolute refusal — and `PRIVACY-page.test.mjs` now asserts **both**
outcomes, so a page cannot quietly re-promise the refusal-only version.

**Verification.** `ACCOUNT-DELETION.test.mjs` — **13 cases, 12 pass, 1 intentionally skipped in DB
mode, 0 fail**: the old refusal case was replaced by two real ones. ★ *closes the whole business
when its only member deletes their account*: an audit row, a conversation **and its message** and a
second tenant's live session exist first; after the call the business row, every user of it, its
audit rows, its conversations, its messages and the deleted person's sessions are **all gone**, the
old token answers **401**, and the other tenant's business, user and session are untouched. ★
*refuses while another member remains, and a second owner unlocks the account-only path*: a STAFF
member keeps the 409 in force; adding a second OWNER then answers 200 with the business, the
co-owner and the member all still present and the caller tombstoned. `DEMO-2` **5/5** and the suite
guard files still pass through the moved module; `PRIVACY-page.test.mjs` **9/9**; server
**`test:unit` 1343 / 1288 pass / 0 fail / 55 skipped**; mobile **93 suites / 1114 tests / 0
failures** (the deletion suite's copy assertions updated: 9/9); `tsc`/`eslint`/module-graph clean.

**5. Measured on production, with a disposable tenant (owner-authorised).** The **deployed** server
was driven through the real flow over HTTPS: owner registered **201**, owner signed in **200**,
STAFF created **201**, STAFF signed in **200**, mistyped confirmation **400**, wrong password **400
`INVALID_CURRENT_PASSWORD`**, session still **200** after both refusals, ★ deletion **200
`{deleted:true,changed:true}`**, the deleted account's token **403 `ACCOUNT_DISABLED`**, its login
**401**, the owner unaffected **200**, and the deleted member absent from `GET /api/users` (**0
rows**) — **12/12 checks passed**. The four probe tenants the runs created (two aborted probes
included) were then removed through the same `removeTenant` definition:
`2/2/8/8` rows, leftovers before `1/1/6/6` and **`0` after every one**, `0` probe users and `0`
probe businesses remaining in `inventoryai_prod_db`. No real account, business or Firebase
identity was touched.

**6. Deployed the same evening, and measured end to end.** Commit `a5a8b10` was pushed and Render
auto-deployed it — `GET /api/health` published `commit: a5a8b10…` with `environment: production`.
`GET /privacy` and `GET /account-deletion` then answered **200 `text/html` from the live host,
signed out**, with `Cache-Control: no-store`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`,
`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and the CSP hash recomputed from the bytes served, and **both
carried the two-outcome wording** (*make another member an owner first* … *if you are the business's
only member*). A second API regression against production repeated both shapes — **43 checks, 0
failures** (`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-24-account-deletion/`): the only member's deletion
removes the business row, its users, its audit trail, its sessions (looked up by the deleted user's
id, since `sessions` carries no `businessId`) and its assistant conversations, frees the address to
register again, and the second account created on that same address also closes with its business;
a STAFF member leaving leaves the business **`ACTIVE`**, the owner untouched and the owner's session
alive, the leaver's row a tombstone (`DELETED`, `Deleted user`, `deleted+<id>@deleted.invalid`, no
credential, no `firebaseUid`, `deletedAt` set), one `ACCOUNT_DELETED` audit row with `userId: null`,
and the leaver a 404 detail and a 401 login; then the owner, with only a tombstone left, closed the
rest — business, tombstone and trail to 0. Both runs ended with **0** probe rows in
`inventoryai_prod_db`, and the counts returned to their pre-run values (3 businesses / 3 users /
8 sessions / 27 audit rows / 1 conversation / 8 messages / 5 categories / 5 locations).

**7. The screen on the phone.** The installed production-profile APK (`12829e5d…`) predates the
feature, so the screen could only be there through an over-the-air update: two were published to the
`production` channel that day, and the second (`c7a108b1-…`, built from `a5a8b10`) carried the
**re-ordered card and the new banner**, which the frames show — so delivery and content were verified
together. On the OPPO CPH1969, signed in as a throwaway legacy-password account created through the
API: Profile lists **Delete account** below Sign out; the screen states the consequences before the
button; pressing it with the word blank answers *Type DELETE to confirm* with **no request**;
`DELET` answers *Type DELETE exactly*; `DELETE` with the password returned the app to **Login**, and
the user row, the business row and the old password were all gone (login **401
`INVALID_CREDENTIALS`**). The `production` channel and branch were then **deleted**, so no
future store build — same `appVersion`, therefore same runtime — can pick up a test update, and
the manifest answers 404 again.

**8. The Firebase branch, on the same handset.** Every run above used a **password** account; this one
used an identity with **no password at all**, so the screen had to ask the provider instead of asking
the person. The fixture was a **real Firebase identity** created through the Admin SDK in the project
the server uses (`emailVerified: true`), taken through the app's own onboarding — sign-in answered
`403 REGISTRATION_REQUIRED`, Login said *"This sign-in is not linked to an Inventory AI account
yet"*, and **Create your workspace** made the tenant — so the stored user was `OWNER`/`ACTIVE` with a
`firebaseUid` and **no `passwordHash`**. On the delete screen there was **no password field**, and the
card said *"We will confirm this with your sign-in"*, because the screen read `authMethods.firebase`
from the session rather than guessing from the address. `DELETE` + **Delete my account** refreshed the
provider token, the server confirmed the uid, and the app returned to **Login**; signing in again with
the same address answered **Invalid email or password on the phone**. Afterwards an Admin SDK lookup
by that address answered **`auth/user-not-found`** — the half the password branch cannot demonstrate,
and the one that matters, since an account deleted locally but still able to authenticate is not
deleted. The user row, the business row, its one session and its one audit row were gone; counts
returned to baseline and no `probe.*` user or `PROBE-*` business remained. Evidence:
`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-24-account-deletion/` (frames 05 and 06).

**Not verified:** the Firebase branch was driven with an **Admin-SDK-created identity onboarded through
the app**, not with **Google Sign-In** — the same `firebaseUid` check serves both, and the Google path
is not separately measured here. Play App Signing, an internal-testing install and review are still

# 27EY. The Google button, on a real Google account (2026-10-24)

**Mobile + documentation — one function changed in `mobile/lib/firebase-native.ts`, no route, schema,
permission, session-model, native-module, dependency or environment change.** This closes the gap
§27EX listed: the Firebase deletion branch had only been driven with an **Admin-SDK-created identity**
onboarded through the app. A **real Google account** (`broccolifreebuff05179@gmail.com`, disposable)
went through the real **Continue with Google** button end to end, on the installed
production-facing APK (`versionName 1.0.0` / `versionCode 1`, embedded JS, no Metro, no `adb
reverse`) against `https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com`. Evidence:
`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-24-google-sign-in/` (8 frames).

**1. A defect that only a provider sign-in could show.** The **first** tap of *Continue with Google*
resolved the Google account this app had used before in about a second, **with no account sheet at
all**, and landed in a dashboard belonging to a **different person's** tenant (frame 01: the button's
spinner, no sheet). On a handset holding a single Google account that looks like convenience; on one
holding several it means **the second account can never be reached**, and on a shared device it means
the next person tapping that button is signed into the **previous person's** Google identity and
therefore their inventory. The subsequent tap *did* show the chooser (frame 02), which is what made
the difference measurable rather than a guess.

**2. The fix is one call, in the boundary that owns the provider.** `nativeSignInWithGoogle` now
clears this app's saved Google credential (`GoogleSignin.signOut()`) **before** it asks, so the sheet
is a choice. A failure to clear is **ignored on purpose** — "nothing saved" is the ordinary
first-run case, and `signIn()` below it is the call that decides whether Google sign-in can work at
all, reporting through the classification this boundary already had. It touches only Play Services'
last account for this client: it does not sign the person out of Google and does not touch the
Firebase session. `phaseC-native-google.test.ts` gains the ★ *clears the saved Google account before
asking, so the sheet can offer another one* case and a *still signs in when there was no saved Google
account to clear* case — **19/19**. The change is **JavaScript only**, so it can ship over the air or
in the next build; the APK's embedded bundle predates it, and item 6 records the over-the-air
delivery that reached the phone instead.

**3. Registration through Google.** Choosing the disposable account answered the info banner *"This
sign-in is not linked to an Inventory AI account yet. Create a business account to continue."* (`403
`REGISTRATION_REQUIRED`, frame 03); **Create a business account** then created the tenant
`PROBE-google-broccoli` through the app's own onboarding, producing an `OWNER`/`ACTIVE` user with a
`firebaseUid` and **no `passwordHash`** — the shape that forces the delete screen onto the provider
branch.

**4. Deletion, and the half a password branch cannot prove.** The screen showed *"We will confirm this
with your sign-in. You do not need to type your password."* with **no password field**, *Type DELETE
to confirm* and the *What stays, if others still use your business* paragraph (frame 04). `DELETE` +
**Delete my account** returned the app to **Login** (frame 05). Then, in production:

- **MongoDB** — the user row and the `PROBE-google-broccoli` business row are **gone**, **0**
  `PROBE-` businesses remain, and the other three tenants are untouched at **3 businesses / 3 users**.
- **No dangling references** — 33 audit rows and 1 conversation / 8 messages, **0** pointing at a
  missing business or conversation, and no `DELETE`-shaped audit row, as designed for the sole-member
  branch.
- **Sessions** — 11 rows, every one belonging to a live user and every one `revokedAt`-stamped,
  **0 orphans**, so deletion left no live session behind.
- **Firebase** — `getUserByEmail(...)` answers **`auth/user-not-found`**: the identity is gone from the
  provider, not merely unlinked. ★ **Signing in with the same Google account again cannot get back
  in**: the chooser appears, choosing that account answers the same `REGISTRATION_REQUIRED` banner,
  and no tenant, dashboard or session is reachable (frame 06). The identity that sign-in re-created
  (`fKinxuUtvpYykfVsRpKLguUMuIS2`, provider `google.com`) was deleted with the Admin SDK afterwards →
  `auth/user-not-found`, Mongo still 3 / 3, no row for the address.

**5. One observation, not a defect.** After that identity was deleted server-side, a cold start showed
the AUTH-04-F *"We could not reach the verification service"* state (frame 07); **Try again** landed
on **Login** (frame 08). That is the documented unreachable state doing its job — it shows no cached
account and mints no session by itself — and it cost the user one tap.

**6. The fix reached the phone over the air, because no build was possible, and was measured there.**
`eas build --profile preview` **failed before compiling**: *"This account has used its Android builds
from the Free plan this month, which will reset in 7 days (on Sun Nov 01 2026)."* The installed build
was already on the **`production`** channel at runtime **1.0.0**, so the fix was published there
(group `d4582eda-…`) — and the device answered **`CheckCompleteUnavailable`** for half an hour while
`curl` with the client's own headers received **200** on both channels and the phone could reach
`u.expo.dev` (ping 2/2, 30–33 ms; Chrome rendered the endpoint's 400). An **`eas update:republish`**
(group **`2518ccb8-…`**, update `01a16e79-…`) was picked up on the next cold start — `Update
available` → `NEW_UPDATE_LOADED`, with the logged manifest naming `branchName: production` and
runtime `1.0.0` — the same refusal-and-republish pattern recorded in §27EP. On that bundle, with two
disposable Google accounts on one handset: **sugarcane** signed in through the chooser, created its
owner tenant and signed out; the next *Continue with Google* showed the **chooser again** (frame 09)
— the exact sequence the old bundle answered silently; **carrots** then got `REGISTRATION_REQUIRED`
with **no tenant, no dashboard, no session** (frame 10), so a second Google identity on a shared
device cannot reach the first person's business; and signing back in as sugarcane and deleting it from
the screen returned the app to **Login** (frames 11–12). Afterwards Firebase answered
**`auth/user-not-found`** for **both** addresses (carrots' was removed with the Admin SDK after the
isolation test), Mongo held **no** row for either, **0** `PROBE` businesses remained, the counts were
back at **3 businesses / 3 users**, and all 12 sessions belonged to live users with **0 live and 0
orphans**. The `production` branch/channel now serve this update, so a store build of the same runtime
would receive it on first launch; the rollback is
`eas update:roll-back-to-embedded --channel production --platform android --runtime-version 1.0.0`.

**Verification.** Mobile `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean, **93 suites / 1116 tests / 0 failures**
(`phaseC-native-google.test.ts` **19/19**). No server file touched, so the server baselines of §27EX
stand. **Not verified:** a store-installed build from Play, Play App Signing, Play's review, a
rollback of *this* update group, and iOS.
