# 27EZ. The store artifact was the wrong commit — a parity gate, and no upload (2026-10-24)

The next step was to upload the `versionCode 3` AAB (`4b133d62…`, the permission-trimmed artifact of
§27ET) to Play. Before uploading, the **JavaScript inside it** — not its manifest — was searched for
the copy of the features shipped after it was built. **Neither AAB contains a single occurrence of
any account-deletion copy**: `Delete account` 0, `Delete my account` 0, `Type DELETE` 0,
`delete-account` 0, in both the `versionCode 2` rehearsal AAB and the `versionCode 3` trimmed one.
Both were built before the screen existed (`381c3f8`, 20:56 local; the two artifacts were downloaded
at 16:51 and 17:41), and their bundles are **byte-for-byte the same length, 2,847,364** — the
permission trim changed the manifest, not the JavaScript, which is precisely why every packaging
check in §27ES/§27ET passed on an artifact that could not be submitted.

**Why this is a release-level defect, not a documentation slip.** Play's account-deletion policy
requires the in-app deletion path in the **uploaded build**. The feature had reached the installed
test build only by **over-the-air update** (§27EY), which a fresh install receives on a *later* launch
— unacceptable as the sole answer to a policy requirement, and invisible to a reviewer who tests on
first launch. The two builds were also missing the Google account-chooser fix (`bfc9c6e`), which is
JavaScript-only and would likewise have arrived late.

**What was added.** `mobile/scripts/check-aab.mjs` — a release gate with **two layers**, both of which
must pass, using only the standard library.

*Packaging, against the values this repository declares* (not merely printed): package
`com.inventoryai.app`; `versionName` equal to the embedded config's version; `minSdk 24` and
`targetSdk ≥ 36`; a JAR signature present; channel `production` on the project's own `u.expo.dev` URL;
runtime version equal to that version; `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` absent and `CAMERA`/`INTERNET` present;
the production API host in the bundle and `localhost:4000` absent; and no `expo-dev-menu`,
`expo-dev-launcher` or `react-native-web` entry. The binary manifest is read the way `aapt2` writes
it — each attribute's value sits next to its own name — and only `uses-permission` **elements** are
counted, so an `android:permission` requirement on a component is not mistaken for a request (the
correction §27ET needed).

*Bundle parity*: four **user-visible** sentences — `Delete my account` and `Type DELETE to confirm`
(the policy requirement), `Continue with Google` (the provider entry point) and
`Create your workspace` (the onboarding a new identity needs) — read out of
`base/assets/index.android.bundle` (a ZIP inside a ZIP, Hermes bytecode).

Exit codes follow the repository convention: **0** verified, **1** an expectation failed (each printed
with its reason), **2** not verified (no file, no ZIP, no bundle/config). **Fifteen controls** run
first (`--self-test`): a complete bundle passes, a bundle missing the deletion copy is reported **by
name**, a missing bundle entry returns `null`, a non-ZIP is refused, a compliant synthetic manifest
passes while `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW`, a wrong package id and a development-client entry are each
refused, and **each probe must still be copy that exists in `app/`/`components/`** — so rewording a
sentence forces the list to be updated instead of silently disarming the gate.
`mobile/__tests__/release-aab-parity-guard.test.ts` runs the controls and pins the negative cases at
source; `npm run check:aab -- <file>` invokes it, and `--bundle <file>` checks a bare bundle.

**CI runs the half it can.** A pipeline has no AAB — builds happen on EAS — so the `mobile` job now
exports the app's JavaScript (`npx expo export --platform android`, which needs no build secret) and
runs `--bundle` against the real Metro/Hermes output. That is a different claim from the Jest case
beside it, which reads source: a screen that stopped being bundled would pass a source grep and fail
here. The artifact half runs on the file actually being uploaded.

The step was **reproduced locally with a CI-like environment**, not just reasoned about: the export
was run with every `EXPO_PUBLIC_*` value empty and both Firebase configuration paths pointing at files
that do not exist, and the resulting **3,455,933**-byte bundle passed all four probes — so the step does
not depend on a developer's `.env` or on a build secret. **It has not run on the GitHub runner yet**;
the first push is where that is observed.

**Measured.** Both artifacts pass **packaging** — the JS port reads exactly what the Python record
read: package `com.inventoryai.app`, `versionCode` 2 and 3, `versionName 1.0.0`, `minSdk 24` /
`targetSdk 36`, **11** permissions with `SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW` gone, four ABIs, signature present,
channel `production`, runtime `1.0.0`, `ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com` ×1, `localhost:4000` ×0 — and
both exit **1** on the bundle layer, missing `Delete my account` and `Type DELETE to confirm` while
`Continue with Google` and `Create your workspace` are present. **The positive control is the code
this repository builds today**: `npx expo export --platform android` (run with the Firebase
configuration paths pointed at files that do not exist, proving the export needs no build secret)
produced a **≈3.46 MB** Hermes bundle (3,456,268–3,456,270 bytes across two exports — the byte count
is not stable, which is why the gate checks content and not size) that passes all four probes, exit
**0**. So the gate fails
those artifacts for being old, not because it fails everything it is shown. Raw output:
`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-24-release-aab/bundle-parity.txt`.

**Decision: nothing was uploaded.** Neither existing AAB is uploadable; the store needs a build from
a current commit, and `eas build` is refused until the Free plan's Android build quota resets
(**2026-11-01**). Retried with the `production` profile after the check — the refusal is per
**account**, not per profile (`This account has used its Android builds from the Free plan this
month`), and it came **after** `versionCode` was incremented **3 → 4**, so the first successful build
will be **versionCode 4 or higher**. The order is now: build from a commit containing the features →
`npm run check:aab` must answer **0** → upload to **internal testing** → enroll **Play App Signing** → install **from
Play** → repeat the Google chooser, shared-device isolation, account-deletion and offline-launch
journeys on Play's re-signed artifact.

**Verification.** Mobile `tsc` clean, `eslint .` clean, **94 suites / 1117 tests / 0 failures**; the
docs integrity and route-inventory guards pass. No server, schema, permission, dependency or session
change. **Not verified:** Play App Signing, an internal-testing install, Play's review, and iOS.

# 27FA. The Terms of Use — and the personal data that outlived the tombstone (2026-10-25)

**Server + mobile + documentation — one PUBLIC page (`GET /terms`), one mobile card, one deletion-service
fix and three guard updates; no new dependency, permission, schema, index, session-model or environment
variable, and no change to who may do what.** §27EU recorded the two Play blockers. The privacy policy
shipped (§27ET, corrected by §27EW) and account deletion shipped in the app and on the web (§27EW), but
there was **no terms of use at all** — nowhere, in the app or on a URL, to say what the service asks of
the person or what they may expect from it. Reading the deletion service again to write them found a
defect the tombstone test could not see.

**1. The page.** `GET /terms` (`server/src/pages/termsOfUse.ts`, `server/src/routes/terms.routes.ts`),
mounted **outside `/api`** and **public**, for the same reason as `/privacy` and `/account-deletion`: it is
an HTML page a person or a reviewer reads in a browser, and terms behind a sign-in wall cannot be read
by somebody deciding whether to create an account. It reads no request data, performs no I/O and has no
branch that can fail. No script, an inline stylesheet authorized by a **CSP hash computed from the bytes
served**, and `no-store` / `no-referrer` / `nosniff` / `frame-ancestors 'none'` on every response.

**2. What it says, and why each sentence is there.** Three behaviours a person would otherwise be
surprised by, all of them the software's actual behaviour rather than legal boilerplate: the assistant
is **read-only** *and* **can be wrong** (a read-only claim without a fallibility claim is a promise the
model cannot keep, and an answer is not accounting, tax, legal or safety advice); a **sole member's
business is deleted with the account**, which is what the server decided on 2026-10-24 and what the
deletion page already states; and **nothing in these terms limits a consumer right** that applies where
the person lives, so the liability paragraph cannot be read as taking one away. The operator (Jeffern)
is named, the contact address is the one the other two pages use, the effective date is 25 October 2026,
and the page carries **no placeholder** — asserted, not assumed.

**3. The three pages link to one another.** A privacy policy, a deletion page and a terms page that do not
reference each other are three descriptions of three different products. `/terms` links to `/privacy` and
`/account-deletion`; `/privacy` now links to `/terms` and `/account-deletion`; `/account-deletion` links
to both. `TERMS-page.test.mjs` asserts the whole link set, so **removing any one of the six links fails a
test** rather than leaving a page quietly orphaned.

**4. In the app.** Profile gained a **Legal** card with *Privacy policy* and *Terms of use*. The address is
built from **`API_URL`**, never typed out: a build pointed at the development server opens the development
pages, and a production build opens production — a hand-written domain is the one thing that keeps working
on the machine it was written on. `Linking.canOpenURL` is asked first, and a device that cannot open a
browser gets a sentence instead of a tap that does nothing. Five cases in
`mobile/__tests__/legal-pages-in-app.test.tsx`, including the URL asserted against the imported constant
and a session-is-untouched case.

**5. THE DEFECT THE TERMS WRITING FOUND — a deletion that still left the person readable.**
`users.service.create` records a `USER_CREATED` audit row whose `metadata` holds the created person's
**name and email address**, so that an owner can see who joined. The tombstone set that row's `userId` to
`null` and stopped there — which left **the deleted address and name visible in the audit viewer to every
owner and admin of the business**. The existing tombstone case could not see it because its own audit
fixture carried `metadata: {}`; the new case writes the real shape the service writes. The fix is a second,
narrowly scoped update: `$unset` `metadata.name` and `metadata.email` on **`entityType: 'USER'` rows whose
`entityId` is this account** — nothing else. The person's **role stays**, because it says something about
the business rather than about them, and a **colleague's** `USER_CREATED` row is asserted untouched, so the
test proves the scope rather than only the erasure.

**6. The guard that failed for the wrong reason.** `phaseA-credential-authority` asserted that the deletion
service contained **exactly one `$unset`**, because that operator is how the Firebase link and the password
hash are cleared and the file is a reviewed exception to the "nothing may clear `firebaseUid`" rule. The
metadata fix is a second `$unset`, so the guard failed while the property it exists to protect was intact —
a blade-edge count standing in for a property. It now counts the property: **exactly one block may name
`firebaseUid` or `passwordHash`, and no other block may reach either.**

**7. The one hole that remains, stated rather than papered over.** If a **Firebase-only** account's identity
is deleted by the provider and the request then dies before the tombstone is written, that account is still
`ACTIVE`, and it can no longer re-authenticate — its only credential is the token the provider will not
mint again — so closing it needs an operator. The window is **two writes wide**. Nothing in the application
can shrink it without either weakening the re-authentication requirement or deferring the provider delete;
both were rejected, and the service header now records the hole beside the recovery it qualifies.

**8. Route inventory 79 → 80** (**47 permission-gated, 14 authenticated, 19 public, 0 role-gated**), with a
dated note in design §2.6. The gated tier is unchanged, as it has been through every auth, recovery and
legal-page increment.

**Verification.** Server `test:unit` **1349 tests / 1294 pass / 0 fail / 55 skipped** (the new
`TERMS-page` suite, 6 cases; `PRIVACY-page` 9 cases passing with the new cross-link assertions);
`node --test test/ACCOUNT-DELETION.test.mjs` with `TEST_MODE=db` **13 pass / 0 fail / 1 skipped** over the
real database, which includes the new audit-metadata case; `tsc`, `eslint` and both module-graph checks
clean. Mobile **95 suites / 1122 tests / 0 failures**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean. **Not verified:** the page
is **not live** — it ships with the next server deploy, so the Play listing cannot point at `/terms` yet
*(corrected 2026-10-25: it **is** live and measured, and the Legal card was opened on the phone —
§27FC)*;
**no device pass** was run for the Legal card (it is suite-proven, and it opens the same host the app
already talks to); the full `test:db` mode was not re-run this pass, only the deletion suite it touches; and
iOS remains unverified (no macOS).

# 27FB. Invitations — the first way to join a business you did not create (2026-10-25)

**Server + mobile + documentation — one new collection, five new routes, one new mail template, one
public landing page, two new mobile screens and the invited shape of Create Account; no new dependency,
increment of an existing permission, session-model, index-on-existing-collection or environment
variable.** Since Phase 14A the only way to add a colleague was `POST /api/users`, which made an
administrator invent a password for somebody else and hand it over — a credential known to two people,
and the single structural reason legacy password login could not be retired (`users.service.create`
writes a `passwordHash` and no `firebaseUid`). An invitation moves the credential decision to the person
who will use it: the admin names an address and a role, the invitee proves the address with the AUTH-04
six-digit code and creates their own Firebase identity, and the server reads the tenant and role from
the invitation rather than from anything the invitee sends.

**1. The invitation is not a credential for an account.** The token is 32 bytes of CSPRNG output, mailed
to the invited address, and the collection stores **only its SHA-256 digest** — so a database reader
cannot reconstruct a working link, exactly as the reset flows store digests rather than codes. Holding
the link proves only that somebody received a message addressed to a particular email; acceptance
additionally requires a **verified Firebase identity whose address equals the invited one**, compared by
the server in `resolvePendingForRegistration` (not only by its caller). A leaked link therefore grants
nothing on its own, which is why it can be a plain random value rather than a second managed secret. The
address IS stored in the clear here, unlike the reset challenges, and deliberately: an invitation cannot
function without knowing who it is for, and the mail is sent to it. It is consequently the one field the
deletion path must not retain — see §5.

**2. The tenant and the role come from the row, never from the request.** `POST
/api/auth/firebase/register` gained exactly one optional input, `invitationToken`, and no field for a
business id, a role, a uid or a user id exists to send. When a token is present, `businessName` becomes
optional **because no business is created**: the person joins the inviting tenant, the role is the
invited one, the address is the verified claim, and the uid is the verified token's. `OWNER` is not
invitable (the user API already refuses to mint one, so an invitation must not be a quieter route to
the same grant), an `ADMIN` may not invite an `ADMIN` (the same hierarchy rule as direct creation), and
because `users.email` is globally unique an address that already owns an account is refused **at invite
time** with `INVITATION_EMAIL_IN_USE` rather than merged at acceptance — matching the Phase 32C/32H
position that two tenants are never joined by an address match.

**3. One pending invitation per business and address, seven days long.** Re-inviting an address
**replaces** the pending row and rotates its token, which is what makes a resent link the revocation of
the previous one; expired, revoked and already-accepted all answer the **same** generic 404
`INVITATION_INVALID`, so a holder learns the link is unusable and not which of the three happened. The
partial unique index catches two admins pressing send at once, and the duplicate-key path re-reads and
rotates rather than failing a request that achieved the invariant. **A mail failure withdraws the row**: an
invitation nobody can receive must not sit in the pending list, and its token must not stay redeemable —
the mail is sent after the write and the row is deleted if delivery fails (`503
INVITATION_MAIL_NOT_CONFIGURED` when mail is unconfigured, `502 INVITATION_MAIL_FAILED` when the provider
refused it).

**4. The three management routes sit behind `users.manage`, and the two public ones disclose nothing.**
`GET`/`POST /api/invitations` and `DELETE /api/invitations/:id` require authentication **and**
`requirePermission(USERS_MANAGE)` — the permission that already governs membership, because an
invitation adds a member and a separate key would create a role that may invite yet not manage. **This is
the first change to the gated tier since the Phase 23 contract** (47 → 50), and the Phase 22/23/24 guards
were extended rather than loosened. `GET /api/auth/invitation?token=…` is public because the person
holding an invitation has not signed in yet; it returns the invited address, role, business name and
expiry and nothing else, and it is per-IP rate limited. **The token travels as a QUERY parameter, never a
path segment**, because the access log records the path and never the query — a token in the path would
sit in every log line and every intermediary's record for a week. `GET /invite` is the page an invitation
email's button opens: mounted outside `/api` like the three legal pages, it validates the token's SHAPE
against an allow-list and writes it into a constant `inventoryai://invite?...` address, resolving and
redeeming nothing; `no-store`, `no-referrer`, no script, and a crafted token is refused rather than
reflected. Send is limited per ACCOUNT (20 / hour) and preview per IP (60 / hour), both **after** the
authentication and permission gates.

**5. Deletion and teardown know about invitations.** An invitation is **personal data and a live token**,
so closing an account deletes the invitations addressed to that person — otherwise the tombstone frees the
address for reuse and a pending invitation would then be addressed to whoever takes it next; invitations
the person **sent** are left alone, because they belong to the business's onboarding and name somebody
else. The tenant teardown gained the collection too: closing a business must not leave emails promising a
tenant that no longer exists. Three audit actions (`INVITATION_SENT`, `INVITATION_REVOKED`,
`INVITATION_ACCEPTED`) and one entity type (`INVITATION`) were added, with **no address in any metadata**
— the same rule the account-deletion work established, and the labels were added to
`mobile/lib/auditLabels.ts` so the viewer renders words rather than identifiers.

**6. Mobile.** `app/invite.tsx` is the public screen the link reaches: one public preview, then the four
facts the invitee already knows, then *Create your account*. The token is held in **memory**
(`lib/pendingInvite.ts`) for the length of the journey — never a route parameter, never persisted, since
the email is still there after a cold start and a stored invitation would be a seven-day secret on the
device for no benefit. Create Account in its invited shape **asks for no business name** (the field is
absent, not optional) and **locks the email** to the invited address, because letting it be edited would
only produce a refusal after a six-digit code had been typed; the form names the business and role
instead. The Firebase-onboarding screen (`register-firebase.tsx`, the `REGISTRATION_REQUIRED` path, which
a Google sign-in can reach) has the same invited shape. `app/(app)/users/invitations.tsx` is the
management surface — send, list, revoke with a confirmation — reached from a new **Invite** button on
Users, and it never receives or displays a token. A signed-in device opening an invitation is told that
an invitation creates an account instead of being shown a form the server would refuse.

**7. A test defect the full run found.** The accepting case asserted `Business.countDocuments()` was
unchanged, and **passed alone while failing in a four-file run**: `node:test` runs test FILES
concurrently, so a global collection count is decided by whatever another suite is doing at that instant.
It now asserts on the business this test owns — the inviting tenant holds exactly two members after the
join — which is the property the global count was standing in for.

**8. Route inventory 80 → 85** (**50 permission-gated, 14 authenticated, 21 public, 0 role-gated**), with
§2.6 corrected as well: the two 2026-10-25 notes had been written out of order and one sum was wrong,
which the route-inventory guard could not see because it reads the canonical sentence at §2.6's head.

**Verification.** Server `test:unit` **1359 tests / 1303 pass / 0 fail / 56 skipped**; `test:db` **909
tests / 814 pass / 0 fail / 95 skipped** (the whole mode re-run this pass, against Atlas); the new
`INVITATIONS.test.mjs` carries **18 cases** (8 unit: payload rules, the mail's two links and its escaping,
the landing page's forwarding and non-reflection; 10 over the real app: create + mailed + digest stored,
supersede-on-resend, preview's four fields, expiry as the same generic refusal, tenant-scoped revoke,
delivery failure withdrawing the row, role/address refusals, acceptance by a verified identity for the
invited address joining that business and creating none, replay refusal, and the invitation dying with
the account). `tsc`, `eslint` and both module-graph checks clean. **The public surface was also exercised
over HTTP** on a local boot of this tree: `GET /invite` answers **200** for a well-formed token and emits
the constant `inventoryai://invite?token=…` link, **400** for a malformed one with **no** request value
reflected; `GET /api/auth/invitation` answers **404 `INVITATION_INVALID`** for an unknown token and
**400** for a malformed one; all three management routes answer **401** unauthenticated; and `/privacy`,
`/terms` and `/account-deletion` each answer **200 text/html**. Mobile **96 suites / 1138 tests / 0
failures** — `mobile/__tests__/invitations.test.tsx` adds **13 cases**, including the token reaching the
real `AuthProvider`'s registration request and being forgotten once a session exists. **Not verified:**
**no device pass** — the invited journey has not been walked on the phone (the link, the registration, a
real inbox) and is suite-proven only *(corrected 2026-10-25: the journey **was** walked on the phone and
this deployed — §27FC)*; **the server change is not deployed at the time of writing**, so
`/invite` and the three management routes are not live yet *(corrected 2026-10-25: deployed — §27FC)*; a **real inbox** was not used (the suite
reads the token out of the recorded message); and iOS remains unverified (no macOS).

# 27FC. The invitation flow, on production and on the phone (2026-10-25)

**Deployment, measurement and one dependency decision — no application behaviour was changed after
§27FA/§27FB; the only code-level change in this pass is a lockfile bump.** §27FA shipped the terms page
and found the audit defect; §27FB shipped invitations. Both were verified against a local boot and a
test database, and both were explicit that nothing was live and nothing had been walked on a handset.
This entry is that gap closed, with the limits that survive it stated at the end.

**1. Deployed, and the deploy is what proved it.** The tree was committed as `33bdd54` (50 files) and
pushed to `main`; Render deploys that branch on commit with `rootDir: server`. Two routes that did not
exist before the push answer on the live host — `GET /terms` **200** and `GET /invite` **200** for a
well-formed token — so the deploy is evidenced by behaviour rather than by a green build log. The full
live surface was then read over HTTPS: `/terms` carries `Cache-Control: no-store`,
`Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, `nosniff` and a CSP with the **computed** `sha256-…` of its inline
stylesheet; `/privacy` and `/account-deletion` each link to it; `/invite` answers **400** for a missing
or malformed token and forwards a well-formed one to the constant `inventoryai://invite?token=…`;
`GET /api/auth/invitation` answers a real pending row with exactly `email`, `role`, `businessName`,
`expiresAt`; and `GET /api/invitations` answers **401 `AUTH_REQUIRED`** unauthenticated.

**2. Delivered to the installed app over the air, not by rebuilding it.** The phone's build is the
production-profile APK from the 2026-10-24 rehearsal (`versionCode 1`, runtime `1.0.0`, channel
`production`). A JavaScript-only publish to that channel and runtime — group `936e1e55-…`, from
`33bdd54` — put the new screens on the handset on the next cold launch; the run proves which bytes
were loaded by opening a route that exists only in this commit. **No APK was built, downloaded or
installed for this pass**, which is the OTA claim §27EP made now being used for a feature rather than
for a fix.

**3. The invited journey, measured end to end against production.** A throwaway address with no inbox
(`invite.probe.20261025@gmail.com`) was invited into the disposable demo tenant as **STAFF**; the token
and the AUTH-04 code were minted for the run, because the address cannot receive mail (before using the
laptop's pepper to read a code digest, it was **proved** equal to production's by matching a real
reset-code challenge by exhaustive comparison). On the phone: the `inventoryai://invite` deep link
opened the invitation screen naming the address, the business and **Staff**; *Create your account*
opened the **invited** registration shape — no business-name field, the address prefilled and locked,
the person choosing their own password; six digits auto-verified, and the app landed on **the demo
tenant's own inventory** rather than a new workspace. In the production database afterwards: the user's
`businessId` is the **inviting** tenant, role `STAFF`, `emailVerified` true, **no `passwordHash`**, the
business count unchanged at 5 (4 existing + the demo tenant), the invitation `ACCEPTED` with
`acceptedBy`/`acceptedAt`, and one `INVITATION_ACCEPTED` audit row whose metadata is `{ role: 'STAFF' }`
and carries **no address**. Evidence, frames and the full measurement table:
`docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-25-invitations/`.

**4. The same account then deleted itself, and the business survived.** Profile → *Delete account* said
*We will confirm this with your sign-in. You do not need to type your password* — the Firebase-only
path — and after the type-`DELETE` confirmation the app returned to Login. Measured: the row is the
tombstone (`Deleted user`, `deleted+<id>@deleted.invalid`, `firebaseUid` gone), **0** invitations for
that address, **0** sessions, `ACCOUNT_DELETED` with `userId: null` and metadata `{ role: 'STAFF' }`,
Firebase `getUserByEmail` → **`auth/user-not-found`**, and the demo business still present with its one
owner — the §27FA fate rule (a non-owner's departure never closes a tenant) holding on the live path.

**5. Cleanup, and production restored.** The demo tenant was removed with `cleanup:demo-tenant`
(**0 leftovers** over every collection carrying the `businessId`), and a final read of the production
database shows **4 users / 4 businesses / 0 invitations / 0 probe addresses / 0 demo businesses** — the
exact shape before the run. The forward-only records that remain are the `ACCOUNT_DELETED` and
`INVITATION_ACCEPTED` rows the product deliberately keeps, and those were removed with the tenant they
belonged to.

**6. The dependency audit, decided rather than deferred silently.** `npm audit` on the server reported one
**high** and one **moderate** advisory: body-parser accepted trailing bytes after a compressed request
body (a denial of service any caller could start) and `ip-address` could stall on one long string. Both
had a compatible release, so they were raised in the **lockfile only** — body-parser **2.4.0**,
`ip-address` **10.7.4** — with no dependency added, removed or re-declared, and the suite unchanged at
**1359 tests / 1303 pass / 0 fail**. The mobile package still reports **six high** advisories, all inside
Expo's own build tooling (`@expo/cli`, `expo-updates` code-signing dependencies and a bundled `zod`);
their only advertised fix is installing an older Expo, which would undo SDK 58, so they are **recorded
for the upgrade train and deliberately not forced**.

**Verification.** Server `test:unit` **1359 / 1303 pass / 0 fail / 56 skipped**, `test:db` **909 / 814
pass / 0 fail / 95 skipped**, `tsc`, `eslint`, both module-graph checks and `npm audit` (0
vulnerabilities) clean; mobile **96 suites / 1138 tests / 0 failures**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean. Live
checks and the device run are tabulated in the evidence README.

**Not verified:** **Play App Signing and an internal-testing install** — this is a production-profile APK,
not a Play-signed build, so the store path is still the open gate; **an admin sending the invitation from
the Users screen on a device**, and **a real inbox** receiving the mail (the token was minted, not
mailed); **Google Sign-In converging on an invitation** (suite-covered only); **iOS** (no macOS); and the
three residual V1 security items recorded in checklist §52 are unchanged by this pass.

# 27FD. The invitation, sent by an admin and received in a real inbox (2026-10-25)

**Verification only — no code, route, permission, schema, index, dependency, session or environment
change; the only files this entry adds are an evidence directory and this record.** §27FC closed by
naming two gaps it could not close: *an admin sending the invitation from the Users screen on a device*
and *a real inbox receiving the mail*, because the token and the code were minted for that run. Both are
closed here, on the same handset and the same production server, with the same APK — **nothing was
rebuilt, published or installed**, so the bytes under test are the bytes already on the phone.

**1. The admin half, driven on the phone.** Signed in as the demo tenant's **OWNER**, `inventoryai://users/invitations`
opened the Invitations screen; a colleague's address and the **Staff** role produced *Invitation sent to
…*, an emptied form, and a pending row carrying the role, *Pending*, the expiry and a **Revoke** button.
The row was written to the production database with a `PENDING` status and a `tokenHash` that is the
SHA-256 of the token the recipient was mailed.

**2. The mail reached a real inbox, and the link worked from it.** The recipient was a throwaway mailbox
at `guerrillamailblock.com`, read through that provider's API, and this time nothing was hand-minted. The
invitation arrived **34 seconds** after the tap — `You have been invited to join DEMO PREVIEW — safe to
delete on Inventory AI` — and the message's button resolved `302` from Brevo's click host to
`https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com/invite?token=…`, which answered **200** and forwarded to the
constant `inventoryai://invite?token=…`. The mailed token's SHA-256 equals the stored `tokenHash`, so the
link in the inbox is the link for that row. **Two facts this made visible for the first time:** Brevo
**rewrites the link** onto its own click host, so the token exists inside a third party's click URL for as
long as that provider keeps it (it resolves correctly, but the exposure was previously unstated); and the
sender is whatever `MAIL_FROM` holds, which is today a Brevo-branded address that delivers but does not
look like Inventory AI — a domain-verified sender belongs on the store-readiness list.

**3. Revoking removes the capability, not just the row.** A second invitation (role **Manager**) was sent
to a second real inbox and then revoked from the same screen through its confirmation dialog. Afterwards
`GET /api/auth/invitation?token=<revoked>` answered **404 `INVITATION_INVALID`** while the untouched
pending token still answered **200** with its address, role, business name and expiry — the revoked link
stops resolving for anyone who kept a copy, which is what the token-digest rotation in `revoke` is for.

**4. The mailed invitation was accepted end to end.** Signed out, the emailed token opened the invitation
screen naming the address, business, **Staff** and the expiry; *Create your account* opened the invited
registration shape — **no business-name field**, the address prefilled and locked, the person choosing
their own password (18 characters, the live rule hint counting it); `Create Account` created the Firebase
identity and requested the AUTH-04 code; the code mail arrived in the same inbox (*Your Inventory AI
verification code … 855806*); six digits typed **with no press of Verify** auto-verified, the invitation
was accepted, and the app landed on **the inviting tenant's own Inventory** — not a new workspace — with
the profile showing **Staff** and *member since Oct 25, 2026 · 12:53*.

**5. Measured afterwards, in the production database.** The new user's `businessId` is the inviting
tenant, role `STAFF`, status `ACTIVE`, `firebaseUid` set, `emailVerified` true and **no `passwordHash`**;
the invitation is `ACCEPTED` with `acceptedBy`/`acceptedAt`; and the trail holds `INVITATION_SENT`,
`INVITATION_SENT`, `INVITATION_REVOKED` and `INVITATION_ACCEPTED`, every one of whose metadata is
`{ role }` with **no address** in it. The invited member then deleted their own account from the app
(the Firebase-only path, no password prompt): the row is the tombstone with `firebaseUid` gone, **0**
sessions, **0** invitations for the address, `ACCOUNT_DELETED` with `userId: null`, Firebase
`auth/user-not-found`, and the business still standing with its owner — §27FA's fate rule holding for a
member who arrived through an invitation.

**6. Cleanup, and what production looks like now.** `cleanup:demo-tenant` removed the tenant with **0
leftovers** over every collection carrying the `businessId`; production reads **5 users / 4 businesses /
1 invitation**, all of them the owner's pre-existing accounts and an earlier `ACCEPTED` invitation that
this run did not touch, with **0** demo businesses and **0** probe addresses. The throwaway inboxes and
every token, code and password generated for the run were deleted from the laptop afterwards.

**The one thing this run exposed about its own method, recorded because it is a real exposure.** Checking
the Firebase identity with a throwaway script printed the `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON` value into the
local terminal log, because the variable holds **base64** rather than the JSON the check assumed and the
parse error echoed its input. The value is a local credential — it lives in `server/.env`, never entered
the repository and is not in any committed file — but it has now been displayed in a local transcript, so
**rotating that service-account key is the recommended follow-up** (Google Cloud → IAM → the Firebase
Admin service account → new key → replace it in the deployment and in `server/.env`). No application
change is required, and nothing else in the project was affected.

**Still not verified:** **Play App Signing and an internal-testing install** (this is a production-profile
APK); **Google Sign-In converging on an invitation** (suite-covered); an **ADMIN** sending and the
ADMIN-cannot-invite-ADMIN refusal on a device (suite-covered); and **iOS**, which stays environment-blocked.
The three residual V1 security items in checklist §52 are unchanged. Evidence, frames and the full
measurement table: `docs/evidence/device-runs/2026-10-25-invitations-admin/`. Roadmap §27FB, §27FC.

# 27FE. Release notes: a card that says what changed, and a version to quote (2026-10-25)

**Mobile only — no route, permission, schema, index, dependency, session-model, environment or server
change.** Over-the-air updates had been silent by design (§27EP, §27ER): a copy change simply appeared
on the next launch. The guide that records that behaviour (`docs/guides/7-over-the-air-updates.md`
§7A) could previously describe a What's New card only as something that *could* be built. It is now
built, and it answers the question that started the work: **how will a user know the app changed, and
how can an important change be announced without a new build?**

**The feature.** `mobile/lib/releaseNotes.ts` holds the notes themselves — three ship in this bundle
(this screen, invitations, the legal pages and account deletion). `mobile/hooks/useReleaseNotes.ts`
reduces the whole rule to `seenId !== latest.id`; the marker is one note id in `expo-secure-store`
(`mobile/lib/releaseNotesSeen.ts`), so nothing is added to the server and the list renders offline.
`mobile/components/WhatsNewCard.tsx` renders on the dashboard, below the stale-data warning and above
Overview. **"Got it"** dismisses, **"See what's new"** opens `mobile/app/(app)/whats-new.tsx`, which
lists every note newest first and is also reachable from a new **Profile → About** card. **Both actions
acknowledge**, so a note cannot return; a bundle with no new note announces nothing; and **a failed
storage read shows the card** rather than swallowing the message.

**Profile → About also shows `App version`**, read from `expo-constants` (never typed by hand), which is
the same number `app.json` and `runtimeVersion` use. It is the first place the app states its own
version: without it, "did the update arrive?" was unanswerable from the phone. It deliberately does not
read `Updates.updateId`, so the **version is quotable and the bundle is not** — and the guide says so
rather than implying more than the code does.

**Decisions recorded, not implemented.** The **restart-to-apply prompt is deferred** by the owner
(2026-10-25): safe publishing, and a correct OTA on both a preview build and the store build, come
first. Its precondition is written into the guide — it may only ever be offered when **no form holds
unsaved input**, because `reloadAsync()` discards typing with no prompt and no undo. The **notes stay in
the bundle** rather than in a collection or an endpoint: the note ships with the code it describes, needs
no route, permission or secret, and cannot announce something this build does not have. The cost is
stated plainly in the guide — writing one is a code edit plus a publish, not a dashboard edit — and a
server-driven list is recorded as the upgrade path, not smuggled in now.

**Tests.** New `mobile/__tests__/release-notes.test.tsx`, **21 cases**: unique non-empty ids, newest-first
order, the announced note being the first, date formatting that cannot shift by timezone, the card's two
actions, the marker's six behaviours (unseen when nothing is stored, quiet when acknowledged, re-announced
when a newer note arrives, flipped and written on acknowledge, fail-open on a read error, no wait on a
failed write), the screen's exits with and without history, and four dashboard cases proving the card
appears, acknowledges on both actions and never returns. It also pinned the test library's contract in
this repo: **`fireEvent` is async in RNTL 14**, and an un-awaited press leaves an act scope open, which
makes every later render in that file commit nothing.

**Verification.** Mobile **97 suites / 1162 tests / 0 failures**, `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean. No server
file was touched, so its baselines stand unchanged.

**Published, and measured on the phone (2026-10-25, 14:44 local).**
`eas update --channel production --environment production --platform android` published group
`f8ca02a3-5b4e-4f2c-948f-c53825736301` at commit `4c0a60a` (runtime `1.0.0`, Android update
`01a171cd-8fa4-70ff-ae3f-b13e9fd48bb1`) — JavaScript only, no build, no install. On the OPPO CPH1969 the
next launch logged `UpdatesController onBackgroundUpdateFinished: Update available` →
`DownloadCompleteWithUpdate` (`isUpdatePending=true`) → `ErrorRecovery: remote load status changed:
NEW_UPDATE_LOADED`; the force-stop and relaunch after it ran the bundle with **no `FATAL EXCEPTION` and
no JavaScript error**, and the app rendered normally. **The new route is in the running bundle and its
guard holds:** the handset was signed out (its old session had ended — this change writes only its own
marker and never touches the token, so it cannot have caused that), and `inventoryai://whats-new`
answered **Login**; a bundle without this screen would have rendered the unmatched-route page instead.

**Still not seen: the card itself.** The dashboard needs a signed-in session, and this host resolves **no
MongoDB database** (`config/env.ts` reports no URI), so the documented `seed:demo-tenant` route to a
demo sign-in was unavailable and no production record was touched. Everything below the screen — the
marker, the card, both actions, the list, the dashboard wiring — is covered by the **21 cases** above; the
one sentence this entry cannot yet write is "the card appeared on the handset". iOS unverified. Guide
§7A.1 is the operating record.

# 27FF. A publish that no commit described, and a dismissal that was not final (2026-10-25)

**Mobile and documentation — no route, permission, schema, index, dependency, session-model,
environment or server change.** This entry is a review of the update workflow, requested by the owner
after the first live over-the-air publish (§27FE), and it records two defects the publish exposed, both
of which are now fixed, plus the corrective publish that is serving production today.

**What the owner did, and what it proved.** On the production-profile build on the OPPO, the owner
drove the What's New card end to end **without USB, without mirroring and without building or
installing anything**: the note appeared, the app had changed, and the change had arrived over the air.
That is the first confirmation of the OTA path from the person holding the phone rather than from a
logcat read, and it is the strongest evidence this guide has that "silent JavaScript update" is real
here and not just configured.

The same run also published a second note — *A small test update* — to `production` (group
`48f7bbcc-64d6-46f4-8475-8aabe1b09f7a`, runtime `1.0.0`, update `01a17205-70d2-73d9-9125-1908e22d59ed`,
created `2026-10-25T07:45:21Z`) together with one sentence on the login screen. Both edits were then
**undone on the laptop, and nothing was published again**. The repository was clean and `main` was
committed. The channel was not: production kept serving the test note to every install.

**The workflow defect, stated exactly.** `eas update` publishes the **working tree**, not a commit,
and this CLI gives an operator no way to notice afterwards: `update:list --json` returns `branch`,
`message`, `runtimeVersion`, `group` and `platforms`, and **no commit hash at all** (checked against
`eas-cli/24.7.0`, installed here). So a bundle that no commit describes is undetectable downstream —
`eas update` prints the commit when it publishes, but nothing later can be joined back to git. A save
is a draft; only a commit is a release, and nothing enforced that sentence.

**The code defect it exposed, which is the more serious of the two.** The release-note marker was a
**single stored id**, and `seenId !== latest.id` cannot distinguish "a newer note arrived" from "this
bundle is older than the last one". A rollback, a republish of an earlier group, or simply deleting
the newest note from `RELEASE_NOTES` makes `latest` go **backwards**, and the note somebody had already
dismissed announced itself again. The remedy for a bad publish is exactly one of those actions, so the
one moment the marker mattered most was the moment it was wrong. It is now the **set of acknowledged
ids** (`lib/releaseNotesSeen.ts`), capped at **100** with the newest kept, read through the single id
the old build wrote under `…releaseNotes.seenId` so an upgrade loses nothing; the hook tests
membership (`!seenIds.includes(latest.id)`) and **refuses to write before the stored list has been
read**, because writing in that window would replace every earlier dismissal with one id. Fail-open is
preserved in both directions: an unreadable marker still shows the card, and a device that never
acknowledged a note is still told about it.

**The workflow fix.** New `mobile/scripts/check-ota-publish.mjs`, run as `npm run check:ota`. It
refuses any modified or untracked path in the repository (with `--allow-dirty` for the genuine
emergency, printed as a warning), re-checks the contract that decides delivery at the moment somebody
is about to reach every phone — `runtimeVersion.policy === "appVersion"`, `updates.enabled`,
`checkAutomatically: "ON_LOAD"`, `fallbackToCacheTimeout: 0`, a project URL, and a build profile whose
channel is the one being published to — and prints the exact publish command, so `--platform android`
stops being the flag that is forgotten. It **warns** rather than fails on a non-`main` branch and on
commits absent from `origin/main`: both are legitimate, and both change what the printed commit hash
means later. It does not run the tests and does not read the EAS environment store; those are
`npm test` and `check:build-env --live`.

**Verification.** `mobile/__tests__/release-notes.test.tsx` is now **31 cases** (10 new): the two
rollback directions (a newer note acknowledged before an older bundle suppresses it; a note never
acknowledged still appears), merge-on-write, the unread-window refusal, and six marker-file cases
(list read, legacy single-id migration, dedupe, the 100-id cap, a read failure, a write failure). The
two `*rollback*` cases fail against the old `seenId !== latest.id` rule. Mobile **97 suites / 1172
tests / 0 failures**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean; the docs-integrity and route-inventory guards **16/16**,
the secret guard clean over **852 files**, `check:build-env` clean for all four profiles. The preflight
was proven **both ways**: on the dirty tree it exited **1** with six findings naming the five paths, and
after the commit it printed `ready` and exited **0**.

**The corrective publish, and how it was verified without a phone.** `0547569` published
`production` group **`62654350-7268-487f-8518-8ca7b6a8dfc9`** (update `01a17222-d4c1-718f-8b0f-f1f07bef4275`,
created `2026-10-25T08:17:27Z`), which withdraws the test note. The channel's own manifest now reports
`"updateGroup":"62654350-…"`, so the served bundle is the committed one — a check that needs no device
and is now written into the guide (§7), including its two measured constraints: `accept:
multipart/mixed` is mandatory (the host answers **406** without it) and the bundle/asset URLs answer
**403** to a plain `curl`, so the command proves **which group** is served, not its contents. For the
contents, the export the publish had just made was read: `A small test update` **absent**, the three
real notes **present**, and a control string (`Hello`) absent, which is what makes the first two
readings mean anything.

**Still open, recorded rather than rounded off.** There is **no preview install** on the handset, so
every OTA still goes to `production` first and the phone is the only staging environment (§12.1);
**code signing is off** (§12.2); `update:list` still cannot be joined to git (§12.7); and the app shows
its **version** but not `Updates.updateId` (§12.8), so a support conversation can establish the build but
not the bundle. The guide's §6 now carries the incident as the reason its first step is a tool, §7A.1
states that a dismissal is final in both directions, §9 gained the "a note you deleted is still on the
phone" row, and §12/§15 were reconciled. Nothing was written to production to manufacture a demo
session: the corrective publish is the only production write in this entry.

# 27FG. A large tenant in production, and the assistant measured there (2026-10-25)

**Server tooling and documentation — two new commands (plus one sign-in helper module), one shared
guard, one probe flag, one test-guard extension, and the evidence folder. No route, permission, permission matrix, schema, index, dependency,
session-model, mobile, environment variable or deployment change.** The owner asked for the
development seeders' production equivalent, and for the assistant to be exercised against a large
production dataset from the deployed server.

**The gap, stated exactly.** `seed:perf` is the query-measurement tool. It refuses production by
design (`assertSafeTarget`), writes no suppliers or purchase orders, and **creates no login** — so its
tenant can never be opened in the app. The only database a store build reaches is
`inventoryai_prod_db`, and the assistant a phone talks to is the deployed one. A "large dataset on the
phone, answered in production" therefore could not be built from the existing commands without
weakening the guard their other callers rely on.

**New commands, with guards that make the target deliberate rather than merely permitted.**
`npm run seed:perf-tenant` and `npm run cleanup:perf-tenant` resolve through a new
`assertNamedDatabaseTarget` in `server/scripts/perf/lib.mjs`: `--database=<name>` is **required** and
must equal the database `config/env.ts` actually resolved (the URI's path segment never decides it),
the **test** database is refused outright, and each command requires a phrase **of its own**
(`seed:perf-tenant` / `cleanup:perf-tenant`) rather than `seed:perf`'s `seed-perf-ai` — so a shell
history entry cannot reach the wrong tool. Production is allowed here on purpose, because that is the
only place the deployed assistant can be given a dataset; everything else keeps refusing it.

**What the seeder does.** It creates the fingerprinted tenant (`PERF SEED — AI assistant stress test
(do not use)`) and one verified `OWNER` identity (`perf-seed-ai@example.invalid`, a reserved domain
that cannot receive mail) **in that tenant only**, attaching the uid through the same `resolveIdentity`
helper `seed:demo` uses — which is also why a re-run **refreshes** the password from
`DEMO_ACCOUNT_PASSWORD` instead of silently keeping the first run's. It writes through the same
`seedTenant` core as `seed:demo` (categories, locations, suppliers, products, inventory, purchase
orders with real receipt movements) and then, before printing OK, **re-counts every collection,
re-checks the arithmetic of every stock movement and asserts the `SEEDSKU-0` anchor** the probe asks
about. The cleanup deletes only the `businessId` both fingerprints agree on, **refuses** when they
disagree (the one state in which it could reach a stranger's business), **re-queries to prove 0
documents remain**, and **keeps the Firebase identity** — F-50, because the reverse direction is the
unrecoverable one. It is not, and cannot become, `cleanup:prod-mongodb`.

**New probe capability: `perf:turns --login`.** A deployed server's `JWT_SECRET` is not on a laptop
(correctly), so the locally minted session the probe used was refused there. `scripts/perf/firebaseLogin.mjs`
now signs in through Firebase's REST password endpoint and exchanges the ID token at the
application's own `POST /api/auth/firebase/exchange` — the production authentication path itself, not
a copy of it. The public web API key is passed in (`EXPO_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_API_KEY` or
`--firebase-api-key=`), no token is printed, and no credential is written to a file. Because the
probe also reads its ground truth from the database, anything outside development/test must be
**named** with `--database=` and confirmed with `PERF_TURNS_CONFIRM=perf-turns:production`
(`assertMeasurementTarget`), before a session is minted or a request spent.

**Measured on production, 2026-10-25.** `--size=60000` wrote 18 categories, 6 locations, 240
suppliers, **13,500 products**, 27,200 inventory rows, 17,836 movements and 1,200 purchase orders in
**110 s**, and the read-back found no problems. `perf:turns --login` against
`https://ai-inventory-l1mi.onrender.com` then **answered 6/6 and grounded 6/6**: 3,275 / 3,380 /
4,220 / 5,938 / 7,366 / **13,321 ms** (slowest 13.3 s), one tool call per question
(`getInventorySummary` ×3, `getReorderNeededProducts`, `getProduct`, `getLocationBreakdown`),
`nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free`, no degraded mark, with the allowance at 43/50 before the run.
Evidence: `docs/evidence/production-ai-scale-2026-10-25/` (the seed output and the probe's own
`turns.json`, checked to contain no token or credential field).

**Verification.** `server/test/script-environment-guards.test.mjs` gained the new refusals — a missing
`--database=`, one the run is not connected to, the test database, a wrong phrase — the measurement
path's two production terms (un-named or unconfirmed refused; named and confirmed allowed), and the two
new scripts joined the "every data-touching script calls a guard" scan, which now reads **11** rather
than keeping its old list. Documentation: guide 6 gained **Part 3G** (the production pair, both guards,
the `NODE_ENV=production` + `MONGODB_DB_NAME` interaction and the measured timings) and the
**Measuring the deployed assistant** section in Part 4, with both tables and the command tables
updated; guide 4 now points at 3G from its throwaway-tenant section. `server/.env.example` was not
touched: these commands read the existing `MONGODB_URI`, `DEMO_ACCOUNT_PASSWORD` and
`EXPO_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_API_KEY`, and add no variable of their own.

**Verified this pass.** Server `test:unit` **1371 tests / 1315 pass / 0 fail / 56 skipped**,
`typecheck`, `eslint`, both module-graph checks (549 modules) and the repository secret guard
(**853 files**) clean; the two production runs above; and a read-only production probe confirming the
tenant's product and stock counts and its linked, verified `OWNER` before the measurement.

**Still open, recorded rather than rounded off.** The seeded tenant is **left in place** so the owner
can sign in to it; `cleanup:perf-tenant` removes it and proves 0 remaining, and the Firebase identity
survives by design. The probe's password was generated for the run, never printed and not stored, so
signing in from the phone needs a re-run with a password the owner chooses (which also resets the
tenant's data). **What is not proven:** a phone signed in to this production tenant (the OPPO runs are
separate evidence), the same latency spread above ~13,500 products, and provider behaviour on a day
with less allowance. The run is one sample, not a benchmark.

# 27FH. Production seeding through the same commands (2026-10-25)

**Server tooling and documentation — two guard additions, one shared tenant-naming rule, four CLIs
and their guard tests. No route, permission, schema, index, dependency, session-model, mobile,
environment-variable or deployment change.** The owner asked for the production database to support
large-scale seeding and assistant testing the same way development does; §27FG had added one
dedicated-tenant pair, but the commands the guides actually teach (`seed:demo`, `seed:accounts`,
`seed:roles`, `verify:demo`) still refused production, so a dataset inside the owner's **own**
deployment could not be built with them.

**The rule, stated once.** Naming the database is what makes production reachable. `assertSafeTarget`
gained an optional `database` — the `--database=` value — and, when it is present, hands the decision
to the existing `assertNamedDatabaseTarget` (the name must equal the database `config/env.ts`
resolved, the test database is refused, the command's own phrase is still required). Called without
it, the guard is exactly the development-only check it has always been, so a shell that forgets the
flag cannot reach a real deployment. The same change makes `seed:demo-tenant`/`cleanup:demo-tenant`'s
story and the account seeders' story one story rather than two.

**The second act a destructive run needs.** Those commands replace a tenant's data, so `seed:demo`
and `seed:accounts` require the business being reset to be **named** in production, through a shared
`assertTenantNamedForReset`: `--business=<id>` for one account, the third field of
`--accounts="address:documents:businessId"` for several. A brand-new tenant has no id to name until
the run creates it, and creating one deletes nothing, so creation is allowed without it; once the
business exists, a missing or mismatched id is refused **before** `clearTenantData`. `seed:accounts`
additionally **refuses its default plan** in production — that plan exists to compare three sizes in
development and would otherwise reset three real businesses — so every production account must be
listed explicitly.

**Credentials are not seed data.** `resolveIdentity` gained `refreshPassword` (default true, preserving
the behaviour §27BB introduced for test identities). The account seeders pass `!production`, so an
**existing** login in a real deployment is never given a new password by a seeding run; only a
brand-new identity gets the one supplied in `DEMO_ACCOUNT_PASSWORD`, because it has none otherwise.
The commands that own their addresses (`seed:perf-tenant`, `seed:roles`) keep rotating theirs, which
is how their password is set.

**The rest of the surface.** `seed:roles`/`cleanup:roles` take `--database=` like every other seeder
and still find the fixture by its two fingerprints, never by a supplied id. `verify:roles` takes it
too, and refuses `--signin`-less runs against a remote `--base`: a session minted locally is signed
with the laptop's `JWT_SECRET`, which the deployed server does not share, and reporting that as 96
role mismatches would be a false alarm. `verify:demo` is read-only and gained
`assertNamedReadTarget`: development and test need no naming, anything else must be named, and there
is deliberately no phrase because nothing is written, deleted or spent.

**Measured on production, 2026-10-25 — read-only and dry-run only, deliberately.**
`verify:demo --database=inventoryai_prod_db` read the 60,000-document tenant §27FG seeded back and
printed `(PRODUCTION)`: 18 categories, 6 locations, 240 suppliers, **13,500 products**, **27,200**
stock rows, **17,836** movements, **1,200** purchase orders, ledger arithmetic and referential
integrity clean, 2,109 products at or below minimum. `seed:demo` refused a missing `--business=` and,
separately, a wrong one, each before a write and each naming the tenant it would have replaced.
`seed:accounts` refused the default plan and accepted an explicit tenant-named plan under
`--dry-run`; `seed:roles --dry-run` printed the named database and the four reserved addresses. **No
production write was performed**: the existing tenant was left exactly as §27FG left it, because
replacing real data to prove a guard is not a test this project should run.

**Verification.** `server/test/script-environment-guards.test.mjs` grew from 23 to **39** cases: the
named form's acceptance under the command's own phrase, its refusals (no `--database=`, a name the
run is not connected to, the test database, another command's phrase), the read-only guard's naming
rule and lack of a phrase, the shared tenant-naming rule in all four states (development, new
tenant, missing id, wrong id, matching id), and a source pin that both account seeders pass
`refreshPassword: !production`. `verify-role-access.mjs` and `verify-demo-data.mjs` joined the
"every data-touching script calls a guard" scan. Server `test:unit` **1387 / 1331 pass / 0 fail / 56
skipped**, `test:db` **909 / 814 pass / 0 fail / 95 skipped**, `tsc`, `eslint`, both module-graph
checks (549 modules) clean. Documentation: guide 6's Part 3 intro and tables, Part 3G rewritten as
G.1 (dedicated tenant), G.2 (your own account, id first), G.3 (several accounts and the role
fixture) and G.4 (verify), Part 6's exceptions paragraph and the quick-reference table; guide 4's
database table, safety-net list and section A.

**Not proven, recorded rather than implied.** A production write through `seed:demo`,
`seed:accounts` or `seed:roles` was **not executed** in this pass — only their guards and dry runs
were. The write path itself is the one `seed:perf-tenant` exercised at 60,000 documents, plus the
tenant-naming check measured above; a first real run should be a small `--total` against a business
the owner is willing to replace. `seed:demo`'s suggested `perf:turns` line hardcodes this project's
deployment host, as the guide already did. iOS remains unverified.

# 27FI. Emptying a tenant without deleting its login, and a repeat at 80,000 (2026-10-25)

**Server tooling and documentation — one new command, one guard parameter, one raised cap, one
corrected printed command and one new guard case. No route, permission, permission matrix, schema,
index, dependency, session-model, mobile, environment-variable or deployment change.** §27FH made
production seeding possible, but left a gap the owner met immediately: `seed:demo` has a reset (re-run
it) and `seed:perf-tenant` has a teardown, but a dataset written into the owner's **own** business had
no way back except a whole-database wipe or a re-seed at a smaller `--total`. Guide 6 said so in as
many words (*"There is no `cleanup:demo`"*). That is not a repeatable test cycle.

**`npm run cleanup:demo`** (`scripts/cleanup-demo-account.mjs`) removes **one tenant's data** and
nothing else: inventory, movements, purchase orders, products, categories, locations, suppliers,
audit rows, invitations and the assistant's conversations and messages — the shared
`clearTenantData` list, so it cannot drift from account deletion's or the other cleanups' idea of
"this tenant's data". It then re-reads the same collections and prints `verification found 0
remaining`. Its `--dry-run` counts the same collections in the same order and prints `would remove
N document(s); nothing was deleted.` **It keeps the MongoDB user, the business row, its members, every session and the
Firebase identity**, deliberately: deleting a login whose database record still exists is the one
unrecoverable state (F-50), and emptying a business is reversible by re-seeding it. The command is
the data-only half of account deletion, usable on a live test account.

**Two identifiers, and they must agree.** `--email=` resolves the account; `--business=` names what
will be deleted; a mismatch is refused before `clearTenantData`, and the id is validated as a
24-character object id before connecting. Needing both is what makes a typo a refusal instead of a
different tenant — the email decides *which account*, the flag decides *which tenant*, and neither
is allowed to answer the other's question.

**`assertSafeTarget` gained `confirmEnvVar`** (default `SEED_CONFIRM`). A cleanup reads
`CLEANUP_CONFIRM=cleanup:demo-account`, so a `SEED_CONFIRM` left exported in a shell cannot satisfy a
destructive command, and the two families stay separate while sharing one target rule. Without
`--database=` the command is development-only like every other seeder; with it, the name must equal
the resolved database, the test database is refused, and the phrase is required.

**The cap went from 60,000 to 400,000 documents** in `seed:perf-tenant` (the same ceiling
`seed:demo` already had), because the 60,000 cap was arbitrary and the owner asked for 80,000-scale
tests. `--size` is documents across all collections; 80,000 is 18,000 products.

**Measured on production, 2026-10-25.** `seed:perf-tenant --database=inventoryai_prod_db
--size=80000` reused the fingerprinted tenant, removed 60,016 rows from the previous run and wrote
**24 categories, 6 locations, 300 suppliers, 18,000 products, 36,104 inventory rows, 23,966
movements, 1,600 purchase orders** in **171,465 ms**, with no read-back problems. `perf:turns
--login` then answered questions 1–2, **2/2 grounded**, in **8,713** and **16,419 ms** (18,000
active / 2,777 low / 1,109 out of stock; reorder total 2,777), one tool call each, starting from 20
of the day's 50 free requests. `cleanup:demo` removed **80,006** documents (the dataset plus 1
conversation, 4 messages and 1 audit row) and reported **0 remaining**; a deliberately wrong
`--business=` had already been refused with nothing deleted. Its `--dry-run` was exercised in
development against a 5,000-document tenant: it previewed exactly 5,000 rows and a read-back still
found all 1,125 products. `cleanup:perf-tenant` then removed the
empty tenant (1 user, 2 sessions, 1 business), again 0 remaining, and kept the `.invalid` Firebase
identity. Production now holds no seed tenant. Evidence:
`docs/evidence/production-ai-scale-2026-10-25/` (`80k-turns.json` and the README's *Repeat at
80,000* section).

**Two transient connection failures, recorded rather than smoothed over:** `cleanup:perf-tenant`
answered `connect ETIMEDOUT …:27017` twice, and a DNS lookup of the Atlas host failed between the
attempts. The retry a minute later completed. Both failed before any write, so neither left partial
state. Guide 6 Part 9 now names that symptom so it is not mistaken for a guard refusal or a bad
flag.

**The printed next step was wrong for production.** `seed:perf-tenant` printed a `perf:turns` line
without `--base=`, which would have measured `localhost`; it now prints the deployed URL and the
`node --env-file=../mobile/.env scripts/measure-ai-turns.mjs` form, which is what was actually run
and needs no key exported. Documentation: guide 6 G.1 (the 80,000 run), G.2 (the way back, replacing
the *no `cleanup:demo`* paragraph), Part 3G's route table and one-cycle table, Part 4's key note and
80,000 measurement, the quick-reference table and Part 9's network note; guide 4's production routes
(two → three); this record and CLAUDE.md.

**Verification.** `server/test/script-environment-guards.test.mjs` **40** cases (was 39): the new
cleanup joined the guard scan, and a source pin asserts it uses `clearTenantData`, requires
`--business=`, never calls `removeTenant`, and reads `CLEANUP_CONFIRM`. Server `test:unit` **1388 /
1332 pass / 0 fail / 56 skipped**, `tsc`, `eslint` and both module-graph checks clean (550 modules,
2614 relative specifiers, 0 unresolved). `test:db` was not re-run: no server module, model, route or
query changed, and the new command was exercised against production instead. **Still open:** a phone
signed in to this production tenant (it is gone now), a store-signed build, and iOS.

# 27FJ. Two advisories that cannot be fixed here, and the watch that says when they can (2026-10-25)

**Dependency triage and documentation — no route, permission, schema, index, session-model, environment
or application-code change. No package was upgraded, no build or OTA publish was made, and both
alerts remain open.**

GitHub reported two high Dependabot alerts on `mobile/package-lock.json` after the documentation push
(§27FE–§27FI). This entry is the triage the owner asked for: what each advisory is, whether the
vulnerable code can run here, and what the safest upgrade path is. The answer to the last question is
**there is no safe upgrade today**, and the work is therefore to prove that rather than to install
something.

## What the two alerts are, measured rather than summarised

The alerts API was re-read on **2026-10-25**: **two open**, `0` dismissed, `0` auto-dismissed, `8`
fixed. Both rows below come from that API and from the installed tree, not from a scanner summary.

| Alert | Advisory | Sev / CVSS | Installed | Consumer (declared range) | Patched release |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| #10 (opened 2026-10-24) | **GHSA-mrhx-c7xc-m3w5** — `zod` exhausts memory validating an oversized array against a length-unconstrained array schema (CWE-770) | high / **7.5** | `3.25.76`, at `mobile/node_modules/expo/node_modules/zod` | `expo@58.0.16 → @expo/cli@58.1.13`, declares **`^3.25.76`** — and the newest published CLI, 58.1.15, declares the same | **4.6.6** (all 3.x is inside the advisory's `< 4.6.6`) |
| #5 (opened 2026-10-09) | **GHSA-86w9-cpqp-85rv** — `node-forge` accepts extra nested `DigestAlgorithm` elements when verifying RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signatures (CWE-347); an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-33894 | high / **7.5** | `1.4.0` | `expo-updates@58.0.18 → @expo/code-signing-certificates@0.0.7`, declares **`^1.4.0`**; `@expo/cli` declares the same | **none exists** — 1.4.0 is both the newest release (2026-03-24) and inside `<= 1.4.0` |

**Neither package is in a shipped bundle**, and that was measured rather than assumed:

- `expo-updates`' own runtime JavaScript (`node_modules/expo-updates/build/**.js`) contains **no
  reference** to `@expo/code-signing-certificates` or `node-forge`; its dependency on the former is
  used by the CLI-side signing tooling.
- The only files that `require()` node-forge outside the package itself are
  `@expo/code-signing-certificates/build/main.js` and
  `@expo/cli/build/src/run/ios/codeSigning/Security.js` — certificate generation and iOS keychain
  signing, both on a developer's machine.
- `zod` is reached by `@expo/cli` from exactly two files, `DevToolsPlugin.schema.js` and
  `createMCPDevToolsExtensionSchema.js`: the **dev-server** plugin-manifest validator. Its input is a
  developer's own local plugin descriptor, not attacker-supplied data, and it never runs inside the
  app, the API server or an EAS build.

Both advisories also need a precondition this repository does not supply: the zod one needs an
application to validate a large attacker-controlled array, and the node-forge one needs an application
that **verifies** an untrusted RSA signature — here the package only generates certificates and reads
Apple-signed ones from the keychain.

## Why no override, and what `READY` will mean

An `overrides` entry can force either version past its consumer's declared range. It was refused, for
the reason the owner's instruction names: that is an unreviewed upgrade of build tooling, and it would
buy a silenced alert rather than a fixed risk.

- **zod** — 4.6.7 is patched, but `@expo/cli` declares `^3.25.76`. Forcing zod 4 into a v3 consumer is
  a major-version substitution inside a dependency Expo owns; the failure mode would land in `expo
  start`'s plugin validation or, worse, in an EAS build, for code that never runs in the product. The
  fix belongs to Expo, and it is a one-line range change upstream.
- **node-forge** — there is **nothing to upgrade to**. No release outside `<= 1.4.0` has been
  published, so no bump, override or patch can close it. This is the same state §27AK recorded, now
  re-measured five weeks later.

What can be automated is the question "has upstream moved yet?". `scripts/check-upgrade-watches.mjs`
gained a **generic advisory gate** — `decideAdvisoryUpgrade` — that answers `READY` only when a
published release is **both** outside the advisory's range **and** admitted by the consumer's own
declared range, which is precisely the condition under which a plain bump closes the alert with no
override. Two watches now use it (`zod (advisory)`, `node-forge (advisory)`), reading the advisory from
GitHub's public API and the consumer range from the **installed** manifests.

## One watch retired, and a prediction that came true

While re-reading the alerts, `decode-uri-component` was found **fixed** — `fixed_at
2026-10-24T14:39:37Z` — and the package is now **absent from the lockfile entirely** (`0` occurrences).
The route was the one §27AK predicted: `expo-router` 58 no longer depends on `query-string`, so the
CommonJS consumer that made 0.5.0 unusable is gone. The watch that tracked it, its CJS-requireability
decider and its eleven controls were **retired** rather than left printing `DEFERRED` about a package
that is no longer installed; the history stays in §27AK/§27CJ and in git. `braces` (3.0.3) and
`sprintf-js` (1.0.3) are still installed and are no longer flagged by the alerts API.

## Verification

The controls are the proof that the new gate can fail in both directions: **23 pass** (`4` must-fire,
`17` must-not-fire, `2` range), including the two live shapes as must-not-fire and a patched release
admitted by its consumer as must-fire in **both** advisory shapes — with a published
`first_patched_version` (zod) and range-only (node-forge). The live report prints both watches
**`DEFERRED`** with the reason in the line: *4.6.7 is patched … but @expo/cli@58.1.13 declares
^3.25.76 — a bump cannot reach it*, and *the newest published release 1.4.0 is still inside the
vulnerable range*. `SECURITY.md`'s known-open row was corrected from the stale four-advisory text it
carried since 2026-10-16 to the two that are actually open.

**No dependency was upgraded by that commit, so no mobile build or test run was owed by it** — and per
the owner's instruction, nothing was published to EAS for a documentation and tooling commit. Both
alerts stay **open**, undispositioned by suppression, until the gate says `READY`.

## The patch bump this entry led to, and the gates it did not move (2026-10-25, same session)

`expo install --fix` was then run against the sanctioned pin table and took the family from
**`expo@58.0.16` to `expo@58.0.19`**: camera 58.0.12, constants 58.0.13, dev-client 58.0.15, font
58.0.10, linking 58.0.14, router 58.0.26, sharing 58.0.20, status-bar 58.0.4, updates 58.0.18 and
jest-expo 58.0.12 — **47 lockfile entries**, every one of them inside the Expo chain (the widest
sideways move being `xcode` 3.0.1 → 4.0.0, which also let `uuid` leave the tree entirely, so the
§27CJ override is now inert). `--fix` exits **1** here by design of this project's own config:
`app.config.js` is dynamic, so the CLI cannot append the `expo-sharing` / `expo-status-bar` plugins
it suggests, and it stops after installing. The three ranges it left behind were set by hand from
`bundledNativeModules.json`, and the SDK-pin guard (`mobile/__tests__/expo-sdk-pins.test.ts`)
**caught a fourth**: `expo-updates` was declared `~58.0.17` while the new SDK pins `~58.0.18` — the
guard doing the job it exists for, not a test to relax. `expo install --check` now answers
**Dependencies are up to date**.

**The advisory gates did not move**, which is the measured answer to the question the bump was for:
`@expo/cli` is now **58.1.15** and still declares **`zod ^3.25.76`**, so that watch stays `DEFERRED`,
and node-forge is still **1.4.0** — its newest release — with no patched version to take. The bump
neither closes nor worsens either alert.

**The native side did move, and that has an operational consequence.** `bundledNativeModules.json`
changed **36 entries** and `expo-modules-core` went **58.0.23 → 58.0.26**, with `expo-modules-jsi`
and `expo-modules-macros` alongside it. The installed `1.0.0` builds on the phone were compiled
against the **previous** native modules, and `runtimeVersion` is `appVersion`, which does not
change — so **an OTA published from this tree would deliver JavaScript expecting native modules
those binaries do not have.** Per the standing rule, **a new build is required before the next
OTA**; nothing was published, built or installed by this entry.

Verification: mobile **97 suites / 1172 tests / 0 failures**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean,
`expo install --check` clean, no invalid or missing entries in `node_modules`, and the watch
self-test unchanged at **23 controls**.
