# 27FK. The runtime boundary made mechanical, and the build that could not run (2026-10-25)

**Mobile tooling and documentation — no route, permission, schema, server behaviour or dependency
change.** `expo.version` and `mobile/package.json` move to **1.0.1**, `check:ota` gains a
native-runtime rule with its own controls, and one new test file (11 cases) pins it. **No build was
produced:** the EAS free plan's Android builds for October are exhausted, and that is recorded here
rather than worked around.

## Why the label had to move

§27FJ's patch bump took `expo-modules-core` **58.0.23 → 58.0.26** under `runtimeVersion: {"policy":
"appVersion"}`, whose label was still `1.0.0`. Every binary on the phone and every artifact in EAS had
been compiled against the old modules. `eas update` would have accepted a publish from that tree — the
label matched — and the incompatibility would have surfaced as a crash *after* the update had already
been installed. The label is the only protection the mechanism offers, so it moves when the native
side does. `1.0.1` rather than `1.1.0`: this is a patch-level SDK refresh, and nothing has been
uploaded to Play, so 1.0.1 becomes the first store version rather than an upgrade to a nonexistent
1.0.0 line.

## What the preflight now refuses

`mobile/scripts/check-ota-publish.mjs` reads a committed record — `mobile/ota-native-runtime.json` — of
the versions the **last build** was compiled with, and compares it with the installed tree:

| Condition | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| No record file | **fail** — no build has claimed this runtime |
| Record missing a version field | **fail** — an incomplete record is not evidence |
| Recorded `appVersion` ≠ `expo.version` | **fail** — a bundle with no installed binary to serve |
| `expo`, `expo-modules-core` or `react-native` moved | **fail**, unless `--allow-native-change` says so out loud |
| All equal | pass, and the publish command is printed |

The record is **deliberately absent** until a build exists; that is why the committed tree refuses to
publish with one finding rather than passing on an assumption. `--allow-native-change` downgrades the
native comparison to a warning but never excuses an unbuilt version — the two questions are different,
and the controls keep them apart.

## The build attempt, and the quota that stopped it

`npx eas-cli build --platform android --profile production --non-interactive --no-wait --json` reached
the upload and fingerprint, incremented the remote `versionCode` **4 → 5**, and then answered:

```
This account has used its Android builds from the Free plan this month, which will reset in 6 days
(on Sun Nov 01 2026). …
    Error: build command failed.
```

No build record was created, so there is no build id to poll; `eas build:version:get` confirms the
remote counter now reads **5**, which means the next successful production build takes **6** and
`versionCode` 5 has no artifact. A gap is harmless to Play (the counter only has to increase), and
rewriting remote versioning to reclaim it would be a risk taken for cosmetics.

**A local Gradle build is not a substitute.** The Android SDK and Android Studio's JDK are on this
laptop, but `google-services.json` and `GoogleService-Info.plist` are **not** (owner decision P-1: they
are injected by EAS as file environment variables), so `expo prebuild` would fail inside the Firebase
plugin; and an APK signed with a debug key cannot install over the EAS-signed app that is already on
the phone. The build waits for the quota to reset or for the plan to change — an owner decision, not a
repository one.

## Verification

Server `test:unit` **1399 tests / 1343 pass / 0 fail / 56 skipped** (11 new; the new file is classified
in `scripts/run-tests.mjs`, which refuses an unclassified suite). Mobile **97 suites / 1172 tests / 0
failures**, `tsc` and `eslint` clean. `check:build-env --profile production --live` and `--profile
preview --live`: no findings. `check:ota` on the committed tree: runtime `1.0.1`, one finding
(`native-record-missing`), exit **1** — the refusal the guard exists for.

CI failed once on the way, honestly recorded: run on `b517657` failed the **server lint** step over an
unused binding in the new test's incomplete-record fixture. The fixture was rebuilt explicitly in
`a47b129`, and run **40199460249** is green on all four jobs (`server`, `mobile`, `secret-guard`,
`attribution-guard`).

## What is still open

The **build** (production AAB + preview APK) once quota allows, the **phone pass** on the `1.0.1`
runtime, then the **record file** written from that build — only after which `check:ota` passes and an
OTA may be published. Code signing before the public build remains open. Nothing was published to
EAS and no store artifact was produced by this entry.

Dependabot **PR #95** was handled separately on the owner's instruction: updated from `main`
(`mongoose` 9.11.3, `eslint` 10.13, `typescript-eslint` 8.72.0 — server only, no security fix), its
four checks passed, and it was **squash-merged as `cbbf7b1`**; `npm ci` and the 1399-test unit suite
were then re-run on this laptop against the merged lockfile and stayed green, and the follow-up CI run
on `cbbf7b1` passed all four jobs.

# 27FL. The session cap the roadmap had twice recommended and never built (2026-10-25)

**Server only — one service rule, one constant and one new DB suite; no route, permission, schema,
index, dependency, mobile or environment change, and nothing deployed or published.**

Two roadmap sections listed *a per-user session cap* under "Still open (recommended, not started)"
(§27EN, §27EO), and the same list still carried invitation onboarding after it had shipped (§27FB).
This increment closes the cap and corrects both lists rather than leaving a second stale
recommendation standing beside the first.

## What was actually unbounded

Since Phase 26A a session is the only thing that makes a token revocable, and nothing limited how many
could exist: every sign-in, every app reinstall and every Firebase exchange minted a row that stayed
usable for the full 14-day absolute cap. `listActiveSessions` capped what the **screen shows** at 50,
but the rows themselves were never bounded, so the only way to end a forgotten device's credential was
`revokeAllSessions` — which signs the owner out of the device in their hand.

## The rule

`MAX_ACTIVE_SESSIONS_PER_USER = 20`, enforced in `createSessionForToken` — the single creation point
for both the legacy login and the Firebase exchange — by `enforceSessionCap`:

| Property | Why it is the property |
| --- | --- |
| newest-first ordering | the session just created is the newest, so a member's sign-in is never what gets revoked |
| oldest rows go first | a member cannot see an idle clock; they can see which device had to sign in again |
| revoked, never deleted | a stale token must not silently resolve to a recreated row |
| an audit row per eviction | `SESSION_REVOKED` with `metadata.reason = "session-cap"`, so a device that signed out is explainable |
| best-effort, never fatal | the login has already succeeded; a cleanup failure is logged and retried on the next sign-in |

20 is a bound, not a policy: a shared shop tablet, a personal phone and the occasional reinstall sit
far below it, so the rule should never fire for an ordinary member. A tight "three devices" cap was
rejected because it signs people out of a device they still use, and a member cannot see or choose
which one — that is a product decision nobody has made.

## What it is not

Not login throttling, and not a shortening of the 14-day cap: a stolen token is live until its session
is revoked or expires, exactly as before. It bounds **accumulation**, so a forgotten credential
eventually stops working, and the existing per-device and sign-out-everywhere controls keep their
current meaning. **A new-device sign-in email remains open** (§27EN/§27EO) — it is the control that
*detects* a takeover, and this one does not.

## Verification

New suite `server/test/AUTH02-session-cap.test.mjs`, classified PURE_DB in `scripts/run-tests.mjs`
(which refuses an unclassified suite): **8 cases** (6 at first, 2 added on deployment day — see the
amendment below), each a direction that matters — the full cap is
held without revoking anything (positive control); crossing it revokes the **oldest** and keeps the
new one; an already-revoked row does not consume a slot; a row past its own cap does not either; the
rule is per account; and the eviction is written to the audit trail with its reason. Against the real
test database, **8 pass / 0 fail**.

**The suite was proved able to fail**: with `enforceSessionCap` commented out it answers
`✖ revokes the OLDEST session …` and `fail 1`; the file was then restored and the call re-asserted
(`grep -c` = 1). Server `test:unit` **1399 / 1343 pass / 0 fail / 56 skipped** (unchanged — the new
suite is DB-only), `tsc` and `eslint` clean, and the four auth suites most exposed to a session rule
(`phaseAUTH03-session-renewal`, `phase03-auth`, `phase07b-auth-security`, `ACCOUNT-DELETION`) ran
**73 tests / 71 pass / 0 fail / 2 skipped**.

**Amended 2026-10-25, on deployment.** Two properties the record above had left as prose are now
pinned as tests: the literal `20` (so changing the bound has to reach the specification's prose too)
and the cleanup-failure path (a simulated write timeout leaves the sign-in working, its session
usable, and the bound exceeded until the next login tries again). That took the suite to **8 cases,
8 pass / 0 fail**.

The commit was then pushed to `main` (`11a9c49`), CI run **40212286545 passed in 5m4s**, and Render
deployed that exact commit — `/api/health` reports `commit: 11a9c498…`, `environment: production`,
`db: connected`, and `/api/health/ready` answers **200**. After the auth-surface probes (`401`
without a token, `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` on an empty body, a uniform `401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS`) the
counters read **0 5xx and no server error**. The rule therefore applies at every session creation
from that moment: it needs no migration, and because a session is a row in MongoDB, the restart
that carried it signed nobody out. What is still **not** verified: a signed-in production session
under the new build — no production credential is held here, so that check needs the owner.

## Limits, recorded rather than rounded off

* **Two concurrent sign-ins can overshoot by one.** Both read the count before either row is written,
  so the next sign-in corrects it. A transaction or a unique-index trick would buy a guarantee nobody
  can observe here.
* **Not on hardware.** No phone run: the change is server-side and invisible in the UI, and the
  runtime that would have carried a client change is the one blocked by the build quota (§27FK).
* **Deployed 2026-10-25** — see the amendment below. The rule is live in production; until that
  deploy it reached nobody.

# 27FN. Three EAS questions answered: the vanished production builds, the quota, and the plan gate on signing (2026-10-26)

**Documentation and read-only verification — no build, no publish, no key generated, no plan change.**
The owner asked whether the production build records were really missing, when the build quota returns,
and how OTA code signing is enabled. Two of the three answers changed what the project should do next.

## 1. The two production builds no longer exist on EAS

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---|
| Builds in the project, all filters cleared (`build:list`, limit 50, 26 returned) | 26, every one `INTERNAL`; **0 `STORE` builds** |
| `build:view 09d77d3d-0f1c-4f8e-948f-7a99ccaa2a56` (the §27ES AAB) | **does not exist** |
| `build:view 4b133d62-30a9-4e18-a7ca-950b06e0cfed` (the §27ET store artifact) | **does not exist** |
| Its artifact URL `…/3sCYPhYme…aab` followed | **HTTP 400** |
| A build from the same day and account `ea941bb7…`, same request | **HTTP 206, bytes served** |

Same project id, same owner, same account, same day — so this is not filtering, pagination, retention
or a transfer: the two records **and their artifacts** were deleted. Nothing in this repository deletes
builds (no `build:delete` in its scripts, docs or workflows), and the CLI exposes no audit trail, so
*which* action removed them cannot be observed from here. What can be stated: the AAB that §27ES inspected cannot be downloaded
again, and a recorded build id is a pointer, not a copy.

**Consequence for the next build.** The build id goes into `mobile/ota-native-runtime.json` and the
evidence record, and it is checked to resolve (`eas build:view <id>`) in the same pass that records it.

## 2. The quota is a calendar month, and October's is spent

Expo's pricing page: the Free plan includes **15 Android and 15 iOS builds a month**. The CLI said on
2026-10-25 that the month's Android builds were used and would reset in six days. No build was
attempted to test that boundary — an attempt that succeeds spends a build, and this pass is not
building anything.

## 3. Code signing is plan-gated, so it cannot be enabled for free

Expo's code-signing guide states it plainly: *"EAS Update Code Signing is only available to accounts
subscribed to the EAS Production or Enterprise plans."* Production is listed at **$199/month**. That
conflicts with the standing constraint — free services only — so signing is **not** being turned on.

The dangerous half-state is worth recording: `codeSigningCertificate` in the app config is compiled
into the binary (CNG regenerates the native project with it). A binary carrying a certificate verifies
every update against it, so a publish that is not signed is **rejected on the device** — the installed
app would keep running its old bundle while the channel claims a newer one. Enabling the config is
therefore not a switch to flip before the plan exists; it is the second half of a build-and-publish
pair. Guide 7 §11 now says so, and §12 no longer recommends doing it "before the public build".

## 4. The preflight, run rather than described

`npm run check:ota` (mobile) answers with exactly one finding — `native-record-missing`: no build has
claimed runtime `1.0.1`, so publishing is refused. That is the guard working as designed, and it stays
in place. Both channels are still `Unprotected`; that is now an accepted residual risk with a named
condition (the plan), not an unfinished task.

## Verification

The four documentation guards (section integrity, route inventory, fact drift, issue records) pass;
the record count and the `CLAUDE.md` index move together to **168**. No test suite was affected: no
server or mobile source changed.

**Not done, deliberately:** no build (quota), no publish (guard), no key pair generated (it would sit
unused and must be backed up by the owner), no plan change (owner decision).

record bodies *are* the evidence — an edited measurement is no longer evidence, and compressing the

specification is the behavioural contract; it is long because behaviour is. The real fix for both is
orientation, not deletion: `docs/README.md` now says plainly that the roadmap is an archive and you
never need to read it to change the project.

**What this pass itself cost:** no source, test, workflow, dependency or configuration file changed.

# 27FP. The advisories re-measured, and no published release can close either (2026-10-26)

**The question was whether a compatible fix had appeared.** None has — and that is now a measurement
rather than a standing assumption. Every package that could carry a fix was asked for its newest
published version, from `mobile/`:

| Package | Installed | Newest published | What it declares |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@expo/cli` | 58.1.15 | **58.1.15** | `zod: ^3.25.76` |
| `expo` | 58.0.19 | **58.0.19** | `@expo/cli: ^58.1.15` |
| `expo-updates` | 58.0.18 | **58.0.18** | `@expo/code-signing-certificates: ^0.0.7` |
| `@expo/code-signing-certificates` | 0.0.7 | **0.0.7** | `node-forge: ^1.4.0` |
| `node-forge` | 1.4.0 | **1.4.0** | itself inside the advisory's `<= 1.4.0` — **no patched release exists** |

A patch inside the current line therefore cannot clear either advisory. Only an `overrides` entry
could, and **D-6 refuses that**: it would install a major the consumer never declared (zod 3 → 4) or
a package that does not exist (a patched forge). `npm audit fix` remains the four-SDK-major downgrade
D-5 rejected. **No dependency was changed.**

**Reachability, named rather than assumed.** The two packages are confined more tightly than "build
tooling" suggests:

- **zod** — imported by exactly **two** files in `@expo/cli`, `start/server/createMCPDevToolsExtensionSchema.js`
  and `start/server/DevToolsPlugin.schema.js`: the DevTools/MCP plugin-manifest validation that
  `expo start` runs on the developer machine. Nothing under `mobile/app|lib|components|hooks` imports it.
- **node-forge** — required only by `@expo/code-signing-certificates/build/main.js`, which `expo-updates`
  reaches from two **CLI scripts** (`cli/build/configureCodeSigningAsync.js`,
  `cli/build/generateCodeSigningAsync.js`) and **not** from `expo-updates/build/index.js`, the module the
  app imports. Code signing is off in this project (§27FN), so neither script runs here.

`npm audit` on 2026-10-26: **`server/` 0**, **`mobile/` 6 entries = 2 advisories**, both high. The
six are dependents, not six defects. D-4 stands, now with D-8 recording that no release can change it.

### OTA readiness, measured on EAS rather than assumed

`eas build:list --platform android` answered with the actual state, which is narrower than "a build
exists":

| Build | Profile | Version | Runtime | Artifact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `18a0af93…` (2026-10-23), `6ee0c10f…`, `4b9a79dd…` | `preview` | 1.0.0 / vc 1 | 1.0.0 | APKs |
| `c23a59ff…`, `b1fecde3…`, `70497184…` | `development` | 1.0.0 / vc 1 | 1.0.0 | APKs |
| — | any `production` | — | — | **none exists** (§27FN deleted both) |

So the phone's installable APK is a **preview** build of runtime **1.0.0**, and the remote production
`versionCode` is **5** with no artifact behind it. Both channels are `Active` / `Unprotected` and both
carry a newest group at runtime `1.0.0`; neither has anything for `1.0.1`.

**`ota-native-runtime.json` was deliberately not written.** It must describe the versions a **build**
was compiled with; writing it from the tree today would claim a binary that does not exist and would
disable the one check that stops a bundle being published to a runtime no install can accept.

### CI caught an over-specified assertion, not a defect

The docs-only push `07c1b0e` failed the server job — **2164 pass, 1 fail** — on
`spends its own attempt on a concurrent invalid confirmation`
(`phaseAUTH04B4-email-verification-confirm.test.mjs`): it expected `attempts === 2` and measured **1**.

**The service is correct in both cases.** The reservation is one conditional `findOneAndUpdate` on
`{ uid, usedAt: null, expiresAt > now, attempts < cap }`, so a submission that arrives after the winner
stamped `usedAt` **misses and spends no attempt** — the locked AD-11/AD-13 behaviour, and the same
answer the miss branch gives every other refusal. The case asserted the interleaving it was written
under ("both reservations are dispatched before either resolves"), which a loaded runner can schedule
the other way. The assertion now accepts **1 or 2** and says why; the property it exists to protect —
a wrong code arriving while the challenge is live spends its own attempt — stays pinned
**deterministically** by `the attempt is spent even though the code was wrong`, and the other side by
`a reservation miss spends no attempt`. **No production file changed.**

Verified locally in unit mode: **19 pass, 1 skipped** (the DB suite); the DB-backed proof is the CI run
on the fix.

**Unchanged and still open:** L-17 (console-only reset action URL), the Play release, iOS verification,
and OTA code signing (plan-gated). None of them was marked complete.

`mobile/package.json` and both lockfiles are untouched, which is the point of the record.

# 27FQ. The empty state the harness could not read, and the production walk it was hiding (2026-10-26)

**The first smoke run on a signed-in production tenant failed a step that was not a defect.** 6/8,
exit 1, stopped at `expect product rows on screen` with *"nothing matches, and the screen is in no
state the harness knows"*. The same screen, read seconds later, was saying *"No products found /
Add your first product to start tracking stock. / Add product"* — a complete, correct empty state in
the app's own words.

**The harness knew two of the app's thirteen empty-state titles.** `EMPTY_COPY` held exactly
`/^Nothing (here yet|to show)\b/i` — the copy the *shared* list shell uses, which is why Inventory
was read correctly and Products was not. Every other screen names its own `emptyTitle`: `No products
found`, `No locations yet`, `No suppliers yet`, `No movements yet`, `No active sessions`, `No items`,
`Nothing left to receive`, … So on a tenant with no data, a screen that had finished loading and had
nothing to show was reported as a **failed assertion** rather than the BLOCKED verdict the harness
already has for exactly that case.

**The fix is the shape those titles share, plus a guard that ties it to the app.** The pattern became
`/^(?:Nothing|No)\b[^.!?]{0,48}$/i` (a short "No …"/"Nothing …" phrase, never a sentence), and
`server/test/device-harness.test.mjs` now **reads every `title`/`emptyTitle` out of `mobile/app`** and
requires each one to be recognised — with a floor of eight titles found, so a scan that silently
returned nothing cannot pass. A rename now breaks a unit test instead of turning an empty list back
into a false failure. The harness suite went from 58 tests to **59**.

**Re-run, same phone, same tenant: 22/24, exit 2** (`2026-10-26T04-51-29-455Z-smoke`). Every one of
the seven screens opened and named itself, all five "loaded without an error" assertions passed, and
the two data assertions reported **BLOCKED** with the copy they saw — `Nothing to show` (Inventory)
and `No products found` (Products) — because the tenant holds none. Exit 2 is the harness's "could not
check", and it is the honest answer: nothing about data was proven either way.

**Third run, once the tenant had a product: 24/24, exit 0** (`2026-10-26T05-27-39-113Z-smoke`), all
seven screens, and both data assertions now proving rows rather than blocks — `4 row(s), e.g. "Smoke
Widget, Smoke shelf, 0 available · 0 on hand, Low, Out"` and `1 row(s), e.g. "SKU SMOKE-1"`. The
BLOCKED verdict was therefore a fact about the tenant, not a soft pass for a broken list.

## The harness could not write, so the write paths were walked by hand — on production

The tenant has no product, no location and no supplier, so `stock`, `transfer`, `label` and `draft`
did not apply (`--product` is an id, and no id exists to pass). Rather than seed a tenant to feed a
harness, the flows were driven through the app itself on the owner's own account, which also tests the
*create* paths the journeys assume have happened already. Every number below is the app's own
confirmation line, read off the screen:

| Flow | The app said |
| --- | --- |
| Create location "Smoke shelf" | appeared in the list as `Active` |
| Create product "Smoke Widget" (SKU `SMOKE-1`, 9.99) | detail shows `SKU SMOKE-1`, `Selling price 9.99`, `No stock yet` |
| Stock in 5 | `Done. Smoke Widget at Smoke shelf: 0 → 5` |
| Stock out 5 | `… Smoke shelf: 5 → 0` |
| Stock in 1 | `… Smoke shelf: 0 → 1`; the transfer form then showed **`AVAILABLE TO TRANSFER 1`** |
| Transfer 1 → "Smoke" | `Smoke shelf: 1 → 0` / `Smoke: 0 → 1` — one confirmation, both legs, one reference `TRF-6adee029e81b7012668a7155` |
| Transfer 1 back | `Smoke: 1 → 0` / `Smoke shelf: 0 → 1` |
| Stock out 1 | `… Smoke shelf: 1 → 0` — the tenant ends net **zero**, as the journeys are designed to |

**The ledger agrees, on a different screen.** Inventory history read *"7 movements, newest first"*
with per-row `from → to`, `+1`/`−1`, timestamps and the **same** transfer reference on both legs of
each transfer; the Inventory list showed `Smoke Widget, Smoke shelf, 1 available · 1 on hand` beside
`Smoke Widget, Smoke, 0 available · 0 on hand` — per-location rows, not one total.

## The assistant answered from the ledger, not from the prompt

Asked on the phone, *"How much Smoke Widget stock do I have, and at which locations?"*, the assistant
answered **"You have 1 Smoke Widget in stock: Smoke shelf – 1 unit available; Smoke – 0 units
available (out of stock / low‑stock) … That's the total on‑hand quantity across both locations"** and
printed its own footer, **`Read: Product search · Inventory rows`**. The number matches the ledger and
the screen, the tools are named, and nothing was written. That is AI tool-calling verified against
production data, not against a fixture.

## Three device behaviours recorded because they cost time

- **An unlinked Google identity is refused, not provisioned.** Signing in with a Google account that
  has no `User` row returned to the login screen with *"This sign-in is not linked to an Inventory AI
  account yet. Create a business account to continue."* — no session, no partial user, no silent
  sign-up. The exchange resolves by `firebaseUid` only, and this is that rule visible on a screen.
- **`uiautomator dump` returned `null root node` for several minutes.** ColorOS's
  `AssistOverlayBottom` / edge-bar windows *were* flagged visible at the time — **and they are visible
  while dumps work, including during the 24/24 run, so they are not established as the cause.**
  **HOME then relaunching the app cleared it**; the harness was not at fault and no code changed. The
  procedure is now in Guide `DEVELOPING_ON_A_PHYSICAL_DEVICE.md` §9b, stated as symptom + workaround
  rather than as a diagnosis.
- **On the product and location forms the inputs are absent from the accessibility dump** while their
  labels are present, so the flows were driven by geometry (tap below the label) and the typed value
  then appeared as text. The login and register screens *do* expose their `EditText` nodes. Not chased
  further and **not claimed as a defect** — recorded because it is both a constraint on this harness
  and a possible screen-reader question for a later pass.

**Residue, stated plainly:** the production tenant now holds two locations (`Smoke shelf`, `Smoke`),
one product (`Smoke Widget`, 0 on hand everywhere) and eight ledger rows. Products are archive-only,
so this is archive-or-keep, not delete. None of it was seeded by a script.

# 27FR. The journeys stopped needing an id, and four false verdicts fell out of it (2026-10-26)

**The obstacle was a number nobody can see.** `stock`, `transfer` and `label` each took
`--product=<id>`, an internal ObjectId. The app displays no id anywhere, so the only way to have one
was to have written it down while seeding the tenant — which made three of the four specialised
journeys unrunnable by anyone who had not. A stale id was worse than useless: a deep link to a
deleted product loads a screen that fails for reasons that look exactly like an app defect.

**A SKU is on the screen, so a SKU is what a journey takes.** Two verbs do the work, both of them
pure-function judgements in `lib.mjs` where CI can assert them:

| Verb | What it does on the phone | The judgement it must pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `findProduct` | types the SKU into the products search, opens the row | the product screen must print that **exact** SKU before any later step acts (`findProductRow`, anchored so `SMOKE-1` cannot select `SMOKE-10`) |
| `pick` | opens the form's own picker, scrolls to the option, taps it | the option must match **exactly and once**, the sheet must **close**, and the field must then show it (`optionTarget`, `sameRow`) |

The name `pick` searches for is not supplied: it is the name the product screen printed, read off
the phone by `findProduct`. `--product` is gone from the runner, and passing it is now an unknown
option rather than a flag that silently does nothing.

## Measured, on the installed preview build against production

| Journey | Steps | Result | The arithmetic the app itself reported |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `smoke` | 24 | **24/24, exit 0** | unchanged by this work — the baseline still holds |
| `stock` | 18 | **18/18, exit 0** | `0 → 5` then `5 → 0` |
| `transfer` | 39 | **39/39, exit 0** | stock in `0 → 1`; `1 → 0` / `0 → 1`; back `1 → 0` / `0 → 1`; stock out `1 → 0` |
| `label` | 2 of 7 | **blocked, exit 2** | `findProduct` passed; `readCode` blocked — this product has no barcode, and the build is not debuggable (`run-as: package not debuggable`) |
| `draft` | 4 of 14 | **blocked, exit 2** | no sheet opened for `Supplier` — the tenant has no suppliers, so the picker is disabled |

The transfer journey now stocks its own unit in and out. A transfer moves stock that must already
exist, so on a source location at zero the form's submit is **disabled** ("Only 0 available to
move"), and the first run at 39 steps reported a failed movement on an app that was right to refuse.
Supplying one unit and removing it at the end leaves the tenant where it started at any starting
quantity.

## Four false verdicts, and what now prevents each

1. **"The Products screen has no search box" on an app that was still booting.** A deep link into a
   cold-started build lands on *Restoring session…*; a 15 s budget called that a missing control
   and FAILED the step. The wait is 30 s, and the failure text now names the state it found.
2. **A one-product sheet reported as ambiguous.** Two separate mistakes, both measured: the sheet's
   search box carries the typed text as its own label (so it counted as a second option), and one
   row reaches the tree **more than once** (a `ViewGroup` `[0,1422][1080,1575]` and its `TextView`
   `[48,1467][1032,1530]`). `optionTarget` now skips edit boxes and clusters duplicates by
   **overlapping band on screen** (`sameRow`) — identity is the row, not the node count.
3. **`tapFirst` reported PASS by tapping a form row.** On a tenant with no suppliers the picker is
   **disabled**, so no sheet opens; the form's own `Supplier *` label carries the same word as the
   sheet heading, so it was taken as one and the control below it was tapped. The purchase order then
   failed with *"Supplier is required."* — a false green pointing at the wrong control. Every sheet
   renders a labelled **`Done`**, so `hasSheetClose` is now the gate, and an unopened picker is
   **BLOCKED** (nothing to choose here) rather than a defect.
4. **A blocked precondition kept running.** With no barcode the `label` journey blocked at
   `readCode` and then FAILED the next step with `expected "Barcode label"` — an app defect invented
   on a product that simply has no barcode. A blocked step now ends the journey, except `expectData`,
   whose "this tenant has no rows" says nothing about the next screen.

## An app defect found and NOT fixed, on purpose

**A searchable picker hides the results it just filtered.** With the keyboard up, the product sheet
was 530 px tall and its only row sat in the hierarchy at `[0,1422][1080,1575]` while being painted
**nowhere** — the screenshot shows empty space above the IME. With the keyboard down the same row is
at `[0,2055][1080,2208]` and tappable. `BACK` and `ESCAPE` both close the whole sheet (the `Modal`'s
request-close), so there is no keyboard-only dismissal: type a filter and there is no way to press
what it found.

It is recorded rather than fixed because **it cannot be verified from here**. The installed app is a
preview APK of this code; a JavaScript change needs a new build, the free plan's October Android
quota is spent, and publishing an OTA is exactly what the preflight gate refuses
(`native-record-missing`). A layout change shipped blind is the failure this repository's records
exist to prevent. The harness therefore reaches picker rows by **scrolling**, which needs no keyboard
and is a gesture a person can make.

## Verification

- `node --test test/device-harness.test.mjs` — **71 pass, 0 fail**, including a control per judgement
  above: a prefix SKU that must not match, the search-box twin, duplicated rows of one option, the
  form label that is not a sheet, and the two malformed verbs `validateJourneys` must refuse.
- `node scripts/device/run.mjs --self-test` — **5 journeys, 102 steps, controls pass**.
- Six device runs of 2026-10-26 in `docs/evidence/device-runs/`, each kept because it proves a
  different thing: `11-03` stock **18/18**, `11-22` transfer failing at **available 0** (the finding
  that made the journey supply its own unit), `11-25` transfer **39/39**, `11-35` label **blocked** at
  `readCode`, `11-36` smoke **24/24**, `11-42` draft **blocked** at the unopened `Supplier` sheet.
  The intermediate iterations were deleted; their findings are the four fixes above.
- No application source changed: `mobile/` and `server/src/` are untouched, and the only code edited
  is `scripts/device/{lib,journeys,run}.mjs` plus its test.

**Unchanged and still open:** both mobile advisories (§27FP — still no patched release), the OTA

supplier to exist before it can run, and `label` needs a product with an EAN-13 on a debuggable build.
None of the three was marked complete.

# 27FS. Two phrases that were both required and only one documented, and the cleanup guard that could not see its own trap (2026-10-26)

**The question.** `cleanup:prod-mongodb` refused to run with `CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM=DELETE-PRODUCTION-DATA`
set, and the documentation read as though that one variable were enough.

**It was by design, and the documentation was the defect.** Two independent gates answer two different
questions: `CLEANUP_CONFIRM` names *which command* (its own name, `cleanup:prod-mongodb`), and
`CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM` acknowledges that the data is real. Neither may substitute for the other — a
habitually exported `CLEANUP_CONFIRM` must not reach production on its own, and the acknowledging phrase
must not run a command the operator did not name. Measured in this shell: with neither phrase the run
stops one gate earlier (`Refusing to clean PRODUCTION data`); with only the production phrase it stops at
`Refusing to clean: confirmation phrase did not match … CLEANUP_CONFIRM=cleanup:prod-mongodb`. Exit 1
both times, no connection opened, nothing deleted. Guide 6 and Guide 4 each named only the production
phrase in their tables, so both now say **both**, print the working command, and explain the split.

The prompt order changed too: the production phrase is now checked **before** the interactive read. It
used to be checked after it, so an operator typed the command phrase and was then refused for a phrase
they had never been asked for.

**The guard that could not see its own trap.** `cleanup:firebase-accounts` refuses to delete an identity
a MongoDB user still references, because §27BB's state — no identity to sign in with, `409 EMAIL_IN_USE`
blocking registration — cannot be repaired by anything in the application. It asked that question of
`firebaseUid` **only**. Measured on the development database: three user rows, uids
`IWzTZ…`/`MyydZ…`/`6QZZZ…`; Firebase held **one** identity, `jefferndullamalinaozxc@gmail.com`, with uid
`j4me8…`. Every stored uid was stale — an identity deleted and re-created under the same address keeps
the row's old uid forever — so `User.countDocuments({ firebaseUid: uid })` returned 0 and the script
printed **`will delete`** for an address a MongoDB user still owned. A `--dry-run` proved it without
touching anything. Run for real it would have created the unrecoverable state the script exists to
prevent.

**The fix** is a pure classifier in `scripts/cleanup/lib.mjs` (`classifyFirebaseAddress`) that takes both
counts and returns one of four verdicts: `refused-linked`, `will-delete`, `no-identity`, and `orphaned`.
The address itself is the durable link — `email` is unique, lower-cased and indexed, and it is what
registration collides on. The CLI now measures `firebaseUid` **and** `email` for every address, refuses
the whole run when either matches, and reports the already-damaged case as
**`ORPHANED — identity already gone, database row remains`** with exit 1 instead of counting it as
"0 deleted" and printing that the address is free to register. That claim is now only printed when it is
true for every address named. All-or-nothing is unchanged: every refusal is decided before the first
deletion.

**Verification.** `phase-cleanup-test-utilities.test.mjs` **56 pass** (four new cases, including the
measured stale-uid case the old rule called deletable); the full server suite, `eslint` and
`tsc --noEmit` green. Live and read-only: the one live identity now reports `REFUSED — still linked`
(exit 1), the already-orphaned address reports `ORPHANED` (exit 1), the absent address still reports
`no identity` and deletes nothing (exit 0). No production record and no Firebase identity was deleted.

**Unchanged and still open:** both mobile advisories (§27FP), the OTA publish gate
(`native-record-missing`), L-17, the Play release, iOS verification and OTA code signing.

---

# 27FT. One seeding command, and a production target that costs a third phrase (2026-10-26)

**The problem was that the two environments cost the same.** Four seeders (`seed:demo`, `seed:accounts`,
`seed:roles`, and the perf tools) all reached production through `assertSafeTarget` with ONE phrase. A
throwaway development tenant and a real business were distinguished only by which database the shell
happened to resolve — the check was correct, but it priced a real write the same as a test write.

**One command, one guard, two or three phrases.** `npm run seed -- --plan=<demo|accounts|roles>
--database=<name>` dispatches from a table in `scripts/seed/guard.mjs`; it holds no dataset logic and no
second copy of the rule. `assertSeedTarget` requires the target to be NAMED and to equal the resolved
database, refuses the test database and any database outside `{development, production}`, and then
counts phrases by target class:

- **development — two**: `SEED_CONFIRM=<the plan's phrase>` (what) and `SEED_DB_CONFIRM=<database>` (where)
- **production — three**: both, plus `SEED_PROD_CONFIRM=SEED-PRODUCTION-DATA` (that the data is real)

A refusal reports every missing phrase at once and states the count. `seed:demo`, `seed:accounts` and
`seed:roles` remain as the same command with the plan preselected — the role-fixture test pins their
package.json entries — so nothing that was documented stops working, and a phrase names the dataset
rather than the wrapper that launched it. `seed:perf*` and `seed:demo-tenant` stay outside this
workflow: they are measurements and a fixed demo fixture, each with its own guard.

**Dry run added to `seed:demo`.** `--dry-run` now exists on all three plans. It runs the full guard and
prints the plan, then returns before `resolveIdentity` and before `mongoose.connect`, so it cannot
create a Firebase identity or open a connection. `verify:demo` is unchanged and still read-only, with
its 0/1/2 contract: verification is not a dry run.

**Measured, without touching data.** No plan → refused (exit 1). Development with zero phrases →
`two confirmation phrase(s) … 2 are missing or wrong: SEED_CONFIRM=seed-demo-account AND
SEED_DB_CONFIRM=inventoryai_dev_db`. With one → the same message naming only the missing one. With
two → `confirmed: 2 phrase(s) accepted`, then `dry run complete — no connection was opened`. Production
with two → `three confirmation phrase(s) … 1 is missing or wrong: SEED_PROD_CONFIRM=…` (exit 1); with
three → `confirmed: 3 phrase(s) accepted` and a dry run that never connected. The `accounts` and
`roles` plans ran the same way through the same command, and `npm run seed:demo` still accepted its
original invocation plus the database phrase. Nothing was written to any database.

`seed-target-guard.test.mjs` — **19 pass**, DB-free: both phrase counts, the missing-phrase enumeration,
a production phrase that does not substitute for a development one, `--database` missing/mismatched/
test/unknown, `MONGODB_URI` absent, the `--plan=` and `--plan ` spellings, an unknown plan refused, a
source scan proving the three seeders call the unified guard (and no longer the one-phrase one), and
the stale-identity-link refusal below.

**The end-to-end run found a second defect, and it was the §27FS landmine in a new place.** Seeding the
first development account died on `E11000 duplicate key … users index: email_1`. Cause: every stored
`firebaseUid` in that database is stale (the identity was deleted and re-created under the same
address), so `ensureTenantForIdentity`'s uid lookup missed and it tried to CREATE a second `User` for an
address that already had one. The driver's message said nothing about why.

Two things were wrong, and only one of them is a code bug. The code bug is the error path: an
email collision is now detected explicitly and refused by a pure `assertIdentityLinkUsable` in
`scripts/seed/lib.mjs`, which names both uids and states that re-pointing an identity link is not
something a data seeder does implicitly. The other is a **data state** that no command here should
repair by guessing: those rows can neither sign in (uid mismatch) nor re-register (`EMAIL_IN_USE`), so
`seed --plan=demo` and `--plan=accounts` refuse until the link is repaired deliberately. Auto-relinking
was considered and rejected — §27BB and the exchange's uid-only rule make it an identity operation, and
this phase is about data.

**The workflow itself was then proved on the development database.** A disposable address
(`seed-probe-2026-10-26@example.invalid`, password generated in-shell and never printed) seeded **300
documents / 68 products in 2,349 ms** through `npm run seed --plan=accounts` with two phrases (exit 0);
`verify:demo` read it back clean (exit 0, ledger and referential integrity hold); `cleanup:demo` removed
**300 documents, 0 remaining**, keeping the login and business row. The owner's first account was
re-verified afterwards and still holds its **1,125 products** untouched — the refusal happens before any
tenant is cleared.

**Documentation.** New [Guide 9](guides/9-seeding-development.md) — the database, the phrases, the one
command, dry run, verification, what resets versus what is read-only, and large-data practice — plus
the seeding examples in Guides 4 and 6 rewritten to commands that actually run.

**Unchanged and still open:** both mobile advisories (§27FP), the OTA publish gate, L-17, the Play
release, iOS verification and OTA code signing — plus the three development accounts stranded by
stale identity links, which need a deliberate repair decision. No production data was read or written
while testing these safeguards.

# 27FU. One cleanup command, and a Firebase check that reads both databases (2026-10-26)

**The problem was that deleting still had two rules.** Seeding had just been unified (§27FT) around one
question asked three ways — *what*, *where*, *is this real*. Cleanup still answered different ones:
four npm scripts (`cleanup:test-mongodb`, `cleanup:dev-mongodb`, `cleanup:prod-mongodb`,
`cleanup:all-mongodb`) selected the target by alias, a non-production target refused unless `NODE_ENV`
was **explicitly** `development`, production carried a second phrase, and `cleanup:firebase-accounts`
had a third variant of the same idea. An operator who had learnt the seeding rule was wrong about the
cleanup one, and the rule that mattered — where is this pointed? — was the one nobody had to type.

**One command, the same guard shape, two or three phrases.** `npm run cleanup --
--target=<database|firebase> --database=<name>` dispatches from a table in `scripts/cleanup/guard.mjs`.
The rule, checked before any connection opens:

- the target must be one of the two — there is no default;
- `--database=` is required and must equal the database `config/env.ts` resolved, and the connection
  uses the resolved value, never the flag;
- only `inventoryai_dev_db` and `inventoryai_prod_db` are cleanable; the test database is refused by
  name because `npm test` owns it;
- a `MONGODB_URI` whose **path** names a different database is refused, because the shell is configured
  for the other environment even when the flag, the phrases and the resolved name all agree — the one
  way an operator could be right about every value they typed and still be somewhere else;
- **development — two**: `CLEANUP_CONFIRM=cleanup:<target>` (which command) and
  `CLEANUP_DB_CONFIRM=<database>` (where);
- **production — three**: both, plus `CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM=DELETE-PRODUCTION-DATA`;
- a phrase that belongs to the *other* command is refused and named, so `CLEANUP_CONFIRM` cannot be
  satisfied from memory by the wrong run.

A refusal reports every missing phrase at once and states the count. The old `NODE_ENV` rule is gone:
the database name and its phrase are the proof, which is what lets one command serve both environments.
The four selector scripts and `cleanup:firebase-accounts` were **removed** rather than aliased — unlike
the seeders, their flags were the contract that changed, so keeping them would have preserved the rule
this record replaces.

**Deleting still happens in the same two engines, and a dry run now proves the target.**
`cleanup-mongodb.mjs` clears every document in the named database and preserves the database, its
collections and its indexes; `--dry-run` counts and stops. `cleanup-firebase-accounts.mjs` deletes only
the addresses named with `--email=`, and now verifies each deleted uid is really gone. Both keep their
phrases-only confirmation: no interactive prompt remains, and `--yes` is accepted but does nothing.

**The Firebase check had a hole, and the first measurement fell into it.** There is one Firebase
project, so an address is one identity, but user rows in **both** databases can reference it. The
engine checked only the resolved database. The first development address tried was referenced by both
development and production, so the old check would have deleted a login that production still uses —
the exact unrecoverable state (§27BB) the check exists to prevent, one database away. It now counts in
dev and prod, by `firebaseUid` **and** by `email` (a re-created identity leaves a stale uid behind), and
a refusal names the database(s) still holding the address.

**Measured, and nothing was destroyed.** No `--target` → usage plus `no --target was supplied; refusing
to guess` (exit 1). `--target=database` with no `--database` → the resolved name is printed in the
refusal (exit 1). `--database=inventoryai_prod_db` from a development shell → `--database is … but this
process resolved "inventoryai_dev_db"` (exit 1, no connection). Development with only the command
phrase → `two confirmation phrase(s) … 1 is missing or wrong: CLEANUP_DB_CONFIRM=…` (exit 1).
Production with two phrases → `three confirmation phrase(s) … 1 is missing or wrong:
CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM=DELETE-PRODUCTION-DATA` (exit 1, and no banner, because the guard precedes the
connection). Development with all three → the extra phrase is ignored and the dry run ran:
**17 collections, 274 009 documents would be deleted; nothing was deleted**. A Firebase dry run against
an absent address reported `no identity` (exit 0); against a real development address it reported
`REFUSED — still linked to a MongoDB user  [inventoryai_dev_db, inventoryai_prod_db]` and exited 1.
With `MONGODB_URI` pointed at `…/inventoryai_prod_db` while the resolved database stayed development,
both commands refused with `MONGODB_URI names the database "inventoryai_prod_db"` (exit 1) and neither
attempted a connection; the message contains no part of the URI beyond the database name.

**One row is enough, and it is summed rather than judged per database.** The counting moved into a pure
`summariseFirebaseReferences` in `scripts/cleanup/lib.mjs`: it totals each database's `byUid` and
`byEmail`, records which databases contributed, and takes the verdict on the totals. A development-only
check is not a subset of this — it is the defect above, and the test asserts a production-only reference
refuses a deletion started from development.

**Tests.** New `cleanup-target-guard.test.mjs` — **41 pass**, DB-free: both phrase counts, the
missing-phrase enumeration, a phrase from the wrong command, the test-database and unknown-database
refusals, the `MONGODB_URI` path refusal (with a control proving the URI itself is never echoed), the
`databaseNameInUri` cases, one reference refusing a deletion in either database and by either link,
`--target` spellings, a refused run that never opens a connection, a live-name mismatch that deletes
nothing, a dry run that deletes nothing, and two source scans proving the guards precede
`connect`/`deleteUser`. The suite also pins the command surface: `cleanup` exists and the five removed
scripts do not. `seed-target-guard.test.mjs` gained the same two URI cases (**21 pass**), because a
stale connection string is the same hazard on the write path.

**Documentation.** New [Guide 10](guides/11-deleting-development.md) — the one command, the two targets, the
phrases, the ordering rule and what is *not* replaced — plus Guides 4 and 6 rewritten to commands that
actually run, and `scripts/cleanup/README.md` reduced to the same rule. Guide 6's old "production needs
two phrases" section was replaced, not amended: it described a message that no longer exists.

**Unchanged and still open:** both mobile advisories (§27FP), the OTA publish gate, L-17, the Play
release, iOS verification and OTA code signing — plus the three development accounts stranded by stale
identity links (§27FT), which this command deliberately does not repair.

# 27FV. The seeding scripts reviewed — four defects, and a read-back that makes OK a measurement (2026-10-26)

**The review was of the workflow §27FT had just unified, and it found four real defects.** None of
them was in the guard — the guard held. All four were in what surrounds it.

**1. `Int` parsing quietly accepted a size nobody typed.** `Number.parseInt('900abc')` is 900 and
`parseInt('12.9')` is 12, so `--total=900abc` seeded 900 documents and reported success. A seeded size
is the input to every later measurement, so a value that was silently changed is a measurement that
cannot be reproduced. All three seeders now use one strict parser (`parseCount`): digits only, a stated
range, and a refusal that says nothing was written. The PRNG seed uses the same parser with no upper
bound, so `--seed=1.5` no longer becomes 1.

**2. The address was normalised on WRITE and not on LOOKUP.** `User.email` is `lowercase: true`, which
Mongoose applies when saving; `findOne({ email })` is exact. A mixed-case `--email` therefore found the
Firebase identity (case-insensitive) and could miss the MongoDB row, then try to create a second one
and die on `users.email_1` — the §27FT symptom again, from a different cause. `normaliseEmail` now
lower-cases and trims at every boundary: the CLIs, `resolveIdentity`, `ensureTenantForIdentity`, and the
`--accounts` plan (which also dedupes on the normalised address, so `A@x.com` and `a@x.com` in one plan
are one entry, refused as a duplicate).

**3. `seed:accounts` promised an all-or-nothing check and did not do one.** Its comment said every
identity was resolved first "so a plan that cannot be satisfied fails before any tenant has been
reset", but tenant resolution and the production naming check ran inside the RESET loop. A plan whose
third account was misnamed therefore wiped the first two before refusing — a half-seeded suite, which
is exactly what biases the comparison the plan exists to support. The loop is now three phases:
identities, then every tenant (resolve, prove the businesses differ, prove every replaced tenant was
named), then reset and write. Nothing is cleared until every account has passed every check.

**4. The role fixture's teardown was confirmed by the wrong family's phrase.** `cleanup:roles` required
`SEED_CONFIRM=seed-roles`, while Guide 6 documented `CLEANUP_CONFIRM=cleanup:roles` — so the documented
command refused, and the working one contradicted the rule that a seed phrase must not authorise a
deletion. It now reads `CLEANUP_CONFIRM=cleanup:roles`; the command the seeder prints also names the
database, because the unnamed form is refused in production.

**And `OK` stopped being the seeder's own opinion.** `seed:role-accounts` counted four of the seven
collections back; `seed:demo` and `seed:accounts` counted none. All three now use one
`readTenantCounts` for the seven collections it writes, compared by a pure `countDisagreements`, and
refuse by name (`products: wrote 10, found 9`) rather than report a dataset that is not there. The
summary lines print the read-back, not the tally.

**Measured, read-only against the real development database.** `readTenantCounts` on the largest tenant
(**50 625 products, 101 374 inventory rows**) returned all seven counts in **475 ms** — small enough to
do on every run. Dry runs for all three plans printed their plan and opened no connection. `--total=900abc`
refused with `--total must be a whole number between 100 and 400000, not "900abc"`; `--seed=1.5` refused
the same way (`at least 0`); a plan naming `A@example.invalid` and `a@example.invalid` refused the second
as a duplicate. `npm run seed` now prints the RESOLVED database and the exact `SEED_DB_CONFIRM` value,
because the old banner read the raw `MONGODB_DB_NAME` and would have omitted the third phrase from a
production run selected by `NODE_ENV` alone.

**Tests.** `seed-target-guard.test.mjs` — **29 pass** (was 21): the strict parser's accepted and refused
shapes, the address normaliser, the read-back comparison (including a missing collection), and a source
scan pinning that all three seeders use these helpers and none parses a size with `parseInt`.
`phase27ct-role-fixture.test.mjs` gained two assertions: the teardown reads `CLEANUP_CONFIRM=cleanup:roles`,
and the line the seeder prints carries `--database=`.

**Documentation.** Guide 6's `cleanup:roles` examples were already right, which is how the code was
found wrong; its phrase-variable summary now names the perf exception. Guide 9 gained the two-phrase
PowerShell form for production, the `--accounts=` production rule, and the role fixture's real
`--total` range (100–20 000, not 100–400 000). The three seeders' headers now name `assertSeedTarget`
rather than the retired `assertSafeTarget`, and `cleanup:roles` no longer advertises a seed phrase.

**Unchanged and still open:** both mobile advisories (§27FP), the OTA publish gate, L-17, the Play
release, iOS verification and OTA code signing — plus the stranded development accounts (§27FT), which
this batch deliberately still does not repair.

# 27FW. The scoped cleanup that was cheaper than the rule (2026-10-26)

**The finding.** `npm run cleanup -- --target=database|firebase` had cost two phrases in development
and three in production since §27FU. `cleanup:demo` — the tenant-scoped command a production test
uses to remove its own data while keeping the login — still cost **one** phrase, and Guide 10 called
that “as it is”. A scoped command was therefore the cheaper way to delete production rows, which is
exactly the habit the phrase rule exists to prevent.

**The fix.** The database half of the cleanup rule moved into one private `assertCleanupDatabase`
(resolved name equals `--database`, known and cleanable, no `MONGODB_URI` disagreement), and a new
`assertScopedCleanupTarget` applies the same phrase count as the dispatch targets:

```text
development   CLEANUP_CONFIRM=cleanup:demo-account  CLEANUP_DB_CONFIRM=inventoryai_dev_db
production    both of the above, plus CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM=DELETE-PRODUCTION-DATA
```

`cleanup:demo` uses it. The phrase names the command, the database phrase names where, and the
production phrase states that the rows are real. The tenant proof is unchanged and still comes
after: `--email` and `--business` must resolve to the same account, and every delete is filtered by
that one `businessId`. The Firebase identity is never touched.

**Measured, non-destructively.** With one phrase in development the command refused and named
`CLEANUP_DB_CONFIRM=inventoryai_dev_db`; in production with two it refused and named
`CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM=DELETE-PRODUCTION-DATA`; with both, a dry run against the 300-document probe
tenant counted exactly 300 and deleted nothing. The shared guard's new tests cover the accepted
shapes, the missing phrase, the database mismatch, the test database and a contradicting
`MONGODB_URI`.

**Still deliberate.** `cleanup:roles`, `cleanup:demo-tenant` and `cleanup:perf-tenant` are fixture
tools with their own single phrase; they still name the database and locate their tenant by two
fingerprints. Guide 10 now says which rule each command follows instead of implying one rule for
all. Making every fixture cleanup cost three phrases is a separate change, not a claim made here.
`cleanup:perf-tenant`, `cleanup:roles` and `cleanup:demo-tenant` took it on 2026-10-27 — see §27FX.

---

# 27FX. The fixture cleanups take the rule, and the dry run counts (2026-10-27)

**The finding.** §27FW put `cleanup:demo` on `assertScopedCleanupTarget` and recorded
`cleanup:perf-tenant`, `cleanup:roles` and `cleanup:demo-tenant` as still carrying their own single
phrases. That left the scoped commands that can delete a production tenant as the cheapest way to
delete production rows — while `cleanup:perf`, which cannot reach production at all, already had a
dry run. `seed:perf-tenant` had the same asymmetry: its own `assertNamedDatabaseTarget` guard
required one phrase, not the two/three every other seeder costs.

**The fix.** All four commands now call the shared guards and none has its own copy of the rule:

```text
seed:perf-tenant     assertSeedTarget           SEED_CONFIRM    + SEED_DB_CONFIRM    (+ SEED_PROD_CONFIRM in production)
cleanup:perf-tenant  assertScopedCleanupTarget  CLEANUP_CONFIRM + CLEANUP_DB_CONFIRM (+ CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM in production)
cleanup:demo-tenant  assertScopedCleanupTarget  CLEANUP_CONFIRM + CLEANUP_DB_CONFIRM (+ CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM in production)
cleanup:roles        assertScopedCleanupTarget  CLEANUP_CONFIRM + CLEANUP_DB_CONFIRM (+ CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM in production)
```

`cleanup:perf-tenant --dry-run` is new and is a real dry run, not a description: it runs the same
guard, resolves the same tenant by both fingerprints, and calls a new `countTenantRemoval` that walks
the same collections, in the same order, as `removeTenant` — then stops. It costs the same phrases as
the real run because a dry run proves the destination rather than skipping it. The seed command now
prints both the preview and the delete, with all three phrases in production. The role and demo-tenant
teardowns keep their own tenant proofs (two fingerprints, then `0 remaining`) and add the shared
phrases; the role fixture keeps its identities unless `--delete-firebase`.

**Measured.** The new guard/source suite (`test/perf-tenant-workflow.test.mjs`) passes **14/14**, and
the adjacent guard, environment and documentation suites pass with it (**145/145** in one unit run).
The database suite passed **6/6**, including a new test that seeds a whole tenant, previews it,
compares the preview's per-collection counts **byte for byte** with the real removal, and confirms the
preview deleted nothing. The full unit suite then passed **1,516 tests, 0 failures** (56 DB-backed
suites skipped in unit mode), with `tsc` and `eslint` clean.

The CLI was then exercised end to end in **development**: a 50-document tenant was seeded (2 phrases),
a dry run counted **60 documents** and deleted nothing, a second dry run still counted **60**, and the
real run removed **60** with verification finding **0 remaining**. In production, all four commands
with their first two phrases (and no connection attempted) refused and named the missing
`SEED_PROD_CONFIRM` / `CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM`. No production row was read or deleted in this pass.
Guides 4, 6, 9 and 10 now show the two/three phrases, including the two remaining fixture teardowns.

# 27FY. The preview and the delete share one plan (2026-10-27)

**The finding.** `countTenantRemoval` was described as the mirror of `removeTenant`, but it was a
second copy of the same order. `cleanup:demo`'s dry run was a third copy, and the two fixture
cleanups had no dry run at all — the commands that can delete a production tenant could only be
inspected by deleting it or by reading their source.

**The fix.** `TENANT_TEARDOWN_PLAN` is now the one ordered list: assistant messages (through their
conversations), assistant conversations, every collection carrying `businessId`, the account-scoped
rows (sessions, reset tokens, reset challenges), users, and the business row. A single
`executeTenantTeardownPlan` is the only place a step becomes a query; `mode: 'count' | 'delete'`
selects the operation, and `selection: 'data' | 'all'` selects the half. `removeTenant` and
`countTenantRemoval` walk all of it; `clearTenantData` and the new `countTenantDataRemoval` walk the
data steps; `countTenantLeftovers` walks the same plan after a removal. `cleanup:demo` now previews
through `countTenantDataRemoval` instead of its own loop.

**The fixture cleanups gained a real preview.** `cleanup:roles --dry-run` and
`cleanup:demo-tenant --dry-run` run the same guard, resolve the same tenant by both fingerprints and
count the same full plan as their real runs, then stop. They cost the same two/three phrases because
the preview proves the destination rather than skipping it. The role cleanup also stopped deleting
sessions, reset tokens and its audit/assistant extras in separate loops: `removeTenant` already
walks those plan steps, and a second loop was the drift this change removes.

**The last preview copy — the database-wide one.** The tenant plans were shared, but
`npm run cleanup -- --target=database` still counted in its own loop in the dry run and again inside
`clearMongoDatabase` before deleting. Both now call one `countCollections`, so the preview lists the
same sorted collections, with the same counts, that the delete is about to clear. A new test runs the
preview and the real cleanup over two copies of one fake database and asserts the two maps are equal,
and a source guard pins the collection listing to one call site.

**Measured.** The DEMO-2 database suite passed **7/7**, including a new data-only test that compares
`countTenantDataRemoval` with `clearTenantData` byte for byte and proves the preview deleted nothing.
The guard/source suites passed **125/125**, the full unit suite passed **1,521 tests, 0 failures**
(56 DB-backed suites skipped), and `tsc`/`eslint` were clean. The shared counter was then verified by
the DB-backed full suite: **2,284 tests, 0 failures, 0 skipped**, including DEMO-2's teardown and
AUTH-02's HTTP cases. In development, two throwaway fixtures
(one role, one demo tenant, each with 9 documents) were previewed at **9** each, then removed at
**9** each with **0 remaining**; the dry runs deleted nothing. `cleanup:demo` was exercised on a
third fixture: the preview and the real run both counted/removed **2** data rows, while its user,
session and business row stayed behind as designed. No production row was read or deleted in this
pass.

# 27FZ. Each topic gets one guide, and the data commands move into theirs (2026-10-27)

**The finding.** Five guides each carried part of the same rule. Guide 4 explained the accounts and
then reproduced the seeding and cleanup commands; Guide 6 promised "every script" and reprinted both
families in full — two nearly identical tables of the same commands; Guides 9 and 10 owned the rules
but not every command that used them; Firebase deletion was mentioned in three places and explained in
none. The cost is maintenance, not length: the perf-tenant production example existed twice, so a
change to its phrases had to be made in both or drift.

**What changed — one subject per guide.**

| Guide | Owns | No longer contains |
|---|---|---|
| 4. Test accounts and mock data | which accounts exist, which tenant each owns, what the seeded data looks like, the irreversible rule | seeding and cleanup command lines |
| 6. Scripts and commands | start, check, measure, maintain, CI, backup and restore | the two data families, replaced by a pointer table |
| 9. Seeding data | every seeder: the one command, the plans, the database rule, the phrases, verification, the tools with their own guards | — |
| 10. Deleting data | every MongoDB deletion: the dispatcher, the tenant cleanups, the ordering rule, verification | Firebase identity detail |
| 11. Firebase identities (new) | which commands create logins, how they are verified, how to delete one, both refusals, the test-project wipe | — |

**What is guarded.** `perf-tenant-workflow.test.mjs` pinned the perf-tenant example to Guide 6's G.1.
It now reads the two guides that own each half — the seed in Guide 9, the cleanup in Guide 10 — and
bounds each section at the next heading, so a phrase surviving elsewhere in the same file cannot

# 27GA. The command audit — one false pass, one bad message, and four flags that were ignored (2026-10-27)

**What was checked.** Every `npm run` name in the documentation against both `package.json` files, and
every script target on disk. 44 distinct names appear in prose; the only ones that are not scripts are
`cleanup:test-mongodb` and `cleanup:dev-mongodb` (quoted by a dated record as *removed*) and one
illustrative placeholder. Every guard path was then exercised against a dead URI, so nothing connected.

**The defects.**

1. **`verify:demo` could pass the wrong account.** With no `--email`, `User.findOne({ email: undefined })`
   drops the key, so the query became `findOne({})` — the first user in the database. A run that forgot
   the flag would verify, and could exit 0 for, an account nobody named. It now refuses **before
   connecting**, with exit 2. Measured: `npm run verify:demo` and `-- --database=…` both answer
   `--email=<address> is required, and nothing was read` and exit 2.
2. **The demo-tenant refusal named no variable.** It read `set seed:demo-tenant confirmation to
   "seed:demo-tenant"`, which never told the operator what to export. It now reads
   `set SEED_CONFIRM=seed-demo-tenant to proceed`.
3. **Four data commands accepted `--dry-run` and ignored it** — `seed:perf-tenant`, `seed:demo-tenant`,
   `seed:perf` and `cleanup:test-firebase`. On a live database the first three would have **written**
   during a preview, and the last would have prompted to delete every identity. Each now previews and
   stops before its first write. Measured: `seed:perf` opened no connection; `seed:perf-tenant` and
   `seed:demo-tenant` reported create/replace without touching Firebase and without needing the
   password; `cleanup:test-firebase --dry-run` counted 2 identities and deleted none.
4. **`cleanup:perf` was the only cleanup with no preview.** It now counts the shared teardown plan:
   measured 517 documents previewed twice (identical both times), then 517 removed with `0 remaining`,
   then `nothing to clean`.

**Documentation.** Guide 6 described `npm run android` as `expo start --android`; the script is
`expo run:android` — a **native build**, not a Metro launch. Guides 9, 10 and 11 now show the new
previews and state which ones read the database and that none touches Firebase.

**Guarded.** `script-environment-guards.test.mjs` gained a command-audit suite: each of the four
previews must read `--dry-run` and its branch must appear **before** its first write; `cleanup:perf`
must count before it removes; the demo refusal must name `SEED_CONFIRM`; and `verify:demo`'s refusal
must precede its connection.

**Measured.** Unit suite **1472 passed, 0 failed, 56 skipped**; database suite **824 passed, 0 failed,
95 skipped**; `eslint` and `tsc --noEmit` clean.

# 27GB. The three accounts by address — a products-sized plan, a pre-flight check, and a cleanup that keeps every login (2026-10-27)

**What was asked for.** One workflow for the owner's own accounts: check that they exist, seed them by
product count, and delete that data again by address — the same three steps in development and in
production, with distinct confirmation phrases for each, and nothing that deletes a login by accident.

**What already existed, and was reused rather than rewritten.** `seed:accounts` was already the
several-accounts seeder, already defaulted to these three addresses, already wrote no SKUs or barcodes
(so the app's own barcode generation is what first assigns a code), already reset only the tenants it
resolved, and already refused to touch Firebase. `clearTenantData` / `countTenantDataRemoval` were
already the one teardown plan every cleanup and account deletion shares. The gaps were the unit, the
pre-flight check and the deletion by address.

**The unit was documents, and a person thinks in products.** `--accounts="a@x.com:225000"` meant
225 000 DOCUMENTS (~50 600 products). Entries and the preset are now counted in **products** — the
number the app's own product list shows — and the console prints the derived document figure beside
every entry, so both numbers are true. A `d` suffix still asks for documents
(`address:400000d`), and products → documents goes through `documentsForProducts`, which verifies the
round trip rather than assuming it: the generator rounds too, so the budget moves a document until the
product count is exact.

**A real defect, found by that round-trip test.** The first version floored the document budget at
`MIN_DOCUMENTS` (100), which is already 23 products — so "5 products" was unsatisfiable and the
conversion threw instead of returning a budget. The floor belongs to a DOCUMENT count; it was removed
from that direction. The test walks every size from 5 to 2 000 and asserts the product count that comes
back is the one that was asked for.

**The ceiling is stated, not guessed at.** 112 500 products ≈ 500 000 documents, because the whole plan
is built in memory before it is inserted. One million products (≈4 400 000 documents) is refused with
that reason in the message, and a plan at or above 90 000 products prints a LARGE RUN warning with the
measured rate it is estimated from (production seeded 80 000 documents in 171 s on 2026-10-25) and the
honest note that this size has not been measured end to end.

**Three new commands, and two new phrases.** `check:accounts` reads the Firebase identity and the user
row in a FIXED list of databases — development, plus production when `--with-production` asks — and
prints, through the same teardown plan a cleanup executes, how many documents a seed would reset. It
writes nothing, so it needs no phrase; exit 0 ready / 1 not ready / 2 not checked. `cleanup:account`
and `cleanup:three` remove tenant data only, require a businessId per account in production, and never
delete a user row, a business row, a session or an identity. The phrases: `seed-three-accounts`,
`seed-accounts`, `cleanup-account-data`, `cleanup-three-accounts` — two in development, three in
production, and a phrase from the other family is refused.

**Measured (all read-only; no production write was performed).**

* The preset plan: 30 000 / 50 000 / 90 000 products → 133 333 / 222 222 / 400 000 documents, and it
  prints the LARGE RUN line for the 170 000-product total.
* A custom plan: `:100000` → 100 000 products ≈ 444 444 documents; `:50000d` → 50 000 documents ≈
  11 250 products.
* The refusals, each naming what to set: a bare `seed:accounts`; `:1000000` (the ceiling); an entry with
  no size; `seed:three` with `SEED_CONFIRM=seed-accounts`; `cleanup:three` with a seeder's phrase.
* `check:accounts`: **0 of 3** account/database pairs are READY in the development database alone, and
  **1 of 6** once production is read. Account 1 has an identity and owns
  `6adfb57dcd2aa24e547d0f02` ("royal kludge", 0 products / 19 documents) in **production**, with no row
  in development; accounts 2 and 3 have no identity and no row anywhere yet. The production seeding
  command it prints names the existing tenant by id and leaves the two that do not exist unnamed —
  which is exactly the rule the seeder enforces.
* `cleanup:three --dry-run`: the three addresses are not in the development database, so it reported
  `nothing to delete` and exit 0 without touching anything.

**Guarded.** `accounts-workflow.test.mjs` (new, DB-free): the conversion round trip, the two modes and
their phrases, the ceiling's reason, the preview running before the connection, and the source guards —
`check:accounts` calls none of the write primitives, reads a fixed list, and takes no `--database=` flag;
`cleanup-accounts.mjs` calls `clearTenantData`/`countTenantDataRemoval` and none of `removeTenant`,
`auth.deleteUser`, `User.delete*/Business.delete*` or `Session.deleteMany`.
`cleanup-accounts.mjs` was added to the data-touching list in `script-environment-guards.test.mjs` and
the new file classified in `run-tests.mjs`.

**A guard caught this record's own citation.** The first run of the unit suite refused `§27GB` in a
source comment because no such record existed yet — the section-integrity guard doing exactly its job,
and the reason this record was written before the guides.

**Measured.** Unit suite **1551 passed, 0 failed, 56 skipped**; `eslint` and `tsc --noEmit` clean.

**Not done here.** No production data was written or deleted: the only production touch was the
read-only `check:accounts --with-production`. The database suite was not re-run (nothing in this change
touches a model, a route or a service's query).

**The documentation pass, and the full suite.** Every guide that names these accounts was brought onto
the new commands: Guide 4 now states the preset's real sizes (30 000 / 50 000 / 90 000 products —
≈133 000 / 222 000 / 400 000 documents, replacing a stale 5 000 / 44 000 / 225 000) and points at the
three commands that read one list; Guide 6 gained `check:accounts` in its data table and the read-only
row it belongs to; Guides 9 and 10 already owned the seeding and deletion halves. The full suite
(**2312 tests, 380 suites**) then ran green except one assertion — the roadmap's own record-count
sentence, which still said **181** where the file now declares **182**. That is the fact-drift guard
working on the file that declares its own totals; the sentence was corrected and the three
documentation-integrity files re-run clean (15/15). `typecheck`, `eslint`, `check:extensions`,
`check:specifiers` and the secret guard (897 files) were clean.

**The deletion half measured against production, read-only.** `cleanup:account --dry-run` there named
the one tenant production holds — `jefferndullamalinaozxc@gmail.com`, 19 documents (all `audit_logs`),
business `6adfb57dcd2aa24e547d0f02` — and deleted nothing. The four refusals were each exercised and
each names what to set: the preset in production; an address without its businessId; a businessId the
account does not own (`belongs to business …, not …`); and a run with no phrase at all. Re-counting what
remains still fails a real run rather than reporting it as done.

**A seed writes to TWO stores, and only one of them was ever named.** Deletion has pinned its Firebase
project since the cleanup guard existed (`assertFirebaseProject`, `inventoryai-d0d20`), but seeding
took the project from the shell's credentials and named nothing — so a shell pointed elsewhere would
create the login THERE while the tenant landed here, and the two could never be joined, because the
application resolves a user by `firebaseUid` only. The result would have read as an account that
exists and cannot sign in. `assertSeedFirebaseProject` now runs inside `resolveIdentity`, the one
function every seeder creates or refreshes an identity through, and it runs **before the first read**,
so a refused run has touched neither store; the approved id is imported from the cleanup guard rather
than restated, because two literals would be two opinions. `check:accounts` refuses the same way — a
wrong project makes it report `MISSING` for accounts that exist, which is a wrong answer rather than a
missing one — and exits 2, its "not checked" code.

**Measured for that pin.** The normal shell (service-account JSON) resolves `inventoryai-d0d20` and
`check:accounts` proceeds unchanged; with the credentials pointed at another project it stops before
connecting and exits **2** (`this shell is configured for Firebase project "some-other-project", but a
seed creates identities only in "inventoryai-d0d20"`), while a normally-configured run over the same
accounts exits **1**, its not-ready code. Both refusal paths print that nothing was read or written.

and verify each tenant afterwards.

| Tenant | Products | Documents | Time | Rate |

| small `jefferndullamalinaozxc@gmail.com` | 30 000 | 133 333 | 170 682 ms | 781 docs/s |

| large `jeffernmalinaoqwe@gmail.com` | 90 000 | 400 000 | 587 461 ms | 681 docs/s |
| **total** | **170 000** | **755 555** | **1 131 s (18 min 51 s)** | — |

So the `LARGE RUN` warning's **27 minutes was conservative**, and it says why: that estimate was built
on the 470 documents/s measured on 2026-10-25 from a 60 000-document PRODUCTION run, while this shape
ran at 596–781 documents/s. The warning is still right to exist — the plan was held in memory (the
seeder's process was at **~370 MB** while writing the 400 000-document tenant). Each tenant's previous
data was reset first (`removed 1333 previous document(s)`), and **nothing was written to Firebase**: all
three identities were reported `already existed, verified`.

(30 000 / 50 000 / 90 000 products; 133 333 / 222 222 / 400 000 documents), and stock health scales with
the catalogue as expected (4 656 / 7 623 / 13 683 at or below minimum; 1 892 / 3 030 / 5 481 at zero).

reads the name. The three production tenants, which the next run fills, carry their own.
