# 27GE. The 512 MB ceiling was the real constraint, and the index allocation was hiding in it (2026-10-27)

**What was asked for.** Seed production at 30 000 / 50 000 / 90 000 products for the three accounts
and verify each tenant. The run was stopped **before its first write**, for a measured reason.

**The measurement that stopped it.** The cluster is Atlas M0, whose documented ceiling is **512 MB of
data plus indexes** (§27BZ's own arithmetic). The development copy of exactly this dataset measured
**337.7 MB**, taking the cluster to **349.9 MB** of 512. A second copy in production would have been
~688 MB — and an M0 that runs out of storage does not degrade, it **blocks writes** (the 2026-10-18
incident, `using 520 MB of 512 MB. Writes are blocked on your cluster.`). So the deployed app would
have lost the ability to record a movement or an AI turn. Nothing was written; the owner chose to
empty development first.

**What emptying actually freed, and what it did not.** `cleanup:three` removed all 755 555 documents
and re-counted every tenant at 0 remaining — and the counted figure fell only **337.7 → 214.4 MB**.
The residue was **index allocation**: three collections holding **zero documents** still counted
`inventory` **94.8 MB**, `inventory_transactions` **77.3 MB** and `products` **39.9 MB**. Disk went
*up* in the same window (205.5 → 266.2 MB) because the deletes were journalled while the allocation
stayed. A delete frees documents; it does not return the space their indexes were given.

**Reclaiming it.** Dropping those three indexes and rebuilding them from the models' own declarations
(`dropIndexes()` + `syncIndexes()` per model) took them to **7.2 / 13.2 / 9.2 MB**, index allocation
across the database from **215.1 MB to ~30 MB**, and the cluster from 226.5 MB to **44.9 MB**. The
declaration is the source of truth, so a rebuild cannot invent or lose an index — proved rather than
assumed with `npm run audit:indexes`: **71 declared indexes across 17 collections, 0 disagreements**.

**The production seed, then.** One run, `EXIT=0`, 755 555 documents into the three named tenants:
133 333 in 203 s, 222 222 in 423 s, 400 000 in 759 s (**23 min 6 s** total — slower than development's
18 min 51 s on the same cluster). Every identity was reported `already existed, verified`, so **nothing
was written to Firebase**, and the production rule held: no existing password was rewritten, and each
tenant was emptied only after being named by id. A mid-run sample read **255.8 MB**, matching the
projection; the final cluster stands at **379.9 MB of 512 MB — 132.1 MB free**.

**Verified independently.** `verify:demo` returned OK for all three tenants — counts, ledger
arithmetic and referential integrity — and the stock-health figures are **identical to development's**
(4 656 / 1 892, 7 623 / 3 030, 13 683 / 5 481), which is the PRNG seed doing what it promises across two
environments. `check:accounts --with-production` reads production READY at 30 000 / 133 335, 50 000 /
222 224 and 90 000 documents, and development READY at **zero** (login, business row and identity
kept). The SKU/barcode rule held in production too: **0 of 170 000** products carry either field.

**What this adds to the guides.** Guide 10 now says that a cleanup frees documents but not index
allocation, names the measured figures, and gives the reclaim (rebuild the three indexes, then
`audit:indexes`) — so the next large re-seed is not refused by residue nobody can see.

# 27GH. The reference documents measured against the tree — three stale sentences, four undocumented variables, and the tables that were already right (2026-10-27)

**What was asked for.** The same audit the guides got (§27GG), applied to the **reference**
format: not "is this misplaced?" but "is this still true?" — every figure a document states that the
tree can measure, checked against the tree rather than read and believed.

**How it was checked.** By reading the documents' claims against files, not by re-reading the claims:
`git hash-object` against `git rev-parse HEAD:<path>` for the protected register; a parser over
`docs/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md`'s two tables against `mobile/lib/theme.ts`; the `npm run …` names printed in
every document against the two `package.json` script registries; and `UPPER_SNAKE` config names against
both `.env.example` files. Three of the four are mechanical, which is the point: a claim that can be
measured should be measured by something that runs again.

**Three stale sentences, and one stale number.**

1. **`server/.env.example` was missing two rate-limit pairs.** `rateLimit.ts` reads **36**
   `AUTH_*_RATE_LIMIT_*` names; the template named **32**. `AUTH_INVITATION_SEND_RATE_LIMIT_*`
   (3600000 / 20, per account) and `AUTH_INVITATION_PREVIEW_RATE_LIMIT_*` (3600000 / 60, per IP, for
   the public `GET /api/auth/invitations/:token`) shipped with the invitation surface on 2026-10-25
   and were documented nowhere — a production knob with no name in the repository, which the project's
   own rule (`the repository holds the **names**`) exists to prevent. Both pairs are now in the
   template with the comment style the other blocks use. No value was ever missing, which is why
   nothing else noticed.
2. **`README.md` stated the old count** — `(32 variables, 16 pairs)`. It agreed with the *file* and
   disagreed with the *code*, so the number and the list were both stale and only one of them was a
   number. Now `(36 variables, 18 pairs)`, and both are guarded.
3. **`SECURITY.md` still listed the RNFirebase PII log as Open.** ISS-02 was patched on 2026-10-10
   (§27AJ) and verified in the shipped dex and on a device on 2026-10-12 (§27BA); the checklist's own
   sensitive-logging row reads resolved. The disclosure page was asking readers to consider reporting a
   finding that had been closed for two weeks.
4. **`docs/TS-MIGRATION-MANIFEST.md` named a file that does not name the module.** §3 listed the places
   that spell `services/entitlement.service.js` — "`CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, the Phase 10 record".
   `README.md` does not contain that string; `SYSTEM_SPECIFICATION.md`, `constants/plans.ts` and the
   Phase 10 test's import do. The sentence's conclusion was right; its list was wrong, and a list that
   sends a reader to check three files that are not the three would fail the reader who did check.
5. **`docs/README.md` sized the roadmap at "~21,000 lines"** — a figure that moves every time a record
   is appended (it is over 22,700 now, and this record makes it more). Reworded to "over 20,000", which
   stays true without being re-measured.

**What was measured and found already right — recorded so the check does not have to be repeated.**

- **All five protected paths** match the register in `AUTH_SECURITY_MASTER_CHECKLIST.md` §8, by
  `git hash-object` against `HEAD` (the two dated plans included).
- **`DESIGN_SYSTEM.md`'s tables match `mobile/lib/theme.ts` exactly** — 38 colour cells and all 10 type
  rows, 0 mismatches. The token table is hand-written prose about code that the theme comments already
  discuss in ratios; it is the document most likely to drift, and it has not.
- **Every `npm run …` name in the documents resolves** to a script, apart from two false positives that
  were checked by hand: the five `cleanup:*-mongodb` names in dated records (quoted as removed by a
  later record, §27FS/§27FT) and Guide 6's deliberate `some:command` placeholder.
- **The two open advisories, the accepted decisions and the watch** agree across `SECURITY.md`,
  `SECURITY_DEPENDENCY_DECISIONS.md`, `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` — same packages, same severities,
  2 open, no in-range fix.

**The guard, extended rather than duplicated.** `server/test/phase-docs-fact-drift.test.mjs` gains two
assertions over files it did not previously read: **every rate-limit variable the server reads is named
in `server/.env.example`**, and **README's stated count is the template's count** — the second alone
would have passed while the first failed (both were 32), which is why the two lists are compared rather
than two numbers. Its stated limits are unchanged and now wider: it parses six files, it still cannot
see a plan or a judgement, and the control that compares a count now compares a **planted** template
rather than the live one — the first version of that control moved with the tree and stopped failing
whenever the tree broke in the same direction.

**Proved on the real tree, not promised.** The two invitation pairs were renamed out of template form
and README's count reverted to 32/16: the missing-name test failed and named all four variables, the
count test **passed** (both sides read 32), and every other test in the file stayed green. Both files
were then restored byte-identically (md5 `8314c926…` / `d97d7871…`, verified with `md5sum -c`) and the
suite re-ran 9/9, exit 0.

**Left alone, deliberately.** `docs/SOURCE_PROTECTION.md`'s claims are GitHub-side (visibility, forks,
branch protection) and no repository file can measure them — the document already says so and lists the
settings it could not read. `docs/freebuff/*` is frozen at its dates by its own statement, the dated
plans and evidence directories are records, and the roadmap's historical command names are history
rather than instructions.

# 27GI. The production dry run checked nothing, and said the run would go ahead (2026-10-28)

**What was asked for.** Make the production seed dry run check each `:businessId` against the account
so a wrong id is refused *before* the real run.

**What was there.** `seed:accounts --dry-run` printed its plan and returned **before opening a
connection**. In development that is correct and cheap — an id is optional there and never compared.
In production it was a preview that could not see what it was previewing, and the consequences were
measured against the live database:

| Entry, `NODE_ENV=production … --dry-run` | Printed | Exit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jaffy…:2000:6ae14e4e…` — another business's id | `business 6ae14e4e…`, no refusal | **0** |
| `jaffy…:2000` — no id, tenant already exists | the plan, no refusal | **0** |
| `jaffy…:2000:6ae14f14…` — the id it owns | the plan, no count | 0 |

The same first line for real refuses (`names business …, but this account owns …`), so the preview
said the opposite of the run on the exact input an operator uses a preview to check. The second line
would have **replaced** an existing tenant's data; the preview accepted it. And none of the three
could say how much a reset would delete, which is the other question a preview exists to answer.

**Why it happened.** There were two lookups and only one of them was shared. The real run resolved
the tenant through `ensureTenantForIdentity`; the preview had no read-only way to ask the same
question, so it asked none. The defect was not a missing check — it was a **second, weaker copy of the
path**, which is the shape that drifts.

**What changed.** The lookup now has a read-only half and both callers use it.

- `seed/lib.mjs`: `readIdentity(email)` returns the Firebase identity or `null` and never creates or
  updates (unlike `resolveIdentity`, which does both). `ensureTenantForIdentity` is split into
  `resolveExistingTenantForIdentity` — the two lookups (by `firebaseUid`, then by email with the stale-
  link check), the business-existence check and the status check — and the create step, which stays in
  `ensureTenantForIdentity`. The error text is unchanged; only its placement moved.
- `seed-accounts.mjs`: in production, `--dry-run` now connects (read-only), resolves each login and
  tenant through that resolver, applies the **same** `assertTenantNamedForReset` rule as the write
  path, and prints the document count the reset would remove via `countTenantDataRemoval` — the
  counting half of the same teardown plan the cleanup runs, so the number is what would actually be
  deleted rather than an estimate. A wrong or missing id now fails the preview. Development keeps the
  connection-free preview, and its message still says so.
- Guides 10 and 9 state the two behaviours as they now are; Guide 9's table row had claimed the
  development preview reports resets, which it does not and never did.

**Measured after the change.** Wrong id: exit **1**, `names business 6ae14e4e…, but this account owns
6ae14f14…`. No id: exit **1**, `the third field of --accounts is required in production` plus
`would REPLACE the data of business … (“republic of gamers”)`. Correct id: exit 0, `reusing
6ae14f14bcf1b24131c7cf26 (“republic of gamers”) — 0 document(s) would be reset`. Then the real paths,
which the refactor touched: production seed at `200` products → **889 documents**, `verify:demo`
**OK** (exit 0), `cleanup:account` **889 removed, 0 remaining**; and the create branch (an account with
no `User` row) in development → `CREATED 6ae15947d9032c245ca21c6a`, 34 documents, deleted to 0. The
production database was left empty: 4 users, 4 businesses, 0 documents in every data collection.

**The test that failed, and why it was right to fail.** `accounts-workflow` located the *first*
`mongoose.connect(` in `seed-accounts.mjs` and asserted the preview printed before it. The shared
helper’s connect now precedes the development message, so the assertion broke on a real change of
contract — not on a rename. It now asserts both halves: development prints before `main` connects
(nothing opens), and the production preview may call only `readIdentity`,
`resolveExistingTenantForIdentity`, `assertTenantNamedForReset` and `countTenantDataRemoval` — never
`resolveIdentity`, `ensureTenantForIdentity` or `seedTenant`. That list is the property worth pinning:
the preview may read, and may not create.

**Verified.** `npm run test:unit`: **1566 tests, 1510 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0; `npm run
lint` 0; `npm run typecheck` 0. Committed as `e109e19` (5 files, 190 insertions, 70 deletions).

**Two behaviour changes this record owns, and one thing it did not prove.** A production dry run now
needs the database reachable *and* `FIREBASE_*` configured, because it reads the identity before it
resolves the tenant; the old preview returned before either was touched, so on a host without them
the preview now refuses where it previously printed a plan. That refusal is the correct
trade — a preview that cannot read cannot check — but it is a change, not a free gain. The connection-
failure path (`the ids were NOT checked`) is written and lint-clean and was **not** exercised: breaking
the network to watch it fire was not worth the risk to a live target.

# 27GJ. The production check was judged by the development database, and every command's boundary re-measured (2026-10-28)

**What was asked for.** `npm run check:accounts -- --with-production` was expected to check production;
run against a shell whose development database held no user rows, it reported **NOT READY (exit 1)**
for accounts that were READY in production. Make production the only database that run judges, then
re-check that every data command is confined to the environment it names.

**What the checker did, measured.** `databases` was built as `[development, ...(withProduction ?
[production] : [])]` — production **appended** to development, never replacing it — and readiness was
summed over every database read. One run therefore produced: development **0 of 3** (all `MISSING`),
production **3 of 3 READY**, and exit **1** because `notReady` counted the development rows. The exit
code described the environment nobody was about to seed.

**The fix, in one place.** `seed/lib.mjs` gained two pure functions: `databasesToCheck({withProduction,
databaseNames})` returns exactly one database (development by default, production instead), and
`summariseReadiness(checked)` returns `{pairs, notReady, ready}` over the databases that were actually
read. `check-accounts.mjs` now builds its list from the first and takes its verdict and exit code from
the second; the second counter that lived inside the print loop (`notReady += 1`) is gone, because two
counters can disagree and only one of them was tested. The printed label, the hint text and the
next-step commands follow the selected database: a production check prints the three-phrase production
line, a development check prints the two-phrase one and no longer suggests `--with-production`.

**The same defect in the seeder's printed hint.** `seed-accounts` printed `npm run check:accounts --
--with-production` after **every** dry run, including a development one. With the new semantics that
line would have sent a development operator to check production. It now emits the flag only when the
run itself targets production.

**The boundary audit, command by command** (source, plus the guards' own tests):

- **Every production-capable writer names its database and proves the name.** `seed:demo`,
  `seed:accounts`, `seed:three`, `seed:roles`, `seed:perf-tenant`, `seed:demo-tenant`, and every
  scoped cleanup including `cleanup:firebase` pass `--database=` to a guard that requires it to
  **equal** what `config/env.ts` resolved; the connection uses the resolved value, never the flag, and
  the connection string's own database is refused if it names a different one. Two phrases in
  development, three in production.
- **The development-only tools cannot reach production at all.** `seed:perf` and `cleanup:perf` call
  the guard without a database, which refuses production and an unrecognised `NODE_ENV`; the
  Firebase-wide `cleanup:test-firebase` is fenced by `assertNonProductionEnv`.
- **Read-only tools do not judge an environment they were not asked about.** The checker is now one
  database; `verify:demo` names production explicitly before reading it; `backup:db` and
  `audit:indexes` read only the resolved database.
- **One deliberate two-database read remains, and it is not a verdict.** `cleanup:firebase` reads user
  rows in development **and** production before deleting an identity, because an identity may only go
  when no row in either database references it. That is a reference check; conflating it with
  readiness is exactly the defect above.
- **One deliberate single-phrase exception remains.** `seed:demo-tenant` keeps `SEED_CONFIRM` alone and
  may still target production, as Guide 10 already documents; it names the database and refuses a
  mismatch, so it cannot cross environments — it is cheaper to confirm, not less targeted.

**Tests added.** `accounts-workflow` now asserts the one-database rule, that the script uses it rather
than rebuilding a list, that a `MISSING` row outside the selected database cannot change the verdict
(the reported failure, reproduced as a unit), and that the summary is the only counter driving the
exit code. `script-environment-guards` gained the call-site sweep: every production-capable writer
hands its guard `--database=`, the development-only tools never gain it, and the checker selects one
database while `cleanup:firebase`'s two-database read is asserted as a reference check.

**Tested against both environments, read-only where production was concerned.**

| Run | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run check:accounts` | dev only, **0 of 3** (rows are absent there), exit **1** |
| `npm run check:accounts -- --with-production` | prod only, **3 of 3 READY**, 0 products / 2 documents each, exit **0** |
| dev shell naming `inventoryai_prod_db` (seed and cleanup) | refused: "resolved inventoryai_dev_db … not connected to", exit **1** |
| production run with two phrases | refused: `SEED_PROD_CONFIRM=SEED-PRODUCTION-DATA` missing, exit **1** |
| development `seed:accounts` at 5 products | created `6ae16216…`, **34 documents** in 652 ms |
| `verify:demo` on that tenant | **OK (exit 0)** — counts, ledger, referential integrity |
| `cleanup:account` dry run, then real | 34 counted, **34 removed, 0 remaining**, rows and identity kept |
| production after all of it | still **3 of 3 READY, 0 products / 2 documents** — the dev work touched nothing |
| production `seed:accounts --dry-run` (2000 products) | read-only check named `6ae15d1b…` ("royal kludge"), 2 documents would reset, exit **0** |

**What is not changed, and why.** `seed:demo-tenant`'s single phrase is a documented decision, not an
oversight, and weakening or tightening it is a separate one. `cleanup:test-firebase` still deletes
every identity in the one Firebase project both environments share, fenced by environment rather than
by database — the narrower `cleanup:firebase --email=…` remains the per-account tool, and the risk is
unchanged by this record rather than introduced by it.

**Verified.** `npm run test:unit`: **1572 tests, 1516 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0 (the
documentation guards included); `npm run lint` 0; `npm run typecheck` 0. The database-backed suite was not re-run: every change here is either a pure function, a print
statement, or documentation, and the behaviour was exercised directly against both databases above.

# 27GK. Production seed and delete at 10 000 products — and a connection failure that read like a partial write (2026-10-28)

**What was asked for.** A production-only pass over the seeding and deletion commands: the three fixed
accounts, a large tenant, verification, scope and isolation checks, and a fix for anything it found.
No development command was run.

**What was run, in order, and what it proved.**

| Operation (production, three phrases where it writes or deletes) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `check:accounts --with-production` before any write | 3 of 3 READY, **0 products / 2 documents** |
| `seed:accounts` — three ids named, 50 products each | **666 documents**, identities already existed and were verified |
| `verify:demo` per tenant | **OK ×3** — 50 products, 6 low, 1 out, 0 integrity failures |
| `check:accounts --with-production` after | **222 documents each** — equal, isolated counts |
| `cleanup:account` dry run, then real | **666 counted → 666 removed, 0 remaining** |
| `seed:accounts` — `jaffy…` at **10 000 products** | **44 444 documents in 65 093 ms** |
| `verify:demo` on it | **OK** — 10 000 products, 1 535 low, 612 out, 462 receipt lines, 178 suppliers, 0 missing references |
| `cleanup:account` dry run, then real | **44 444 counted → 44 444 removed, 0 remaining** |
| final read-only count of the whole database | **4 businesses, 4 users, 0 products, 0 inventory, 0 transactions, 0 purchase orders** |

**Every refusal fired before a connection**: a cleanup naming another account's `businessId`
(`belongs to business …, not …`); a cleanup with only two phrases (`CLEANUP_PROD_CONFIRM` missing); a
production shell pointed at the development database (equality refusal); `cleanup:three` in production
(a development convenience, refused); `seed:perf` in production (development-only tool, refused).
`seed:demo-tenant --dry-run` in production reported `would CREATE a new tenant` and wrote nothing.

**The defect.** The first three-account seed reported only `connect ETIMEDOUT 159.143.174.111:27017` and
exited 1: no database named, and no statement about whether anything had been written. The first
10 000-product cleanup **dry run** was worse — it printed its `DRY RUN` header and then exited 1, which
reads like a delete that may have run. Both were connection failures before the first write or delete;
both succeeded on an immediate retry, and the tenants were confirmed unchanged in between. `seed-accounts`
and `cleanup-accounts` now wrap their connection attempt and refuse with the target database named, an
explicit `No tenant data was written` / `No document was deleted`, and the advice that one retry is
the right response to a transient failure. A source test pins both messages.

**Deliberately not exercised, with the reason.** The documented 30 000 / 50 000 / 90 000 preset was not
run: it is ≈756 000 documents against a 512 MB tier whose ceiling §27GE already measured. `seed:demo-tenant`
and `seed:roles` were not written for real — both rotate fixture credentials this shell does not hold
(the demo preview's password in particular) — so only the demo tenant's read-only preview ran. The
whole-database wipe and the Firebase-wide identity delete were not run at all: both destroy more than
the tenants under test, and no test needs them.

**Remaining risks, stated rather than closed.** Atlas connection timeouts were observed twice in one
session; the new messages make them honest but nothing retries automatically. The large-size ceiling
is unchanged: a 30/50/90 production preset can exhaust the tier regardless of these fixes. And the
whole-database and Firebase-wide commands remain the two ways to destroy more than a tenant, unchanged
by this pass.

**Verified.** `npm run test:unit`: **1573 tests, 1517 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0; `npm run lint`
0; `npm run typecheck` 0.

# 27GM. Each account chooses whether its products carry a SKU and barcode (2026-10-29)

**What was asked for.** `seed:accounts` could seed products with generated codes or without them, but
the choice was one `--include-sku` flag applied to the whole run: three accounts in a single command
could not mix them. The request was for each `--accounts` entry to choose for itself, with the existing
default and every safety rule unchanged.

**What changed.** The entry grammar gained one optional field:
`address:products[:businessId][:codes=both|none|sku|barcode]`. The two product fields are written
INDEPENDENTLY — `both` writes the generated `sku` and `barcode`, `sku` and `barcode` write that one,
and `none` omits both, which is what leaves the app's own barcode generation the first code to assign.
The id and the choice are recognised by their own shapes — 24 hex, or a `codes=` prefix — and accepted
in either order, so naming a tenant never forces a position for the new field. An entry that states
nothing takes the run-wide default: `none` as before, or `both` when `--include-sku` is passed, so every
command line written before this record behaves exactly as it did.

The parser moved from `seed-accounts.mjs` into `parseAccountsPlanEntry` in `seed/lib.mjs`, where it is
pure and throws `SeedSafetyError` instead of exiting. That is what makes the resolutions and refusals
assertable without a database: the default, all four modes, the override of the run default, four
accounts configured independently in one plan, both field orders, the unchanged product/document units,
an unknown mode, a repeated `codes=`, and a field that is neither an id nor a mode. `seedTenant` now
takes `includeSku` and `includeBarcode` as separate booleans (the demo, role and performance seeders
pass both), the CLI passes the entry's pair straight through, and its plan output states the choice per
account.

**What did not change.** `assertSeedTarget`, the two/three confirmation phrases, the pinned Firebase
project, production's tenant resolution and OWNER rule, the `:businessId` comparison, the reset scope
and the read-back verification are untouched — the choice is a property of the dataset, not of the
target. The `seed:three` preset keeps the run-wide default, because it has no entry list to configure.

**Limits, stated rather than discovered later.** At the time of this record a seeded barcode was still
an opaque string (`ACCTBC0`), not EAN-13, so it was stored and searchable but not printable or
scannable — §27GN closes that. The `--include-sku` flag keeps its historical meaning (both fields) and
has no `--include-barcode` partner; a run that wants a different default sets it per entry.
`seed --plan=demo`, `seed --plan=roles` and `seed:perf-tenant` still always write both; changing them
was not asked for, and the performance tenant's own verifier requires the `SEEDSKU-0` row its
measurement asks about.

**Verified.** `npm run test:unit`: **1608 tests, 1552 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0 (nine new
assertions); `npm run lint` 0; `npm run typecheck` 0.

# 27GN. Seeded barcodes are valid, unique EAN-13 — printable and scannable (2026-10-29)

**What was asked for.** With `codes=both` and `codes=barcode` available (§27GM), a seeded barcode was
still an opaque string (`ACCTBC0`): stored and searchable, but neither renderable by the product screen
nor decodable by the scanner. The request was for valid EAN-13 — thirteen digits with a real check
digit, unique per tenant, compatible with the app's scanning.

**What changed.** `allocateEan13Barcodes` in `seed/lib.mjs` reuses the generator the API already owns,
`internalEan13Candidates` in `src/utils/internalBarcode.ts`: deterministic from the product's
ObjectId, GS1 "restricted distribution" prefix 2, standard mod-10 check digit — the same values
`POST /api/products/:id/generate-barcode` issues. `seedTenant` now pre-generates each product's `_id`
and allocates the whole batch before the insert, so no two products in a tenant can share a code even
when their 64-candidate windows overlap. A product whose candidates are all taken is a
`SeedSafetyError` rather than a duplicate; the partial `(businessId, barcode)` unique index remains
the final authority. `taken` is empty in every seeder because each caller clears the tenant first.

**Why a check digit, and not just thirteen digits.** The mobile predicate `isEan13` is `/^\d{13}$/`
— it decides whether the label card renders at all, and it does not verify the check digit. Padding a
number to thirteen digits would therefore produce a label that renders and does not decode. The code
is built with `ean13Value(payload12)`, and the tests assert the check digit digit by digit.

**Scope.** Every seeder that writes through `seedTenant` with barcodes — `seed:accounts` and the
`seed:three` preset, `seed --plan=demo`, `seed --plan=roles`, `seed:perf-tenant` — now writes EAN-13.
SKUs are unchanged (`ACCTSKU-0`). `seed:perf` still writes its separate `SEEDBC` fixture and
`seed:demo-tenant` has no barcodes; neither was in scope.

**Uniqueness.** Within a tenant, by the batch Set and the index; across tenants a repeated value is
legal and expected, because the index is `(businessId, barcode)`. A 5 000-product batch is asserted
unique and check-digit-valid, and a one-off allocation at the 112 500-product ceiling produced
**112 500 distinct codes in 214 ms**. Omitting both fields remains legal for any number of products.

**Not exercised, with the reason.** The write itself was not run against a database: unit mode skips
the 56 DB-backed suites, and no suite calls the shared `seedTenant`. The allocator, the batch rule and
the seeder's wiring are covered; the document that MongoDB would store is not.

**Verified.** `npm run test:unit`: **1614 tests, 1558 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0 (six new
assertions); `npm run lint` 0; `npm run typecheck` 0.

---

# 27GO. `--include-sku` is replaced by `--codes=`, and refused rather than ignored (2026-10-29)

**What was asked for.** With the per-account `codes=` field (§27GM) and real EAN-13 values (§27GN), the
old `--include-sku` boolean looked redundant: one switch for the whole run, and only one thing it could
say. The request was to remove it — after a review, and only if that were safe.

**What the review found, and why it could not simply be deleted.** Since §27GM the flag had exactly one
job: it set the run-wide default that every `--accounts` entry without a `codes=` field inherits. That
includes the `seed:three` preset, which takes no entry list at all — so `--include-sku` was the only way
to seed the three comparison accounts WITH codes. Deleting it would have quietly removed a capability,
not a duplicate. Nothing in CI, no npm script and no workflow passed it, but three guides described it,
§27GB's record named it, and one test asserted the raw `process.argv.includes('--include-sku')` scan.

**What changed.** `--codes=both|none|sku|barcode` is now the run-wide default, parsed by
`parseRunwideCodes` in `seed/lib.mjs` — pure, like the entry parser, so every refusal is assertable
without a process. It is a strict superset of the boolean: `both` is what the flag meant, and `sku` /
`barcode` are choices the flag could never express, now available to the preset too. `--include-sku` is
REFUSED, with a message naming `--codes=both`, rather than ignored: ignoring it would seed neither field
on a command line that asked for both, and the plan would print `none` as if that had been chosen. That
is the rule the removed cleanup selectors already follow. `codeFields(mode)` turns a mode into the two
booleans `seedTenant` takes, so the translation exists once instead of three times (the entry parser,
the preset, the CLI), and the plan line prints the default it will use.

**What did not change.** `seedTenant`'s own `includeSku` / `includeBarcode` parameters — six seeders call
them — the per-entry `codes=` field and its precedence over the default, the default itself (`none`), the
two/three confirmation phrases, `assertSeedTarget`, the pinned Firebase project, production's tenant
resolution and OWNER rule, the reset scope and the read-back. The guides say what a saved command line
must now type instead of the flag.

**History, not rewritten.** §27GB's command list and §27GM's account of the flag describe the surface as
it stood on their dates; both are left as written, and this record is the current one.

**Verified.** Focused suite **61/61** (four new assertions: the default and all four modes, a cased
value, the `--include-sku` refusal with and without a `--codes=` value, and the three malformed forms);
`npm run test:unit`: **1618 tests, 1562 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0; `npm run lint` 0;
`npm run typecheck` 0. Both behaviours were also run as commands: `--include-sku` exits 1 with the
replacement named, a `--codes=both` list seeds `both` by default and lets an entry override it to
`sku only`, and `seed:three --codes=barcode` — a choice the boolean could never express — printed
all three accounts as `barcode only` with no connection opened.

The sizes match the parsers: `seed:accounts` 5–112 500 products (500 000 documents), `seed --plan=demo`
100–400 000 documents (default 80 000), `seed:perf-tenant` 50–400 000 documents (default 4 000), and the

2. **Guide 6 said the comparison seeders "leave SKUs and barcodes blank on purpose".** True as a default,
   false as a rule: `--codes=both` seeds them. The step now says which is which.
3. **No guide contained a runnable `--codes=` command.** The option was described in prose only. Guide 9
   now carries a complete PREVIEW/EXECUTE pair with a different choice per account.
4. **The dictionary had no `barcode` or `SKU` entry**, although Guide 4's glossary line points readers
   there. Both are added, with the EAN-13 range and the independence of the two fields.
5. **Guide 9/10 did not state the single-account form.** One entry is the same command; both guides say so.
6. **`SYSTEM_SPECIFICATION.md` §39 still called scanning "not required for the first release" and put the

   the scanner resolves the code through the business-scoped lookup, shows the product's per-location

banner and frozen status table; it is declared historical and is not reworded. The roadmap's own §27GB /
§27GM / §27GO records keep the wording of their dates. Guides 11–13 were read and needed nothing: their

# 27GQ. A typed tenant id is a claim, and it is checked in every environment (2026-10-29)

**What was asked for.** A continued improvement pass over the seeding and cleanup surface: review the
scripts, commands, validation, code generation, verification and cleanup for defects, and fix what is
verifiable without touching production data.

**Three defects, all one shape: a tenant id that was typed and then not read.**

1. **`seed:accounts` checked the third `--accounts` field only in production.** In development the
   entry's `businessId` was parsed and then dropped (`tenant = existing ?? ensureTenantForIdentity(…)`),
   so `alice@x.com:1000:<bob's businessId>` REPLACED ALICE'S OWN TENANT while the console printed alice's
   id. The operator believed they had named bob's tenant; the run reset a different one. The seeder now
   applies `assertRequestedTenantMatches` on the development path too, before the tenant is reset.
2. **`seed --plan=demo` did the same with `--business`.** The flag was compared with the resolved tenant
   only inside the production branch, so a mistyped id in development replaced the caller's own tenant
   and said nothing. The same rule now runs there, on the tenant the address already owns.
3. **An id that named NO tenant was silently replaced by a generated one.** `ensureTenantForIdentity`
   never accepted a chosen id, so a development run given `--business=<id>` for an address with no
   tenant created a DIFFERENT tenant and printed its id — after the operator had named one. Both seeders
   now refuse through `assertRequestedTenantKnown`, before any business row is written, and say that a
   run creates a tenant only when no id is named.

**And one cleanup defect the same review found.** `cleanup:account` is a list of ACCOUNTS, but every
count and every delete is scoped to a TENANT. Two members of one business — exactly the shape the role
fixture (`seed:roles`) creates — were accepted, and the tenant's documents were counted and reported
twice. `seed:accounts` already refused that plan, with an inline check and its own wording. Both now
call one shared rule, `findDuplicateTenant` / `assertDistinctTenants` in `server/scripts/seed/lib.mjs`,
and it runs on the RESOLVED ids: two different typed ids can still land on one tenant, which is the case
a typed-id check cannot see.

**The pre-flight had to learn the same answer.** `check:accounts` is what an operator runs before
seeding, and for that plan it printed two `READY` lines — one per address, both naming the same tenant —
while the seeder would refuse it. `markSharedTenants` (pure, beside the rules above) now labels each
READY row of a shared tenant `SHARED TENANT`, naming the other address, so the check's `ready/total`
count and its exit code (1) agree with the run it is predicting. A row already refused by another rule
is left as it is.

**The development preview is honest about what it cannot check.** A dry run opens no connection, so no
address can be resolved and neither claim-check can run there. The preview therefore does not pretend
to have validated an id; the real run does, before the first write, and the messages above are the ones
it prints.

**What did not change.** Every confirmation phrase, the target guard (`--database=` must equal
`MONGODB_DB_NAME`), the production OWNER/ACTIVE checks, the one-tenant-per-plan premise, and the
`codes=` / `--codes=` surface. Production already refused all three id cases; the production paths and
their messages are untouched. No database was seeded, deleted or otherwise modified while verifying
this record.

**Verified.** `npm run test:unit`: **1625 tests, 1569 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0; `npm run lint`
0; `npm run typecheck` 0. The new cases are in `server/test/accounts-workflow.test.mjs`: the two claim
rules (omitted id, matching id, mismatched id, unknown tenant), the duplicate-tenant rule (a shared
tenant, a plan with no tenant, two differing tenants), the pre-flight's shared-tenant verdict and its
effect on the `ready/total` count, and source assertions that both seeders, the cleanup and the check call
the shared guards rather than a private copy. No database was seeded, deleted or otherwise modified.

# 27GS. One verification command for the accounts workflow — and the expected size made checkable (2026-10-29)

**What was asked for.** Simplify production inventory testing to five operations: check the accounts, seed,
verify the seed, delete only that data, and verify the deletion. The audit found step three still needed
`verify:demo` once per account, and none of those runs could assert the size the seed was asked for.

**The change, and what it deliberately did not add.** `verify:demo` now accepts
`--accounts="address[:products],…"`: one connection, one process, one exit code. `--email=` is unchanged
for one account, and `--expect-products=` supplies a default for entries that omit a size. There is no new
npm script and no second verifier; the existing command and its read-only target guard do the work.

**One exit code for several accounts.** Every account is read before the verdict is chosen: **0** all
verified, **1** at least one violation, empty tenant or expected-size mismatch, **2** none failed but at
least one could not be checked. A database that cannot be reached is still **2**. Each account is resolved
through its own `businessId`; duplicate addresses, a missing address and an entry with more than one size
are refused before the connection.

A1.1 records:

```text
Database : inventoryai_prod_db (PRODUCTION)
Accounts : 3
... 1,000 products — expected 1,000 / 4,444 documents / 1,829 ledger rows, 0 bad, 0 negative
    0 missing references / 166 low / 58 out of stock ...
Result   : SUCCESS — 3 account(s) verified.        [exit 0]
```

No production row was created, changed or deleted; the three tenants still hold the 13 332-document
dataset and no cleanup was run after the seed.

**Guarded.** `DEMO1-demo-tenant.test.mjs` pins the account/size parser and its refusals.
`command-runbook.test.mjs` now requires A1.1 to carry one `--accounts` block with three expected sizes and
to omit `--email=`, and accepts either form in every `verify:demo` block. The source guards that require
the address refusal before the connection, the quoted `process.argv[2]` test and the
`tenantEmptinessProblem(counts)` call still pass.

**Verified.** `node --test test/DEMO1-demo-tenant.test.mjs test/command-runbook.test.mjs
test/script-environment-guards.test.mjs`: **89 tests, 89 pass, 0 fail**, exit 0. The full unit
suite (`npm run test:unit`): **1 653 tests, 1 597 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0. The refusal
cases were also run: no address and `--accounts` combined with `--email` each exited **2** before a

**Remaining, deliberately.** The post-delete isolation proof still covers the named tenants and their

# 27GT. The unrelated-tenant witness for `cleanup:account` (2026-10-29)

**What was open.** §27GS recorded P1: the post-delete isolation proof covered the named tenants and their
logins, but not a tenant outside the plan. `cleanup:account` scopes every delete by the `businessId`
resolved from each named account, so the isolation was structural — and nothing read a different tenant to
show it.

**The change.** `cleanup:account` now accepts an optional `--witness="<address>"`. It is read-only: the
witness is resolved from its own user row, and the command captures the data-only teardown counts plus the
login row (id, email, business id, role, status, Firebase linkage) and the business row (name, status)
before the first `clearTenantData`. After the deletes — or after a dry run's `Would remove` block — it
repeats those reads and fails on any difference. The Firebase UID is compared but never printed. A witness
with no account, no tenant, an `address:businessId` value, or a tenant already in the plan (same address or
same business) is refused before anything is deleted. The witness never enters the deletion plan.

**Where the code is.** `server/scripts/cleanup/witness.mjs` holds the pure parser, scope rule and snapshot
comparison; `cleanup-accounts.mjs` holds the DB reads and the two calls, so every rule is assertable without
a connection.

**Guarded.** `server/test/cleanup-witness.test.mjs` has 13 DB-free tests: optional parsing and
normalisation, the address-only refusal, in-plan and same-business refusals, the no-tenant refusal, the
exact snapshot shape, changed count/login/business/Firebase-linkage failures, the UID never appearing in a
failure, and source wiring that resolves the witness before the first delete, re-checks it before
`SUCCESS`, and never passes it to `clearTenantData`.

**Measured.** `node --test test/cleanup-witness.test.mjs`: **13 tests, 13 pass, 0 fail**, exit 0.
`node --test test/cleanup-witness.test.mjs test/data-guide-commands.test.mjs test/command-runbook.test.mjs
test/cleanup-target-guard.test.mjs`: **98 pass, 0 fail**, exit 0. `npm run test:unit`: **1,673 tests,
1,617 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0. `npm run lint`: **0**. A read-only development dry run with one
planned account and a witness in another business printed `Witness  : … — 4,444 documents (outside the
plan, read-only)` and `Witness  : unchanged — …`, then `DRY RUN SUCCESS`; no document was deleted, and no
production command or destructive run was made.

**Two integration points.** The unit runner refused the new file as unclassified (exit 2) until it was
registered in the pure-unit group. The older missing-account guard in `accounts-workflow.test.mjs` now
anchors on the plan's own refusal message, because the witness introduced a second `if (!user)` block

**Documented, and a stale sentence corrected.** Guides 11, 12 and 14 describe the flag and when the

# 27GU. The seed's SKU/barcode mode becomes verifiable — from the products, not the plan (2026-10-30)

**What was open.** The one-account production workflow asked for the seeded SKU/barcode setting to be
verified, but `verify:demo` read only counts, ledger arithmetic and references. The seed printed the mode
it intended, and the seeder's own read-back counted documents, not fields; neither was evidence that the
products actually carried the requested codes. A plan could say `both` while every product was `none`.

**The change.** `verify:demo` now accepts `--expect-codes=both|none|sku|barcode`, and an `--accounts`
entry may state its own `codes=` mode. The run always prints the four disjoint counts it read from the
products — both, SKU only, barcode only, neither — plus the observed mode (`both`, `sku`, `barcode`,
`none`, `MIXED` or `empty`). An explicitly named mode that does not match fails the account with exit
**1** and names the expected mode and all four counts; a malformed or valueless flag is refused with exit
**2** before the database is opened. Without an expectation the line is informational only, so existing
callers keep their previous pass/fail contract.

**Read-only by construction.** The new `scripts/demo/codeCoverage.mjs` exports one function built from
four `Product.countDocuments` calls, filtered by the account's own resolved `businessId`. It has no write
call. The product counts mean a non-empty `sku`/`barcode` string; the check does **not** validate EAN-13
check digits or uniqueness.

**Guarded.** `DEMO1-demo-tenant.test.mjs` pins the parser (run-wide default, per-entry override, duplicate
or malformed fields, bare flag), the classifier (all four modes, `MIXED`, `empty`, impossible counts), the
exact `Codes` line and the mismatch sentence, plus the source order (mode parsed before connecting) and
the read-only coverage module. A new DB suite, `DEMO3-code-coverage.test.mjs`, inserts products in every
combination and proves the counts against real MongoDB; it is registered in the runner's `PURE_DB` list.

**Measured.** `node --test test/DEMO1-demo-tenant.test.mjs`: **24 pass, 0 fail**. `TEST_MODE=db node
--test test/DEMO3-code-coverage.test.mjs`: **3 pass, 0 fail** against `inventoryai_test_db`.
`TEST_MODE=unit node --test test/DEMO1-demo-tenant.test.mjs test/command-runbook.test.mjs
test/data-guide-commands.test.mjs test/script-environment-guards.test.mjs`: **109 pass, 0 fail**. The full
`npm run test:unit`: **1 677 tests, 1 621 pass, 0 fail, 56 skipped**, exit 0. `npm run lint`: **0**;
`npm run typecheck`: **0**.

**Production, read-only.** All three accounts read `Codes : 0 both, 0 SKU only, 0 barcode only,
1 000 neither — none`; the three-account run with `--expect-codes=none` exited **0**. The first account
with `--expect-codes=both` exited **1** with `code coverage is none, expected both — 1 000 products:
0 both, 0 SKU only, 0 barcode only, 1 000 neither`; the bare flag exited **2** before reading. No
production document was created, changed or deleted, so no production tenant currently carries a
non-`none` mode to measure; the four non-empty modes are covered by the DB suite against the test
database, not by production data.

**Documented.** Guides 6, 9, 10 and 14 describe the flag, the per-entry form, the `Codes` line, the
exit-code change and the fact that coverage is not format validation. No seed or cleanup command was
changed, and nothing was committed or pushed.

# 27GV. The empty-tenant CLI verdict becomes an executed test (2026-10-30)

**What was open.** §27GU tested the coverage reader against real products and exercised the CLI's
mismatch path, but the `empty` branch was only asserted through the helper and a source scan. A change
that moved the coverage line after the empty-tenant return — or removed it from that path — could have
left the helper tests green while the command an operator runs printed no `Codes` line at all.

**The change.** `DEMO4-verify-cli.test.mjs` creates one disposable `Business` and one `User` in the test
database, with no categories, locations, suppliers, products, inventory, movements or purchase orders.
It then runs the real `scripts/verify-demo-data.mjs` as a child process and pins the exact
`Codes    : 0 both, 0 SKU only, 0 barcode only, 0 neither — empty` line, the
`the tenant is empty — it holds no seeded documents` failure, exit **1**, and the fact that the fixture
business and user still exist afterwards. The file is registered in the runner's `PURE_DB` list.

**Measured.** `TEST_MODE=db node --test test/DEMO4-verify-cli.test.mjs`: **1 pass, 0 fail**. The same
file with `TEST_MODE=unit`: **1 skipped**, with the DB-backed reason. `npm run lint`: exit **0**.

**Documented.** No command or guide changed; this record pins the behavior §27GU documented. Nothing
was committed or pushed.

# 27GW. The barcode report checks the value, not just the field (2026-10-30)

**The gap.** `verify:demo` read four counts — total, SKU, barcode, both — so it could prove a product
*had* a barcode and nothing about the value. Two products could share one code, or a thirteen-digit
value could carry a wrong mod-10 check digit, and the report would still print `Codes … both`. The
seeder allocates valid, unique EAN-13 values, but the verifier's job is to disbelieve the seeder: a
partial write, an edited tenant, a missing index or a legacy row can all produce a value the count cannot
see.

**The change.** `scripts/demo/codeCoverage.mjs` now projects each product's `barcode` in the same
read-only batch (`Product.find(filter).select('barcode').lean()`), and returns the non-empty strings.
`classifyBarcodeHealth` in `scripts/demo/verify.mjs` classifies every value into four mutually exclusive
buckets — a 13-digit value with a correct or wrong check digit, and every other string as non-EAN-13 —
and counts duplicate values with the number of extra rows that share them. `formatBarcodeHealth` prints
one line beside `Codes`; `barcodeHealthProblem` turns an invalid check digit or a duplicate into the
failure sentence. Non-EAN-13 values are reported but do not fail, because a manufacturer code need not
be EAN-13. `scripts/verify-demo-data.mjs` prints the line on every account, including an empty tenant,
and adds the failure to the existing exit-1 path. It is still read-only: no write call was added.

**Guarded.** `DEMO1-demo-tenant.test.mjs` asserts all six counters, the exact line with singular and
plural labels, the joined failure sentence, the empty line, and that a valid EAN-13 or a non-EAN-13 value
alone is not a failure. `DEMO3-code-coverage.test.mjs` writes one valid and one wrong-check-digit product
and reads them through the real counter, and writes a non-EAN-13 value to prove it is counted without
being failed. `DEMO4-verify-cli.test.mjs` runs the actual command against a disposable two-product tenant
and pins `Barcodes : 2 present — 1 valid EAN-13, 1 invalid check digit, 0 duplicate values, 0 non-EAN-13`,
the failure reason and exit **1**. Duplicate detection is asserted on the pure classifier rather than on
real rows: the model's partial unique `(businessId, barcode)` index makes a duplicate impossible while
the suite has created the indexes, and dropping it would break every DB suite sharing the collection.
The verifier keeps the duplicate check as a defensive read for a legacy tenant or a missing index.

**Measured.** `TEST_MODE=unit node --test test/DEMO1-demo-tenant.test.mjs`: **25 pass, 0 fail**.
`TEST_MODE=db node --test test/DEMO3-code-coverage.test.mjs`: **5 pass, 0 fail**. `TEST_MODE=db node
--test test/DEMO4-verify-cli.test.mjs`: **2 pass, 0 fail**. The documentation suites: **49 pass, 0 fail**.
`npm run lint`: exit **0**.

**Documented.** Guides 9, 10 and 14 now describe the `Barcodes` line, its four counters, which conditions
fail the run and which are reported only. Guide 14 records the new line as covered by the three suites
but **not yet observed against production data**; the production `Codes` evidence it already carried is
unchanged. Nothing was committed or pushed.

# 27GX. The one Dependabot alert that could be closed, and the two that cannot (2026-10-30)

**What was measured.** The public default branch carried **three** open Dependabot alerts on
`mobile/package-lock.json`: **#10** `zod` GHSA-mrhx-c7xc-m3w5 (high), **#5** `node-forge`
GHSA-86w9-cpqp-85rv (high), and **#13** `deepmerge` GHSA-gcqx-w48m-w2h4 (low). `npm audit` counted
**17 entries** for the same tree, but only **two** distinct advisories — the rest are dependents. The
three questions that decide a fix are separate, and were answered from the tree rather than the alert
count: is there a patched release, does the consumer's own declared range admit it, and is the package
reachable from shipped code.

**The fix.** `node-forge` was the only yes. `1.4.2` had been published outside `<= 1.4.0`, and
`@expo/code-signing-certificates@0.0.7` already declares `^1.4.0`, so a plain lockfile bump could take
it with no override and no `package.json` change. `mobile/package-lock.json` moved from `1.4.0` to
`1.4.2` in three lines. The package was never in a shipped bundle — its only importer is
`@expo/code-signing-certificates/build/main.js`, reached from two `expo-updates` CLI scripts that do
not run because code signing is not enabled (§27FN) — so the bump removes the alert without changing
app behaviour.

**What was refused, and why.** `zod` is patched only at `4.6.6+`, while `@expo/cli@58.1.15` declares
`^3.25.76`; the vulnerable copy is nested for the CLI's DevTools-plugin schema, and the top-level
`zod@4.6.7` is already outside the range. `deepmerge@4.3.1` is both the newest release and inside
`>= 4.2.0 <= 4.3.1`, so **no patched release exists**; it is used by `@expo/config`'s build-time config
loader and by `jest-config`. `npm audit fix` offers `expo@51.0.39`, a seven-major downgrade, and an
`overrides` entry would force a version neither parent declared. Both remain accepted, reachable only
from build/test tooling, and recorded in `docs/SECURITY_DEPENDENCY_DECISIONS.md`.

**Guarded.** `scripts/check-upgrade-watches.mjs` now reads the **installed** version as well as the
registry and the consumer range. A tree already outside the vulnerable range reports `CLOSED` instead
of `READY`, so the next session is not sent to re-take a fix that is already in the lockfile. All
three advisories are watched: the report reads `zod` `DEFERRED` (installed `3.25.76`), `deepmerge`
`DEFERRED` (installed `4.3.1`) and `node-forge` `CLOSED` (installed `1.4.2`). Two new controls pin the
`CLOSED` shape and the live `deepmerge` shape, and `--self-test` passes **25 controls** (4 must-fire,
19 must-not-fire, 2 range).

**Measured.** `cd mobile && npm run typecheck` → exit **0**. `npm test -- --runInBand` → **97 suites,
1 172 tests, all pass**. `npm run lint` → exit **0**. `node scripts/check-upgrade-watches.mjs
--self-test` → **25 passed**. No server source, route, model, workflow or mobile application file was
changed.

**Documented.** `docs/SECURITY_DEPENDENCY_DECISIONS.md` (D-9 and the updated D-4/D-7/D-8),
`SECURITY.md`, `CLAUDE.md`'s open items and this record. The GitHub alert for `node-forge` closes when
the lockfile change reaches the default branch.

# 28. Phase Gate System

Claude Code must NOT automatically move to the next phase after completing a phase.

After every phase, produce:

```text
PHASE STATUS
────────────
Phase:
Status:

IMPLEMENTED
- ...

FILES CHANGED
- ...

TESTS
- ...

VERIFICATION
- ...

ISSUES
- ...

SPECIFICATION CONFLICTS
- ...

REMAINING WORK
- ...

RECOMMENDED NEXT PHASE
- ...
```

The project owner decides whether to proceed.

---

# 29. Change Control

If Claude discovers that the current specification is incomplete or incorrect:

Do NOT silently redesign the system.

Instead:

1. Identify the issue.
2. Explain why it matters.
3. Propose a solution.
4. Explain affected components.
5. Wait for approval before making major architectural changes.

Minor implementation improvements that do not alter architectural decisions may be applied normally.

---

# 30. Bug Handling

If a bug is discovered during a phase:

### If related to the current phase

Fix it before declaring the phase complete.

### If unrelated to the current phase

Do not immediately expand scope.

Report it as:

```text
Unrelated issue discovered:
...
Recommended future phase:
...
```

Only fix it immediately if it blocks the current phase.

---

# 31. Refactoring Rules

Refactoring is allowed when it:

- Improves maintainability
- Fixes architectural problems
- Removes duplication
- Improves security
- Improves testability

However:

Do not perform large unrelated refactors during feature implementation.

Keep changes focused.

---

# 32. Dependency Rules

Before adding a dependency:

1. Determine whether the feature actually requires it.
2. Check whether an existing dependency already provides the functionality.
3. Prefer established and maintained libraries.
4. Avoid unnecessary packages.
5. Explain significant new dependencies.

Do not add dependencies simply for convenience.

---

# 33. Git Checkpoints

A Git commit should be created after a stable phase.

Recommended:

```text
phase 00: planning complete
phase 01: foundation complete
phase 02: backend database complete
phase 03: authentication authorization complete
phase 04: inventory core complete
phase 05: mobile application complete
phase 06: AI assistant complete
phase 07: production hardening complete
phase 08A: structured request logging complete
phase 08B: ESLint baseline complete
phase 10A: commercialization foundation complete
phase 10B: commercialization documentation close-out complete
phase 11A: inventory intelligence + restock alerts complete
phase 11B: inventory intelligence documentation close-out complete
phase 14A: user management foundation complete
```

Before committing:

- Run relevant checks.
- Review changed files.
- Verify no secrets are included.
- Confirm scope is correct.

# 36. Final Development Rule

The goal is not to produce the largest amount of code as quickly as possible.

The goal is to produce a:

- Secure
- Correct
- Maintainable
- Testable
- Scalable
- Production-ready

inventory management system.

Every phase must leave the project in a better and verifiable state than before.

# 27GZ. One operation, one movement — inventory writes deduplicated (2026-11-01)

**The report.** The owner saw the dashboard's Recent Activity list the same stock-in,
stock-out and purchase-order operation more than once, from a single tap. The first
half of this record is what the investigation found; the second half is the fix.

**Recent Activity is the ledger, one row per event.** `dashboardService.summary()`
reads the newest `InventoryTransaction` rows and maps them to the list; its only
transformation is `recentActivities()`, which merges a transfer's TWO legs into one
event and leaves every other type as the single row it already is. The screen maps
that array directly with a stable id. So a duplicate entry is a duplicate ledger row —
never a rendering artifact and never an activity log of its own.

**PO creation writes no ledger row at all.** It cannot produce a Recent Activity entry;
what appears for a purchase order is its RECEIPT (each line becomes one `STOCK_IN`).
A duplicated PO create therefore shows as two DRAFTs in the PO list, and duplicate
receipt rows show as two stock-ins. Both are covered by the same key.

**Nothing in the services was duplicating.** Each movement writes exactly one ledger
row: `recordMovement` creates one `InventoryTransaction` and one audit row, and a
transfer writes its two legs and a single audit. `stockIn`, `stockOut`, `adjust` and
`transfer` each issue one guarded inventory update; `receive` stock-ins once per line,
after winning that line's claim. So a duplicate on screen could only be the same
operation being DELIVERED twice — applied once per delivery rather than once per
operation. No duplicate was found in the query, the grouping or the rendering.

**Three delivery paths were unguarded, and one was left open by the first pass.**
(a) A second press can reach the handler before the `busy` state is rendered as a
disabled button, because `busy` is a rendered signal rather than a guard on the handler.
(b) The client's request budget can expire while the server is still working: the form
is told the movement failed, the member submits again, and the first delivery lands
after all — this is the path that matches "I only did it once". (c) The transport's own
AUTH-03 recovery retry dropped the `Idempotency-Key` header, so the one automatic retry
in the app re-sent a movement as a NEW operation. None of these is proved to be the
instance the owner saw (no production request log naming it), but each produces exactly
the reported symptom, and all three are now closed.

**A fourth hole was in the first pass's own rule.** A purchase-order receive that loses
its last line answers 409 `RECEIVE_CONFLICT` carrying the `applied` lines. Treating every
4xx as "nothing happened" released the claim, so a duplicate delivery of that same
request could re-run the batch and apply a PARTIAL line twice (a full line is stopped by
the remaining-quantity bound; a partial one is not). That answer is now recorded as an
outcome and replayed.

**The fix is a transport concern, not a domain one.** `inventory.service.ts`,
`transactions.service.ts` and `purchase-orders.service.ts` are unchanged, so none of
their compensation paths moved.

* `middlewares/idempotency.ts` + `models/idempotencyRecord.model.ts`: a request that
  carries `Idempotency-Key` claims `{ businessId, key }` (unique index, 24 h TTL). A
  claimed key that is still running answers 409 with `Retry-After`; a completed key
  replays the stored status and body; a completed key with a DIFFERENT body fingerprint
  (SHA-256 of method, path and body) is refused as 422 `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` and
  applies nothing; no header leaves the request untouched, which is what keeps an older
  installed build working. A 4xx/5xx that applied nothing releases the claim; one that
  reports `applied` lines is recorded (`appliedWork()`) and replayed. A replayable
  outcome is written BEFORE its answer is sent, so a duplicate cannot arrive in a gap
  where the answer exists but is not yet recorded. A claim older than 60 s is taken over
  atomically, so a dead request cannot block its own retry until the TTL expires.
* Mounted on the four movement routes (`stock-in`, `stock-out`, `adjust`, `transfer`) and
  on purchase-order `create` and `receive`.
* `mobile/lib/idempotency.ts` mints one key per operation ATTEMPT and exports
  `endsOperation()`: a transport failure (status 0) and a 409
  `IDEMPOTENT_REQUEST_IN_PROGRESS` keep the key, because neither is a final answer to
  this operation; every other answer ends it. The movement, transfer, PO-create and
  receive forms reset the key when their inputs change — but NOT while a request is in
  flight, since an edit during a slow delivery must not rename an attempt that may
  already have landed — and each gained an in-flight ref guard. A deliberate, identical
  repeat is therefore two operations and two keys, never swallowed as a duplicate.

**Operations covered, by their own test.** Stock in, stock out, adjustment, transfer and
PO receipt each deliver the same request twice and assert one ledger row, the correct
quantity, and exactly one Recent Activity entry for the returned transaction id. PO
creation asserts one DRAFT; the receipt case deliberately uses 3 of 10 units, because a
second application of that line still fits the remaining bound — the case the service's
own guard cannot catch.

**Verification.** `server/test/INVENTORY-IDEMPOTENCY.test.mjs` — **10 DB-backed cases,
all passing** (6 before this pass): same key twice writes one row and replays the first
response; a different key applies in full; a reused key with a changed body is 422 with
no row; no key behaves as before (two rows, the pre-fix reproduction); a duplicated PO
create leaves one DRAFT; a duplicated transfer leaves two legs and one activity; plus
the three new operation cases and the `applied`-refusal replay. Two controls were
watched fail before the code was trusted: removing `idempotent()` from the stock-out
route fails that case with two different transaction ids, and removing the key from the
AUTH retry fails the header case with `undefined`.

`mobile/__tests__/inventory-submit-once.test.tsx` — **3 cases**: a transport failure
keeps the key, a 409 in-flight keeps the key, an answered refusal mints a new one.
`mobile/__tests__/phaseAUTH03-client-renewal.test.ts` gained the header-across-retry
case. `phase04-inventory`, `phase13-purchase-orders`, `phase13-receiving`,
`phase-index-integrity` and `phase23-authorization-contract` pass (**59 pass, 0 fail, 1
intentional skip**); both `tsc` runs and both linters are clean. `phase-index-integrity`
iterates the model barrel and compares declarations with the connected database, so it
proved the unique claim index and the TTL index exist in `inventoryai_test_db`.

**Not verified here:** no production database was written — there is no production
credential on the development host, and the owner's other users share that database, so
the controlled tests ran against the isolated `inventoryai_test_db` only. The production
ledger was not re-scanned for historical duplicate rows, so this record claims the
mechanism and the prevention, not a count of past rows. Any rows written before this
increment stand as they are, and rectifying them would need an owner-authorised
reconciliation, not a bulk delete.

**Deployment note.** The unique `{ businessId, key }` index is what makes two concurrent
deliveries unable to both own a key; it is declared in the model and is built by
Mongoose's default `autoIndex` at connect time. Before relying on the guarantee in
production, run `npm run audit:indexes` against it — that is the read-only check that
asks the database whether the claim index and the TTL index were built, and this record
did not run it (no production credential here).
